0.title: The King Has Come
0.overview:
Matthew begins where the Old Testament ends — with promises. His opening genealogy is not a genealogy at all; it is a theology compressed into names. Abraham to David to the exile to Jesus: the whole arc of Israel’s story, told in three movements, arriving at the one name toward which every other name was pointing. Matthew’s first words are biblos geneseos — the book of origins, the book of genesis. A new creation has begun.

Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, probably in Antioch, in the decades after the destruction of Jerusalem. His readers knew the Old Testament. They had grown up with the promises of a coming King from David’s line, a new Moses who would deliver God’s people, a suffering servant who would bear the sins of many, a son of man who would receive an everlasting dominion. Matthew’s argument, sustained across twenty-eight chapters, is that all of these promises find their yes in Jesus of Nazareth (2 Cor. 1:20). The fulfillment formula — to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet — appears again and again like a refrain, stitching the Old Testament to the New until you cannot see the seam.

The great theme of Matthew is the kingdom of heaven. Where Mark asks who this man is, and Luke traces the universal reach of grace, Matthew announces the arrival of a reign. Heaven’s rule has broken into earth’s disorder in the person of the King. He teaches with authority (not as the scribes). He heals with a word. He calms the sea. He feeds the multitude. He raises the dead. And then he goes to the cross not as a victim of circumstances but as the King who lays down his life to ransom many (20:28) — the supreme act of royal authority disguised as utter weakness.

Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses, but greater. Moses gave the law from Sinai; Jesus gives the new law from the mountain (chapters 5–7). Moses delivered Israel through the Red Sea; Jesus passes through death and comes out the other side. Moses saw the promised land from a distance and died; Jesus enters it, conquers it, and invites all nations to follow him in. “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them” (5:17). In Jesus, the Old Testament does not end — it arrives.

The name given to him in chapter 1 is the key that unlocks the whole: Emmanuel — God with us. And the Gospel ends with the same promise, spoken now in resurrection glory: I am with you always, to the end of the age (28:20). Matthew is bracketed by the presence of God. What began in a manger in Bethlehem does not end at a tomb in Jerusalem. It ends with a commission that will reach every tongue and tribe and nation — because the one who sends is the one to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given.

Read Matthew as someone meeting the King for the first time. Let the authority of his teaching arrest you. Let the tenderness of his healing move you. Let the cross unmake your comfortable religion. And let the resurrection send you — into all the world, making disciples, baptising, teaching. The Gospel of Matthew is not a story that ends; it is a commission that begins.

1.title: Emmanuel — God With Us
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. <sup>2</sup>Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers, <sup>3</sup>and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, <sup>4</sup>and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon, <sup>5</sup>and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, <sup>6</sup>and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah, <sup>7</sup>and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, <sup>8</sup>and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, <sup>9</sup>and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, <sup>10</sup>and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah, <sup>11</sup>and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. <sup>12</sup>And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, <sup>13</sup>and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, <sup>14</sup>and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, <sup>15</sup>and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, <sup>16</sup>and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ. <sup>17</sup>So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations. <sup>18</sup>Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. <sup>19</sup>And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. <sup>20</sup>But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. <sup>21</sup>She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” <sup>22</sup>All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: <sup>23</sup>“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us). <sup>24</sup>When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, <sup>25</sup>but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
1.overview:
Matthew opens not with a manger scene but with a list of names — and the list is the point. Every name in the genealogy is a promise kept. From Abraham, through whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 12:3), to David, whose throne would endure forever (2 Sam. 7:16), to the exile and back: the whole history of Israel’s faithfulness and failure, strung together like beads on a single cord that ends at the name Jesus. God’s covenant faithfulness spans every generation, including the dark ones. Especially the dark ones.

The genealogy contains surprises that Matthew intends. Four women appear — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and “the wife of Uriah” — each associated with scandal, foreignness, or irregularity. Matthew is signalling from the first page that this King comes not for the respectable but for the broken, not only for Israel but for the nations. Grace does not run through clean lines; it runs through history as it actually happened, mess and all.

Then the birth narrative proper, and its two names. Jesus: he will save his people from their sins (v. 21). The name carries the whole gospel in four letters — Y’shua, the LORD saves. And Emmanuel: God with us (v. 23). The fulfilment of Isaiah’s sign (Isa. 7:14) is no longer a child born in the eighth century BC as a near-term reassurance to Ahaz; it is the Son of God entering human flesh, the Creator wearing the creature’s nature, the infinite becoming finite — without ceasing to be infinite. This is the doctrine of the incarnation, announced in a single breath in a single verse, and it changes everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew opens not with a narrative but with a name-list, and in doing so announces that the gospel is rooted in real history. The genealogy traces Jesus' legal descent through Joseph from Abraham and David, grounding him in both the Abrahamic covenant (promise of blessing to all nations, Gen. 12:3) and the Davidic covenant (promise of an eternal throne, 2 Sam. 7:12–16). Three groups of fourteen generations form a theological argument, not an exhaustive record: Jesus is the divinely appointed culmination of redemptive history. Four women — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — appear unexpectedly, each associated with scandal or Gentile origin, signaling that this King's grace reaches beyond the expected. Three kings are missing at verse 8 — Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah (1 Chron. 3:11-12) — which is not an error: the phrase rendered "father of" means ancestor of throughout Scripture, and a Jewish genealogy was a legal document establishing descent rather than a birth register. Matthew wants his three fourteens and prunes to get them; all three omitted kings descended from Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Two names look wrong — "Asaph" for king Asa and "Amos" for king Amon — and these are simply the fuller Greek forms Matthew used, which modern translations keep rather than tidy. The third group has thirteen names, not fourteen; Jeconiah is probably counted twice, standing as the hinge of the exile. And Jeconiah carries a curse: God had sworn that none of his offspring would sit on David's throne (Jer. 22:30), yet the royal line runs straight through him — which the virgin birth resolves, since Jesus receives the legal throne-right through Joseph without receiving Jeconiah's blood. Luke's genealogy, tracing physical descent, comes down through David's other son Nathan and never touches him. The dark names are the point: Ahaz burned his own son as an offering (2 Kgs. 16:3) and is the very king to whom Isaiah 7:14 was spoken — the verse Matthew quotes at v. 23. Manasseh, the worst man in the list, repented in a Babylonian prison and was heard (2 Chr. 33:12-13). And the six names after Zerubbabel appear nowhere else in Scripture, spanning the five-hundred-year silence between the return from exile and the carpenter's shop. Finally, verse 16 breaks the pattern: thirty-nine times Matthew has written "A was the father of B" with an active verb, and at the fortieth link he goes passive and feminine — "of whom Jesus was born" — asserting the virgin birth in the grammar two verses before he explains it.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy establishes Jesus as Messiah (Christ = Anointed One), Son of David (royal heir), and Son of Abraham (heir of the covenant). The 14-14-14 structure — possibly reflecting the numerical value of David's name in Hebrew — underscores divine superintendence: God has been ordering history toward this moment across centuries of faithfulness, failure, exile, and return. Providence is not the absence of scandal; it is the sovereign use of all things toward the appointed end.
verseByVerse.examples: This genealogy reminds us that salvation is not a timeless philosophy but a historical event rooted in a long chain of real covenantal faithfulness. God's promises survived murder, adultery, exile, and foreign domination to arrive at their fulfillment. What he has promised, he performs — across generations, across continents, across every human failure. The God who kept his word to Abraham keeps his word to you.

verseByVerse.quote: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, and Isaac the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Judah and his brothers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew opens by calling Jesus the Christ, the son of David and the son of Abraham, and begins his family line with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Judah. Jesus is the promised King of David’s line and the promised blessing of Abraham’s line — the one in whom God keeps every promise he has made across the centuries.

A new beginning. Matthew’s first words, “the book of the genealogy” (literally “the book of the genesis”), echo the opening chapters of the Bible (Genesis 2:4; 5:1). A Jewish reader would hear the claim: the story is starting again.

Two titles. Before a single event, two titles. “Son of David” — the heir with a claim to a throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16). “Son of Abraham” — the heir of a promise that one family would bless every nation on earth (Genesis 12:3). The order matters. Matthew gives Israel its King first and then opens the door to everyone else, which is the shape of the whole Gospel, right to its last verses: “make disciples of all nations” (28:19).

Why seventeen verses of names? This is the page most readers skip, and skipping it costs something. First, it says this happened. Myths don’t come with paperwork. Matthew lists generations his readers could check against the Old Testament — like putting your address at the top of the page. He isn’t offering a story about the human condition; he is reporting on a man with ancestors. Second, a genealogy was a legal document. In Israel it established title — to land, priesthood, a throne. Matthew enters Jesus’ claim to David’s crown into the record in the first breath, because everything afterward depends on it. Third, it tells you where the story starts, and it isn’t Bethlehem. It starts two thousand years earlier, with a promise to a childless man called out of Ur.

Receipts. So read the names not as a register but as receipts. Each is a generation in which God didn’t abandon what he had said — including long stretches when nothing visible happened, when the family was enslaved, exiled, forgotten or faithless, and the promise was carried by people who never saw it land. Most of God’s work in the world has looked like that. If you are in such a stretch yourself, this is your chapter: the record of a God who keeps promises across centuries, at a pace that looks from underneath like nothing at all. A test: are you judging God’s faithfulness by how quickly you see results?
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” marks Jesus as the promised king; “son of Abraham” as the one through whom the nations would be blessed.

parallels.desc: Luke’s genealogy, traced back to Adam
the promise of a son of David on the throne forever
all the families of the earth blessed in Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and Perez the father of Hezron, and Hezron the father of Ram, and Ram the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab the father of Nahshon, and Nahshon the father of Salmon,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line runs through Judah, who fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, and on through Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon and Salmon. By naming Tamar, Matthew shows that God’s promise came through a family scarred by sin and injustice — grace, not respectability, carries the line.

A woman named. Two things would have stopped a first-century reader. A woman’s name appears in a Jewish genealogy, which wasn’t how they were written. And it is this woman. Tamar was probably a Canaanite, and Perez — through whom the line runs to David and to Christ — was conceived by the roadside when she disguised herself as a prostitute and was hired by her own father-in-law. Matthew didn’t have to mention her. He puts her in the third verse.

The story behind the name. Tamar married Judah’s eldest son, who died. By custom the next brother was to father a child in the dead man’s name; he refused, and died too. Judah, afraid for his last son, sent her back to her father’s house, promising the boy when he was grown. He never gave him. He simply left her there — not divorced, not free to remarry, a childless widow with no standing and no future, waiting for a wedding he had privately decided wouldn’t happen.

A shameful remedy. What she then did was disgraceful, and Genesis doesn’t soften it. She veiled herself and sat by the road; Judah, after his wife’s death, took her for a prostitute and hired her. She kept his seal, cord and staff as a pledge — his identification. About three months later, told his daughter-in-law was pregnant by immorality, Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.” She sent him his own seal, asking whose it was. And he said: “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah” (Genesis 38:26).

What Matthew invokes. That is what Matthew invokes with one name: not a colourful ancestor but a woman wronged first, owed something and denied it, who took a desperate and shameful route to what was hers by right — and was pronounced, by the man who had failed her, the more righteous of the two. Grace doesn’t excuse either of them; it works through both.

Perez. The child is Perez, “breach,” named because he burst out ahead of his twin (Genesis 38:29). The royal line runs through a boy named for pushing in where he wasn’t expected, and generations later the neighbours blessed Ruth’s marriage by his name (Ruth 4:12). A test: do you think your family’s failures put you beyond God’s use?
verseByVerse.note: Tamar is the first of four women Matthew includes before Mary, each with an irregular story.

parallels.desc: the line from Perez to Nahshon

verseByVerse.quote: and Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, and Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David the king. And David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salmon fathers Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathers Obed by Ruth, and the line reaches Jesse and David the king, who fathers Solomon “by the wife of Uriah.” Matthew deliberately names outsiders and a royal scandal, showing that the Messiah’s family, like ours, needed grace — and that God writes such people into his story.

Two foreigners and a silence. Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho, a city under sentence of destruction, who hid two spies under the flax on her roof (Joshua 2). Ruth was a Moabite, from a people barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Then Matthew writes that Solomon was born “by the wife of Uriah” — and doesn’t write Bathsheba’s name. He gives her husband’s instead, so you can’t get through the sentence without saying the name of the man David had killed. David stands here as king and as adulterer in one breath, and the line runs straight through the sin.

The four women. Look at the four together; Matthew has done it deliberately. Jewish genealogies traced men, and these aren’t the matriarchs you would expect — not Sarah, Rebekah or Leah. They are Tamar, who disguised herself as a prostitute; Rahab, who was one; Ruth, a Moabite; and a woman Matthew won’t name, identified by the husband David murdered. Foreigners and scandals. If you were forging a royal pedigree you would strike out every one; Matthew writes them in on the first page.

Your family’s line. Consider what that means for your own family. Most have a name that isn’t mentioned, or a stretch nobody talks about — the affair, the child born outside marriage, the drinking, the violence, the prison sentence, the parent who left. People carry it quietly and assume it has disqualified them, that God works with families of a different kind. Matthew’s answer is the first page of the New Testament. The Messiah’s family tree reads like that, and God didn’t tidy it before he used it. He wrote it down. A test: is there a part of your story you think God can’t use?

Two guards. This mustn’t be mistaken for something cheaper. It doesn’t mean the sin was small: Matthew’s refusal to name Bathsheba is there so you remember a murdered soldier, and grace that pretends nothing happened isn’t grace. And it works the other way: you can’t inherit standing from a good family any more than a verdict from a bad one, as John will tell those who said, “We have Abraham as our father” (3:9). What runs down this list isn’t merit but a promise, and promises are kept by the one who makes them.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and Ruth a Moabite — Gentiles in the royal line. “The wife of Uriah” is Bathsheba.

verseByVerse.quote: and Solomon the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asaph, and Asaph the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The royal line runs from Solomon through Rehoboam, Abijah, Asaph (Asa), Jehoshaphat and Joram to Uzziah — good and bad kings alike. The promise depended not on the quality of the men who carried it but on the faithfulness of the God who made it.

No verdicts. Read slowly and notice what Matthew declines to do. Jehoshaphat “sought the LORD with all his heart” (2 Chronicles 22:9). Joram murdered all his brothers to secure the throne (2 Chronicles 21:4). Uzziah died a leper for forcing his way into the temple to burn incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). They are set down in the same rhythm, with no adjective attached to any of them. What is traced isn’t the quality of the men but the durability of the promise that passed through their hands — and it didn’t falter once in the hands of people who did. A test: do you think God’s purposes depend on your faithfulness more than on his?

Three kings missing. A reader who checks this against the Old Testament will notice two things. First, Matthew writes that Joram fathered Uzziah, but Chronicles has Joram followed by Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah, and only then Uzziah (1 Chronicles 3:11–12). Three generations are gone. That isn’t a slip. “Father of” in Hebrew and Greek can mean “ancestor of,” as Jesus is called “son of David” a thousand years after David. A Jewish genealogy established descent; it wasn’t a birth register, and skipping generations to make a memorable pattern was ordinary practice no first-century reader would call an error. Matthew wants his three groups of fourteen (v. 17), and prunes to get them.

Why these three? Perhaps because all three descended from Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, who brought her family’s idolatry into David’s line, and God had pronounced judgment on Ahab’s house (1 Kings 21:21). Matthew may be letting that sentence stand. We can’t be certain, and he doesn’t say. What is certain is that the line itself is unbroken; names left out of a list don’t remove men from history.

Asaph and Amos. Second, the names. Your Bible probably reads that Abijah fathered “Asaph,” and later that Manasseh fathered “Amos,” and a reader may object that Asaph was a psalmist and Amos a prophet. The kings meant are Asa and Amon. The oldest manuscripts have Asaph and Amos, and modern translations keep that reading, noting Asa and Amon in the margin. These may be variant spellings, or Matthew may be glancing at the psalmist and the prophet. Either way, the kings are the same.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Asa for Asaph. Matthew’s list skips several kings between Joram and Uzziah; “father of” can mean ancestor.

verseByVerse.quote: and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amos, and Amos the father of Josiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line continues through Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amos (Amon) and Josiah — the best and worst kings Judah ever had. God carried his promise through men who had no claim on it, and even the worst of them was not beyond his mercy.

The best and the worst. Ahaz shut the doors of the LORD’s house and burned his son as an offering. Manasseh went further: he set a carved image in the temple and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood from one end to the other (2 Kings 21:7, 16). Between them stand Hezekiah and Josiah, Judah’s two best kings. All four are links in one chain, and the chain doesn’t thicken at the good names or wear thin at the bad ones. It isn’t a record of achievement but of a promise kept through people with no claim on it.

Ahaz and the sign. Ahaz burned his son “according to the despicable practices of the nations” (2 Kings 16:3) — child sacrifice by a son of David, in Jerusalem. He stripped the temple to buy Assyrian protection and copied a pagan altar he admired in Damascus for the LORD’s house (2 Kings 16:10–11). And Ahaz is the king to whom Isaiah 7:14 was spoken. The verse Matthew will quote at the end of this chapter — “Behold, the virgin shall conceive” — was given to this man, in his terror, after he had refused to ask God for a sign. The greatest promise in the Old Testament was handed to one of its worst kings, who didn’t want it. The promise doesn’t depend on the man holding it.

Manasseh. Fifty-five years on the throne, the longest reign in Judah’s history, and he used it for idols in the temple, sorcery, burning his sons, and innocent blood, until the LORD said he would “wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish” (2 Kings 21:13). By any reckoning the worst man in this list. And Chronicles records what Kings doesn’t. The Assyrians took him with hooks and bronze chains to Babylon, and there “he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly,” and God “was moved by his entreaty” and brought him home (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). He spent his last years tearing down what he had built.

No one too far gone. So the darkest name in the genealogy is the strongest case in Scripture against the idea that anyone is too far gone. Manasseh’s sins weren’t the ordinary kind; he sacrificed his own children, and God heard him when he finally asked. A test: name the person you have privately given up on, for whom you have stopped praying seriously because the case seems closed. Then notice that the man who filled Jerusalem with blood stands in the line that leads to Christ — and that he repented in a foreign prison at the end of a wasted life.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Amon for Amos. Hezekiah and Josiah were reforming kings; Manasseh was the worst.

verseByVerse.quote: and Josiah the father of Jechoniah and his brothers, at the time of the deportation to Babylon. And after the deportation to Babylon: Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah is the ancestor of Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon, and after the exile Jechoniah’s line continues through Shealtiel to Zerubbabel. God’s promise survived even the exile and even a divine curse, and the virgin birth is how God kept both his curse and his promise.

The line breaks — and continues. Here the list breaks. Fourteen generations of kings run out at a deportation, and to those who lived through it, it looked like the end of everything promised: no throne, no temple, no land, and Judah’s king in a Babylonian prison. Matthew builds the spine of his genealogy around the worst thing that ever happened to his people rather than around a victory. And the line doesn’t stop. It goes into exile and comes out the other side — Shealtiel, then Zerubbabel, who led the first company home. A test: is there a loss in your life that you have treated as the end of God’s promises?

A cursed name. But a shadow lies over Jechoniah, and a reader with an open Bible will find it. Of him God had sworn: “Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not succeed in his days, for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah” (Jeremiah 22:30). And Matthew runs the royal line straight through him. How can the Christ inherit David’s throne through the one man God cursed off it?

Legal heir, not blood descendant. The answer comes a few verses later. Jesus is Joseph’s son legally, and that conveys the right to the throne, descending through Solomon and Jechoniah. But he isn’t Joseph’s son by blood: “of whom Jesus was born” refers to Mary alone (v. 16). So the legal title passes through Jechoniah, while the blood doesn’t. And Luke’s genealogy, which on a common reading follows physical descent, comes down through David’s son Nathan (Luke 3:31) and never touches Jechoniah.

Another omission. Josiah was Jechoniah’s grandfather, not his father; Jehoiakim stands between them (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). As with the kings left out at verse 8, “father of” can mean “ancestor of,” and Matthew omits Jehoiakim to keep his pattern. The omission sharpens the point: Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah’s scroll (Jeremiah 36:23), and the curse on his son is the curse this genealogy must pass through.

Both words kept. The curse stands; God doesn’t quietly revoke it. And the promise stands: “your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). Two divine words that look as though both can’t be true, and the virgin birth threads them together. God didn’t go back on his word; he found a way through it that nobody saw coming. He generally does.
verseByVerse.note: The deportation to Babylon came in 597 and 586 BC. Zerubbabel later led the return and the rebuilding of the temple.

parallels.desc: Zerubbabel as the LORD’s signet ring

verseByVerse.quote: and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Zerubbabel the line runs through Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim and Eliud — men mentioned nowhere else in Scripture. Through five silent centuries God was quietly carrying his promise in ordinary, unknown lives, and an unrecorded life can still be essential to God’s purposes.

The light goes out. After Zerubbabel, names follow about whom history says nothing: no throne, no prophet, no chronicle, no psalm, not one recorded sentence. They lived in an occupied backwater under Persian, Greek and then Roman rule, and what they did was work, marry and raise children. Search the rest of the Bible and you won’t find them. They appear here and nowhere else.

The longest silence. This stretch covers the longest silence in the story. Between Zerubbabel, who returned from Babylon around 538 BC, and Joseph the carpenter, roughly five centuries pass — Persia giving way to Alexander, his generals dividing his empire, Antiochus desecrating the temple, the Maccabees revolting, Rome arriving. Israel lived through it all, and no prophet spoke. Generations of a family lived quietly through centuries in which God seemed to say nothing at all.

Not emptiness. But the silence wasn’t emptiness. The promise was moving the whole time, through men whose names survive only because Matthew wrote them down. They married, worked, raised children, buried parents and died without the least idea where the line they carried would end.

Load-bearing lives. Consider how much of your own life will be visible to anyone in three hundred years. For nearly everyone, none of it — and these men prove that isn’t the same as insignificance. Not one did anything the Bible thought worth recording, and every one was load-bearing. A test: are you measuring the worth of your faithfulness by whether anyone will remember it?
verseByVerse.note: These men after Zerubbabel are mentioned nowhere else in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line reaches Jacob, the father of Joseph, “the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” Matthew changes his pattern at the last link to show that Jesus is Joseph’s legal son but not his natural son: born of Mary alone, he is the promised Christ.

A broken drumbeat. Thirty-nine times Matthew has used the same construction, “A was the father of B,” with an active verb — a man fathering a son — like a drumbeat down the page from Abraham to “Jacob the father of Joseph.” Then, at the last link, it stops. He doesn’t write, “Joseph the father of Jesus.” He writes, “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born.” The verb turns passive, and “of whom” is feminine and singular in Greek: it can refer only to Mary.

Said first in the grammar. So Matthew has built thirty-nine identical links to establish a legal line, and broken his own pattern at the last, where breaking it changes everything. The chain reaches Joseph and doesn’t continue through him; it turns aside to a woman, and the child is “born” rather than “fathered.” He hasn’t yet said a word about a virgin; that comes shortly (vv. 18–25). But he has already said it in the grammar, and a careful reader would stop at that verb and go back to check.

How Scripture works. The doctrine isn’t asserted first and defended later. It is built into the structure of a list of names, so the shape of the sentence makes the claim before the story explains it.

“Who is called Christ.” “Christ” means “anointed one,” the Messiah. The whole list has been heading for this title. Every promise to David and to Abraham lands on this one man. A test: is Jesus to you simply a figure of history, or the Christ — the King God promised?
verseByVerse.note: Matthew breaks the pattern at the end: Jesus was born of Mary, not fathered by Joseph. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

parallels.desc: “being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph”

verseByVerse.quote: So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew sums up the genealogy in three sets of fourteen generations: Abraham to David, David to the exile, and the exile to the Christ. History is not random; God was steering it through promise, apparent ruin and fulfilment, to Jesus.

His working shown. Matthew stops and shows his working, as no other evangelist does. Three sets of fourteen: Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to Christ. The number is chosen. In Hebrew the letters of David’s name add up to fourteen, which may be part of the point; a list that says fourteen three times has said “David” three times. And the three panels form a shape: a promise given, a promise apparently destroyed, a promise kept. In this Gospel history isn’t a sequence of events but an argument going somewhere. A test: can you trust that God is steering the confusing chapters of your life toward his purpose?

Only thirteen? Count the third group and you find thirteen names. Matthew says fourteen. The usual answers are that Jechoniah is counted twice, closing the second group and opening the third as the hinge of the exile, or that Matthew counts generations rather than men. We can’t be certain. What is certain is that Matthew isn’t careless but schematic, and his first readers, who knew genealogies were shaped for teaching rather than kept as archives, wouldn’t have blinked.

Why do Matthew and Luke differ? Luke’s genealogy doesn’t match this one (Luke 3:23–38). From David the two lines part: Matthew goes through Solomon, Luke through Nathan, and Luke calls Joseph the son of Heli where Matthew calls him the son of Jacob. Christians have answered in several ways: that Luke gives Mary’s line, Joseph being Heli’s son-in-law; that a levirate marriage gave one man both a legal and a natural father; or that Matthew traces the legal royal succession while Luke traces physical descent. We can’t be certain, but the third is the most likely, and it is the reading assumed at verses 11–12: Matthew traces the legal, royal line through Solomon and Jechoniah, by which the throne passed to Joseph’s son, while Luke follows physical descent through Nathan. Each of the other views is held by careful readers, and none involves an error in Scripture.

What both agree on. Notice what the two genealogies never disagree about, which is what Matthew wants you to have: this man is the son of David and the son of Abraham, and every promise God made to either lands on him.
verseByVerse.note: Three sets of fourteen give the story its shape: rise to David, fall to exile, and the wait for the Christ. The counts are arranged, not exhaustive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Birth of Jesus Christ: God with Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew tells the nativity through Joseph's eyes. He discovers Mary's pregnancy, intends to divorce her quietly (sparing her public disgrace), and is then visited by an angel who reveals the child's supernatural origin. Joseph's response is exemplary and immediate: he did as the angel commanded. Two names define the child — Jesus (he will save his people from their sins) and Immanuel (God with us). The birth fulfills Isaiah 7:14, establishing the pattern of scriptural fulfillment that runs through Matthew's entire Gospel. Two things more. Verse 22 introduces the formula that will ring out ten times in this Gospel — "all this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet" — which is not proof-texting but the claim that these events complete Israel's whole story; and the verse-by-verse handles the controversy over Isaiah's word for "virgin" (Hebrew almah), including the fact that Jewish scholars translating their own Scriptures into Greek nearly two centuries before Christ rendered it parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for a virgin. The "virgin" reading was not a Christian invention. Verse 25's "knew her not until she had given birth" is Scripture's modest way of speaking about a husband and wife (as at Gen. 4:1), and the little word "until" fixes attention on the one thing at issue — that Jesus was conceived with no human father — rather than hinting at anything else. Note also that this is the first of four times God speaks to Joseph in a dream (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22), and that he obeys immediately every time; and that Joseph never speaks a single recorded word anywhere in the New Testament.
verseByVerse.theology: The virgin birth is not incidental decoration but theological necessity. If Jesus is to be the sinless substitute for sinners, he cannot enter the world through ordinary generation under fallen Adam. The Holy Spirit's agency in the conception ensures both his full humanity (born of woman, Gal. 4:4) and his freedom from the entail of the first Adam's sin. The two names capture the whole gospel: he is God who has come to be with us (Immanuel), and in being with us he saves us from our sins (Jesus). Doctrine and salvation are inseparable from the first moment.
verseByVerse.examples: Joseph's obedience is one of Scripture's quietly great acts of faith. He received no applause, no public vindication, no explanation beyond the angel's word. He obeyed at enormous personal cost — accepting social suspicion, raising a child not his own, surrendering his right to defend his reputation. In an age that demands visible proof and public validation before any commitment, Joseph's silent, costly fidelity is a rebuke and a model. God still calls his people to act on his word before the full picture is visible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. And her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary, betrothed to Joseph, is found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit before they come together, and Joseph, a just man unwilling to shame her, resolves to divorce her quietly. Joseph shows that true righteousness joins justice with mercy, choosing the least harmful honest course even when wronged.

Betrothal. Betrothal wasn’t engagement in our sense. It was legally binding from the day it was made: the couple didn’t yet live together, but only a divorce could end it, and unfaithfulness was treated as adultery (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). So when Mary is found pregnant, Joseph isn’t a disappointed young man reconsidering a wedding. He is a husband with a legal case, a public remedy available, and everyone’s sympathy. Matthew calls him “just” — and reports that he resolved to end it as quietly as the law allowed.

Holding every card. Put yourself in the room; this is one of the most practical scenes in the Gospel. Joseph held every card. The law was on his side, the evidence looked conclusive, and the village’s sympathy was his; he could have destroyed her and been praised for his piety. Most of us meet some version of this: someone has, as far as we can tell, wronged us badly, and we have the power to expose them and the right to use it.

The least destructive honest course. Watch what he decides. Not to pretend nothing happened, nor to waive the matter: he still intended to divorce her. What he refused was the destructive version of a legitimate act. He would take the ambiguity onto himself, let the village think what it liked about him too, and cost her as little as possible. Mercy isn’t denial; it doesn’t mean a wrong can never be named or acted on. Joseph chose the least destructive of the honest options — nearly always available, and nearly always costlier. Righteousness asks not “What am I entitled to do?” but “What does love permit me to do with what I am entitled to?” A test: when you have been wronged, are you seeking the remedy that heals or the one that humiliates?

Mary’s silence. Spare a thought for Mary, silent in these verses. She carried something she couldn’t explain in a way anyone would accept; whatever she said would sound like what a guilty girl says. She was obeying God and losing her reputation for it in a village where reputation was survival, and her vindication, when it came, came privately to Joseph in a dream and never to the neighbours. If you are doing right and paying for it in the eyes of people whose opinion matters to you, that is where she stood.

God met him on the road. Note when heaven moved: the angel came while Joseph was considering the merciful course. God met him on the road he had already begun to walk.
verseByVerse.note: Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; ending it required a divorce. The couple did not yet live together.

parallels.desc: the law on a betrothed woman

verseByVerse.quote: But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel tells Joseph in a dream not to fear taking Mary as his wife, because her child is conceived by the Holy Spirit; she will bear a son, and he is to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins. Jesus is the sinless Son, conceived by God’s Spirit, who came to rescue his people from sin itself — its penalty, its power, and one day its presence.

“Joseph, son of David.” The angel calls him by a title this Gospel otherwise keeps for Jesus, and it matters: the man asked to take this child is the one through whom the child will inherit a throne. Then “do not fear,” said to a man whose fear was entirely reasonable — not argued with, only answered. A test: what reasonable fear is keeping you from obeying what God has made clear?

From the Holy Spirit. “That which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.” No human father stands behind this child, and that is everything. Every other child of Adam inherits Adam’s fallen nature: “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5). This conception is a fresh act of God. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) overshadows Mary, so that “the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). So Jesus is fully man — truly Mary’s son, real flesh and blood — yet without the sin every child of Adam carries. And only such a Saviour can save: a Redeemer under Adam’s guilt would need redeeming himself. Salvation comes wholly from God’s side; the life within her is the Spirit’s gift, not human achievement.

How was Jesus sinless if Mary was a sinner? Not because Mary was sinless; she called God “my Savior” (Luke 1:47), as only a sinner can. The Roman Catholic teaching that Mary was conceived without sin has no basis in Scripture, and it doesn’t solve the problem anyway, since it would simply move the question back a generation. The answer Luke gives is the Spirit’s work in the conception itself: “the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy” (Luke 1:35). God sanctified what he created in her womb.

The name. “You shall call his name Jesus” — the Greek form of Joshua, “the LORD saves.” Not “may save.” And the sentence says what he saves from: not Rome, not poverty, but sin. To a first-century Jew, “his people” meant Israel and salvation meant rescue from Rome. Matthew overturns both. The enemy isn’t Caesar but sin, and “his people” proves wider than Israel: by the last verse it reaches “all nations” (28:19). The name echoes the psalm: “he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities” (Psalm 130:8). And Matthew shows how it will be done, at the table on the night of betrayal: “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28). The manger aims straight at the cross.

Saved from sin. What is it to be saved “from their sins”? From sin’s penalty: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). From sin’s power: “sin will have no dominion over you” (Romans 6:14). And one day from sin’s very presence: into the city “nothing unclean will ever enter” (Revelation 21:27). Guilt cancelled, grip broken, shadow one day gone — all folded into one name. A test: have you come to Jesus to be saved from your sins, or only from your troubles?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

parallels.desc: the name given to Mary too
he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities

verseByVerse.quote: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel" (which means, God with us).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew says all this fulfilled the Lord’s word through Isaiah: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel,” meaning “God with us.” In Jesus, God himself has come to be with his people — truly God and truly man in one person — and he will never leave them.

Fulfilled. Matthew’s formula, “all this took place to fulfill,” recurs throughout his Gospel. It isn’t proof-texting but fulfilment: the events of Jesus’ life complete Israel’s whole story.

Isaiah’s sign. Isaiah 7:14 was spoken around 734 BC to faithless King Ahaz, terrified as Syria and Israel marched on Jerusalem. God offered him a sign; Ahaz refused; so God gave one anyway — a child would be born, and before he knew right from wrong the two kings Ahaz dreaded would be gone (Isaiah 7:16). In its own day the sign said: God hasn’t abandoned his people. He is with us. But it outran its first fulfilment by seven centuries, waiting for the day God would be with his people not by sending help from afar but by coming himself.

“Virgin.” The Hebrew word Isaiah used, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age, in the Old Testament always unmarried, so a virgin is naturally in view (the narrower word is betulah). Critics say Matthew over-read it. But nearly two centuries before Christ, Jewish scholars translating their Scriptures into Greek rendered almah with parthenos, the ordinary Greek word for a virgin. The “virgin” reading wasn’t a Christian invention; it was already in the Jews’ own Greek Bible.

Are there virgin-birth stories in other religions? The supposed parallels don’t hold. The pagan myths tell of gods who had sexual union with women, as Zeus did; some of the stories most often cited, like those of Mithras or Horus, either describe nothing of the kind or come from sources later than the Gospels. None describes a conception without any union at all. And Matthew’s first readers were Jews, the people in the ancient world least likely to borrow a pagan myth and least prepared for a virgin-born Messiah. Matthew grounds it in Isaiah, not in anything around him.

God and man. The virgin conception means this child is truly man, without Adam’s sin, and truly God come in our flesh. The church fought long to keep both halves, and the Council of Chalcedon (AD 451) confessed two natures in one Person. Remaining what he was, he became what he was not. He didn’t lay aside his deity to take a body, nor merely appear human. He isn’t God in a costume, nor a good man promoted upward, but one Person, the eternal Son, in whom true human nature and undiminished divine nature are joined without confusion and without separation. Remove either and there is no gospel: a Christ less than God can’t save us, and a Christ less than man hasn’t saved us. Immanuel means both, in one cradle.

Immanuel. No one in the New Testament actually calls Jesus “Immanuel.” He is named Jesus. So how is the prophecy fulfilled? Because Immanuel isn’t a label but a confession of who he is. Matthew makes it the bracket around his Gospel: it opens with “God with us” (1:23) and closes with the risen Christ’s promise, “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (28:20). Everything between is God with us. The God whom the highest heaven can’t contain wrapped himself in our flesh and was laid in a feeding trough; “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Not encouragement mailed from a distance, but God himself, with us — and he has never left. A test: do you live as though God is truly with you today?

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him: he took his wife, but knew her not until she had given birth to a son. And he called his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Joseph wakes, he does as the angel commanded: he takes Mary as his wife but has no union with her until she gives birth to a son, and he names him Jesus. Joseph’s quiet, immediate obedience protected the virgin birth and brought Jesus legally into David’s line — a model of faithful, unseen service.

Woke, and did. “When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” No interval, no consultation, no negotiation. And what he agreed to wasn’t small: marrying a visibly pregnant woman, enduring the village’s arithmetic about the dates for the rest of his life, and raising as his own a child he was told wasn’t his. It is the first of four times God speaks to Joseph in a dream, and he responds the same way each time: take the child to Egypt, and “he rose and took the child and his mother by night” (2:14); go back (2:21); turn aside to Galilee (2:22). Four instructions, four immediate obediences, and not one recorded question. A test: when God’s word is clear, how long do you take to obey it?

Adopted into David’s line. “And he called his name Jesus.” Naming the child carried legal weight. By giving him his name, Joseph formally received him as his son, bringing him into the line of David.

“Knew her not.” The Bible’s modest way of speaking of a husband and wife coming together, used since the beginning: “Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived” (Genesis 4:1). There is beauty in the word: marriage’s union isn’t treated as a mere physical act but as two people truly knowing each other. Matthew tells us, plainly and reverently, that Joseph had no union with Mary until after Jesus was born. He guarded her, so no one could say the child was his. The child was God’s alone.

Did Mary have other children? Matthew’s “until” says only what didn’t happen before the birth. But the natural reading of the whole Gospel is that Joseph and Mary lived as husband and wife afterwards, and Matthew names Jesus’ brothers and mentions his sisters (13:55–56; cf. 12:46). The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that Mary remained a virgin for life, and take the “brothers” as cousins or as Joseph’s children from an earlier marriage. Nothing in the text requires either explanation, and the plain reading is the more likely: Mary was a faithful wife who bore other children after her firstborn.

The silent man. Joseph never speaks. Not one word of his is recorded in the New Testament. He is spoken to and about, and acts decisively at every turn — and the man who headed the household in which the Son of God grew up leaves no line of dialogue. He is present when Jesus is twelve (Luke 2:41–51), and then he disappears; by the time of the ministry Mary appears without a husband, and he had very likely died. He was given the hardest assignment of any man in the Christmas story, carried it out without complaint, received no vindication we know of, and left no words behind. Faithfulness doesn’t need an audience.
verseByVerse.note: “Knew her not” means they had no sexual relations until the birth.

1.theology:
The Incarnation and the Hypostatic Union. Matthew 1:23 is the first New Testament statement of what the Council of Chalcedon (451 AD) would define as the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. Emmanuel — God with us. The one born of Mary is not a divine being wearing a human costume, nor a human being elevated to divine status. He is the eternal Son of God who took to himself a true and complete human nature, remaining what he was while becoming what he was not.

Reformed theology has insisted on both sides of this confession with equal force. Against those who diminish the humanity (docetism), the reformers affirm: he was born of a woman, grew in wisdom, wept, hungered, died. Against those who diminish the divinity, the reformers affirm: he is the Lord who saves, the one who forgives sins, who raises the dead, who will judge the living and the dead. The incarnation is not a compromise between deity and humanity; it is the union of both in one Person, the only foundation on which salvation is possible.
1.examples:
Then: The women in the genealogy — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba — represent the scandalous grace of God that runs through broken and foreign vessels to accomplish his purposes. The rabbis of Matthew’s day would have found their inclusion in a royal genealogy offensive. Matthew includes them precisely because the gospel offends the self-righteous and welcomes the unlikely. The same grace that wrote Rahab the harlot into the ancestry of the Messiah writes sinners into the family of God through faith.

Now: We live in a world that determines worth by background, achievement, and social position. The genealogy of Matthew 1 demolishes every such calculation. The line of the King runs through exiles, foreigners, adulterers, and the forgotten. If your story has chapters you would rather not name in public, you are in good company in this genealogy. The God who included Rahab and Ruth and Tamar in the ancestry of his Son includes broken people in his family — not despite their stories but through them, weaving even the darkest threads into the tapestry of his redeeming purpose.

2.title: The King and the Nations
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, <sup>2</sup>saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him.” <sup>3</sup>When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; <sup>4</sup>and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. <sup>5</sup>They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: <sup>6</sup>‘And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’” <sup>7</sup>Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. <sup>8</sup>And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, “Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him.” <sup>9</sup>After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. <sup>10</sup>When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. <sup>11</sup>And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. <sup>12</sup>And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way. <sup>13</sup>Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him.” <sup>14</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt <sup>15</sup>and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” <sup>16</sup>Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. <sup>17</sup>Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: <sup>18</sup>“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.” <sup>19</sup>But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, <sup>20</sup>saying, “Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead.” <sup>21</sup>And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. <sup>22</sup>But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee. <sup>23</sup>And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is a chapter of contrasts. From the east, pagan Magi travel hundreds of miles to worship a Jewish king they have never met, guided by a star and driven by a longing they cannot fully name. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes know exactly where the Messiah is to be born — they can quote the prophecy from memory — and do not move a single step toward Bethlehem. Knowledge without seeking is useless; seeking without knowledge leads to Jerusalem first and then to the star. The Magi needed both, and they found the King.

The flight to Egypt is Matthew’s second great fulfilment: Out of Egypt I called my son (Hos. 11:1). What Hosea said of Israel, Matthew applies to Jesus — because Jesus is the true Israel, recapitulating the nation’s story in his own person. Israel went into Egypt to be preserved; Israel came out of Egypt to receive the law at Sinai. Jesus goes into Egypt as an infant; he comes out to receive baptism at the Jordan and give the new law on the mountain. He is not just a figure from Israel’s history; he is Israel’s history compressed and completed.

The massacre of the innocents is the chapter’s darkest moment, and Matthew does not diminish it. Rachel weeping for her children (Jer. 31:15) — the ancient lament of exile reactivated by Herod’s paranoid terror. Children died because the King had come. This is not a comfortable note, and it should not be. The incarnation provokes powers that kill to protect themselves. And yet those children are the first martyrs — the first to die because of the King who would die for all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Visit of the Magi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wise men from the East arrive in Jerusalem following a star, seeking the one born King of the Jews. Their arrival triggers the first of Matthew's great ironies: Gentiles travel from afar to worship the Jewish Messiah, while the Jewish king plots his murder and the religious establishment is unmoved. Herod's response — feigned interest concealing murderous intent — foreshadows the opposition that will culminate at Golgotha. The magi's worship, their gifts, and their Spirit-warned departure set the pattern: the nations come to the light while those who hold the Scriptures remain in darkness. Two things more. Verses 7-8: Herod's secrecy is his first tell — he does not want Jerusalem to know what he is planning — and the detail he extracts from the magi, the time the star appeared, is precisely the data that produces the age-range of the massacre at verse 16. His "that I too may come and worship him" is a lie welding devotion to murder, which is the enemy's own signature (Jn. 8:44). Verses 9-10: the star resumes only after the Scriptures have sent them to Bethlehem, and by verse 9 the light is behaving less like an object in the sky than like the pillar of fire that went before Israel (Exod. 13:21) — it goes ahead of them at walking pace and halts over one house. Matthew's Greek for their reaction piles up four words where one would do: they rejoiced with joy exceedingly great. And note what caused it — not the sight of the child, whom they had not yet reached, but a light they had followed for months finally standing still.
verseByVerse.theology: The magi's journey is the fulfillment of Isaiah's vision: the nations streaming to Zion's light (Isa. 60:1–6). Their gifts — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one destined to die — have long been read as prophetic of Christ's three offices. Herod represents all who will acknowledge Christ's kingship only to oppose it: knowing who he is changes nothing if the heart is not transformed. The Scripture the chief priests quote from memory (Micah 5:2) but do not obey is a standing rebuke to knowledge without submission - and the loose form of their quotation, examined at vv. 5-6, only sharpens the point: they had the text near enough to recite and far enough to ignore.
verseByVerse.examples: The magi traveled perhaps a thousand miles, following light they only partially understood, to bring costly gifts to a child. Their worship was costly, inconvenient, and preceded by great uncertainty. Many who have never left their town have more theological knowledge than these men had — and far less devotion. The question the magi's story presses: what are you willing to travel, spend, and risk to find and worship Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star when it rose and have come to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem, in Herod’s reign, wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews is, for they have seen his star and come to worship him. God draws Gentile outsiders to worship Israel’s true King, while the city that should have welcomed him is unaware.

Bethlehem. Bethlehem of Judea is named not for geography but for prophecy: the city of David, where the Messiah was to be born (Micah 5:2). The wise men ask the right question — “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” — in the wrong place. They come to the palace looking for a newborn king and find only Herod. The star brought them as far as Israel; Scripture would carry them the last miles to Bethlehem.

Herod. History calls him Herod the Great — great as a builder (he lavishly rebuilt the temple), monstrous as a man. An Idumean, of Esau’s line, he was given the title “King of the Jews” by Rome and clutched at his throne all his life: he murdered his wife Mariamne, three of his own sons and many others. Augustus is said to have joked that it was safer to be Herod’s pig than his son. So when word comes of a child “born king of the Jews,” the old tyrant’s terror, and the slaughter in verse 16, are grimly in character. Two kings of the Jews now face each other: one crowned by Rome and drenched in blood, one born of God and worshipped by strangers.

The wise men. The “magi” were learned men from the East, probably Persia or Babylon — royal advisers who studied the heavens. They were Gentiles, outside the covenant, and yet they are the first in this Gospel to seek the King and bow down. Where would they get a hope of a Jewish Messiah? Perhaps from the long memory of the East, where Daniel had once been set over Babylon’s wise men (Daniel 2:48), and where the old prophecy still lingered: “a star shall come out of Jacob” (Numbers 24:17). Scripture never calls them kings or numbers them; the three crowns and the names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar are later legend, the “three” guessed from the three gifts. What matters is the picture: the nations coming to the light of Israel’s King with gold and frankincense, as Isaiah foresaw (Isaiah 60:3, 6).

What they sought. “King of the Jews” — not a petty local ruler, but a King whose birth the heavens marked, who plainly mattered to the nations, or why travel so far? Roman historians (Tacitus, Suetonius) record a widespread expectation in that era that rulers would arise from Judea. “His star” — we aren’t told what it was, and shouldn’t pretend to know; but it later goes ahead of them and stops over one house (v. 9), which no ordinary star does. God met these men inside their own field, the study of the skies, and used a light they couldn’t ignore to draw them to his Son. “To worship him” — at least to do a king homage; but at the house they fall down and pour out their treasures (v. 11), giving this child what belongs to God.

Far and near. Gentiles travel hundreds of miles to worship the King, while Jerusalem, holding the very Scriptures that name his birthplace, won’t walk six miles to see him. A test: are you near to Christ in knowledge yet far from him in worship?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “wise men” renders the Greek magi — scholars of the stars, probably from Persia or Babylon. Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC.

parallels.desc: a star shall come out of Jacob
nations bring gold and frankincense to the light

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and assembling all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod is troubled at the news, and all Jerusalem with him, and he summons the chief priests and scribes to ask where the Christ is to be born. Knowing the Scriptures is not the same as submitting to Christ, and religious knowledge can coexist with complete indifference to him.

Trouble instead of joy. The city that should have erupted in joy at its King’s arrival trembles instead. Herod’s trouble is that of threatened power; Jerusalem’s is fear of what Herod might do. The chief priests and scribes are summoned not for worship but for information — used as a reference library by a man with no intention of bowing. The religious establishment had every text and no intention.

The scholars exposed. Before that lands comfortably on someone else, notice who is most exposed. The men in this scene aren’t sceptics or pagans; they are the Bible scholars. They can produce the right chapter and verse from memory, at speed, under pressure from a king — and won’t walk six miles down a road they have just identified. That isn’t a failure of information but of appetite.

The reader at risk. The person most at risk here is the person reading a commentary. If you can locate a doctrine, follow an argument about the Greek and hold an opinion on a disputed text, you have the very equipment these men had. The chapter asks not whether you know where Christ is to be found, but whether knowing has ever once made you get up and go. Study can become a substitute for what it is meant to serve — a comfortable one, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing.

The honest question. So ask it now rather than at the end of your life: over the last month, what has knowing moved you to do? If the answer is only that it moved you to know more, you are standing with the scribes, and Bethlehem is still six miles away. A test: what is one thing you know from Scripture that you have not yet obeyed?
verseByVerse.note: Herod was notoriously jealous of rivals; he had members of his own family killed. The chief priests and scribes were the experts in the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet: 'And you, O Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scholars answer that the Christ is to be born in Bethlehem of Judea, quoting the prophet: from little Bethlehem will come a ruler who will shepherd God’s people Israel. God brings his King from an overlooked place, and his grace makes small things great.

Quoted and ignored. Micah 5:2 comes to their lips at once and is obeyed not at all. They know exactly where the Messiah is to be born, and not one makes the six-mile journey to check. Foreigners travel far to worship; Israel’s scholars travel no distance at all. And the text calls the coming ruler a shepherd — evoking David, Moses, and the one who will say, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). He came to shepherd his people, and the shepherds of his people wouldn’t go to find him.

Turned around. Look up the prophecy, and something will stop you. Micah wrote: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah” (Micah 5:2). The version here says nearly the opposite: “by no means least among the rulers of Judah.” Too little — by no means least. And the closing line, “who will shepherd my people Israel,” isn’t in Micah 5:2 but in God’s word to David: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel” (2 Samuel 5:2).

Not carelessness. Notice whose words these are: the chief priests and scribes answering a king, quoting as scholars do and joining to Micah the promise to David that belonged beside it. But there is more than loose citation. Micah’s point was that Bethlehem was too small to matter — that God delights to choose what the world overlooks. The point here is what that smallness has now become. The village too little to count among Judah’s clans is, now that this child is born there, by no means least.

Grace doesn’t leave little things little. Both are true, and the second is what the first was always going to produce. Read that way, the apparent misquotation is the gospel in miniature. It is the logic Paul preaches — “God chose what is low and despised in the world” (1 Corinthians 1:28) — and the logic of Bethlehem, of Nazareth, and of every unremarkable person Christ has laid his hand on. A test: do you think your smallness puts you beyond God’s great purposes?
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem, David’s hometown, lies about six miles south of Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: “You shall be shepherd of my people Israel”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Herod summoned the wise men secretly and ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. And he sent them to Bethlehem, saying, "Go and search diligently for the child, and when you have found him, bring me word, that I too may come and worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod secretly finds out from the wise men when the star appeared, then sends them to Bethlehem to search for the child and report back, “that I too may come and worship him.” The deadliest hatred of Christ often disguises itself as devotion — yet God protects his Son and guides even outsiders to him through his Word.

A murderer’s secrecy. Herod’s secrecy is the first mark of his intent; he doesn’t want Jerusalem to know what he plans. The time of the star’s appearing becomes the data for the massacre: “two years old or under” (v. 16). His claim to want to worship is one of history’s most transparent lies — and it has been repeated by every power that has tried to co-opt Christ for its own ends. True worship dethrones the worshipper; Herod wanted information to eliminate a rival.

The star and astrology. In the ancient East it was assumed that the heavens spoke — that the births and deaths of kings were written in the sky for those trained to read them. Astrology was the respected learning of the day, and the magi its scholars. Yet the Bible forbids God’s people to steer their lives by the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19), and Isaiah mocks “those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars” (Isaiah 47:13). So how does God use one? In grace he met these outsiders where they were, speaking in the language they knew — not to bless astrology, but to draw them out of it and onto the road to Bethlehem. And the star brought them only as far as Israel; it was Scripture that brought them to the King (vv. 5–6). God often calls a person through the dim light he already has, but never leaves him there; he leads him to his Word. We aren’t to scan the skies for messages: “we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed” (2 Peter 1:19).

Murder dressed as worship. “That I too may come and worship him” — meaning, that I may find him and kill him. To weld lying and murder in one breath is the devil’s signature: “He was a murderer from the beginning… a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). Herod is doing the serpent’s work, and Revelation shows the picture behind it: the dragon crouching before the woman “so that when she bore her child he might devour it” (Revelation 12:4). The deadliest hatred of Christ rarely comes snarling; it comes dressed in devotion. The same evil will later kiss him in a garden. A test: do you ever use the language of faith to cover what you really want?

The lie fails. But see how the lie ends. God need only warn the wise men in one dream and Joseph in another, and the child is gone before the swords arrive. The cradle the tyrant meant to empty, God was guarding; and the King Herod couldn’t kill would one day lay down his life of his own accord — and take it up again.

parallels.desc: rulers take counsel against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After hearing the king, the wise men set out, and the star they had seen goes ahead of them until it stops over the place where the child is; seeing it, they rejoice with exceedingly great joy. God himself guides those he is calling to his Son, and great joy comes when we find that the road of faith was the right one.

A guiding light. “The star… went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was.” No star in the ordinary sense does that. Astronomers have proposed a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, a comet, a nova — and whatever stood in the sky at its rising (v. 2), none of these travels ahead of tired men at walking pace down the Bethlehem road and halts above one roof. By now this light behaves less like an object in the heavens than like the pillar of fire that went before Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21): a light God set before people to bring them exactly where he wanted.

He doesn’t lose them. We aren’t told what it was. We are told the point: God moved heaven itself to bring these outsiders to his Son’s feet. He doesn’t lose those he is calling. If it takes hanging a light in the sky and walking it down a road to bring a Persian scholar to Bethlehem, he will do it.

Joy piled up. Matthew’s Greek is doing something odd: literally, “they rejoiced with joy exceedingly great” — a verb, its own noun, an adjective and an adverb piled on one another. It isn’t elegant Greek. It is the sentence of a man reaching for four words because one won’t do, the strongest expression of gladness in this Gospel.

The road was right. And notice what produced it. Not the sight of the child — they haven’t reached the house yet — nor any word or deed of the King. They rejoiced because a light they had been following stopped moving. What they had was confirmation that the journey hadn’t been foolish: months on the road, a wrong turn into a hostile palace, an audience with a man they would be warned to avoid — and then the thing they had sought standing still over a roof before them. Most Christians have known some version of that joy: not yet arrival, but the moment it becomes clear the road was the right one after all. A test: are you willing to keep following God’s light before you can see where it ends?

verseByVerse.quote: And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Entering the house, the wise men see the child with Mary his mother, fall down and worship him, and offer gold, frankincense and myrrh; then, warned in a dream, they return home another way. True worship bows before Christ without needing outward splendour, and God provides for his Son’s needs and protects him from his enemies.

Worship without trappings. They found not a palace but a house; not a king enthroned but a child with his mother. And they fell down and worshipped. Authentic worship doesn’t need the trappings of majesty to recognise its reality. A test: does your worship depend on impressive surroundings, or on Christ himself?

Not the stable. The text quietly refuses to say what every Christmas card says. It doesn’t say there were three magi; three gifts are named, not three men. It doesn’t call them kings. And this isn’t the stable. Luke’s shepherds came on the night of the birth and found “the baby lying in a manger” (Luke 2:16); the magi come to a house, to a “child” — and Herod’s “two years old or under” (v. 16) suggests the visit came some time after the birth. The nativity scene that sets the wise men beside the manger folds many months into one night. The truth is better: not a crowd round a cradle on one evening, but the patient, sovereign gathering of the nations to Christ, begun with a handful of foreign scholars and still going on.

The gifts. Take them first as what they plainly were: portable wealth. Gold needs no explanation; frankincense and myrrh were resins brought from southern Arabia at great cost. A fortune arrives in a working family’s house — immediately before a flight into a foreign country. Joseph is about to be told to leave in the night, with no means of support in Egypt, and the funds arrive first, carried far by strangers who had no idea what they were for. The old reading — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one who would die — is ancient and may be right; myrrh reappears at his burial (John 19:39). Matthew doesn’t say so.
