But the plainer providence is remarkable enough: God provided for the exile before he announced it. Sometimes a provision that seems out of proportion to anything happening now is for later.

Another way. “Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.” God actively protects his Son from those who would destroy him. And those who have met Christ often go home by another way.
verseByVerse.note: By now the family is in a house, not a stable. Frankincense was a resin burned in worship; myrrh a fragrant resin also used in burial.

parallels.desc: kings bring gifts to the king

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infant boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth — each movement fulfilling a specific Old Testament text. Matthew sees in these events not merely historical geography but the recapitulation of Israel's story: Jesus relives the Exodus (out of Egypt), the Exile (the weeping of Rachel), and Israel's wilderness sojourn (settling in a despised region). The Son of God is doing in himself what Israel failed to do: he is the true Israel, perfectly faithful where the nation was not. Three items the summary passes over. Verses 19-20 contain a quiet oddity: "those who sought the child's life are dead" is plural, though only Herod had died — because Matthew is quoting Exodus 4:19 almost word for word, God's word to Moses in Midian, with the direction of travel reversed. Herod died at Jericho in the spring of 4 BC, which is why Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1 — an error not in Scripture but in the sixth-century monk who built the calendar. Verses 21-22 are the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and the verse-by-verse takes up the question readers actually carry: whether God still guides this way, and what to do with a vivid dream. Note that Joseph's fear of Archelaus was reasonable on its own terms and the dream confirmed his ordinary judgement rather than overruling it. Verse 23 is the hardest fulfilment quotation in the Gospel, because no Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene — and Matthew signals as much by writing "prophets" in the plural, naming nobody and quoting nothing. The strongest reading is Isaiah 11:1, where the shoot from Jesse's stump is a netser; the theme of the despised one (Isa. 53:2-3) very likely stands behind it too. And the name stuck: it is what Pilate wrote over his head, how the angel identified him at the tomb, and what the risen Christ called himself from heaven on the Damascus road (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's three fulfillment quotations here (Hos. 11:1; Jer. 31:15; and possibly Isa. 11:1 or Judg. 13:5 for "Nazarene") reveal his typological reading of history: Israel's great narrative events were not merely past occurrences but prophetic templates waiting for their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt. The slaughter of the innocents does not merely echo Rachel's weeping; it is the event that makes the older weeping fully intelligible. This is not proof-texting but fulfillment theology.
verseByVerse.examples: The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is the event that silences easy answers about suffering. Matthew does not explain it; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and moves on. Rachel weeping for her children who are no more: there are moments when the only honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's birth caused suffering for the innocent. His death would be the answer to that suffering — not by explaining it away, but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the wise men leave, an angel tells Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt with the child and his mother, because Herod is about to search for the child to kill him, and Joseph sets out that very night. The Son of God shared the life of refugees, and God carries his purposes forward through the immediate obedience of ordinary believers.

By night. Joseph obeys at once — “by night,” without waiting for morning. The danger is real; Herod will move quickly. Egypt, the land of Israel’s ancient bondage, becomes the Messiah’s refuge. The one who will lead a new exodus first relives the sojourn in Egypt. Joseph is told, and he does — the faith that acts without arguing and obeys without understanding the whole plan, harder than heroism: silent, sustained obedience to a voice only he heard.

Refugees. Say plainly what is happening, because familiarity has smoothed it over. A family wakes in the dark, takes what it can carry, and crosses a border to escape a ruler who wants their child dead. They arrive in a foreign country with no standing and no idea how long they will stay. There is a word for people in that position: refugees. The Son of God spent part of his childhood as one.

A face on the command. God could have protected the child in Bethlehem — he had just redirected a caravan with a dream. Instead he sent him down the road displaced families have walked. So when Scripture commands care for the sojourner and the stranger, reminding Israel that they were strangers in Egypt themselves (Exodus 23:9), the command now has a face. Christians in good conscience differ on borders and policy, but no follower of this King is free to speak with contempt of people fleeing violence. He was carried out of such a night in his mother’s arms. A test: how do you speak of the stranger and the displaced?

For the uprooted. And there is comfort here. If your life has been marked by upheaval you didn’t choose — moved on, uprooted, made to start again somewhere that wasn’t home — you aren’t outside the experience of Christ or the plan of God. Those years in Egypt weren’t an interruption of his mission but part of it, and Matthew says next that Scripture had them written down beforehand.
verseByVerse.note: Egypt had long been a refuge; large Jewish communities lived there.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family stays in Egypt until Herod’s death, fulfilling “Out of Egypt I called my son”; meanwhile Herod, furious at being tricked, kills all the boys of two and under in and around Bethlehem. Jesus is the true Son who relives and fulfils Israel’s story, and his coming provokes the violent hostility of worldly power against the defenceless.

Out of Egypt. Hosea 11:1 originally referred to the Exodus — God calling Israel, his son, out of Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus as the true Son who fulfils that pattern: where Israel as God’s son failed again and again in the wilderness, Jesus will succeed.

Is Matthew bending Hosea? Hosea wasn’t predicting the future; he was looking back at the Exodus. So is Matthew forcing his words to fit Jesus? The sound answer is that “fulfil” doesn’t always mean a prediction has come true; often it means “filled full,” brought to the completion God always intended. God wrote a pattern into Israel’s history: Israel was his “son” (Exodus 4:22), taken down into Egypt and brought out again. That pattern was a shadow cast ahead, waiting for the true Son who would walk the same road and never fail. Matthew is reading the Old Testament as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it — one story, by one Author, about one Saviour (Luke 24:27). Two rules keep this honest: we never erase what a text meant in its own day (Hosea did mean the Exodus), and we read every text in the light of the whole Bible, whose centre is Christ. That is no licence to make a verse say whatever we please; it is learning to see the Author’s single design.

The massacre. Herod’s fury at being “tricked” shows he knew he was pursuing a child, not an army — and killed infants anyway. Worldly power meets the presence of Christ with violence against the most vulnerable, an early shadow of the cross.

Why doesn’t Josephus mention it? No writer outside Matthew records this massacre, and Josephus, who chronicles Herod’s reign at length and spares him nothing, is silent; that silence is often offered as proof Matthew invented it. Start with the scale, which Christmas art distorts. Bethlehem was a village of perhaps a few hundred people; its boys of two and under would have numbered perhaps a handful to a score — a few families and one terrible morning. Then set it against the reign. This man murdered his wife Mariamne, executed three of his sons, had his young brother-in-law drowned in a pool for being too popular, and on his deathbed ordered the nation’s leading men shut in the hippodrome at Jericho and killed when he died, so the country would weep at his funeral. Beside that, the deaths of a few peasant infants in a village near Jerusalem is, horribly, the kind of thing a historian of such a reign might not think worth recording. An argument from silence is weak, and weakest for small events far from the centre of power. And Matthew wrote for readers in the region within living memory — the worst possible audience for inventing a local atrocity.

God’s ledger. But don’t let the answer make it small. The reason it didn’t trouble the chroniclers is the reason it should trouble us: in the ledgers of power, poor children in an unimportant village don’t count. God keeps a different ledger. Matthew gives these families verses and the words of a prophet, and heaven hasn’t forgotten one of them. A test: do the people the world overlooks count in your ledger?
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem was a small town; the number of boys killed was probably small, but the act fits Herod’s known cruelty.

parallels.desc: “Out of Egypt I called my son”
Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys killed

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew says the massacre fulfilled Jeremiah’s word of Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more. Scripture doesn’t explain away grief; it honours it — and in Christ, who later suffered himself, God enters our sorrow and holds out sure hope.

Rachel weeping. Jeremiah 31:15 was originally the voice of exile: Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, pictured mourning as her descendants were led past Ramah into Babylonian captivity. Matthew hears that ancient lament in the weeping of Bethlehem’s mothers — Rachel was buried on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). He doesn’t soften it or explain it; he names the grief.

A page of promise. As in verse 15, this is fulfilment in the fuller sense: an ancient pattern brought to its deepest point. And Jeremiah’s words carry a buried comfort Matthew surely means us to find. That cry stands in the most hopeful chapter the prophet wrote. The next lines are: “Keep your voice from weeping… there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back” (Jeremiah 31:16–17), and a few verses on comes the promise of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Even Bethlehem’s tears are quoted from a page soaked in promise.

Why was one child warned? The question underneath must be asked aloud. God sent an angel to Joseph. He sent no angel to the house next door. Why was one child carried to safety while the others were left to the swords? It is the sharpest form of the oldest question, set at the very beginning of the Gospel. Scripture’s first answer is to refuse to explain. Matthew offers no reason or consoling remark. He quotes a mother who “refused to be comforted,” and leaves her refusal uncorrected. Anyone who has been told that grief is a failure of faith should hold onto that. The Bible puts an inconsolable woman in the Christmas story and doesn’t rebuke her.

The limit. We aren’t told why the warning came to one house. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29), and a commentary that manufactures an answer here is presumptuous, not faithful. If you have lost a child, no one on earth can tell you why, and anyone who offers a reason is guessing.

Not a guess. But this isn’t a guess: the child rescued that night was rescued for Golgotha. The reprieve was real and temporary; thirty years later the sword that missed him in Bethlehem found him outside Jerusalem, and this time the Father sent no angel. Whatever else is true, God doesn’t keep his own family clear of the grief he permits in yours. He entered it at its deepest point. That isn’t an explanation of your loss, but the presence of someone in it with you who knows what it cost — and it is why “your children shall come back” isn’t poetry but a promise with a cross and an empty tomb behind it. A test: will you bring your unanswered grief to the One who suffered it himself?
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay north of Jerusalem, on the road into exile. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was buried near Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: Rachel buried on the way to Bethlehem

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Herod dies, an angel tells Joseph in Egypt to take the child and his mother back to the land of Israel, because those who sought the child’s life are dead. Jesus relives Moses’ story as the greater deliverer, and God’s timing and guidance can be trusted through long and uncertain waiting.

Moses’ words. There is a small oddity in the angel’s wording: “those who sought the child’s life are dead.” Plural — but only one man, Herod, had sought the child’s life and died. The sentence is a quotation. In Midian God told Moses, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Matthew reproduces it almost word for word, plural and all, and reverses the direction: Moses is sent back to Egypt, Joseph brought back from it. Jesus is the new Moses — and more. Moses led Israel out of Egypt; Jesus leads his people out of bondage to sin and death.

Herod’s end. Josephus describes Herod’s death in detail: a disease of fever, ulcers, convulsions and decay, borne with mounting rage, at Jericho in the spring of what we call 4 BC. During that final illness he gave the order to have the nation’s leading men killed at his death; his sister quietly cancelled it.

The calendar. That produces a surprise: if Herod died in 4 BC and Jesus was born before that, Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1. The error isn’t in Scripture but in a sixth-century monk, Dionysius Exiguus, who built a calendar from the incarnation and miscalculated by a few years. The date on the wall is wrong; the events aren’t.

Waiting without a date. Recall what Joseph had been told: “remain there until I tell you” (v. 13). No duration. He was told to go and told he would be told when to return, and then he waited in a foreign country with a small child, not knowing whether it would be months or a decade. It turned out to be a few years, and he knew that only afterward. That is the ordinary shape of waiting on God. Joseph wasn’t given a date; he was given a Person who promised to speak again, and the promise was kept. A test: are you able to wait on God without knowing how long?

parallels.desc: “all the men who were seeking your life are dead”

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph returns to Israel, but hearing that Archelaus rules Judea in Herod’s place, he is afraid to go there, and, warned in a dream, he withdraws to Galilee. God guides his people through ordinary wisdom and circumstances as well as special revelation, and now he guides us chiefly by his finished Word.

A reasonable fear. Joseph’s fear of Archelaus was well founded: he was as brutal as his father, and Rome deposed him in AD 6. Divine guidance doesn’t override prudence; here the dream confirms what ordinary wisdom suspected. God’s providence works through human fears, political realities and family decisions, not only through dramatic interventions. He is as sovereign in the ordinary as in the spectacular.

How does this fit Luke? In Luke the family returns to Nazareth after the presentation in the temple (Luke 2:39). Most likely the order was: birth in Bethlehem, where they had come for the census (Luke 2:1–5); the presentation in Jerusalem forty days later; a stay in Bethlehem, now in a house (2:11), where the magi found them; the flight to Egypt; and then Nazareth. Luke compresses the story and Matthew supplies the episode Luke leaves out. Matthew writes as if Nazareth is a new decision because from his angle it was: Joseph’s first thought was to settle in Judea.

Rare dreams. This is the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), which raises a real question: does God still guide like this? Notice how rare such a cluster is. Across thousands of years, guidance by dreams gathers at a few hinge-points of redemption — Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and here at the Messiah’s arrival. It wasn’t the ordinary way God led his people; the Israelite in the next village had the law, the priest and the counsel of the wise. And these dreams told Joseph things he couldn’t have known and needed urgently — a murder plot, a death, a danger ahead. None told him what to believe or how to live; for that, God had already spoken.

Does God still guide by dreams? Some Christians believe God still guides through dreams and visions today, pointing to Joel’s promise that “your old men shall dream dreams” (Acts 2:17), and to the dreams in Acts. The more likely reading is that those revelations belonged to the founding of the church, and that God now guides his people by his finished word. That does not stop God from using a dream in his providence, for example to send someone to read the Bible. But a dream is never a word that binds the conscience, and it must always be tested by Scripture.

The means God has given. Notice what sits beside the dream here: Joseph’s reasonable fear, which God doesn’t scold but confirms. That is the pattern. God guides most of us most of the time through the means he has given: Scripture, prayer, wisdom, circumstances and the counsel of people who know us. Anything contrary to what he has already said in his Word isn’t from him, however vivid it felt in the night. We have something steadier than dreams: “the prophetic word more fully confirmed” (2 Peter 1:19). A test: are you seeking guidance in Scripture and wise counsel, or waiting for a sign?
verseByVerse.note: Archelaus, Herod’s son, ruled Judea so brutally that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee was ruled by his brother Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph settles in Nazareth, fulfilling what the prophets said, that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene. Jesus is the promised Branch of David who came from a despised village, and he still bears that humble name in glory.

No single verse. This is the hardest of Matthew’s fulfilment quotations, and the difficulty should be stated: no Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene. And Matthew knows it. Elsewhere he writes “by the prophet,” singular, often naming him, and quotes. Here he writes “by the prophets,” plural, names no one, and quotes no text. He is pointing to a theme running through the prophets rather than citing a line.

The Branch. The strongest explanation: Isaiah promised “a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots” (Isaiah 11:1), and the Hebrew for “branch” there is netser, the same consonants as Nazareth. Jeremiah and Zechariah take up the image with another word, calling the coming King a righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12), which may be why Matthew says “prophets.” On this reading the village name is a play on words God arranged: the Branch grew up in Branch-town. And note the image. A stump is what is left when a tree is cut down — David’s royal house reduced to a dead-looking stub, and a green shoot coming from it. By Joseph’s day that was literally so: the heir of David’s throne was a carpenter in an occupied province.

Not a Nazirite. Some suggest “Nazirite,” the consecrated one, like Samson (Judges 13:5). It sounds close, but it is probably wrong: Jesus wasn’t a Nazirite, since he drank wine and was accused of enjoying it too much (11:19).

The despised one. A third reading takes “Nazarene” as what everyone understood it to mean: a nobody from a nowhere village. Nazareth appears nowhere in the Old Testament, Josephus or the Talmud; it was a small settlement. Nathanael gave the local verdict: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). On this reading the prophets foretold it in a theme: “he had no form or majesty that we should look at him… He was despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:2–3). The readings aren’t rivals so much as layers, and Matthew’s plural likely allows them all.

The name stuck. He is “Jesus of Nazareth” to the crowds, to demons, to a blind man on the road. It was written over his cross (John 19:19). The angel at the tomb says, “You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified” (Mark 16:6), and Peter preaches it at Pentecost (Acts 2:22). And the risen, glorified Christ uses it of himself from heaven: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 22:8). He was given a village that was a byword for insignificance, and he kept its name. He could have dropped it; Bethlehem had the prophecy, Jerusalem the temple, heaven his eternal home. What he answers to in glory, with the wounds still on him, is the name of the poor village nobody expected anything from. A test: are you ashamed to be associated with the humble Christ the world looks down on?
verseByVerse.note: No single prophecy says “he shall be called a Nazarene”; Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in general. Nazareth was a despised backwater, and the prophets foretold a despised Messiah.

parallels.desc: a branch from the stump of Jesse
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

2.theology:
Typology and the Unity of Scripture. Matthew 2 demonstrates the Reformed doctrine of the unity of the two Testaments through typological fulfilment. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not wresting Hosea from its context. He is reading with the grain of Scripture’s own logic: Israel was God’s son (Exod. 4:22), whose history was a pattern that pointed forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a collection of proof texts waiting to be claimed; it is a single story moving toward a single climax.

Reformed biblical theology, developed through scholars like Geerhardus Vos and continued by Edmund Clowney, has called this “redemptive-historical” interpretation: reading every text in the light of its place in the one story of God’s redemptive purpose. Matthew 2 is a masterclass in this method. Every Old Testament quotation is not forced but organic — the story was always moving here, toward the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settlement in Galilee of the nations (Isa. 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The Magi represent the first fruits of the Gentile mission that will be formally commissioned in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, guided by general revelation (the star), and are brought to special revelation (the Scriptures) and to the King himself. This is the pattern of mission throughout Acts: Cornelius, the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer — each guided by a mixture of seeking and sovereign orchestration to the one who is the answer to every longing.

Now: In our world, the contrast of chapter 2 repeats daily: people with no theological background travelling great distances (literally and metaphorically) to find Jesus, while those with full access to Scripture never move toward him. Church membership without worship, theological knowledge without seeking — this is Jerusalem troubled but not travelling. The question Matthew 2 poses is not “how much do you know?” but “are you moving toward the King?” The Magi found him because they went. That remains the condition of finding him today.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first voice is John’s: rough, wilderness-forged, prophetic, urgent. He wears the clothes of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. The kingdom is not arriving on your terms. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit — now, because the axe is already laid to the root. John’s preaching is the sound of the law doing its proper work: exposing the bankruptcy of religious privilege and the urgency of genuine turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: tender, declarative, public. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. It comes from heaven, over the Jordan, spoken in Matthew's account as a declaration to those watching: This is my beloved Son. The Father is not waiting to see how the ministry goes before rendering his verdict; he speaks it before the first sermon, before the first miracle, before the temptation is overcome. The approval is unconditional, grounded not in performance but in person and covenant.

Between the two voices stands the baptism — and the question it raises: why does the sinless one need a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers it: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is identifying with sinners. The one who needs no baptism submits to it on behalf of those who need it most. This is the logic of substitution, enacted in water before it is enacted in blood. The baptism of Jesus is the first act of the atonement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice preparing the way. His ministry draws crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, but he reserves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees — those who came for baptism without repentance. Jesus then comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and at his baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public ministry. Several things the summary passes over, all treated in full below. Verse 4's clothing and diet are not a costume: camel's hair and a leather belt are Elijah's uniform (2 Kgs. 1:8), whose return was promised before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5); locusts were among the few insects the law permitted (Lev. 11:22) and wild honey is what the wilderness gives away, so John lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody — which is precisely why nobody can buy him. The Jordan itself matters: it is where Israel crossed into the land (Josh. 3), where Elijah was taken up (2 Kgs. 2), and where Naaman went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kgs. 5:14). Note the direction of travel — the crowds go out of the towns to the river, leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it and coming back in through the water. John is asking Israel to start again from the beginning. Verse 9 contains a pun English cannot show: in Aramaic, stones are abanim and children are banim — take away a letter and the rubble becomes the family of God — and he says it standing at the river where Joshua set up twelve stones from the riverbed as a memorial to the twelve tribes (Josh. 4:1-7). Verses 13-14: Nazareth to the Jordan is sixty to eighty miles, three or four days on foot; and behind that walk lie eighteen years of which Scripture says nothing at all, since Luke last showed him at twelve and now says he was about thirty. The Son of God spent roughly nine-tenths of his life on earth doing work nobody recorded — and that was not preparation for obedience, it was obedience. John's protest is an imperfect verb, "he kept trying to prevent him", and his theology in it is impeccable while his conclusion is wrong: right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what God will do next. Verse 15's "to fulfil all righteousness" is the answer and the hinge of the chapter — not personal repentance but substitution enacted in water before it is enacted in blood.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, anticipating the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His insistence on fruit worthy of repentance cuts against every form of religious privilege — ancestry, tradition, institutional membership. You cannot inherit faith; you must repent. Jesus's baptism is not a baptism of personal repentance (he has no sin) but an act of identification and consecration: he enters the waters of judgment on behalf of sinners and emerges declared righteous by the Father. The Spirit's descent and the Father's voice confirm him as the inaugurator of the new age.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the religious establishment with their false security: "Do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.'" The same temptation runs through every tradition — to substitute membership for repentance, heritage for faith, attendance for transformation. John's question to each worshiper is still the right one: is there fruit? Not feeling, not knowledge, not ancestry — fruit. The tree is known by what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist preaches in the Judean wilderness, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” God’s King is arriving to reign, and the only fitting response is a wholehearted turning from sin to God.

Repent. John’s first word isn’t “God loves you” or “you are enough” but a call to turn round. Repentance isn’t mere regret or a change of habits; it is a change of mind so deep it reorients the whole life. The reason is the nearness of the kingdom: God’s rule, in the person of his King, is arriving, and the right response to a holy King’s arrival is honest self-examination. It is good news — but good news that demands a reckoning with who you are before the King you are about to meet.

What it meant on the riverbank. To a Jew, repentance was an old, weighty idea — “returning,” coming home to the LORD. The prophets had cried it for centuries: “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God” (Hosea 14:1); “rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). It was concrete: confession of sin, often with fasting, and a real forsaking of idols. John pressed it to a shocking edge. He called Jews — sons of Abraham, temple-goers, law-keepers — into the water as though they were outsiders who needed to come in. It meant letting go of every proud “we have Abraham as our father” (v. 9). And John demanded visible proof: “bear fruit in keeping with repentance” (v. 8) — share your coat, deal honestly, stop extorting (Luke 3:10–14).

And today. The heart of it hasn’t changed. Repentance is still a Spirit-given change of mind, turning from sin to God and from self-trust to Christ — not one tearful moment but the daily direction of a life; Luther’s first thesis was that the believer’s entire life is one of repentance. Our temptation is the old one in new dress: leaning on churchgoing, baptism, a decent name, a Christian family — our own “child of Abraham.” None of that is the turning itself. Yet this isn’t a demand to earn God’s favour. It is “godly grief” that “produces a repentance that leads to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10), a heart grace has begun to thaw turning home. We don’t repent to make the King come near; we repent because in Christ he already has. A test: what are you leaning on in place of turning to God?

Kingdom of heaven, kingdom of God. Matthew uses “the kingdom of heaven” some thirty times where Mark and Luke say “the kingdom of God.” They are one thing. Writing for Jewish readers, Matthew keeps their reverent habit of saying “heaven” in place of God’s name, as the prodigal says, “I have sinned against heaven” (Luke 15:21), and Daniel, “Heaven rules” (Daniel 4:26). Matthew proves it himself: it is hard for a rich man “to enter the kingdom of heaven,” and in the next breath, “to enter the kingdom of God” (19:23–24). Some have taught that the kingdom of heaven is an earthly kingdom for Israel and the kingdom of God a separate spiritual reality; those who hold this love the Scriptures, but those two verses are hard to get past. (The question is taken up further at 4:17.)

A reign, not a place. “Kingdom of heaven” doesn’t mean heaven, and John isn’t preaching about where you go when you die. A kingdom is a reign before it is a realm: a King exercising rule. What is at hand isn’t a place opening up but a throne being occupied, here on earth, in a man about to walk down to this river. That is why the only fit response is to turn round.
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Judea is the dry, barren land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven” where the others say “kingdom of God” — the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is the voice Isaiah foretold, crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord, and he dresses and lives like Elijah. John prepares for the coming of the LORD himself in Jesus, and repentance is how a sinner makes ready the road for the holy King.

The way of the LORD. Isaiah 40:3 announced a voice preparing the way of the LORD — God’s own name — for his coming. Matthew applies it to John preparing the way for Jesus: a staggering identification. Jesus is the LORD coming to his people.

A road for a King. “Prepare the way… make his paths straight” is the language of a royal arrival. Before a great king travelled, crews went ahead to ready the road — filling valleys, levelling hills, clearing rocks — so the procession could pass unhindered. Isaiah’s next verse says it: “Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low… and the rough places a plain” (Isaiah 40:4). But the King is no earthly monarch; it is the LORD. Isaiah 40 opens the book of comfort to a people in exile, promising a new exodus: God coming in person to lead his people home across the desert like a shepherd-king (Isaiah 40:10–11).

A watchword of hope. By Jesus’ day the verse was a watchword. The community at Qumran by the Dead Sea took these words and withdrew into the desert “to prepare the way,” sure God was about to act. So when John appears in that wilderness crying Isaiah 40:3, devout ears caught it: the King is coming — ready the road. And the roadwork is the heart: the hills of self-righteousness brought low, the valleys of despair filled with hope, crooked dealings made straight. A test: what in your life needs levelling or straightening before the King?

Elijah’s dress. John’s camel-hair garment and leather belt mark him as a prophet like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), whose return before the great day of the LORD Malachi promised (Malachi 4:5). His food fits: locusts were among the insects the law allowed Israel to eat (Leviticus 11:22), and wild honey is what the wilderness gives away. He lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anyone — which is why no one can buy him. It isn’t a costume. He lives the prophetic calling with his whole life, refusing comfort and the establishment, a sign in the wilderness that the old order is passing and something new is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People from Jerusalem, all Judea and the Jordan region go out to John and are baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. To be ready for the King, even the covenant people must humbly admit their sins and start again by grace.

Even Jews. Washings were familiar in Judaism, and later sources describe a washing for Gentiles converting to Israel’s God. John applies a washing of repentance to Jews — a radical provocation. He is saying: you need cleansing too; you are no cleaner before God by birth than any Gentile. And confession of sin was essential; the washing is pointless without the honesty it pictures.

What they confessed. We aren’t left to guess. When the crowds asked, “What then shall we do?” John named sins. To ordinary people: you keep two coats while your neighbour shivers — that tight-fisted selfishness is sin (Luke 3:11). To tax collectors: your greed, collecting more than you should (Luke 3:13). To soldiers: your extortion, false accusations, and discontent with your wages (Luke 3:14). To the religious leaders: pride, hypocrisy, and smug trust in being Abraham’s children (vv. 7–9). Behind them lay the sins the prophets exposed: cheating workers of their wages (Malachi 3:5), worship that was all lips and no heart (Isaiah 29:13), the quiet idolatry of loving money and reputation more than God. If we are honest, we meet ourselves in the list. A test: which of these sins would you need to confess?

Why the Jordan. The river wasn’t incidental. It is the water Israel crossed to enter the land: the priests stepped in, the flow stopped, and a nation walked over into its inheritance (Joshua 3). It is where Elijah struck the water with his cloak and was taken up (2 Kings 2:8–11), and where Naaman the Syrian went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kings 5:14). Entry, ascent and cleansing, all at one muddy, unimpressive river.

Starting again. And notice the direction. The people aren’t going to the temple. They are going out — out of Jerusalem and the towns to the wilderness and down to the river, leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it and coming back in through the water. That is what John’s baptism meant. He wasn’t offering another ceremony to add to their religion. He was asking Israel to start again from the beginning: to go back outside, admit they had no more claim on God than a Gentile convert, and come in by grace. That is why the establishment couldn’t bear it, and why the crowds came in thousands.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism, John calls them a brood of vipers, asks who warned them to flee the coming wrath, and demands fruit in keeping with repentance. Religious privilege is no shelter from God’s judgment; only real repentance, shown in a changed life, is.

The sharpest words for the most religious. The Pharisees and Sadducees were rivals, but John addresses them as one brood. “Vipers” recalls the serpent of Eden: children of the deceiver, poison under religious clothing. “Who warned you?” — he doubts their motives: social, political, curious, but not repentant. A baptism received without repentance is just getting wet.

Two rival parties. They could hardly have been less alike. The Pharisees were the great lay movement — their name likely means “the separated ones.” Zealous for the law, they surrounded it with a “tradition of the elders” to guard every commandment, and were scrupulous about tithing, purity and the Sabbath. They believed in the resurrection, angels, a coming judgment and Messiah. Devout and admired, they were undone by what they prized; their religion soured into the self-righteous show Jesus would expose (chapter 23). The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who ran the temple. They held the five books of Moses as binding and denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8) — worldly men who kept comfortable terms with Rome to protect their power, and who vanished when the temple fell in AD 70. Bitter rivals, yet they come to the Jordan together, and one day they will conspire together against the Lord. Nothing unites enemies like a shared threat to their religion.

The wrath to come. Their own Scriptures spoke of the Day of the LORD, when God would judge sin and set the world right: “A day of wrath… a day of distress and anguish” (Zephaniah 1:15); “the day is coming, burning like an oven” (Malachi 4:1); “who can endure the day of his coming?” (Malachi 3:2). Amos warned the complacent it would be darkness, not light (Amos 5:18–20). But the deadly assumption John shatters is that this wrath was for Gentiles and obvious sinners, and that the sons of Abraham would watch safely. The fire is for every unrepentant heart, the religious first of all — and the only shelter isn’t ancestry but repentance, and the Coming One who himself will pass through the fire for his people.

Fruit. “Bear fruit in keeping with repentance.” The picture is an orchard: a tree shows what it is by what hangs on its branches, not by its leaves. Israel was God’s vineyard, looked to for a harvest of justice (Isaiah 5:1–7). John says: don’t show me your pedigree or ceremonies; show me a changed life. Paul uses the same phrase: “performing deeds in keeping with their repentance” (Acts 26:20). But notice the order. Fruit doesn’t make a tree good; a good tree bears good fruit. John isn’t telling them to manufacture good works to earn standing — that was the Pharisees’ mistake. Real repentance always shows; a turning no one can see is no turning at all. And a branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine (John 15:5). A test: what has changed in your life because you turned to God?
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law; Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, who denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warns them not to rely on being Abraham’s children, for God can raise children for Abraham from stones, and the axe is already at the root of every tree that doesn’t bear good fruit. Being born into God’s people saves no one; saving faith always shows itself in fruit, and judgment is near for those without it.

No security by birth. Descent from Abraham was the deepest form of Jewish religious security — covenant membership by birth. John demolishes it: God could make children for Abraham from the pebbles underfoot. The covenant isn’t a biological inheritance but a gift received by faith and shown by fruit. A test: is any part of your confidence before God resting on your family or background rather than on Christ?

A pun. There is wit here English can’t show. In Hebrew and Aramaic the two words sit almost on top of each other: stones are abanim, children banim. From these stones God can raise up sons. And notice where John stands. When Israel first entered the land, Joshua had twelve men carry twelve stones up from this riverbed as a memorial for the twelve tribes, “that this may be a sign among you” (Joshua 4:6). John stands at that river and tells the sons of Abraham that God could begin the tribes again from the rocks. God has never been short of raw material; he made Adam from the ground and gave Abraham an heir from a womb as good as dead (Romans 4:19).

The axe. “Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees.” Not a gentle warning but an imminent verdict. The fruitless tree isn’t warned again; it is cut down. Grace is real, but so is the axe.

Is this salvation by works? Verse 10 can sound like it: bear fruit, or be cut down and burned. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; our works add nothing to the verdict (Ephesians 2:8–9). But the faith that justifies never stays alone. A living faith bears fruit as surely as a living tree; “faith apart from works is dead” (James 2:26). So John isn’t saying fruit earns life; he is saying fruitlessness exposes death. The barren tree is cut down not because it failed to earn its place but because its barrenness shows it was never alive. When Scripture says God “will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6), the works are evidence brought into court, not the price paid — they reveal the root; they don’t become it. We are saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. And even the fruit is grace: God must first make the tree good. An axe never turned a dead tree into a living one; that making-alive is the Coming One’s work.

parallels.desc: every tree that does not bear good fruit

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John says he baptizes with water for repentance, but the mightier One coming after him will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, and will separate wheat from chaff, gathering the wheat and burning the chaff with unquenchable fire. Jesus is both the Saviour who gives the Spirit and the Judge who will divide humanity finally, so we must come to him now.

The sign and the substance. “I baptize you with water for repentance.” The water was a sign — an outward washing picturing the inward cleansing the people sought, marking their turning as they prepared for the King. It could wet the body, not change the heart; it pointed to One who could. Ezekiel had joined the two: clean water sprinkled, and a new heart and spirit given (Ezekiel 36:25–27).

Not worthy to carry his sandals. Carrying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task. John, the greatest of the prophets, says he isn’t fit even for that. He gives the sign; Jesus gives the substance. John can lower you into the river; only Jesus can baptize you with the Spirit. A test: do you rest in an outward rite, or in the Christ it points to?

Spirit and fire. The Spirit-baptism is the great gospel promise: the Coming One pours out God’s Spirit to give new birth and to indwell and transform, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2). And the fire? Some take it as the Spirit’s refining work on believers, recalling Pentecost’s “tongues as of fire.” But the context points to judgment: the fruitless tree is “thrown into the fire” (v. 10) and the chaff burned “with unquenchable fire” (v. 12), and wheat isn’t refined with unquenchable fire. John speaks to a mixed crowd, and Messiah’s coming divides it: the repentant he baptizes with the Spirit to life; the impenitent he meets with fire. And the wheat need never dread that fire, because the Coming One would pass through it for them at the cross.

Is baptism with the Spirit a second experience that comes after conversion? Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians teach that it is: a distinct empowering, often marked by tongues, which believers should seek. They point to the disciples at Pentecost, the Samaritans (Acts 8:14–17) and the Ephesian disciples (Acts 19:1–7), who received the Spirit after believing. The more likely reading is that every believer is baptized with the Spirit at conversion: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). The episodes in Acts mark unrepeatable turning points as the gospel crossed from Jews to Samaritans to Gentiles. What Christians are told to seek is to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), not baptized again.

How does John’s baptism relate to Christian baptism? John’s looked forward to the One who was coming; Christian baptism looks back to his death and resurrection and is given in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19). That is why the disciples at Ephesus, who knew only John’s baptism, were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:3–5). Christian baptism rests on Jesus’ command, not on his own baptism, which was unique.

The threshing floor. Picture a threshing floor on a breezy hilltop. The grain is trodden until the kernels break from their husks; then the farmer tosses it into the wind with a winnowing fork. The heavy grain falls back; the light chaff blows aside. He gathers the wheat into his barn and burns the chaff. Until the Coming One acts, wheat and chaff lie mingled; the truly repentant and the merely religious stand side by side and look alike. His coming is the wind that sorts them. There are two heaps and two destinations, barn or fire, and “unquenchable” means the verdict is final. The prophets used the image: the wicked “are like chaff that the wind drives away” (Psalm 1:4). And the fork is already in his hand. The chaff isn’t bad wheat but empty husk, and the way to be found wheat isn’t to be impressive in yourself but to come to the Coming One in repentance and faith — the One who took the fire in his people’s place.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back, the chaff blew away and was burned.

parallels.desc: tongues as of fire at Pentecost

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, but John tries to stop him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” The sinless Son humbly identifies with sinners, and those most aware of their own need are often the most godly.

A long walk to a queue. “Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan.” From Nazareth to the Jordan crossings was some seventy miles, several days on foot. He walked the better part of a week to stand in a line of sinners.

The silent years. And consider what he was walking from. Luke says he was “about thirty years of age” when he began (Luke 3:23). Matthew last showed him as a small child; Luke gives one scene at twelve. Between that and this river lie some eighteen years about which Scripture says nothing — years in a workshop in a small village, with no sermons, miracles or disciples. The Son of God spent most of his earthly life doing work nobody thought worth recording, and it wasn’t wasted or mere preparation. It was obedience, part of the righteousness he is about to say he came to fulfil. A test: do you treat your ordinary, unseen work as obedience to God?

John’s struggle. “John would have prevented him” — the verb means he kept trying to stop him: not one polite objection but a struggle at the water’s edge. And his protest is theologically precise. His baptism was for repentance, and Jesus had nothing to repent of. The sinless one shouldn’t be washed by a sinner; the one who baptizes with the Spirit shouldn’t be baptized with water.

“I need to be baptized by you.” This is the man who has just called the religious leaders a brood of vipers and said he wasn’t fit to carry the Coming One’s sandals. Of all on that riverbank he had least reason to think himself unclean, and he is the one who says he needs washing. Jesus calls him the greatest born of women (11:11), and his instinct on meeting Jesus is to change places in the water. Those most conscious of their need are seldom the ones you would nominate.

Did John know him? They were relatives (Luke 1:36). Yet in John’s Gospel he says twice, “I myself did not know him” (John 1:31, 33). There is no contradiction: he means he didn’t know him as the Messiah until the promised sign came — the Spirit’s descent he is about to see.

Right premises, wrong conclusion. John’s theology is impeccable and his conclusion wrong. He rightly recognised who Jesus is, rightly understood his own baptism, rightly reasoned that the sinless one doesn’t need it — and on those premises tried to stop the Son of God doing what he came to do. A useful warning for those who reason carefully about God: right premises don’t guarantee a right conclusion about what he should do next, because he always sees more of the picture than we do. Jesus corrects him in one sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells John to allow it, “for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness”; as Jesus comes up from the water, the heavens open and he sees the Spirit of God descending like a dove and resting on him. Jesus took his place with sinners to fulfil all righteousness on their behalf, and the Father anointed him with the Spirit for his saving work.

All righteousness. “Fulfill all righteousness” is a key phrase in Matthew: Jesus came not to bypass God’s requirements but to meet them all on behalf of his people. His baptism isn’t personal repentance but solidarity. He enters the waters with sinners as their representative, identifying with those he came to save. This is what theologians call his active obedience: not only dying in our place but living the life we owed and never lived, so that what is credited to the believer is not a blank record but a kept one. A test: are you trusting Christ’s perfect obedience, or trying to present your own?

The heavens opened. The opened heavens signal that the long silence since the prophets is over. The Spirit descending like a dove echoes the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2): a new creation is beginning. At the start of Jesus’ ministry the Father, the Son and the Spirit are all present and active.

Was the Spirit not already with him? He was, fully, from the first. This child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20); the eternal Son was never for an instant without the Spirit. So the Spirit isn’t arriving where he had been absent, and Jesus doesn’t become the Son or the Christ here, as some old errors taught. What happens is twofold. First, his anointing. “Christ” means “Anointed One,” and the Father visibly anoints him to begin his public work as the promised Servant: “Behold my servant… I have put my Spirit upon him” (Isaiah 42:1; cf. Isaiah 61:1; Acts 10:38). Second, a sign for others: John tells us he knew the Messiah by seeing the Spirit descend and remain on him (John 1:32–34). And the Spirit comes to rest — to remain, not to come and go as with the prophets of old. The One on whom the Spirit settles will pour that Spirit out on all who are his (v. 11).

Does “went up from the water” show that Jesus was immersed? It fits immersion well, as does the word baptize itself, which means to dip or plunge, and this is the natural picture of a believer’s burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4). Christians who baptize by pouring or sprinkling argue that the text describes where Jesus stood, not how the water was applied. The immersion reading is the more likely. But Jesus’ baptism was unique, the anointing of the sinless Son, so it does not by itself settle who should be baptized; that rests on the command to baptize disciples (28:19).
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records John’s protest and Jesus’ reply.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice from heaven says, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” The Father declares Jesus his beloved Son and King, the Servant in whom he delights — and through faith in Christ that delight rests on all who are in him.

King and Servant. The Father’s words join two texts: Psalm 2:7, “You are my Son,” the royal psalm of the messianic King; and Isaiah 42:1, “my servant… in whom my soul delights,” the first song of the Servant who suffers. From the start the Father defines his Son as both triumphant King and obedient Servant.

Before he had done anything. “With whom I am well pleased” is spoken before Jesus has preached, healed or gone to the cross. The Father’s delight isn’t earned but given, and from that secure identity all his ministry flows.

Is it said over anyone else? Every human being is trying to hear that word from someone. We spend our lives auditioning — for a parent whose approval never quite came, for an employer, a congregation, an audience of strangers on a screen — and underneath is the ache to hear a voice we trust say: you are mine, and I am pleased with you. Matthew records that sentence said aloud over a man in a river. Does it have anything to do with us?

In the Beloved. Everything — and the link isn’t imitation but union. The Father speaks this over his Son, and the believer is in the Son. So Paul can say God “has blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6) — not accepted alongside him or for trying to be like him, but accepted in him, our life “hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). So the Spirit of the Son cries “Abba! Father!” in our hearts (Galatians 4:6), and “bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs” (Romans 8:16–17).

The exchange. At the Jordan the sinless one stepped into the place of sinners, taking a washing he didn’t need. At Golgotha he did so again, taking a judgment he didn’t deserve — the guilt, the verdict, and on the cross the silence where a voice from heaven should have been. What he gives in exchange is what was always his: sonship and the Father’s welcome. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For the frightened. If you are frightened by the winnowing fork a few verses back, notice when the Father speaks: before a single sermon or miracle. If his delight in his Son wasn’t produced by performance, his delight in those who are in his Son isn’t produced by theirs. You won’t settle it by inspecting your feelings, but by looking to the one you have come to. The way in is the way John preached: turn, and come.

Why do the Gospels word it differently? Mark and Luke report the voice as “You are my beloved Son,” addressed to Jesus; Matthew reports it as “This is my beloved Son,” announced to those watching. The Gospel writers often give the sense of words rather than a transcript, and both forms say the same thing. John the Baptist saw and heard (John 1:32–34), and whether others did, the declaration was for Jesus and for those who would follow him.

A guard. This isn’t the modern idea that God approves everyone as they are. The same chapter has an axe at the root and unquenchable fire. The word is spoken over those who are in the Beloved, and there is a door to walk through. But once through it, the verdict on your life has been announced by the only voice that finally matters — not earned, and not forfeited by a bad week. He is well pleased: not with your performance, but with his Son, and with you in him. A test: are you still auditioning for God’s approval, or resting in Christ’s?

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights
the same voice at the transfiguration

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. Matthew 3:16–17 is one of the clearest Trinitarian texts in the New Testament. The Son stands in the water; the Spirit descends upon the Son; the Father speaks from heaven. Three distinct persons, one divine act. Reformed theology has always insisted that the doctrine of the Trinity is not a late addition to Christian thought but the grammar of the gospel itself — the structure of reality that makes salvation possible.

The baptism of Jesus is a Trinitarian event. The Father approves; the Spirit empowers; the Son obeys. This pattern runs through the whole New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. The atonement is Trinitarian (the Father gave, the Son died, the Spirit regenerates); the church is Trinitarian (baptised in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit, Matt. 28:19); the Christian life is Trinitarian (praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit). The Jordan reveals the shape of everything that follows.
3.examples:
Then: John the Baptist stands in a long line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action: Moses before Joshua, Elijah before Elisha, Isaiah before the return from exile. Each was a voice, not the Word; each pointed away from himself. John is the culmination of this pattern — the last and greatest of the preparers. His greatness lay precisely in his self-effacement: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher, teacher, and leader stands in John’s tradition: making straight the way, getting out of the way.

Now: The Father’s declaration over Jesus at the baptism — This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — is the word every human being is searching for. We spend our lives seeking approval: from parents, employers, social media, achievement. The gospel announces that in Christ, the deepest possible approval has already been given — not because of what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done. The restless search for significance ends not in achievement but in adoption: we are accepted in the Beloved. That is the word the Father spoke at the Jordan, and it is addressed to everyone who is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the axis on which the Gospel turns. The Spirit who descended at the baptism immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness — not as abandonment but as commission. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where God’s people failed at every test. Jesus succeeds at every one, and he does it using the same weapon available to Israel and to us: the written Word of God. Three times the devil attacks; three times Jesus answers with Deuteronomy. The true Israel passes where the nation failed.

Each temptation targets a specific aspect of Jesus’ identity and mission. Turn stones to bread: use divine power for personal comfort. Throw yourself from the temple: leverage God’s promises for public spectacle. Bow to me: gain the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is a shortcut past suffering to glory — and Jesus refuses every one. There is no crown without the cross, no glory without the grave, no kingdom without Calvary. Satan offers the destination without the path; Jesus insists on the path.

Then the ministry begins — in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isa. 9:1), the region of mixed ethnicity and questionable reputation, the last place a respectable rabbi would choose as his base. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The light does not go to the well-lit; it goes to the dark. And the first disciples he calls are working men with nets and boats — not scribes with scrolls. The kingdom of heaven is staffed from the margins, then and now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the three temptations echo Israel's great failures — bread, testing God, idolatry. But where Israel fell, Jesus stands. He defeats each temptation not by miraculous power but by the word of God alone, quoting Deuteronomy three times. The temptations are not trivial: they are the offer of the kingdom by a shortcut — bread without suffering, glory without the cross, dominion without death. And he overcomes not merely as our example but as our champion — the last Adam and true Israel, whose perfect obedience is reckoned to all who are his, so that we now resist temptation not to win God's favor but from within the victory he has already won for us. Two things the summary passes over. Verse 2's hunger is the ground of the first temptation — the devil does not waste his best offer on a man with full hands, and he waits for the sixth week. And verse 11 is not the end of the matter: Luke adds that the devil departed "until an opportune time" (Lk. 4:13), and Matthew shows where those times came. At Caesarea Philippi, when Peter says the suffering shall never happen, Jesus answers with the same words he used here — "Get behind me, Satan" (16:23) — because it is the same offer, the crown without the cross, arriving from a friend. And at Golgotha the passers-by shout "if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross" (27:40), which is the identical formula the devil used twice in this wilderness (vv. 3, 6). The temptation that opens the ministry is the temptation that closes it. Note also the quiet irony of the angels: the devil had proposed a scenario in which angels would catch him spectacularly before a temple crowd, and Jesus refused — so they come instead in an empty desert with nobody watching, and the verb is an imperfect (they kept ministering) of the ordinary word for waiting at table. What he would not seize, he was given.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation of Jesus is not merely a test of personal willpower but a cosmic conflict at the hinge of redemptive history. The devil who succeeded in Eden now faces the second Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus is revealed as the true Israel — obedient where the nation failed — and the true Adam — resisting the serpent where the first man did not. His weapon is the word of God alone: not angelic power, not divine fiat, but the Scripture he has internalized and believes. This models the Christian's resource in temptation: not mystical experience but the word of God believed and obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: The devil's three temptations all contain a kernel of legitimate desire: food is not evil, protection is real, authority over the nations is Jesus's ultimate inheritance. The temptation is in the shortcut — get the good thing the wrong way, on the wrong timetable, from the wrong source. This is how temptation almost always works: it offers real goods through illegitimate means. Jesus refuses not because the ends are bad but because the path bypasses the Father's will and the cross's necessity.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, and after fasting forty days and nights he is hungry. God appointed this testing of his Son, and Jesus faced real temptation in real weakness — so he can help us in ours.

Led by the Spirit. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness — not away from God’s will but deeper into it. The temptation isn’t an accident or ambush but an appointed trial. Forty days and nights echo Moses on Sinai (Exodus 34:28), Elijah’s journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), and Israel’s forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). And “he was hungry” — genuinely, after six weeks without food. The devil doesn’t waste his offer on someone who has everything; he waits for the moment of need.

Does God tempt? “Led up by the Spirit… to be tempted by the devil.” Did God arrange for his Son to be tempted? What then of “lead us not into temptation” (6:13), or James’s statement that God tempts no one (James 1:13)? The Greek word does double duty: it covers both testing and tempting, where English needs two words. God tests; he never tempts. The difference is the intention. A test aims to prove and strengthen; a temptation aims to break. The same event can be both, aimed at one man from two directions — as here. The Spirit leads him out to be proved; the devil comes to destroy him. Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant the same act for good (Genesis 50:20). God stood behind the testing, the enemy supplied the temptation, and the Son came through.

Could Jesus have sinned? Some answer yes: if he could not, they argue, his temptation was not real. The historic answer of the church is no: Jesus is one person, the eternal Son, and God cannot sin (James 1:13). The second is the more likely. But it does not make the temptation unreal. Jesus felt its full pull in his human nature, and because he never yielded, he felt it longer and harder than anyone who gives in. The soldier who never surrenders is the one who knows the full force of the attack. That is why he can sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and why his victory can be counted for us.

The desert after the blessing. The wilderness wasn’t a wrong turning. He didn’t wander there through carelessness or sin; he was led there immediately after the best moment of his life — the water, the voice, the open heaven. The desert doesn’t only follow failure. Sometimes it follows blessing and is the appointed next thing.

For those in a dry stretch. If that is where you are — prayers that seem to go nowhere, loss or waiting with no visible end — take three things. It isn’t necessarily discipline; the Spirit sometimes leads his own into hard country on purpose. It has a limit: forty days, and Matthew tells you at once that it ended. And you aren’t alone in it, because the One who went through this country came out, and “is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). The wilderness is where the enemy expects to finish you; in God’s hands it is often where you are being made. A test: are you treating your hard season as abandonment or as God’s training?
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls Moses on the mountain and Israel’s forty years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: tempted as we are, yet without sin

verseByVerse.quote: And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tempter urges Jesus, if he is the Son of God, to turn stones into bread, but Jesus answers from Scripture that man lives not by bread alone but by every word from God’s mouth. Jesus, the true Israel, trusted his Father’s word and provision rather than serving himself — and his obedience counts for us and teaches us how to resist.

The “if.” The “if” isn’t genuine doubt; the devil knows who Jesus is. It is a provocation: use your power for your own comfort. There is nothing wrong with bread, or with Jesus’ power; he will later multiply loaves for thousands (14:19). The poison is in the suggestion: prove your sonship by serving yourself, take relief at my prompting, step out from under your Father’s hand and timing.

Why stay hungry? How do we know it was the Father’s will for him to stay hungry? The Spirit had just led him there on purpose (v. 1); the hunger was appointed. And Jesus shows how he reads the moment by the text he chooses. Deuteronomy 8 is Moses looking back over forty years and explaining why God led Israel the hard way: “that he might humble you, testing you… And he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna… that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone” (Deuteronomy 8:2–3). God emptied their hands, then sent bread from heaven to be gathered each morning in trust, to wean them off the lie that life is secured by what we can supply ourselves. By choosing that verse, Jesus names his own situation: this is a God-ordained hunger, and the faithful answer is trust, not self-supply.

The true Israel. Israel mostly failed that lesson, grumbling and demanding bread on its own terms (Exodus 16; Numbers 11). Jesus is the true Son, called out of Egypt (2:15), reliving their test — forty days for their forty years. Where Israel said in effect, “Give us bread or we die,” he says: my life rests not on bread I can conjure but on every word from my Father’s mouth — including his word that I be here, wait, and trust.

Ours by grace. Adam was tempted in a garden where every tree was good, and fell; Israel was tested in the wilderness, and fell; Jesus, starving and alone in a harsher wilderness, was tempted and prevailed. He is the last Adam and the true Israel, keeping the covenant we broke, as our representative. His victory isn’t merely admirable; it is counted to us. And because he lives in us by his Spirit, his way becomes ours: when tempted, we resist not by willpower but with “it is written,” trusting the Father’s word.
