The order is everything: we don’t climb to God’s acceptance by fighting temptation like Jesus; we fight because in him we are already accepted, and never alone (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15). A test: when you are under pressure, do you reach for God’s word or for a quick way to serve yourself?

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, 'He will command his angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and, quoting Psalm 91, urges him to throw himself down so that angels will catch him; Jesus answers, “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.” Genuine faith trusts God’s promises without demanding that he prove himself on our terms.

Scripture as bait. The second temptation is subtler: the devil quotes Scripture. Psalm 91:11–12 promises angelic protection to one who trusts God — though the devil leaves out the line “to guard you in all your ways.” The temptation is to force God’s hand: to manufacture a crisis requiring divine rescue, proving sonship by spectacle rather than obedience. A leap from the temple would have drawn a crowd and commanded instant recognition. But it would have been faith demanding proof rather than resting in promise. The devil can quote the Bible accurately and use it to tempt; knowing a text isn’t submitting to its meaning.

Massah. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16, which in full says, “You shall not put the LORD your God to the test, as you tested him at Massah.” At Massah (Exodus 17:1–7), Israel had no water, and instead of trusting the God who had just split the sea and sent manna, they turned on Moses: “Is the LORD among us or not?” They demanded God prove himself on the spot, on their terms, and the place was named “testing,” a byword for cornering God (Psalm 95:8–9). The devil invites Jesus to do the same — throw himself down and make the Father send angels, a staged emergency to force a rescue. Massah again, wrapped in a Bible verse.

Unbelief dressed as faith. But notice the twist. Israel tested God from open unbelief. The devil dresses the same sin as daring faith: “You trust your Father? Prove it — jump, and let him catch you!” Jesus sees through it. A faith that must have a spectacle isn’t faith but presumption; a trust that demands proof has already stopped trusting. The weak, starving Son trusts the promise without forcing it — what Israel, with full stomachs and water from the rock, wouldn’t do.

Don’t test God. First, praise: where Israel failed this test, and we still do, the true Israel stood firm, and his trust is counted ours. Then a lesson: beware of testing God. We do it when we treat his promises as levers, manufacturing a crisis and calling our recklessness faith — stopping prescribed medicine and announcing we are “trusting God to heal,” or making a rash financial leap and assuming he must catch us. That isn’t faith resting in God but presumption dictating to him. Real faith uses the means God provides and waits on him without demanding proof of his love on cue. A test: are you using God’s promises to excuse your own recklessness?

But doesn’t God invite us to test him, as in Malachi 3:10, “put me to the test”? He does, and that is the difference. Testing God is sin when we set the terms and demand proof of our own choosing; it is faith when we take God at his word where he himself has invited it. Gideon’s fleece (Judges 6:36–40) was a concession to a fearful man, not a pattern for guidance.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall. The devil quotes Scripture but cuts it short.

parallels.desc: Israel tests the LORD at Massah

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil shows Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and offers them all if he will bow down and worship him, but Jesus commands, “Be gone, Satan!” and answers that God alone is to be worshipped and served. Jesus refused to gain his kingdom by a shortcut that bypassed the cross, and we too must worship God alone, whatever is offered.

The escalation. The temptations widen: from personal need (bread), to public recognition (the temple), to world dominion (the kingdoms). The devil climbs toward what Jesus actually came to possess.

How was it shown? No mountain on earth shows all the kingdoms of the world. Christians have answered in three ways: that it was bodily throughout, Satan being a spirit of real power (compare Acts 8:39; Ezekiel 8:3); that it was a vision shown to the mind, as prophets were shown what eyes couldn’t see; or a mixture. Matthew doesn’t say, and nothing hangs on it. A temptation presented to the imagination isn’t a lesser temptation; most of ours come that way, and they are strong enough to ruin us. What matters is that he came with real bait, and the Son of God said no.

The kingdom without the cross. The offer is staggering: everything he came to win, for one act of worship — authority without Gethsemane, inheritance without suffering. The devil could offer “all these” because he has real, though temporary and limited, power in this age (John 12:31; 2 Corinthians 4:4). Jesus doesn’t dispute the offer’s reality; he refuses its terms. “Be gone, Satan!” The worship of God alone isn’t negotiable for any reward.

He won the right way. Jesus would inherit the nations; the Father had promised, “I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). But he wouldn’t take them from the devil’s hand on the devil’s terms. He chose Gethsemane over the easy throne. And he won: by the cross and the empty tomb he could stand on another mountain and say, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (28:18). He gained the kingdoms Satan dangled, but rightly, and for us. The world had a rightful King who couldn’t be bought.

Our version. This temptation comes to us in ordinary disguises, and underneath it is always a question of worship: the prize you long for, offered for a small bow to something other than God. The promotion is yours if you fudge the figures. The comfort, security or applause you crave can be had if you quietly serve money, status or self, and give God the leftovers. Satan shows you the kingdoms and hides the bill. Answer as Jesus did: refuse the shortcut, worship God alone, and trust that his costly road is the only one to a kingdom that lasts; “a disciple is not above his teacher” (10:24). And we can say our own “be gone” as people joined to the Victor, “more than conquerors” in him (Romans 8:37). A test: what shortcut are you being offered that would require you to bow to something other than God?
verseByVerse.note: “Satan” means adversary.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil leaves Jesus, and angels come and minister to him. Jesus’ obedience was vindicated by his Father’s care — what he refused to seize, he was given — though the devil would return with the same temptation at the cross.

Until an opportune time. Luke adds that the devil “departed from him until an opportune time” (Luke 4:13): a withdrawal, not a surrender. And Matthew shows where the opportune times came. At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus speaks of suffering, Peter rebukes him — “This shall never happen to you” — and Jesus answers, “Get behind me, Satan!” (16:23). The same offer again, the crown without the cross, now from the mouth of his closest friend.

The same formula at the cross. Twice here the devil began, “If you are the Son of God…” And at the cross the passers-by say, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (27:40). The same formula and logic: prove it by rescuing yourself, take the shortcut. The temptation that opened his ministry closes it, shouted by a crowd instead of whispered by a spirit. He refused it in the desert with an empty stomach, and on the cross with nails through his hands. A test: where is the voice that says “If you are really God’s child, prove it” speaking to you?

The angels came anyway. There is a deliberate irony. The devil proposed a scene in which angels would catch him spectacularly before a temple crowd. Jesus refused. Now they come anyway — quietly, in an empty wilderness, with no one watching, to a man too weak to stand. The verb means they kept on serving, the ordinary word for waiting at table, and very likely it means what it sounds like. He refused to make bread for himself, and the Father sent others to feed him — as an angel fed Elijah in his exhaustion (1 Kings 19:5–7).

Given, not seized. That is the pattern: what he wouldn’t seize, he was given — not on the terms offered, not on the timetable suggested, not before an audience, but given. Obedience is vindicated, though seldom on our schedule.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — The Beginning of Ministry in Galilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After John's arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about light dawning in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He begins preaching the same message as John — "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" — and immediately calls his first disciples: Peter, Andrew, James, and John. They leave their nets and their father without delay and follow him. Matthew concludes with a summary of Jesus's ministry: teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction, drawing crowds from all of Syria and the surrounding regions. Three details more. The word for John's arrest (v. 12) is paradidomi, to be handed over — not the ordinary word for a legal arrest, but the very verb Matthew will use of Jesus again and again (17:22; 20:18; 26:2), and of what Judas, the council and Pilate each do. The forerunner goes before him in this too. And "he withdrew" is anachoreo, a favourite of Matthew's for keeping to a timetable his enemies are not setting (2:14, 22; 12:15; 14:13; 15:21) — never presented as cowardice. Capernaum has been excavated: a fishing village of perhaps 1,500 on the Via Maris, with a customs house (Matthew's own booth was there, 9:9) and a small garrison (hence the centurion of ch. 8). He based himself among tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and foreigners passing through. And Zebulun and Naphtali were not chosen at random by Isaiah: they were the first tribes deported, carried off by Tiglath-Pileser in 733 BC (2 Kgs. 15:29), a decade before Samaria fell. They went into the dark first — which is exactly why Isaiah 9:1 promises the light dawns there first. God begins the repair at the place that broke earliest.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus's settlement in Galilee of the Gentiles fulfills Isaiah 9:1–2: the regions most despised in Israel — the northern territories given first to Assyrian darkness — receive the first light of the kingdom. This is the pattern of the kingdom: light to the edges, hope to the marginalized, the first shall be last and the last first. The calling of the disciples is not recruitment but sovereign summons: "Follow me" is a command, not an invitation to consider. Their immediate response models discipleship — not eventual obedience after weighing options, but the abandonment of everything for the one who calls.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples left their nets immediately. They left their boats. James and John left their father. The commentaries note what Matthew stresses: the immediacy and totality of their response. Jesus did not give them time to consult, calculate, or negotiate terms. He called; they followed. This is the New Testament pattern of conversion — not gradual warming to the idea of Jesus but the decisive moment of abandonment and allegiance. The question the passage presses: what are your nets? What would obedience cost you to leave behind?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus hears that John has been handed over, he withdraws to Galilee, leaves Nazareth, and settles in Capernaum by the sea in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. Jesus begins his public ministry on his Father’s timetable, among ordinary and overlooked people.

Handed over. Matthew’s word for John’s arrest isn’t casual. It means “handed over,” “delivered up” — the word Matthew will use again and again of Jesus: “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men” (17:22); “delivered over to the chief priests” (20:18); “delivered up to be crucified” (26:2). The forerunner goes ahead of him in this too, and the same verb will follow Jesus to the cross.

Withdrew. “He withdrew” is a favourite of Matthew’s, used of Joseph taking the child to Egypt (2:14) and turning aside to Galilee (2:22), and later of Jesus moving away from danger (12:15; 14:13; 15:21). It is never cowardice. It is a man whose hour hasn’t yet come, keeping a timetable his enemies don’t set.

Capernaum. He left Nazareth — Luke tells us the town had tried to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:29) — and settled in Capernaum. Excavations show it wasn’t much: a fishing town of perhaps a thousand or so on the north shore. But it lay near the great trade road, with a customs post — Matthew’s own tax booth was likely there (9:9) — and a centurion turns up in chapter 8. A synagogue stands on the site, and beneath a later church lies a first-century house venerated very early as Peter’s.

Among ordinary people. That is where the Son of God based himself: not Jerusalem with its temple, not even a large town, but a working village by a trade road, full of the people the respectable wouldn’t have chosen — tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and passing foreigners. He made his home among the kind of people he came to save. A test: are you willing to make your life among the people Christ came for, not just the respectable?
verseByVerse.note: Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, among the first to fall to Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ move fulfils Isaiah’s word about the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, “Galilee of the Gentiles.” God begins his work of restoration in the very place that was first into the dark, and his light is set where the nations pass.

First into the dark. Zebulun and Naphtali weren’t chosen at random. Their land lay furthest north, on the exposed frontier, and they were the first taken. When the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser came in 733 BC, Scripture records that he captured “Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried the people captive to Assyria” (2 Kings 15:29). They went into the dark first, a decade before Samaria fell and more than a century before Jerusalem.

The reversal. That is the point of Isaiah’s sentence: “In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1). The reversal is deliberate and specific: the ground first into darkness is where the light dawns first. Seven centuries later, a man from Nazareth moves to that very shoreline to begin.

Galilee of the Gentiles. Even in Isaiah’s day the north was ethnically mixed, and Judeans looked down on it. That the Messiah brings his first ministry to this mixed region anticipates the commission to all nations (28:19). And “the way of the sea” was a real road, the great highway from Egypt through Galilee to Damascus and the East, on which the nations travelled. God didn’t plant the light in a hidden valley but by the roadside of the world, where every people would see it.

Where the repair begins. This isn’t only geography. God’s habit is to begin the repair at the place that broke first. The part of a life that went wrong earliest, has been dark longest and would be nobody’s choice for a starting point is where he has a documented preference for starting. A test: what part of your life have you assumed is too dark for God to begin with?
verseByVerse.note: “Galilee of the Gentiles”: the region had a mixed population, looked down on by Judeans.

verseByVerse.quote: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s promise is fulfilled: the people in darkness have seen a great light, and on those in the shadow of death a light has dawned. Jesus is that light — not merely showing our lost condition but ending it, bringing life where there was death.

A dawn. Isaiah 9:2, one of the great Old Testament promises, is fulfilled not in a Jerusalem spectacle but in a Galilean teacher by a lake. “Darkness” and “shadow of death” aren’t merely metaphors for ignorance; they describe the human condition before God — estranged, condemned, without hope. The great light isn’t an idea or a movement but a Person. And the image is sunrise: total, irreversible, making everything visible at once. In Isaiah’s day the dawn was first the relief after the Assyrian night; in Jesus the true Sun rises over a deeper darkness, the night of sin and death, for the whole world.

Light that saves. A lamp only shows you the room; this Light saves. It doesn’t merely expose the shadow of death; it breaks it. Malachi promised that “the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2), and Zechariah sang that “the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1:78–79). This light warms the frozen and heals the wounded, speaking life into the dead as God once spoke a world from nothing: “Let light shine out of darkness,” who “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

The night is over. To sit in darkness is to be lost and condemned. But when this Sun rises on a soul, the night doesn’t merely become visible — it is over. That is what dawned on Galilee, and what can dawn on you. A test: have you come out of darkness into Christ’s light, or are you still sitting in the shadow?

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on Jesus preaches, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” In Jesus, God’s saving reign has truly arrived, though its full glory awaits his return, and it calls everyone to turn from sin to him.

The same words, a new moment. Jesus’ first message is John’s (3:2), but the moment has changed: John announced the Coming One; Jesus announces the kingdom’s arrival in his own person. “From that time” marks a turning point.

The hope they had. When a Jew heard “kingdom,” his heart leapt to an old hope: God would act in power, throw off Rome, restore David’s throne, regather his people, judge the wicked and reign in peace from Zion. It was rooted in the prophets — “Your God reigns” (Isaiah 52:7), the everlasting dominion given to the Son of Man (Daniel 7:13–14), the kingdom never destroyed (Daniel 2:44). But for most it was an earthly, national dream: a Messiah on a warhorse.

Fulfilled and transformed. Jesus takes up that hope and fulfils and transforms it. The kingdom he brings is God’s saving reign breaking into history in himself — but it comes first against sin, Satan and death, not Rome; by a cross, not a sword; quietly, like a buried seed, before it fills the earth. “If it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (12:28). It is present in him, yet its full, visible glory awaits his return. It asks not for revolution but repentance.

Repent. Not merely feeling sorry, nor doing penance, but a turning of mind and heart from sin and self to God, shown in a changed life (3:8). Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning (Mark 1:15): we turn from sin as we turn to Christ. It is a command and also a gift (Acts 11:18), and the shape of the whole Christian life. A test: is there a sin you are still refusing to turn from?

What does “at hand” mean? The word means “has drawn near,” and it has been read in a few ways: as a kingdom merely soon to come, as one that has actually arrived in Jesus, or, best, as both at once. The historic Reformed reading is exactly this “already and not yet”: in Christ’s first coming the kingdom has truly and powerfully arrived, present now and advancing through the gospel, the Spirit and the church, and it will be consummated only when the King returns. Here this reading parts, in love, from the dispensational understanding many brothers and sisters hold. On that view, Jesus offered Israel a literal, earthly, Davidic kingdom; when the nation’s leaders refused him it was postponed, the church age came in as an unforeseen interval, and the promised reign will be set up in a future thousand-year kingdom centred on Israel and Jerusalem. The Reformed conviction is different: the kingdom was not postponed but inaugurated; the one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, is the true Israel; and the Old Testament promises of throne and land are not shelved but fulfilled in Christ and, at last, in the new heavens and new earth. We hold this clearly and humbly, remembering what we share with those who differ: that Christ is King, that his promises are sure, and that he is coming again in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls the fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,” and immediately they leave their nets and follow him. Christ calls ordinary people to follow him at real cost, and he himself makes them what they couldn’t make themselves.

An ordinary scene. Two working men casting a net, ankle-deep in routine. The kingdom doesn’t come through unusual people in unusual places; it breaks into the ordinary and calls it to something greater.

The call. “Follow me” is the whole call — no exam, no conditions. “I will make you fishers of men” promises transformation through following, not before it: Jesus makes them what they can’t make themselves; their part is to come. And they respond “immediately” — not after settling their affairs, but at once. The nets were their livelihood and identity, and they left them. Following Christ has always cost something real.

Had they met him before? John tells us that Andrew and Peter had already met Jesus at the Jordan (John 1:35–42). This is not their first encounter but the call to leave their work and follow him for good. Their obedience was still costly, but it was not blind.

Fishers of men. In the prophets, fishing for men meant gathering them for judgment: “I am sending for many fishers, declares the LORD, and they shall catch them” (Jeremiah 16:16; cf. Amos 4:2). Jesus turns the image inside out. These men will gather people not to judgment but out of it, drawing them from the waters of death into the kingdom.

Following today. What does following look like for us? Peter and Andrew left their nets, but not everyone Jesus called did; many followed him where they were. So following is less about which job you leave than about who owns your life: Jesus as Lord of the boat you are in — your work, your family, your ordinary days. It means hearing his voice in his Word and obeying; turning from sin and trusting him afresh each morning; taking up your cross daily (Luke 9:23) — dying to self-rule for his sake; and abiding in him as a branch in the vine, for “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). And it means being made a fisher of men, an ordinary person through whom he draws others to himself.

For the stumbling follower. If you wonder whether you are doing it well, hear this. Following is a direction, not a flawless performance. These men argued about greatness, slept when he needed them, scattered at his arrest, and Peter denied him — yet they were still following, and Jesus restored Peter and made him a rock. “I will make you”: he does the making; you do the coming. If your heart is turned toward him, grieving sin, longing to obey and rising after every fall, you are following. Your standing rests not on the quality of your following but on the One you follow, “who began a good work in you” and “will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). A test: is Jesus Lord of your ordinary working day, or only your Sundays?
verseByVerse.note: A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls James and John, who are mending nets in the boat with their father Zebedee, and immediately they leave the boat and their father and follow him. Christ’s call takes priority even over family, and though his call is the same for all, the road he gives each disciple is his to choose.

Leaving their father. James and John left not only their nets but their father — a detail that sharpens the cost. Zebedee wasn’t abandoned carelessly; he had hired servants (Mark 1:20). But the call of Jesus takes priority over family obligation, the father-son bond that underpinned ancient society. “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (10:37). The kingdom doesn’t abolish family; it reorders priorities.

For the family’s good. And though Christ must come before family, he comes for the family’s good too. The son who loves Jesus first becomes a truer son; love rooted in God receives others as gifts rather than clutching them as idols. Often the Lord uses the one who follows to draw others home: Zebedee’s own wife later followed Jesus to the cross (27:56), and the gospel swept through whole households (Acts 16:31). Sometimes following him brings division (10:34–36), yet even then the disciple holds out to his family the one thing of eternal worth. A test: does anyone in your family come before Christ in your heart?

Mending. They were “mending their nets,” and the verb means to put right, restore to working order, make fit for use. It is the word Paul uses for restoring a brother caught in sin (Galatians 6:1) and for a church united (1 Corinthians 1:10), and Hebrews prays that God will “equip you with everything good that you may do his will” (Hebrews 13:21). They were making torn things fit for use when he called them to do it to people for the rest of their lives.

Two roads. Two brothers: same boat, same father, same trade, called the same morning with the same words. James was the first of the twelve to be killed: Herod “killed James the brother of John with the sword” (Acts 12:2), around AD 44. John, by tradition, was the last to die, living to old age, long enough to write his Gospel, letters and Revelation. One call, two roads that could hardly have been less alike. And when Peter later asked about John, “Lord, what about this man?”, the answer was, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!” (John 21:21–22). The call is identical; the road never is. No one who obeys is told in advance which road he will get, and comparing your road with another Christian’s is a question the Lord has already declined to answer. A test: are you comparing your path with someone else’s instead of simply following?

verseByVerse.quote: And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes throughout Galilee teaching in the synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease, and his fame spreads through Syria as all kinds of sufferers are brought and healed. Jesus’ words and works together show that God’s kingdom has come in him, and his healings are a foretaste of the full healing to come.

Teacher, herald, healer. Matthew’s first summary presents Jesus in three roles at once: teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease. These aren’t separate departments; teaching explains, proclamation announces, healing demonstrates. Word and deed are inseparable in him. And his fame spreading to “all Syria” signals what chapter 28 makes explicit: the kingdom can’t be contained within Israel’s borders.

What the healings meant. They were never mere kindness, though they were kind. First, they were the King’s credentials. Isaiah foretold that when God came to save, “the eyes of the blind shall be opened… then shall the lame man leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:5–6); when John later asked, “Are you the one?”, Jesus pointed to these works (11:4–5). Second, they were a window into a deeper healing. Sickness is a bitter fruit of the fall, and in mending bodies Jesus showed what he came to do for the soul: forgive and make whole. “With his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Disease and demons. Matthew lists disease and demonic oppression side by side, keeping them distinct; this isn’t an ancient way of describing illness. Open demonic activity clusters around Christ’s coming, as the powers of darkness resisted the kingdom. Christians today face real spiritual opposition, but needn’t fear it; they belong to the One who drove the demons out.

What about healing now? We don’t, as a rule, see such healing in the church today. The great tide of miracles clustered around Jesus and his apostles to authenticate the gospel once for all; we aren’t promised that abundance, and should be wary of anyone who guarantees it. Yet God remains free to heal, and does as he wills in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15). And these healings were the firstfruits of a coming world, the future breaking into the present. A day is coming when God “will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Revelation 21:4). Every blind eye Jesus opened was a crack of that dawn. For the believer, healing is never finally denied, only delayed, and the empty tomb makes it certain. A test: in your suffering, are you looking forward to the healing Christ has promised?
verseByVerse.note: Syria was the Roman province to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great crowds follow Jesus from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan. Many are drawn to Jesus, but being near him is not the same as truly following him at cost.

The whole region. The five regions — Galilee; the Decapolis, a league of Greek cities mostly east of the Jordan; Jerusalem; Judea; and beyond the Jordan — span the land of Israel and its neighbours. Jesus’ ministry drew an immediate response from everywhere.

Two kinds of following. The crowds “followed” — the same word used of the disciples, though the crowds will prove less committed. The crowds want healing and teaching; the disciples have left everything. Both are drawn to Jesus, differently, and Matthew spends the rest of his Gospel exploring the difference.

Which crowd? So ask plainly which you are in, because the two look identical from outside. Both are near Jesus and enthusiastic, and both would have said they were following him. The difference isn’t intensity of feeling but what happens when following costs something. The crowd came for what Jesus gave and went home with it. The disciples came for Jesus and left the boats behind. So the useful question isn’t whether you feel strongly about Christ but whether he has ever cost you anything you didn’t want to give — an ambition laid down, money given, a relationship ended, a habit surrendered, a reputation, an evening you would rather have kept. If the honest answer is nothing at all, sit with that. It is possible to enjoy Jesus enormously and never once have obeyed him.

Not a demand to prove yourself. But don’t read that as a demand to prove yourself; he said, “I will make you.” The making is his work; the coming is ours. If the question makes you uneasy, that unease is itself a good sign — the crowds weren’t troubled by it at all. The remedy isn’t to whip up more commitment but to go back to the shoreline where the call was given and answer it again today, in whatever the next costly thing turns out to be. A test: what is the next costly step of obedience Christ is asking of you?
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

4.theology:
Active Obedience and the Imputed Righteousness of Christ. The temptation narrative is crucial to the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness. Jesus does not merely die for our sins (removing the guilt of our disobedience); he also lives in perfect obedience (providing the positive righteousness that we lack). This is called his active obedience — the life of perfect faithfulness to the Father from baptism to cross.

At each point of testing in the wilderness, Jesus does what Adam failed to do in the garden and what Israel failed to do in the desert: he trusts God’s word over his own need, refuses to demand signs, and worships God alone. This perfect obedience is credited to everyone who trusts in him. We are justified not only by the forgiveness of our sins through his death but by the clothing of his righteousness through his life. The temptation narrative is the biography of our justification — the record of the obedience that is now ours by faith.
4.examples:
Then: Israel’s forty years in the wilderness is the extended backstory of Jesus’ forty days. Every test Jesus faces has a corresponding failure in Israel’s wilderness narrative: bread (the manna crisis, Exod. 16), testing God (Massah, Exod. 17), worship (the golden calf, Exod. 32). Jesus passes where Israel failed, using the very Scriptures that Israel was given at Sinai. He is the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who finally does what the nation was always called to do.

Now: Every temptation we face follows one of Satan’s three patterns: use what you have for immediate gratification (stones to bread), demand that God prove himself (test the promise), or compromise your worship for immediate reward (kingdoms without the cross). Jesus’ answers are our weapons too: It is written. The Scripture that armed the Son of God in his temptation is the same Scripture available to every believer in theirs. The difference between victory and defeat in temptation is often simply whether we know the word well enough to wield it in the moment.

5.title: The New Law from the Mountain
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. <sup>2</sup>And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: <sup>3</sup>“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>4</sup>“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. <sup>5</sup>“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. <sup>6</sup>“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. <sup>7</sup>“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. <sup>8</sup>“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <sup>9</sup>“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. <sup>10</sup>“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>11</sup>“Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. <sup>12</sup>Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. <sup>13</sup>“You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. <sup>14</sup>“You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. <sup>17</sup>“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. <sup>18</sup>For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. <sup>19</sup>Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <sup>20</sup>For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>21</sup>“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ <sup>22</sup>But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the hell of fire. <sup>23</sup>So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, <sup>24</sup>leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. <sup>25</sup>Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. <sup>26</sup>Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny. <sup>27</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ <sup>28</sup>But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <sup>29</sup>If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. <sup>30</sup>And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. <sup>31</sup>“It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ <sup>32</sup>But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. <sup>33</sup>“Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn.’ <sup>34</sup>But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, <sup>35</sup>or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. <sup>36</sup>And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. <sup>37</sup>Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil. <sup>38</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ <sup>39</sup>But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. <sup>40</sup>And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. <sup>41</sup>And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. <sup>42</sup>Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. <sup>43</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ <sup>44</sup>But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, <sup>45</sup>so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. <sup>46</sup>For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? <sup>47</sup>And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? <sup>48</sup>You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.overview:
Jesus goes up on a mountain to teach — and every Jewish reader of Matthew’s Gospel would have heard the echo: Moses went up on Sinai. But this is not a repetition; it is a surpassing. Moses received the law and gave it; Jesus gives the law with his own authority: But I say to you. No prophet ever spoke like this. The prophets said “thus says the LORD”; Jesus says “I say.” He does not claim to relay a message from God; he speaks as God.

The Beatitudes are the charter of the kingdom — and they invert every human expectation of what blessed looks like. Poor in spirit, not rich in confidence. Mourning, not celebrating. Meek, not powerful. Persecuted, not applauded. The kingdom of heaven belongs to people the world dismisses. This is not a programme for self-improvement; it is a description of those who have been broken of self-sufficiency and have learned to receive everything from God’s hand. The Beatitudes describe Jesus perfectly — and they describe every person who has been conformed to his image.

The antitheses (“You have heard… but I say”) press the law deeper than the scribal tradition imagined. It is not enough not to murder; the anger that murders in the heart is already culpable. Not enough not to commit adultery; the lust that adultery in the imagination is already a violation. The law reaches inward. And this inward reach is not only a demand; it is a diagnosis. No one can meet the standard of verse 48 — “be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect” — by their own effort. The Sermon on the Mount is the X-ray that shows us the fracture and sends us to the only Physician who can heal it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Beatitudes and the Call to Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes up the mountain — deliberately evoking Sinai, where Moses received the law — and sits to teach, the posture of a Jewish rabbi. His first words are the Beatitudes: nine declarations of blessedness that systematically invert the world's value system. The poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry — these are not character traits to develop but descriptions of those who know their need before God. The section closes with the salt and light metaphors: disciples are to be world-preserving and world-illuminating, not by withdrawal but by visible, costly presence. Two structural things govern this whole section and are set out at length in the verse-by-verse. First, "blessed" is not a wish. Makarios is a flat declaration about how things stand, not a hope that things go well — and it does not mean "happy" in the modern sense, since half the people described are mourning, starving or being driven out. It is the word the Psalter opens with (Ps. 1:1). Second, the eight are one argument, sealed at both ends. Verse 3 and verse 10 share the same six words — "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" — and the bracket is in the tense as well as the wording: v. 3 is present, vv. 4-9 are all future (shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called), and v. 10 returns to the present. Present, six futures, present. And the order is not random: the first four describe a person's need (bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving) and the second four describe what comes out of a person met in that need (merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and consequently hated). Nobody arrives at the second four by trying; they are what the first four turn into. Individual notes: "poor" is ptochos, a beggar who crouches, not penes the working poor; "mourn" is pentheo, the word for grieving the dead; Moses is Scripture's own definition of meekness (Num. 12:3), which settles that it cannot mean timidity; "satisfied" is chortazo, the animal-feeding word, fed until you stop; verse 8 answers the temple question of Psalm 24:3-4 and then promises more than David dared write; and "peacemakers" is eirenopoios, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, where the making is the point — peacekeeping arranges for a difficulty not to be mentioned, which is very often the opposite of this.
verseByVerse.theology: The Beatitudes are not a moral ladder to climb but a portrait of kingdom citizens in their native condition. They describe the same person from different angles: the one who is poor in spirit mourns their sin, is meek before God, hungers for righteousness, shows mercy, is pure in heart, makes peace, and bears persecution gladly. This is not nine different types of Christian but one Christian seen fully. Crucially, the blessings are not rewards for achieving these qualities; they are the condition of those who have already received the kingdom. Grace precedes the beatitudes; they describe those who know it. And before they are a portrait of the Christian, they are a portrait of Christ: he alone was perfectly poor in spirit, mourning over sin, meek, hungering for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, the peacemaker, the persecuted — he kept every blessing flawlessly, and that whole beatitude-life is reckoned to all who are united to him. This is the lens that keeps the Beatitudes from crushing the believer. We do not read them to measure ourselves and despair; we read them resting in the One who fulfilled them for us and who is now, by his Spirit, slowly forming them in us. So the struggler need not flee: the very ache of falling short — the grief over sin, the hunger to be made clean — is itself the first Beatitudes already at work, the early evidence of grace rather than the proof of its absence. Here law and gospel meet: the Beatitudes show us a righteousness we cannot produce, and then point us to the Christ who both gives it freely and grows it within.
verseByVerse.examples: Salt in the ancient world was a preservative — it slowed decay. Light is simply visible; it cannot be hidden without ceasing to be light. Jesus calls his disciples both: agents of preservation in a decaying world, and bearers of visible testimony that draws glory to the Father. Neither metaphor allows for invisible, privatized Christianity. The Christian life is inherently public — not in the sense of performance (that will be condemned in ch. 6) but in the sense of witness. The question is not whether your life will be seen, but what people will see when they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up the mountain, sits down, and teaches his disciples. Like a new and greater Moses, Jesus gives the teaching of his kingdom — not entry requirements to earn God’s favour, but a portrait of the people God has already blessed.

A greater Moses. Moses went up a mountain and came down with the law. Now a Galilean carpenter goes up a mountain and sits down — the posture of a teacher about to speak with authority — and his disciples come to him (cf. Exodus 19:3). Matthew arranges the scene so no one can miss the claim. And notice who is in front of him. The crowds are present and still there at the end (7:28), but the teaching is addressed first to men who have already left their nets. It isn’t a list of entry requirements; it describes what the kingdom does to people once they are inside it.

“Blessed.” The word beginning each line means far more than “happy.” Happiness rises and falls with what happens to us. What Jesus pronounces doesn’t. To be blessed is to be the object of God’s settled favour, and so to flourish at the deepest level whatever the weather of your life. That is why these sentences aren’t cruel: you can’t order a mourner to be happy, but Jesus isn’t describing a feeling. He announces a verdict — God is for this person — and it holds while the tears are still wet. The world keeps “blessed” for the full and the winning; Jesus lays it over the poor, the grieving, the hungry and the hunted.

Not a ladder. Take this to heart before the Beatitudes one by one, or they will crush rather than bless. They aren’t eight exams to pass to earn God’s favour. Every “qualification” is a disqualification in the world’s eyes — poor, mourning, hungry, persecuted. This is grace from the first word: a blessing pronounced over the empty-handed. The Beatitudes aren’t a ladder you climb to God; they are a portrait of people God has stooped down to bless.

A portrait of Jesus. And they are first a portrait of Jesus himself. He was truly poor in spirit, mourned over sin, was meek, hungered for righteousness, was merciful, pure in heart, a peacemaker, persecuted. He lived every line we can’t keep, and his life is credited to all who are his. So read them first as your Saviour’s face, then as what his Spirit is slowly making you. If “pure in heart” stings because you still battle your thoughts, don’t despair: that sting is poverty of spirit, that grief is the mourning, that ache to be clean is the hunger for righteousness — the first Beatitudes already at work. The struggler who keeps running to Christ isn’t shut out of these blessings; he is the person they describe, finished only when “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). A test: are you reading the Beatitudes as demands to earn God’s favour, or as blessings spoken over you in Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach. The mountain setting recalls Moses receiving the law on Sinai.

parallels.desc: Moses goes up to God on the mountain

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed the poor in spirit, for the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Those who come to God with empty hands, knowing they have nothing to offer, are the very people who receive his kingdom as a gift.

Empty hands. Poverty of spirit isn’t low self-esteem but honesty before God: recognising that we have nothing to offer him, no claim, no merit — total dependence on his grace. The tax collector in Luke 18 is the portrait: he names no achievement, only beats his breast and says, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). It shows in specific moments: in prayer, the poor in spirit have nothing to produce, only need; in success, they can’t take the credit; in conflict, they don’t reach for their own righteousness; in failure, they have no excuses left. It is the patient who admits he is ill who calls the doctor; the man who insists he is fine stays sick.

Beggars. Greek has two words for “poor.” One is the working man with nothing to spare. The word here is the other, from a verb meaning to crouch or cower: a beggar, destitute, dependent entirely on what someone puts in his hand. That is the word Jesus chose for the first sentence of his first sermon. And it stands on ground Isaiah laid: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me… to bring good news to the poor” (Isaiah 61:1); “this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2). Of all creation, that is what God says he looks at.

A verdict, not a wish. “Blessed” isn’t a wish — “may you be happy” — but a flat declaration of how things stand. Half the people described in these sentences are in circumstances no one envies; calling them happy would be an insult. Calling them blessed — rightly placed, on the receiving end of God’s favour whatever the week looks like — is the truth. The Psalms open with the word: “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1). What no one had heard was this list of people attached to it.

The shape of the set. These sayings are one argument, sealed at both ends. “Theirs is the kingdom of heaven” opens the set (v. 3) and closes it (v. 10), in the present tense; the six between are all future — shall be comforted, inherit, be satisfied, receive mercy, see God, be called. The kingdom is already yours at the front door and still yours at the back, and everything between is on its way. And the first four describe need — bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving; the second four describe what comes from someone met in that need — merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and hated for it. No one reaches the second four by trying; they are what the first four become.

Luke’s version. Luke records, “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20), addressing disciples who were actually poor, with woes on the rich; Matthew spells out the heart. God has special care for the poor (James 2:5), but poverty saves no one, and a rich man can be poor in spirit. What Jesus blesses is the person who knows he has nothing to bring. And “theirs is” now, because they know how to receive everything as a gift — from him who, though rich, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). A test: do you come to God with achievements to show, or with empty hands?
verseByVerse.note: “Blessed” means truly well off in God’s sight, not merely happy.

parallels.desc: with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed those who mourn, for they will be comforted. Those who grieve honestly over sin — their own and the world’s — will be comforted by God, who exchanges their ashes for joy.

Mourning that follows sight. This isn’t simply bereavement or depression, and confusing it with either has hurt people who needed a doctor rather than a sermon. It is what happens to someone who has seen himself honestly. Poverty of spirit is the sight; mourning is what he does when he can’t look away. Paul calls it the godly grief that leads to life, as opposed to worldly grief that only corrodes (2 Corinthians 7:10).

A heavy word. Jesus chose a heavy word, used for mourning the dead — as Jacob mourned Joseph (Genesis 37:34). Not mild regret, but grief of the kind felt at a graveside, over what sin has done. Picture someone who, after years of excusing his sharp tongue or wandering eye as “just how I am,” finally grieves it before God, and finds the tears aren’t a pit but a doorway. God draws near to the broken-hearted, never to the self-satisfied.

Two guards. This can be twisted into a demand for a certain intensity of feeling, so that people who can’t produce tears conclude they aren’t Christians. Jesus isn’t prescribing a temperature. He is describing what happens when someone truly sees his condition: he doesn’t shrug. Whether it comes as tears or a long quiet ache is temperament, and God doesn’t seem to mind. And it isn’t depression. Godly sorrow moves toward God and produces life; depression is an illness that often makes a person feel further from God and produces only exhaustion. To tell a depressed believer that his flatness is a spiritual failure is a cruelty this verse doesn’t authorise.

The comfort promised. The comfort is Isaiah’s, spoken to exiles who knew why they were in Babylon: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1). The same promise continues in the chapter Jesus read at Nazareth: “to comfort all who mourn… to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit” (Isaiah 61:2–3). Ashes were what you put on your head when someone died. The promise isn’t that the mourning was a mistake, but that the ashes will be exchanged. And the comfort is certain because it was purchased: the Man of Sorrows (Isaiah 53:3) bore our griefs, so ours have an appointed end. A test: when you see your sin, do you shrug, or grieve it before God?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Those who entrust their cause to God instead of grasping and defending themselves will receive the whole renewed creation as his gift.

Strength under control. Meekness isn’t weakness or passivity; it is strength held in submission to God, not deployed for self-vindication. When someone humiliates you in a meeting, meekness isn’t having nothing to say; it is having something to say and choosing not to, because you have entrusted your vindication to God. When someone takes credit for your work, meekness doesn’t agree with their verdict; it leaves the accounting to the One who keeps perfect records. A test: where are you fighting to defend yourself instead of trusting God to vindicate you?

Moses. Scripture defines the word with a man: “Now the man Moses was very meek, more than all people who were on the face of the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Moses — who stood before Pharaoh unmoved, came down a mountain and smashed the tablets, ground the golden calf to powder and made the people drink it (Exodus 32:19–20). That settles what meekness can’t mean: not timidity or an inability to act. What Moses couldn’t do was defend himself. Read Numbers 12: his own brother and sister attack him behind his back, Moses says nothing, and God answers for him. A man with every power he needs and no interest in using it on his own behalf. The Greek word was used of a horse that had been broken — not with less strength than before, but whose full strength now answers to another’s hand.

Trust made visible. The promise quotes Psalm 37:11, “the meek shall inherit the land,” set in a longer call: “Trust in the LORD, and do good… Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act” (Psalm 37:3–5). Meekness is that trust made visible — refusing to take God’s work of vindication into your own hands.

The whole earth. Jesus keeps the psalm’s sentence and widens the word, from the strip of land between the Jordan and the sea to the earth itself. Measure that against how land is actually gained: it has always gone to whoever could take and hold it; every border was drawn by someone with the means to draw it. Jesus’ verdict is that at the end the whole earth will belong to those who never grabbed at any of it. And we learn this from him who said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (11:29), and stood silent before his accusers; in him the meek inherit everything.
verseByVerse.note: “Meek” means gentle and humble before God, not weak.

parallels.desc: the meek shall inherit the land
“I am gentle and lowly in heart”

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. God promises to fill completely those who long, with desperate desire, to be right with him and to see everything set right.

Appetites that won’t be argued with. He could have said those who value righteousness, admire it or work at it. He chose the two appetites a body can’t argue with. Hunger and thirst aren’t preferences weighed against others; they are what make a person unable to think of anything else. Picture the gap between idly wishing you were a little fitter and the gasping thirst of someone lost in a desert. God blesses not the casual wisher but the soul that aches to be made right. A test: has righteousness ever registered with you at that level?

What is hungered for. “Righteousness” covers more than personal holiness. It means being right with God, right dealing between people, and often in the Old Testament justice — the setting right of what is crooked. So the appetite is for everything to be put right, including wrongs out in the world. Someone who aches at the state of the world is inside this verse as much as someone aching at the state of his own heart. And the righteousness we hunger for is first a gift, not a wage: Christ is “the bread of life” (John 6:35), and his righteousness is credited to all who come empty and hungry.

Fed full. “They shall be satisfied” isn’t polite language. The word comes from feeding animals until they stop eating — fed full. The Gospels use it of the five thousand: “they all ate and were satisfied” (14:20), with twelve baskets left over. Those with a beggar’s hunger will be fed like cattle in deep grass. And it is the one appetite God guarantees to fill. Most hungers in this life can be starved, spoiled or fed with the wrong thing; this one he promises not to manage but to fill (cf. Isaiah 55:1–2; Psalm 42:1–2).

A strange test. The question isn’t whether you are righteous — that isn’t what the verse blesses — but whether you are hungry. Someone who has lost his appetite is sicker than someone starving, and the surest sign God is at work in a person isn’t that he has arrived but that he can’t stop wanting.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed the merciful, for they will receive mercy. Those who have truly received God’s mercy show mercy to others, and a heart that refuses mercy shows it has never grasped the mercy it needs.

A description, not a transaction. Read it as a transaction and it becomes unbearable: be merciful enough and God will be merciful back — which would make mercy purchased and therefore not mercy. Read it as a description and it comes right. The person who has actually received mercy finds he can give it; the one who can’t has told you something about what he imagines he received. We don’t work up mercy to earn God’s; we pass on what we have received at the cross.

Not toothless. But that guard mustn’t make the verse toothless, because Jesus doesn’t treat it gently. Of all the Lord’s Prayer’s petitions, this is the one he stops to explain: “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (6:14–15). And the parable of the unforgiving servant ends with a man released from ten thousand talents handed over to the jailers because he wouldn’t release a hundred denarii (18:23–35). Mercy shown doesn’t buy mercy received; but mercy withheld is evidence that mercy was never received.

The arithmetic. Ten thousand talents was an absurd sum, more than the yearly revenue of whole provinces, a debt no one could clear in a lifetime. A hundred denarii was a few months’ wages — real money, a genuine wrong, a debt someone is entitled to be angry about. The parable doesn’t pretend the second debt was nothing; it says the first was so much larger that the comparison should have been decisive.

A concrete test. Bring to mind the person you haven’t forgiven — not a category, but a name — and set beside it what you are asking God to overlook in your own account this week. The two figures aren’t of the same order, and someone who can’t see that has probably never looked properly at his own. And mercy triumphs over judgment (James 2:13). A test: whose debt are you still holding while asking God to cancel yours?

parallels.desc: should not you have had mercy?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed the pure in heart, for they will see God. Those whose hearts are undivided in loyalty to God will be given the greatest gift of all — God himself, seen face to face.

Undivided. Purity here isn’t chiefly about what a person has avoided. The word means clean, unmixed — clear water, metal with the impurities removed. So the opposite of a pure heart isn’t only a dirty heart but a divided one: someone who genuinely wants God and also wants three or four other things, and couldn’t say which he would give up. Think of a man who worships on Sunday with one eye on his money, image and comfort; his heart is divided. The pure in heart is one whose loves have been simplified, who wants God more than God’s gifts.

The temple question. This beatitude answers a question in the Psalms: “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). Who may come up and go in and not be struck down? And to David’s answer Jesus attaches what David didn’t dare write — not only “stand in his holy place” but “see God.”

The largest promise. Measure it against the Old Testament. Moses asked to see God’s glory and was refused: “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was hidden in a rock and shown God’s back. Isaiah saw the Lord and cried that he was undone. No one in the Old Testament sees God’s face and walks away comfortable. The whole arrangement of tabernacle, temple, curtain and priesthood said, in the most emphatic architecture ever built, that this was the one thing not available. And Jesus tells fishermen and farmers on a hillside that some of them will. Everything else a Christian is promised — forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, resurrection, a new creation — is a gift from God. This one is God himself.

Purchased. It was purchased by the only man who ever had a pure heart, who was made sin so that people who never had one could look at his Father and live; at his death the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom (27:51). A divided heart is the honest description of most Christians much of the time, and that is what God is working on; the wanting of single-heartedness is itself evidence of his work. If your heart feels anything but pure, look to him: Christ is our righteousness and sanctification (1 Corinthians 1:30), he cleanses us day by day, and “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). A test: what rival love is dividing your heart from God?

parallels.desc: he who has clean hands and a pure heart
holiness, without which no one will see the Lord
we shall see him as he is

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God. Those who actively and at personal cost work to reconcile people show the family likeness of God, who made peace with us through Christ’s blood.

Makers, not keepers. Notice the word is “makers.” A peacekeeper stands between two parties and stops them fighting; a peacemaker walks into the quarrel and does the costlier work of bringing them back together. One preserves a silence, the other repairs a relationship, and only the second costs anything. The word appears only here in the New Testament: not peace-lovers or peace-wishers, nor people who find conflict distasteful, but people who go and do something about it.

Why it matters. Keeping the peace usually means arranging for a difficulty not to be mentioned. It is cheap and quiet, and often the opposite of what this verse commends, because the unspoken thing goes on rotting. Making peace means going into the difficulty on purpose, which is expensive and nearly always uncomfortable — and that is why this beatitude sits just before persecution. Peacemakers get hit from both sides. Picture the friend who, when two others fall out, won’t take a side but goes back and forth between them, bearing awkwardness and even blame, until clenched fists become clasped hands. A test: is there a quarrel you are keeping quiet about instead of helping to mend?

Sons of God. “They shall be called sons of God” — called by God himself, not by the reconciled parties, who may be ungrateful, nor by the watching community. And “sons of God” speaks of family likeness: in Hebrew idiom a “son of” something bears its character, as “sons of thunder” or “son of encouragement.” To be called a son of God is to be recognised as doing what God does.

The cost God paid. That fixes what peacemaking costs. God didn’t make peace by overlooking anything, or persuading the offended party to be reasonable, or arranging for the matter not to come up. He made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), absorbing the whole cost himself so the wrong could be truly dealt with, not ignored (2 Corinthians 5:18–19). So a peacemaker isn’t someone with a talent for smoothing things over, but someone willing to carry a cost that isn’t theirs so that something broken can be properly mended. And we can only make peace because peace was first made with us: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pronounces blessed those persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Suffering because of faithfulness to God is not a sign of his displeasure but the mark of those to whom his kingdom already belongs.

The bracket closes. “Theirs is the kingdom of heaven” — the same promise as verse 3, in the present tense. The poor beggar at the front door and the hunted disciple at the back are told the same thing, and it is the one thing in the list they don’t have to wait for.

For righteousness’ sake. This qualifier is the whole of the verse’s honesty. Jesus isn’t blessing suffering as such, or every cost a Christian pays. The world doesn’t persecute the harmless; it persecutes those whose faithfulness exposes its darkness. Peter draws the line sharply: “let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler” (1 Peter 4:15). Being disliked for being difficult, tactless, self-righteous or wrong isn’t persecution; it is consequences. A test: is the opposition you face because of Christ, or because of you?

Ordinary forms. It needn’t be a prison cell. It may be the colleague quietly sidelined for refusing to fudge the figures, or the teenager frozen out for not joining the cruelty in a group chat. When obedience to Christ costs you something at others’ hands, you aren’t unblessed; you stand where the citizens of the kingdom have always stood — with the One who was cast out for them (1 Peter 3:14).

Two distortions. The guard runs both ways. In comfortable countries this verse gets reduced to social awkwardness, while much of the church elsewhere is in real danger. Avoid both errors: manufacturing a persecution you don’t have, and quietly deciding the verse belongs to history. The honest position for many Western Christians is to notice that the verse describes a normal condition of kingdom life, to ask why it so rarely touches us, and to be careful what conclusion we draw from the answer.

parallels.desc: if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his disciples they are blessed when insulted, persecuted and slandered on his account, and calls them to rejoice, for their heavenly reward is great and the prophets were treated the same way. Suffering for Christ places believers in the company of God’s faithful messengers and is cause for joy, not despair.

“You.” Eight times Jesus has said “blessed are those” — describing a category. Now: “Blessed are you.” He turns from describing to addressing, after the crowd has had eight sentences to work out whether they are in the list.

“On my account.” Verse 10 said persecution “for righteousness’ sake”; verse 11 says “on my account.” The two are made equivalent, and the substitution is enormous. A man on a hillside replaces the standard of righteousness with himself, in consecutive sentences, without explanation, before people who would stone someone for less. It is allegiance to him, not merely being good, that draws the world’s opposition.

Rejoice. “Rejoice and be glad” — the second word means to exult, the gladness that gets up and moves. He isn’t telling them to pretend slander doesn’t hurt. He gives two reasons for gladness: forward, “your reward is great in heaven” — grace upon grace, not wages owed; and backward, “so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

In good company. That second reason is a strange comfort until you feel its weight. Our natural reading of being attacked for our faith is that something has gone wrong — we have handled it badly, or God has withdrawn. Jesus offers a different diagnosis: this is what happened to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Elijah, and everyone God ever sent. If it is happening to you, you stand where they stood. Not that suffering proves you right — many suffer for being wrong — but that this kind of suffering, for this reason, has a long and honourable history, and the people in it are the ones God kept sending. The apostles left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41). A test: when you are mocked for Christ, do you shrink back or rejoice in his company?

parallels.desc: rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his disciples they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, warning that salt which loses its taste is worthless, and that a city on a hill can’t be hidden. Christ has made his people distinct and visible for the world’s good, and they must not lose that distinctiveness by blending in.

You are. Both pictures declare — “you are” — rather than urge “you should become.” Identity comes before calling. He tells his disciples what he has already made them, then warns them not to waste it.

Salt. In the ancient world salt was the great preservative; packing fish or meat in salt kept it from spoiling, and salted fish from the Sea of Galilee were traded widely. Disciples work like that: they slow moral and social decay by their presence. A community of truthful, faithful, just people doesn’t transform a neighbourhood by force or noise but by the quiet, persistent influence of changed lives — the way salt works through meat, slowly and from the inside.

Salt that loses its taste. Pure salt can’t stop being salty. But the salt of that region, from around the Dead Sea, came mixed with other minerals, and if it lay damp the salt could leach out, leaving a white residue that looked exactly like salt and did nothing. It hadn’t turned into something else; it had lost the one property that made it worth having, while keeping the appearance. And it is never a decision. No one resolves to become indistinguishable. It happens by a hundred small accommodations — the joke you laugh at because not laughing is awkward, the figure you round in your favour because everyone does, the conviction you keep quiet so long that you stop holding it. The result is a life exactly like every other in the office, with a religious residue on top.

Can a Christian lose salvation? Some read the warning that way. But the salt that is thrown out describes those who looked like disciples and had none of the substance, the same people Jesus describes in 7:21–23. Those who truly belong to Christ will be kept (John 10:28). The warning is real, and it is aimed at the danger of a profession without a life.

The better question. Ask the diagnostic question, not the anxious one. “Have I lost my saltiness?” tends to produce despair or a burst of intensity that fades by Thursday. Ask instead: if someone who knows me well were asked what difference Christ has made to how I work, spend, speak and treat people, could they name anything — not something impressive, something different? If nothing comes to mind, that isn’t a verdict; it is information, and the rest of this sermon sets about changing it.

A city on a hill. Light is simpler still: it is visible by nature. A city on a hill can’t choose to be hidden. The Christian life is unavoidably public — not as performance but as testimony. The question isn’t whether to be seen, but what your visible life says about the One who gave it (cf. Philippians 2:15). A test: what does your ordinary week show about Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Salt preserved and flavoured food. Impure salt, such as that from the Dead Sea, could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”
shine as lights in the world

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says no one lights a lamp to hide it under a basket, but sets it on a stand to light the house, so his disciples should let their light shine so that people see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven. Christians are to live visibly good lives, and to be ready to point to God as their source, so that he, not they, is praised.

Witness, not show. The lamp on a stand lights everyone in the house. The purpose of good works isn’t self-promotion (chapter 6 will condemn that) but the Father’s glory. Works done to be seen by others for their praise are hypocrisy; works done before others so that God is praised are witness. The same deed — giving to the poor, visiting the sick, telling the truth — can be either, depending on whose glory it seeks. Light points beyond itself to its source.
