Two failures. What does this look like on an ordinary weekday, without becoming the person everyone avoids? The two pictures do different jobs, and most of us fail at one. Salt works by being different, quietly; light works by being seen. So there are two opposite failures. The first is salt that has leached away: you are pleasant, entirely assimilated, and no one could name anything about your life that would need explaining if there were no God. The second is a lamp under a basket: you are visibly different — honest, unusually kind, unwilling to join the pile-on — and no one has ever been told why. Everyone thinks you are simply nice. The first has nothing to say; the second has something and never says it.

Salt made concrete. The saltiness is mostly unglamorous. It is the accurate expense claim when nobody checks. It is declining to join the character assassination in the group chat, without a speech about it. It is how you speak to the person who can do nothing for you — the cleaner, the junior, the difficult customer — when there is no audience. It is telling the truth when it is costly, and being known for it. None of that needs a platform, and people notice it precisely because it is rare.

Light made concrete. And the light is simply being ready to say why when the question comes — and it comes, eventually, to people who live like that. Not a prepared speech, but a brief, plain answer. Peter puts it exactly: “always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). The manner is part of the instruction (cf. 1 Peter 2:12).

The test in the verse. The aim isn’t that people think well of you, but that they “give glory to your Father who is in heaven.” If the effect of your visible life is that people admire you and never think about God, the lamp is pointing the wrong way, however bright. And if you have been dim and silent for years, remember what a lamp is: it produces no light of its own. It holds up a flame lit from elsewhere, and it can be lit again this morning. A test: when people notice something good in you, are they pointed to God?
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

parallels.desc: they may see your good deeds and glorify God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses the relationship between his teaching and the law of Moses: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill. He then gives six antitheses — "You have heard... but I say to you" — in which he does not contradict the law but penetrates to its interior logic. Murder begins in anger; adultery begins in the look; divorce fractures the covenant; oaths corrupt speech; retaliation perpetuates violence; hatred divides what love should unite. The section climaxes with the demand: "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." — a standard no one reaches by effort, which is exactly why it drives us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The antitheses reveal that the law was always concerned with the heart, not merely the external act. Jesus does not introduce a new, stricter morality; he discloses the full depth of what God always intended. The Pharisees' righteousness was wide but shallow — it covered the surface of behavior without reaching the roots of motive and desire. The righteousness Jesus requires exceeds theirs not by adding more external rules but by going deeper into the same terrain. This is why grace must precede the Sermon on the Mount: no one can produce this righteousness by effort; it must be worked in us by the Spirit of the one who fulfilled the law perfectly. To "fulfill" the law (v. 17) is not to abolish it but to bring it to its goal: by his flawless obedience Jesus meets its every demand, in himself he embodies the types and shadows that pointed forward, and at the cross he bears its curse. And the righteousness that "exceeds" the Pharisees comes in two layers — first the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to us through faith, the only righteousness that truly opens the kingdom, and then the real if imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a regenerate heart. So the very law that drives the unbeliever to Christ by exposing his sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a Spirit-empowered life of love. Read this way, the towering standard of verse 48 humbles without crushing: it sends us to Christ for a righteousness we cannot produce, and then to the Spirit who produces it in us.
verseByVerse.examples: The demand for perfection (v. 48) has driven interpreters in two directions: some make it an impossible ideal that drives us to grace; others read it as a call to wholeness or completeness (the Greek teleios can mean "complete" or "mature"). Both are partially right: the standard is God's own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but which the Spirit progressively conforms us to (2 Cor. 3:18). The sermon is both a mirror that shows us our need and a map of the life the Spirit produces in those who have received the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them, and that not the smallest letter or stroke will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Christ fulfils the whole Old Testament — keeping its demands, completing its shadows, bearing its penalty and revealing its true depth — so that the law now drives sinners to him and shapes the life of love his people live.

Fulfilled, not abolished. Jesus flatly denies that he came to abolish “the Law or the Prophets” — the whole Old Testament. He came to fulfil them, and that means more than obeying. He fulfils their demands, keeping perfectly what Israel and we have broken. He fulfils their types and shadows: the sacrifices, temple, priesthood and feasts all pointed to him (Luke 24:44). He fulfils their penalty, bearing the law’s curse on the cross (Galatians 3:13). And he fulfils their meaning, pressing the commands to their full inward depth, as the rest of this chapter shows. The law demanded a righteousness no sinner could produce; Jesus produced it, and is himself the law’s goal (Romans 10:4).

Not a dot. Not the smallest letter (the iota, the Hebrew yod) nor the tiniest stroke will pass away “until all is accomplished.” The law isn’t scrapped; it is carried to its appointed completion, reached above all in Christ’s life, death and resurrection, with the final consummation still to come. That is why Paul can say the believer has “died to the law” (Romans 7:4). The law wasn’t a mistake; but since Christ fulfilled it and bore it for us, we are released from it as a covenant of works — no longer under its demand to “do this and live,” nor under its condemnation.

The law’s work now. For someone not yet in Christ, the law is God’s faithful schoolmaster: exposing sin and silencing excuses, it drives the sinner to the only Saviour (Galatians 3:24; Romans 3:20). For someone in Christ, the law isn’t a ladder to God’s love, which is already ours. Yet its moral heart — love for God and neighbour (Romans 13:10; 22:37–40) — remains the shape of the redeemed life, and the Spirit writes it on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), enabling us to walk in it as children, not slaves (Romans 8:3–4). Freed from the law as a way to be saved, freed for the law as the way of love. A test: is the law driving you to Christ, and is Christ’s Spirit shaping you by it?

Which parts of the law still apply? Reformed Christians have usually distinguished three kinds of law. The ceremonial law, the sacrifices and purity rules, is fulfilled in Christ and no longer practised. The civil laws of Israel as a nation expired with that nation, though their underlying justice still instructs. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still shows God’s people how to love him and their neighbour. Some, called theonomists, hold that Israel’s civil laws and penalties should still govern nations today. The first view is the more likely: Israel was a unique covenant nation, and the church is not a state (John 18:36; Romans 13:1–7).

How do dispensationalists read this? Many faithful believers read it through dispensational eyes, stressing a sharp distinction between Israel and the church. On this reading the Law of Moses was given to national Israel as a single code, and at the cross that whole code ended for the believer; the Christian now lives under “the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2; 1 Corinthians 9:21), the commands of the New Testament, and many are wary of the threefold division of the law. Classic dispensationalists read the Sermon on the Mount as chiefly law for a coming earthly kingdom, though many today apply it directly to Christian living. The difference from the Reformed reading is real but narrower than it looks. Both confess that we are saved by grace through faith, not law-keeping; that the believer isn’t under the law’s condemnation; that Christ fulfilled it; and that it still drives sinners to him. The divergence lies in the framework: the Reformed see one covenant of grace through both Testaments and the moral law abiding as the believer’s guide; the dispensationalist sees a sharper break. In practice both walk the same road of Spirit-empowered love. (See 4:17 on the kingdom.)
verseByVerse.note: The iota is the smallest Greek letter; the “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter. Nothing in the law is too small to matter.

parallels.desc: Christ is the end of the law

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever relaxes the least commandment and teaches others to will be least in the kingdom, but whoever keeps and teaches them will be great — and unless their righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, they won’t enter the kingdom at all. God demands a righteousness greater than the most religious people’s, a righteousness found first in Christ, given by faith, and then worked out by his Spirit in a changed heart.

A thunderclap. In that world the scribes and Pharisees were the gold standard of holiness. When Jesus says you must out-righteous them or “never enter the kingdom of heaven,” the ordinary listener thinks, “If they fall short, what hope is there for me?” and the Pharisee bristles. Jesus means to unsettle both — closing every road of self-confidence before opening the only door that works.

The great relaxers. “Relaxes” warns any teacher who loosens God’s commands. But there is irony here: the men who looked strictest were the great relaxers. They buried the law under extra rules while hollowing out its weight, and at points their traditions cancelled God’s commands — by “Corban” they let a man neglect his aged parents, “thus making void the word of God” by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). To keep the letter while killing the heart is the worst relaxing of all.

What about the ceremonial laws? Must we still keep the food laws, feasts and Sabbath? Read this with verses 17–18. Jesus upholds the law’s authority, but fulfils it, and its ceremonial shadows — sacrifices, clean and unclean foods, holy days, the Sabbath as a sign — reach their goal in him. “These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). We honour those laws not by repeating the shadows but by trusting the One they pointed to; to rest in Christ isn’t to relax the law but to keep it at its deepest. A rhythm of rest and worship remains God’s good gift, and the moral law abides in full force, pressed deeper in the verses ahead.

Does and teaches. The one commended both “does them and teaches them.” Teaching isn’t enough: “be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22). But this is about the direction of a life, not its perfection. The great in the kingdom are those whose hearts mean to obey, who keep turning back after every stumble, and whose doing springs from grace received.

A righteousness that exceeds. The Pharisees’ flaw wasn’t too much obedience but hypocrisy: good works done for their own honour, as chapter 6 will show. A righteousness that surpasses theirs must be of a different kind, in two layers. First, a righteousness not our own: Christ’s perfect righteousness credited to us through faith (Philippians 3:9). That alone truly exceeds the Pharisees and opens the kingdom. Then, flowing from that gift, a real if imperfect righteousness of the heart, as the Spirit gives a new heart and moves us to walk in God’s ways (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Theirs was wide, shallow and for show; this is deep, genuine and for God.

Does “least in the kingdom” mean saved but given a lower place? Some take it that way, as a difference of reward; others take it as a way of saying he is effectively outside, since verse 20 speaks of not entering at all. The first is the more likely, since he is still in the kingdom. Either way, the point is not how to earn a high rank but how seriously Jesus takes the teaching of his commands.

Driven to Christ. Jesus sets the bar impossibly high not to crush you but to drive you off your own righteousness and into his. Received by faith, it becomes yours, and the same grace sends the Spirit to make you, slowly and truly, the kind of person these words describe. A test: whose righteousness are you counting on to enter the kingdom?

parallels.desc: the righteousness from God that depends on faith

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says the law forbade murder, but he says that anyone angry with his brother, who insults him, or who calls him “You fool!” is liable to judgment, the council, and even hell. God’s law reaches the heart: contemptuous anger is murder at the root and deserves God’s judgment, so we need his mercy and must put such anger away.

To the root. The first of six contrasts takes murder to its root: anger. The law forbade the act; Jesus forbids the inner state from which it grows. He isn’t adding a new law but showing what the old always implied about the worth of people made in God’s image. Every insult attacks someone who bears that image. The rising liability — judgment, council, hell — tracks rising contempt: anger (the feeling), insult (the word), “You fool!” (the verdict that writes a person off as worthless).

Three courts. “Judgment” meant the local court; “the council” the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem, Israel’s supreme court of seventy-one members; and “the hell of fire” is Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem. That valley was notorious: Manasseh burned his sons there (2 Chronicles 33:6); Josiah defiled it to end such worship (2 Kings 23:10); Jeremiah called it the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:32). Its name became the name for final judgment. So the escalation runs from village court to national tribunal to God’s own judgment seat. Jesus treats contemptuous speech as a moral catastrophe, not a social lapse.

Is all anger sin? No. God is “a God who feels indignation every day” (Psalm 7:11); Jesus looked around “with anger” at hard hearts (Mark 3:5). So Scripture says, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). When you hear of a child abused and something in you burns, that can be right — love recoiling at evil. But holy anger is rarer than we think, and it has marks: stirred by God’s concerns, not wounded pride; under control, not flaring into contempt or revenge; slow, for “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20); and spent in doing good, never in writing someone off. Most of our anger, tested, turns out to be about us — our rights, comfort and honour.

Is anger as bad as murder? Jesus is not saying the two do equal harm, or deserve the same penalty from a court; Scripture itself recognizes degrees of sin (John 19:11). He is saying they come from the same root and make a person liable to the same judgment before God. No one can say, “I have never murdered, so I am safe.” The same is true of lust and adultery in verses 27–28. Jesus closes every escape route so that everyone must come to him for mercy.

But Jesus called people fools. Jesus himself called the Pharisees “blind fools” (23:17), and Paul wrote, “O foolish Galatians!” (Galatians 3:1). What Jesus forbids is contempt: writing a person off as worthless. A prophet’s rebuke of folly, spoken in truth and for the hearer’s good, is a different thing. And the warning of hell describes the settled heart of contempt, the kind the gospel exists to forgive. A believer who has spoken in anger is not condemned (Romans 8:1); he is to repent and be reconciled.

When anger rises. Be slow; don’t speak in the heat — “A soft answer turns away wrath” (Proverbs 15:1). Look underneath: ask what was really threatened, and you will usually find bruised pride rather than God’s glory. Take it to God before the person, leaving room for his justice: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19). Remember you are the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (18:21–35). Then move toward the person, as the next verses urge. And when you fail, confess it and receive fresh forgiveness; the Spirit is still retraining your heart. A test: is there someone you have written off in contempt?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “insults” renders the Aramaic term of abuse Raca. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice. “The council” is the Sanhedrin.

parallels.desc: child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom
everyone who hates his brother is a murderer

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are offering a gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave the gift, go and be reconciled first, then come and offer it. God values reconciliation above religious ritual, and those who have wronged others must take the first step to make it right.

Reconciliation before worship. Reconciliation with a brother takes priority even over a temple offering — not after worship, but before. God isn’t honoured by worship from an unreconciled heart. The order is precise: remember, leave, go, be reconciled, return. The gift waits while you mend the relationship, because the God who receives the gift cares more about the brother than the offering. As Jesus says elsewhere, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (9:13). Worship of God and relationship with others can’t be separated.

When you are in the wrong. Notice whose fault is in view: “your brother has something against you.” Here you are the one in the wrong, and the burden to act falls on you. Put it beside 18:15, where someone sins against you and you must go to him. If someone sins against you, go; if you have sinned against someone, go. Neither the wronged nor the wrongdoer may sit still. Love takes the first step in both directions.

What reconciliation looks like. Go humbly. Name the sin plainly: “I was wrong to speak to you the way I did.” Don’t excuse it or slip in blame — no “I’m sorry if you were offended,” no “but you started it.” Own it, show real sorrow, and ask the question pride hates: “Will you forgive me?” Where damage can be repaired, repair it. And the brother is called to forgive as God in Christ forgave him (Ephesians 4:32) — to say and mean “I forgive you,” and then keep that word: not raking it up, holding it over you or rehearsing it to others. Forgiveness is a promise to bury the matter, as God remembers our sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34). A test: is there someone you need to go to this week?

When the other refuses. What if you go, confess honestly, and meet a cold shoulder? Paul gives the limit: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). You are answerable for your part — honest confession and genuine reaching out — not for the other person’s response. Having truly sought peace, you may worship with a clear conscience, leaving him in God’s hands and ready to be reconciled the moment the door opens. Another’s unforgiveness can grieve you, but it can’t hold your worship hostage.
verseByVerse.note: The gift at the altar is a sacrifice brought to the temple.

parallels.desc: forgive, so that your Father may forgive you
so far as it depends on you

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus urges settling quickly with an accuser on the way to court, before you are handed to the judge and imprisoned until you have paid the last penny. Be reconciled now, with others and with God, while there is time — and know that your debt to God can only be settled by Christ’s full payment, never by your own.

Urgency. The court picture presses reconciliation with urgency: settle before it reaches judgment. It applies on the human level as plain prudence, and on the eternal level: settle your account with God while there is time. The “penny” was the smallest Roman coin, so “the last penny” means the whole debt paid in full if reconciliation is refused. The window for reconciliation — with others and with God — is open now; it won’t always be. A test: what account are you putting off settling, with someone else or with God?

Does this teach purgatory? “You will never get out until you have paid the last penny” has long been cited, with Luke 12:59, for purgatory — temporary punishment after death from which the soul is released once its debt is paid. The word “until” seems to promise an end. Three things stand in the way. First, the kind of speech: Jesus isn’t mapping the afterlife but urging two men at law to settle, using an ordinary scene. Doctrine can’t be read off a parable’s furniture; by that method another story would make God a judge who helps people only to stop them pestering him (Luke 18:1–8), the opposite of its point. Second, the idiom: a man in a debtors’ prison couldn’t earn; that was the horror of it. “Until you have paid” isn’t a release date but a closed door — like saying something will happen “when pigs fly.” Third, what the debt of sin cost: never a sum a sinner could work off by degrees, but paid once, by someone else, who said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). A purgatory in which the believer pays off a remainder implies something was still owing when he said it. (The other text cited, “either in this age or in the age to come,” is taken up at 12:32.)

Settle now. So take the urgency as Jesus means it: settle now, while the road to the court still runs. But the settling he wants isn’t the first instalment of a payment plan. It is the empty-handed surrender of someone who has finally understood he can’t pay, throwing himself on the mercy of the One who already has.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” (Latin quadrans) was a small Roman copper coin, worth about 1/64 of a denarius.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says the law forbade adultery, but anyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. God’s law reaches the desires of the heart, so we must fight lust by Christ’s grace, flee temptation, and rest in his forgiveness when we fail.

The heart before the body. The second contrast goes to the root of adultery: the intentional look of desire. Jesus doesn’t condemn involuntary attraction but the cultivated gaze that uses another person as an object for gratification. Adultery begins in the heart before the body. This demolishes every defence that stops at “I haven’t done anything wrong”; the inner life is under God’s law as much as outward acts. Faithfulness in marriage is a matter of the eyes and heart, not only the bedroom.

Where the line falls. It isn’t sin to notice that someone is beautiful; God made beauty. Nor is the first involuntary glance a sin, any more than a tempting thought’s arrival. Being tempted isn’t sinning; Jesus “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). What he condemns is the second look that lingers, the desire deliberately fed, the imagination invited to stay. Luther is said to have put it: you can’t stop birds flying over your head, but you can stop them nesting in your hair.

Is lust as bad as adultery? It is the same sin in the heart, and guilty before God, but it does not do the same damage, and it is not a ground for divorce, which Jesus ties to actual sexual unfaithfulness (v. 32). The point is to expose the heart and send us to the cure.

For the struggler. Suppose your eyes keep being drawn where they shouldn’t linger; you look away, and walk off weighed down with guilt. The looking away isn’t your failure but your obedience, a small daily victory. Much of that burden is false guilt, the accuser heaping condemnation on someone who fought and won: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Where you truly let the gaze linger, don’t wallow; confess it at once and receive the cleansing promised (1 John 1:9).

Tools for the fight. Make Job’s covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1). Turn the glance away quickly and flee rather than negotiate (2 Timothy 2:22). Don’t merely suppress the thought but replace it — turn your heart to Christ, give thanks, even pray for that person as a soul, not an object. And deepest of all, the cure for a wandering eye is a captured heart: as Christ becomes our greater treasure, purity grows less from gritted teeth and more from love. A test: what are you feeding your eyes and imagination with?

parallels.desc: you shall not covet your neighbour’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says that if your right eye or right hand causes you to sin, tear it out or cut it off, for it is better to lose one part than for your whole body to go into hell. Sin is deadly, so we must act decisively and at real cost to remove whatever feeds it — not by self-harm, but by radical repentance.

Violent language, real stakes. The exaggeration is violent because the stakes are real. Jesus isn’t teaching self-mutilation — a blind man can still lust, a handless man can still sin. He is teaching radical, decisive action when sin has a foothold. “Your right eye” — the favoured, dominant one — means even your best faculty must go if it is the instrument of your fall. And the repeated mention of hell shows this isn’t about self-improvement but eternal life. Sin isn’t inconvenient; it is lethal.

Not literal. The church has known this from the start. Origen is reported to have castrated himself over a literal reading of 19:12, and the church regarded it as a tragedy. The decisive argument is in the text: cutting off a hand doesn’t stop wanting, and removing an eye doesn’t touch the heart. Jesus has just moved sin from the act to the desire behind it. What the exaggeration does is set a price: if it came to a choice between a maimed life and a lost soul, the arithmetic isn’t close — and most of us have never made a decision at anything like that rate.

Not despair. Someone who takes sin seriously can hear this as a demand for a purity he knows he lacks, and conclude that the fire is his. But this comes in a sermon that began by giving the kingdom to the spiritually bankrupt, preached by the One who would soon be cut off in his hearers’ place. The severity is real, and it isn’t the last word.

What cutting off looks like. Picture a surgeon amputating a gangrenous limb: better to lose the hand than let the poison take the body. Deal with sin as ruthlessly. If the phone in your pocket has become the doorway to lust through late-night scrolling, install a filter, leave it downstairs at night, or trade it for a simpler one. If a friendship keeps dragging you into gossip, drink or compromise, step back from it. If the road home passes the bar, or the bottle waits in the cupboard, change the road and empty the cupboard. Notice that what is given up is something good or precious — the right eye, the right hand. Jesus asks us to part with anything, however valued, that has become the instrument of our fall, and to do it before the moment of temptation, not during it (cf. 18:8–9; Colossians 3:5). No one haggles with gangrene. A test: what “right hand” do you need to cut off this week?
verseByVerse.note: The right eye and hand were thought the more valuable. Jesus is using deliberate exaggeration to demand radical action against sin, not self-mutilation.

parallels.desc: put to death what is earthly in you

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says the law allowed a man to divorce his wife with a certificate, but he says that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. Marriage is a lifelong covenant that may not be dissolved casually; divorce is permitted only for grave breach, and grace is available to all who have failed.

The concession. The certificate of Deuteronomy 24:1 was a concession to hard hearts, not God’s design (19:8). Jesus restores the original intention: marriage is a covenant, and dissolving it isn’t a legal technicality but a moral rupture. Marriage isn’t a contract to be terminated; it is an image of God’s own faithfulness to his people.

What he meant. In his day divorce had become casual and one-sided: a man could hand his wife a certificate for flimsy reasons (one famous rabbi allowed it even for a spoiled meal), leaving her shamed and destitute; a divorced woman usually had to remarry to survive. When Jesus says such a man “makes her commit adultery,” he means that because the divorce wasn’t on valid grounds, in God’s sight she is still bound to her first husband, so her remarriage counts as adultery — and the guilt traces back to the man who wrongly cast her out. “Whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” follows: if her divorce was illegitimate, she is still another man’s wife in God’s eyes.

The exception. Does this forbid every divorced person from remarrying? The hinge is “except on the ground of sexual immorality.” By making an exception, Jesus shows there is a ground on which a marriage is truly broken, where divorce is permitted and remarriage isn’t adultery. The sweeping “no remarriage” is aimed at remarriage after an unjust, groundless divorce.

Contested ground. Faithful brothers land in different places here, so hold convictions firmly and charity wider. The historic Reformed position (as in the Westminster Confession) recognises two grounds on which divorce is permitted and the innocent party is free to remarry: sexual immorality (here and 19:9), and wilful, irreparable desertion, which Paul addresses: “if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). Others read the exception more narrowly and conclude no remarriage is permitted while a former spouse lives.

Adultery and abuse. If a marriage is broken by adultery, the innocent spouse is, on the mainstream Reformed reading, free to remarry. And abuse: first, without hedging, an abused spouse must get to safety; God never calls anyone to remain in danger, and the church must protect, never pressure. Second, many faithful pastors rightly judge that brutal, unrepentant abuse is itself a profound breaking of the marriage covenant, a desertion of every vow to love and cherish, falling under the principle of 1 Corinthians 7. Some would frame it more cautiously as separation, but none should ever bind a victim to ongoing harm.

What does “sexual immorality” cover? The word is broad. It includes adultery and other serious sexual sins that break the marriage covenant in the same way. Some take it more narrowly, of unfaithfulness during betrothal or of a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship. The broader reading is the more likely. And permission is not command: where there is repentance, forgiveness and reconciliation remain the better path (cf. Hosea 3:1).

Why do Mark and Luke leave out the exception? Most likely because they state the general rule (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18), while Matthew, writing for Jewish readers who knew the debates about divorce, records the exception that everyone assumed. Those who hold that remarriage is never permitted while a former spouse lives rely on these shorter texts, on Paul’s statement that a wife is bound while her husband lives (Romans 7:2–3; 1 Corinthians 7:39), and on the teaching of many early church fathers. Their view deserves respect, but it leaves Jesus’ exception without a clear meaning.

For those who have failed. The way back is the same as for every sin: repentance and forgiveness. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage, not to be broken by a further sin; the call is to live faithfully in it. Whether the guilty party may remarry is disputed among Reformed Christians, and such cases need the elders’ counsel. Through it all, marriage is holy, a picture of Christ’s covenant with his church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and divorce is always a tragedy. Yet for anyone with a broken marriage in their past, these words aren’t a permanent condemnation; there is full forgiveness at the cross. Jesus guards marriage fiercely because he is the Husband who will never divorce his bride. A test: are you honouring your marriage covenant as a picture of Christ’s faithfulness?
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry. Rabbis disputed the grounds for divorce, some allowing it for trivial reasons.

verseByVerse.quote: Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn." But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No"; anything more than this comes from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says the law required keeping oaths, but he forbids swearing at all — by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or one’s own head — and tells his disciples to let their “Yes” be yes and their “No” no. Everything belongs to God, so there is no oath that doesn’t involve him; Christians are to be so consistently truthful that their plain word needs no oath to back it.

No loophole. The law permitted oaths and required them kept (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2). The trouble was the system of evasion that grew around them. People swore by lesser things — heaven, earth, Jerusalem, their own head — treating such oaths as less binding than one sworn by God’s name: a tidy loophole for the careful liar. The rabbis had worked out which were binding; Jesus mocks the scheme in chapter 23 — swearing by the temple, by the gold of the temple, by the altar, by the gift on it (23:16–22). Here he goes to the root: heaven is God’s throne, earth his footstool (Isaiah 66:1), Jerusalem his city, and you can’t even change the colour of one hair. There is no neutral object to swear by; every oath drags God in, and no oath can be quietly broken. The graded system was machinery for lying honestly — words that sounded binding while leaving a back door open. Anyone who has read small print knows the instinct isn’t dead.

A word that needs no oath. The alternative is startlingly small: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No.’” Not a better formula — no formula. The need for oaths exposes how unreliable ordinary speech has become; someone who reinforces his word with an oath half-admits his plain word isn’t trusted. In the kingdom a Christian’s bare word should be as good as another’s sworn oath. Anything more “comes from evil,” a symptom of the fall’s fracturing of speech. A test: is your plain word reliable without needing to be backed up?

Does this forbid wedding vows, membership vows or an oath in court? No. Scripture itself honours solemn vows made before God (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5); God swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13); Paul calls God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23); and Jesus answered the high priest when put under oath (26:63–64). What Jesus forbids is using oaths to prop up ordinary speech, as if a plain statement could not be trusted. Some Christians, notably Quakers and Anabaptists, have refused all oaths, including in court, at real cost. The majority position, and the better one, is that Jesus addresses casual daily oath-taking; but those who take the stricter line deserve respect, for they err, if at all, on the side of taking their Lord at his word.

Truthful, not tactless. Must you then tell everything you know? No. Truthfulness isn’t the same as telling everyone everything. Scripture forbids deceit, not discretion. There is room to keep a confidence, guard what isn’t yours to share, keep a wise silence as Jesus did before his accusers (26:63; 27:14), or decline a question not rightly asked. You may keep silent, but you may not lie; you needn’t say all, but what you say must be true.
verseByVerse.note: People swore by heaven or Jerusalem instead of by God, treating such oaths as less binding.

parallels.desc: do not swear by my name falsely
do all that proceeds out of his mouth
heaven my throne, the earth my footstool
the city of the great King

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says the law said “an eye for an eye,” but he tells his disciples not to resist the one who is evil: turn the other cheek when slapped, and give up your cloak as well when sued for your tunic. Christ’s followers refuse personal revenge and hold their rights loosely, entrusting themselves to God the just Judge — without abandoning justice or the protection of the weak.

A limit, not a licence. “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (v. 38, quoting Exodus 21:24) was never a licence for revenge but a rule for judges, keeping punishment in proportion — a mercy that restrained blood feuds. Jesus carries his disciples beyond even that, from measured justice to refused vengeance.

The cheek and the cloak. “Do not resist the one who is evil” doesn’t mean passively accepting all injustice; it means refusing the spiral of personal vengeance. A slap on the right cheek was usually a backhanded blow — an insult, not an assault. Turning the other cheek isn’t offering to be beaten twice but refusing to be drawn into tit-for-tat retaliation for honour. Giving up the cloak as well as the tunic is a willingness to absorb loss rather than fuel a legal war. Jesus teaches a new relationship to personal rights: hold them loosely, suffer loss without bitterness, refuse the calculus of revenge.

Today. The “slap” is rarely literal for us; it is the insult to our pride — the colleague who belittles you in a meeting, the driver who leans on the horn, the cutting reply waiting to be typed under someone’s post. To turn the other cheek is to let it fall without firing back. The “tunic and cloak” is the grievance over money or property — the neighbour who damages your hedge, the tradesman who overcharges, the relative who never repays — and it means being willing to swallow a loss rather than wage war for every right. It reaches into the home: when a spouse snaps or a teenager throws a barbed word, answer with calm instead of returning fire. A test: whose insult are you itching to answer back?

Does this mean Christians must be pacifists? Some Christians, especially in the Anabaptist tradition, read it that way: a disciple may never use force, even in self-defence or as a soldier. The more likely reading is that Jesus is speaking of personal insult and loss, as the backhanded slap shows, not of violent assault. Scripture allows the defence of life (Exodus 22:2), and the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain (Romans 13:4). A Christian may serve as a soldier or police officer, as the centurion did (8:5–13; cf. Luke 3:14), while refusing personal revenge. And this verse never requires a victim of abuse to stay and take it; it is not a command to remain under violence or to refuse the help of police and church (cf. 5:31–32).

May a Christian ever go to court? Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11) and used his rights as a Roman citizen, so lawful redress is not forbidden. What Jesus forbids is the grasping spirit that will fight for every right. And Paul tells believers not to sue each other before unbelievers but to settle disputes within the church (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). A Christian may defend himself in court, and may seek justice for others, but should first seek peace and be ready to lose.

Rights in safer hands. This isn’t a doormat’s passivity, nor does it cancel protection of the weak or lawful justice; it is the deliberate surrender of personal vengeance. And you can let go of your rights because they are safe in better hands. You follow the One who, “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Secure in such a Saviour, you can afford to lose an argument, swallow an insult and bless the one who wronged you.
verseByVerse.note: “Eye for eye” was a rule for judges, to keep punishment in proportion, not a licence for private revenge. A slap on the right cheek — probably with the back of the hand — was an insult. The cloak was the outer garment, used as a blanket at night.

parallels.desc: a cloak taken in pledge returned by sunset

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says that if someone forces you to go one mile, go two; give to the one who begs, and don’t refuse the one who would borrow. Christ’s followers serve willingly beyond what is demanded and hold their possessions with open, generous — and wise — hands.

The second mile. The forced mile refers to Roman requisition: a soldier could compel a civilian to carry his pack for a mile, as Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross (27:32). Going a second mile is the free act that turns a resentful conscript into a willing servant — grace at work in a coerced situation. Today the second mile is the willing extra: the worker who does more than the minimum, serving “heartily, as for the Lord” (Colossians 3:23); the neighbour who, asked one favour, gladly does a little more; the believer who keeps serving a demanding boss with grace instead of grumbling. A test: where are you doing only the bare minimum, and grudgingly?

Not without limits. Love isn’t the same as having no boundaries. The extra mile is a free gift, not bondage to another’s every demand. It doesn’t mean endless overtime that swallows your evenings and starves your family; caring for your household is God’s command too (1 Timothy 5:8), and someone who neglects his family to chase his employer’s approval hasn’t gone the extra mile — he has only changed which duty he is failing. Jesus himself withdrew to rest and pray. The point is a generous heart, guided by wisdom about the other things God has given you to do.

Must I lend to everyone? Jesus calls for a generous, willing heart, ready to lend without interest and without hope of return (Deuteronomy 15:7–8; Luke 6:35). But Scripture also warns against rash guarantees (Proverbs 6:1–5; 22:26). Love seeks the good of the person asking, which sometimes means helping in another way rather than feeding a pattern that harms him.

Generous and wise. “Give to the one who begs from you” forbids the tight fist that says, “What is mine is mine.” The disciple’s default is open-handed. Yet generosity should be wise, for love seeks a person’s real good. Where begging is organised to exploit both giver and poor, or cash would feed an addiction, love still gives, but shrewdly: a meal rather than money, support to a shelter or mercy ministry that truly helps, time and the gospel alongside the gift. Two ditches line the road: the hard heart that hides stinginess behind “they’d only waste it,” and thoughtless giving that funds what destroys someone. Walk between them — and when in doubt, lean toward mercy; it is better now and then to be taken advantage of than to nurse a miserly heart.
verseByVerse.note: Roman soldiers could compel a civilian to carry their gear for a mile, as Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry the cross.

parallels.desc: Simon compelled to carry the cross
open your hand to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says it was said, “Love your neighbour and hate your enemy,” but he commands his disciples to love their enemies and pray for their persecutors, so they may be sons of their Father, who sends sun and rain on the evil and the good — and to be perfect as their heavenly Father is perfect. God’s children are to show his own undivided, impartial love, even to their enemies, as he first loved us when we were his enemies.

The fence torn down. This last contrast is the most radical. “Hate your enemy” was never in the law of Moses; it was a popular gloss that fenced “neighbour” to shut enemies out. Jesus tears the fence down: love has no exception clause. To love an enemy isn’t merely to tolerate him or refrain from harming him, but active goodwill that seeks his welfare even while he seeks your ruin. Its sharpest form is prayer: to pray for a persecutor is to stand before God on his behalf and begin to want for him what God wants. That is humanly impossible — which is the point; only grace produces it.

The family likeness. Why love like this? Because it is God’s family likeness: he “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.” His kindness falls even on those who curse him. Loving only those who love you is mere reciprocity; even tax collectors and pagans manage that. And we have known this love ourselves: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). We pass on the love that first reached us.

What it looks like. Praying by name for the good of the colleague who undermined you or the relative who has turned cold. The neighbour everyone gossips about finding his path cleared and no note left. Choosing words that bless rather than bite about the one who wronged you, and quietly doing him a kindness. Refusing to gloat when an enemy stumbles. None of it waits for the other person to deserve it. A test: whom do you need to pray for, by name, today?

What it doesn’t mean. To love an enemy isn’t to pretend evil is good or to leave the wicked unopposed. You may love a man and still report his crime, shield the weak from him, and let just consequences fall — God, all kindness, is also the righteous Judge. Nor does it mean staying in harm’s way; loving an abuser doesn’t require remaining his target. Enemy-love seeks the offender’s true good and refuses personal revenge; it doesn’t abolish justice, wisdom or self-protection.

Does loving enemies rule out national defence? Pacifist Christians say it does. The more likely reading is that Jesus is speaking to his disciples about their personal conduct; the state has a different calling, to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and Scripture honours the soldier (8:5–13; Luke 3:14). The bridge between the two is Romans 12:19–21: do not take revenge yourself, but leave room for God’s justice.

How does this fit the psalms that call down curses on enemies? Those prayers (Psalms 35; 69; 109) hand vengeance to God rather than taking it; they cry for his justice. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and yet the martyrs in heaven still cry for justice (Revelation 6:10). The believer prays first for his enemy’s repentance, and leaves the rest to God.

“Be perfect.” The word means whole, complete, undivided as well as flawless: the Father’s perfection here is the wholeness of a love without exceptions. His children are called to that undivided love — not as a crushing legal bar but as the shape of the life the Spirit is growing in them.

Is sinless perfection possible in this life? Some in the Wesleyan holiness tradition teach that a believer can reach a state of entire sanctification. The more likely reading is that God’s standard is perfection and stays perfection, but that no believer is without sin now: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8; cf. James 3:2). We press toward it (Philippians 3:12) and will be made like Christ when we see him (1 John 3:2).
verseByVerse.note: “Hate your enemy” is not in the law; it was a popular inference from it. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators.

parallels.desc: you shall be holy, for I am holy

5.theology:
The Law and the Gospel: The Threefold Use of the Law. Reformed theology has distinguished three uses of the law: the civil use (restraining evil in society), the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving us to Christ), and the normative use (guiding the life of the believer). Matthew 5 exercises the second use with particular intensity: Jesus presses the law so deeply inward that no one can claim compliance, and in doing so drives every hearer to the mercy of the one who fulfilled what we cannot.

But Matthew 5 also exercises the third use: the Beatitudes, the salt and light images, and the love of enemies are not legal demands for the unregenerate but the description of the life the Spirit produces in those who are already citizens of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount is simultaneously gospel (this is what the kingdom looks like) and law (this is what you cannot achieve without the Spirit). Held together, they produce the only life worth living: dependent, transformed, and directed toward the glory of the Father.
5.examples:
Then: The Beatitudes describe the whole history of faithful Israel: Abel the righteous who was persecuted, Abraham the meek who sojourned in a land not his own, Hannah who mourned and was comforted, David the poor in spirit who wrote “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:17). The Beatitudes are not new values; they are the values of the faithful covenant people, now fully embodied in the King who pronounces them and perfectly exemplified in his own life.

Now: The world’s beatitudes are the inverse of Jesus’: blessed are the confident, the successful, the powerful, the popular, the comfortable. The Sermon on the Mount is a collision with that value system at every point. The Christian who takes these beatitudes seriously will find themselves increasingly out of step with the surrounding culture — and increasingly at home in the kingdom. The persecution promised in verses 10–12 is not a possible outcome but a promised one: the world does not celebrate the values of the kingdom because the world is not the kingdom. But the kingdom is coming — and the persecuted will inherit it.

6.title: The Hidden Life of the Kingdom
6.text: <sup>1</sup>“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. <sup>2</sup>“Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>3</sup>But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, <sup>4</sup>so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>5</sup>“And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>7</sup>“And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. <sup>8</sup>Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. <sup>9</sup>Pray then like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. <sup>10</sup>Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. <sup>11</sup>Give us this day our daily bread, <sup>12</sup>and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. <sup>13</sup>And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. <sup>14</sup>For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, <sup>15</sup>but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. <sup>16</sup>“And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>17</sup>But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, <sup>18</sup>that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>19</sup>“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, <sup>20</sup>but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup>For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. <sup>22</sup>“The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, <sup>23</sup>but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! <sup>24</sup>“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. <sup>25</sup>“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? <sup>26</sup>Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? <sup>27</sup>And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>28</sup>And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, <sup>29</sup>yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>30</sup>But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? <sup>31</sup>Therefore do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ <sup>32</sup>For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. <sup>33</sup>But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. <sup>34</sup>“Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is a sustained meditation on hiddenness. Give in secret. Pray in secret. Fast without showing it. The recurring phrase is “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” — and it upends the entire economy of religious performance. If God sees in secret, then the audience that matters most cannot be seen. The religious life that performs for human approval has traded the eternal reward for the temporary one, and the exchange is catastrophic.

At the centre of the chapter stands the Lord’s Prayer — six petitions that together describe the whole of what the kingdom life looks like in communion with the Father. First, God’s glory: hallowed be your name. Then God’s reign: your kingdom come. Then dependence: daily bread. Then forgiveness: both received and given. Then protection: from temptation, from evil. The prayer moves from adoration to petition, from God’s agenda to human need, from the cosmic to the daily. It is the complete grammar of prayer in a few short lines.

The chapter ends with an antidote to anxiety that is also a diagnosis of its cause. Anxiety is the fruit of serving the wrong master (v. 24). When God and money compete for ultimate allegiance, anxiety is the symptom of the conflict. The cure is not financial security but reorientation of treasure: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the birds will add what you need. This is not a prosperity promise; it is a priority promise. When the kingdom is first, everything else finds its proper place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Piety Before the Father: Giving, Prayer, and Fasting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses three practices central to Jewish piety — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — and in each case distinguishes the performance of these acts for human recognition from the genuine practice of them before God. The hypocrites have their reward: human applause, now and fully paid. Those who give, pray, and fast before the Father alone receive what the Father alone can give. The section includes the Lord's Prayer as the model of kingdom-oriented prayer: God-centered in its priorities, dependent in its petitions, and honest about the human need for forgiveness. Some details the summary passes over, all treated in the verse-by-verse. The prayer's shape: six petitions in two halves of three — the first three each say your (name, kingdom, will), the second three each say us (give us, forgive us, lead us not). Nothing about our needs appears until God has been addressed three times, and the first three are not requests for God to acquire anything — his name is already holy and his will already done in heaven; they ask that these become true here. Every pronoun in the prayer is plural. There is not one singular pronoun in it: a man praying alone at three in the morning still cannot say "me", and is asking for bread for people he has never met. Daily (v. 11) is epiousios, a word that appears nowhere in Greek literature before this — Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it. The two likely readings ("necessary for existence" and "for the coming day") arrive at the same place: one day's supply, asked one day at a time, which is the manna arrangement of Exodus 16 put into every Christian's mouth. Debts (v. 12) is Matthew's word, the commercial term for what is owed; Luke has "sins"; the familiar "trespasses" came in through Tyndale and the Prayer Book. A trespass is a line crossed and is over when it is over; a debt is a sum outstanding, which is the truer picture. And the tense of "as we also have forgiven" is past — already done, before the asking — matching 5:23-24, where the gift is left at the altar until the matter downstairs is settled.
verseByVerse.theology: The three acts — giving, prayer, fasting — are not optional extras but the basic disciplines of covenant life: relationship with the neighbor (giving), relationship with God (prayer), and relationship with the self (fasting). Jesus does not question whether his disciples will do these things; he assumes they will ("when you give," "when you pray," "when you fast"). The question is motive and audience. Hypocrisy is not performing religious acts — it is performing them for the wrong audience. The hypocrite plays to the crowd; the disciple plays to the Father. The Father's reward — his presence, his approval, his delight — is infinitely superior to human applause.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord's Prayer contains the whole theology of the kingdom in miniature. It begins with the Father's character and glory (hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done) before turning to human need (daily bread, forgiveness, protection). The order is the order of Christian living: God first, then us. The disciple who prays this prayer daily is being trained in a way of seeing the world: God's kingdom is the primary reality; my needs are real but secondary; forgiveness received must be forgiveness extended.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns against practising righteousness before others in order to be seen by them, for then there will be no reward from the Father in heaven. Our devotion must be lived before God, not performed for human applause — whoever seeks people’s praise gets that and nothing more.

The banner. This verse governs the next three examples — giving, prayer and fasting. It isn’t the deeds Jesus forbids but the audience they are performed for. Showy piety was the air the religious elite breathed: alms with fanfare, long prayers where most would notice, fasting worn on the face. In an honour-and-shame culture, religion was a recognised road to status, and his hearers knew the type.

Seen, or in order to be seen? One chapter ago Jesus said, “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works” (5:16). Now he says, beware of practising your righteousness before others “in order to be seen by them.” The issue isn’t visibility. Almsgiving, prayer and fasting were public in that culture; a man who gave to the poor was seen doing it. What Jesus forbids is visibility being the point — the “in order to.” And the endings pull opposite ways: in 5:16 people see and glorify your Father; here the hypocrite wants them to see and think well of him.

No reward. If you do righteousness for human applause, applause is your whole pay. You chose your paymaster. The word Jesus uses in verse 2 was stamped on ancient receipts: “paid in full.” The account is settled; nothing more is owed from heaven — not because the Father is stingy, but because the deed was never done for him. This reward isn’t earning salvation, which is God’s free gift; it is the Father’s delight in and recompense for what his children do out of love for him. Trading that for a few moments of being noticed is the worst bargain a soul can make.

The real test. So the test isn’t whether anybody knows. It is what you would feel if nobody ever did — and, harder, what you feel when someone else gets the credit for something you did (cf. 23:5). A test: whose approval are you really working for?

parallels.desc: they do all their deeds to be seen

verseByVerse.quote: Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When giving to the needy, don’t sound a trumpet like the hypocrites who want praise; give so secretly that your left hand doesn’t know what your right is doing, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you. Giving should flow from mercy toward the needy and love for God, not from a desire to be admired.

Paid in full. The trumpet is almost certainly a figure of speech for making a show of giving. “They have received their reward” means paid in full, nothing more coming. Human praise is real but small and passing; the Father’s reward is eternal — but it goes to those who weren’t chasing the lesser thing.

Mercy, not reward. What should drive our giving isn’t reward at all but mercy. “Give to the needy” literally means to do an act of mercy — help reaching down because need stirs compassion. We give because we have seen a brother in want and love won’t look away (1 John 3:17), and because we imitate a God “rich in mercy” who gave to us when we could never repay (Ephesians 2:4). The secrecy isn’t coldness; it is love so taken up with the person in need that it forgets itself. Giving to be seen keeps one eye on the mirror; giving for mercy keeps both eyes on the neighbour and on God.

Left hand, right hand. Not letting the left hand know what the right is doing isn’t a command to be deceptive but to be unselfconscious — giving without the inner tally of self-congratulation that counts, remembers and expects recognition. Genuine generosity is hidden not only from others but, ideally, from ourselves. We give and move on. And the Father “who sees in secret” is the most attentive and just audience there is: nothing done for him is missed, undervalued or forgotten (cf. Acts 10:4).

Picture it. You hear of a young family at church who have fallen behind on rent. You could write the cheque after the service, mention it to a few friends, and enjoy being known as generous — and that glow would be your whole pay. Or you could slip the money to the pastor in an unmarked envelope, ask him not to say who, and very nearly forget you did it. No one claps. But the Father saw, and that envelope, given for love and not for show, is laid up with him. God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). A test: would you still give if no one ever found out?
verseByVerse.note: “Sound no trumpet” is probably a figure of speech for making a show of giving.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When praying, don’t be like the hypocrites who pray where they will be seen; go into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret, and he will reward you. Prayer is communion with the Father, not a performance — and private prayer is what keeps all our praying honest.

The spot chosen for the sightlines. Standing to pray was normal Jewish practice. Jesus isn’t condemning the posture but the location chosen for visibility — the synagogue and the street corner, where most people would notice. The alternative isn’t another posture but another room, where the only audience is the Father.

Not against praying together. Taken flatly, “go into your room and shut the door” would close every prayer meeting in the world, and plainly he doesn’t mean that. The prayer he is about to teach says “our Father” and “give us,” assuming company. He prayed aloud at Lazarus’s tomb, saying he did it for the people standing there (John 11:41–42), and his church prayed together from its first days (Acts 1:14; 4:24; 12:12). What he regulates is the audience, not the setting. The hypocrites chose their spot for the sightlines; the sin was in the choosing.

The shut door. So ask not where you are standing but whether you would still say this if no one could hear. The shut door is the cure because it is the one place where the audience has been removed, so the habit formed there comes out honest everywhere else. Someone who prays impressively in the meeting and never once alone has exactly this disease. The closed door isn’t the enemy of public prayer; it is what makes public prayer truthful. A test: is your private prayer life larger or smaller than your public one?

The storeroom. The “room” was a storeroom or pantry, the inner room of a small house, often the only one with a door that shut. It was the least impressive space available. Jesus isn’t describing a study or a prayer corner; he is naming the cupboard. Nobody needs a special place.

Someone is watching. “Your Father who sees in secret” occurs for each discipline. It isn’t mainly a warning that God is watching, but the promise that someone is — that the giving nobody thanked you for, the praying nobody counted, the fasting nobody noticed were all observed. The hypocrite’s real problem isn’t that he wants an audience; it is that he has settled for a small one (cf. Luke 18:10–14).
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing, at set hours; the “room” was an inner storeroom, the one private space in a small house.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee and the tax collector

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When praying, don’t heap up empty phrases as the pagans do, thinking they’ll be heard for their many words, for your Father knows what you need before you ask. Prayer isn’t a technique for working on God but honest conversation with a Father who already knows and cares.

Magic, not length. The pagan error isn’t length but magic — the assumption that words multiply and repetition compels divine attention. Pagan prayer often treated the gods as powers to be worked by the right formula repeated enough, like the prophets of Baal crying from morning till noon (1 Kings 18:26–29). Jesus forbids this not because brevity is always better but because prayer isn’t a technique for bending God’s will. It is the difference between a child speaking to his father and a man operating a machine.

What it doesn’t forbid. This verse troubles many people, so say plainly what it doesn’t forbid. Not long prayers: Jesus spent a whole night in prayer (Luke 6:12). Not asking the same thing more than once: in Gethsemane he prayed the same words three times (26:44), and he told a parable to teach us “always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Not a set form of words — for in the next breath he gives one. Vainness is a quality of the heart, not the vocabulary. The Psalms have been the church’s prayer book for centuries and the Lord’s Prayer said daily for two thousand years, and neither is vain when meant; while someone can babble as emptily off the top of his head as off a page, filling silence or performing fluency.

Your Father knows. “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” That doesn’t make prayer pointless; it makes it a relationship rather than a transaction. We pray not to inform God but to be with him and align our desires with his. So pray at length when your heart is full, and briefly when it isn’t. Bring the same request back tomorrow. Use words others have written when your own won’t come. Only don’t imagine God is worn down by volume or won over by technique (cf. Ecclesiastes 5:2). A test: when you pray, are you talking to your Father or trying to work a mechanism?

parallels.desc: the prophets of Baal cry from morning to noon

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches his disciples to pray: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” Prayer begins with God himself — his name, his reign and his will — and we may come to him as his children because of Christ.

God first. The prayer opens not with our needs but with God — his name, his kingdom, his will — before it reaches bread. The order retrains the heart: we are made for God’s agenda, not merely his assistance. A prayer that begins with me will often never get past me.

“Our Father.” Feel the wonder of the address. The eternal God, who needs nothing and dwells in unapproachable light, invites us to call him Father. We can do it only because the Son has made us sons and daughters and the Spirit cries within us, “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). He is no distant force or stern tyrant, but the Father of the prodigal who runs down the road. And it is “our” Father; we never pray alone, but as part of a family.

Is God the Father of everyone? He is the Creator of all, and he cares for all (5:45; Acts 17:28). But the Father Jesus teaches us to address is the Father who adopts his people in Christ (John 1:12; Galatians 4:4–6). Anyone may come to him through Jesus, and that is how he becomes “our Father.”

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” means treated as holy, honoured, held precious. In the Bible a name stands for the whole person, so God’s name is God himself as he has made himself known. This petition asks that he be revered and taken seriously — in a world that uses his name as a curse or forgets it, in the church, and first in my own heart, lips and life. It asks God to stop being treated as common, and begins with me ceasing to do so (cf. Ezekiel 36:23). A test: does your life treat God’s name as holy or as ordinary?

Your kingdom come. Is the kingdom here or still to come? Both. God’s saving reign has arrived in Jesus (see 4:17) and advances wherever the gospel takes root, yet its full glory awaits Christ’s return. So to pray “your kingdom come” is to ask two things: extend your reign today — in me, in the lost being saved, in your church — and hasten the day you come to make all things new.

Your will be done. In heaven God’s will is done perfectly, gladly and without delay. This petition asks that earth become like that. And it starts at home: it is the prayer of a surrendered heart that says with Jesus in the garden, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42; cf. 26:42). It is submission (let your will rule me), mission (let it sweep over a rebellious world), and hope (let heaven and earth become one).
verseByVerse.note: “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us this day our daily bread,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches his disciples to ask, “Give us this day our daily bread.” We are to depend on the Father, one day at a time, for everything we need — and to pray for others’ needs as well as our own.

Today’s bread. After God’s name, kingdom and will, the prayer turns to our needs, and the first is the humblest: bread, and only for today. Like the manna that fell one morning at a time (Exodus 16:4), it trains us in daily dependence rather than self-sufficient hoarding. Israel couldn’t gather manna for two days without it spoiling; the whole arrangement taught a nation to ask again every morning, and this petition puts the same arrangement in every Christian’s mouth.

Not only for the poor. Someone with a full bank account needs this petition as much as anyone, perhaps more, since wealth tempts us to forget that every loaf comes from the Father’s hand. Money can’t make your heart beat, hold off illness or secure tomorrow; rich and poor alike live each day on mercy. So Scripture prays, “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you” (Proverbs 30:8–9). To ask for daily bread with a full cupboard is to confess gladly that it is all gift. A test: do you thank God for provision you think you earned?

More than food. “Bread” stands for more than food. Under it we may bring God everything we need for body and life: health and work, shelter and provision, strength for the day — and wisdom for the meeting, patience with the children, courage for the hard conversation. Whatever today requires, you may ask your Father for it, one day at a time. He welcomes his children’s small, practical requests.

A puzzling word. The word translated “daily” appears almost nowhere in Greek before the Lord’s Prayer, and Origen, a native Greek speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it. Three readings compete: bread necessary for existence; bread for the coming day (today’s, or tomorrow’s if prayed at evening); or, as Jerome rendered it, “supersubstantial” bread, read by a long tradition as the bread of the Lord’s Supper. The first two are the likely ones and arrive at the same place: enough for one day, asked one day at a time. The third is unlikely; the context — debts, temptation, evil — is ordinary, and the Supper hadn’t yet been given.

“Us.” And notice that every pronoun for the one praying is plural: give us, our bread, forgive us, lead us, deliver us. Someone can pray it alone at three in the morning and still can’t say “me.” He is asking bread for people he has never met — which makes it impossible to pray this prayer and remain unconcerned whether anyone else has any.

parallels.desc: feed me with the food that is needful for me

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
