parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stretches out his hand, touches the leper, says, “I will; be clean,” and he is cleansed at once; Jesus tells him to say nothing but to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded. Christ’s holiness isn’t defiled by our uncleanness but drives it out, and he restores outcasts to God’s people.

He didn’t have to touch him. The next healing in this chapter is done at a distance, by a word. The power didn’t need contact. Nothing was gained by touching except the touch itself. And “stretched out his hand” echoes the outstretched arm of God in Exodus. That hand crossed the distance the law had set and rested on skin nobody had willingly touched in years.

Contagion reversed. He touched first, then said, “be clean.” For a moment Jesus was in contact with an unclean man not yet healed. By the law, touching made a person unclean. Here the flow runs the other way: his holiness isn’t contaminated by the leper’s uncleanness; it expels it. That is the gospel in a gesture. “I will; be clean” — no formula, no process, simply the will of the Creator restoring what disease destroyed. A test: what in you do you think is too unclean for Christ to touch?

Say nothing. The silence wasn’t arbitrary. Mark tells us the man “went out and began to talk freely about it,” so that Jesus “could no longer openly enter a town” (Mark 1:45). A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under crowds, and it did.

Show yourself to the priest. Jesus honours the law (5:17). Only a priest could declare a leper clean and readmit him to Israel’s worship, with the offerings Leviticus 14 prescribes: two birds, cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop, washings, eight days and sacrifices. Every priest knew the ceremony and none expected to use it; in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman are recorded as cleansed. So a man walking into the temple asking for the rite of a cleansed leper was “a proof to them” — handing the priesthood a page they had never had cause to open, and making someone ask who had done this.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Capernaum a centurion comes to Jesus pleading for his servant, who lies paralysed at home in terrible suffering. A powerful Gentile humbles himself for a lowly servant — showing the faith and compassion that please Christ.

A centurion. The backbone of the Roman military system: a career officer nominally commanding a hundred men, risen from the ranks. Capernaum lay in Herod Antipas’s territory, so he may have served Herod’s Roman-style army; either way, he was a Gentile soldier in a force the locals resented. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented sympathetically — a striking fact in an occupied land.

For a servant. He comes not commanding but “appealing,” and for a servant — someone of low status whose suffering moves him. The word can mean servant or boy; Luke says he was a slave the centurion highly valued (Luke 7:2). Those with power often notice only their own needs; this man uses his for the powerless. A test: how do you use whatever power you have — for yourself or for those beneath you?

Did he come himself? Matthew has the centurion speak with Jesus directly; Luke says he sent Jewish elders and then friends, and the two never meet (Luke 7:3–8). That is a difference of reporting, not a contradiction. A man is said to do what he does through his agents, as we say a king built a palace. Matthew compresses the exchange to its principals because his point is the centurion’s faith; Luke, interested in how Jews and Gentiles dealt with each other, keeps the messengers.

Why the elders came. Luke explains why Jewish elders would carry a message for an officer of the occupation: “he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue” (Luke 7:5). The ruined synagogue at Capernaum today is later, but it seems to stand on a first-century foundation, very possibly the floor of his.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus offers to come and heal the servant, but the centurion says he isn’t worthy to have Jesus under his roof — “only say the word, and my servant will be healed.” True faith rests on the power of Christ’s word alone, and humbly recognises its unworthiness before him.

Protecting Jesus. “I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.” This is more than self-abasement. A Jew who entered a Gentile house incurred ceremonial defilement — why Peter needed a vision before going to Cornelius (Acts 10:28), and why the leaders wouldn’t enter Pilate’s headquarters before Passover (John 18:28). The centurion knows it. He is saying, “Coming under my roof will cost you, and it isn’t necessary” — the courtesy of a man who has learned what his neighbours believe, offered while his servant is dying.

A question? Jesus’ words in verse 7 can also be read as a question: “Shall I come and heal him?” — raising the very issue of entering a Gentile house so the centurion can answer it. It can’t be settled, and the sense is much the same.

Only say the word. What makes this faith rather than respect is what it assumes. He doesn’t think Jesus needs to be present, see the patient or touch him. The word alone is enough — which is how Genesis says the world came to be, and what the psalm says of God: “He sent out his word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20). The church has prayed his sentence for centuries before communion: “Lord, I am not worthy… but only say the word.” And it is why we pray to the ascended Lord now: distance is nothing to his power. A test: do you trust Christ’s word even when you can’t see him act?
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house; the centurion spares Jesus the problem.

parallels.desc: unlawful for a Jew to visit a foreigner
he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion explains that he too is under authority and gives orders that are obeyed, and Jesus marvels, saying he has found no such faith in Israel. Faith sees that Christ’s word carries God’s own authority — and such faith can astonish the Son of God.

The argument from authority. The centurion reasons by analogy: because he stands under authority, his commands carry the weight of the power above him. When he says “Go,” Rome stands behind the word. So he sees that when Jesus speaks, God’s power stands behind his word. That is the core of faith: confidence not in the one asking but in the authority of the one asked.

Further than he knew. But press the analogy further than he could. He pictures Jesus like himself, a man under authority whose word carries weight because a greater power backs it. That is true insofar as the Son is sent by the Father. It isn’t the whole truth. Jesus isn’t a prophet holding God’s power on loan, as Elijah and Elisha did; he is the Son in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). When Elisha raised the dead he prayed; when Jesus heals he simply speaks. The centurion had the right end of the truth and didn’t yet know how deep it went.

He marvelled. “With no one in Israel have I found such faith.” Faith isn’t a national or religious achievement; it is seeing who Jesus is, open to anyone. And the Gospels record Jesus marvelling at only two things: this Gentile’s faith, and his hometown’s unbelief — “he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark 6:6). Not storms, demons, crowds or his own betrayal. Faith is what astonished him, in both directions. A test: which would Jesus marvel at in you — your faith or your unbelief?

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says many will come from east and west to feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom, while the “sons of the kingdom” are thrown into outer darkness; then he heals the servant at that very moment. The kingdom belongs to those who believe, whatever their background, and no privilege of birth or membership secures it.

The feast. “From east and west” echoes the prophets’ gathering promises: “I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you” (Isaiah 43:5; cf. Psalm 107:3). And reclining at table is Isaiah’s banquet on the mountain, “a feast of rich food” where God swallows up death (Isaiah 25:6–8). The imagery is wholly Jewish. What is new is who sits at the table: the nations recline with the patriarchs, while the patriarchs’ own descendants stand outside.

Sons of the kingdom. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring phrase for final loss (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30), and the first time he uses it, those in view are “the sons of the kingdom” — insiders by birth. Jesus takes the title people used of themselves with satisfaction and attaches it to the ones put out.

A guard. This verse has been misused. It doesn’t say God has finished with Israel and replaced her. Paul answered that flatly — “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1) — and warned Gentile believers against arrogance (Romans 11:18–21). What Jesus dismantles isn’t Israel but presumption: the assumption that descent secures anything. John the Baptist said the same (3:9), and it is just as false when a Gentile assumes church membership secures it. The warning has been transferred, not retired. A test: are you trusting your religious background, or Christ himself?

Healed that hour. “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” Faith is the channel, not the source. The centurion’s faith didn’t heal his servant; Jesus’ word did. But faith received what only Jesus could give, and “at that very moment” distance collapsed before his word.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring picture of final judgment.

parallels.desc: from the north and from the west

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus entered Peter's house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Peter’s house Jesus finds Peter’s mother-in-law sick with fever; he touches her hand, the fever leaves, and she rises and serves him. Jesus cares for ordinary needs in ordinary homes, and restored life expresses itself in service.

No sickness too small. The miracles flow one into the next: a leper, a paralysed servant, and now a fever in a family home. There is no threshold of severity below which Jesus is unconcerned. He touches her hand — the same touch that cleansed the leper — and the fever goes.

She served. She rises at once and serves him, a detail Matthew notes without comment. That is the New Testament pattern: grace received becomes service given. A test: how is the grace you have received showing itself in service?

Peter was married. Matthew mentions her in passing and so records a plain fact: Peter had a wife. You don’t acquire a mother-in-law any other way. Nor is it an isolated hint: years later Paul asks, “Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?” (1 Corinthians 9:5). Peter was still married, his wife travelling with him, decades after this morning. That is no argument against celibacy freely chosen; Paul was unmarried and commended singleness to those given it (1 Corinthians 7:7; cf. 19:12). But whatever office Peter held, a married man could hold it, and a rule requiring otherwise can’t appeal to him. And there is something homely in learning that the first thing we know of the leading apostle’s household is that Jesus was in it, taking a sick old woman by the hand.

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick, This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening many demon-oppressed and sick people are brought, and Jesus drives out spirits with a word and heals all the sick, fulfilling Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” Jesus’ healings were signs of the kingdom and foretastes of the full healing he secured by his suffering, which will be complete at the resurrection.

All who were sick. The whole town gathered at the door (Mark 1:33), and Jesus healed “all who were sick” — not the most deserving or the most faithful, but all. It anticipates the breadth of the gospel: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Isaiah 53. Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 — from the song of the suffering Servant — to the healings in Galilee. The healings aren’t separate from the atonement; they are its advance expression. The cross is the once-for-all bearing of sin and its consequences; the healings were enacted promises that the One who would bear it all was already at work.

Does God still heal like this, and is healing guaranteed in the atonement? Continuationist Christians point out that no text says the gifts will end, that Paul lists healing among the gifts (1 Corinthians 12:9), and that James tells the sick to call for prayer (James 5:14–16); some also read Isaiah 53:4 as promising healing now. The cessationist reading is the more likely. Miracles in Scripture cluster around the great moments of revelation — Moses, Elijah and Elisha, and Christ and his apostles — to authenticate God’s messengers (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Even in the apostolic age healing was never automatic: Paul kept his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20), prescribed wine for Timothy’s stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Epaphroditus nearly died (Philippians 2:27). God still heals in answer to prayer, but Isaiah 53:4 does not guarantee it in this life. Its final fulfilment is the resurrection, and Peter applies the same chapter to sin-bearing (1 Peter 2:24). Beware the cruel teaching that healing is guaranteed if only faith is strong enough; it heaps guilt on the suffering. Sometimes grace carries us through sickness rather than removing it (2 Corinthians 12:9). A test: are you trusting God when he doesn’t heal as you hoped?

Why so many demons? Demonic powers are real throughout Scripture — behind idolatry, which is sacrificing to demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; Psalm 106:37) — yet open possession is almost absent in the Old Testament. In the Gospels it erupts, because the King has come. His arrival forces the kingdom of darkness into the open: “if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (12:28). And it recedes in the letters not because the demonic vanished but because the decisive battle was won: Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15). The letters reframe the war as the believer’s daily resistance, clothed in God’s armour (Ephesians 6:12; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8–9). One indwelt by the Spirit is not owned by such powers; the Christian fights from within Christ’s victory.

parallels.desc: by his wounds you have been healed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–34 — The Cost of Following and the Lord of Storm and Demons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 8 moves from healing to the cost of discipleship and the authority of Jesus over creation and the demonic. Two would-be followers learn that Jesus offers no earthly security (no place to lay his head, no leave for burial rites). Then Jesus stills a storm with a rebuke and casts demons into pigs, and the Gadarenes ask him to leave. The sequence shows that following Jesus is neither comfortable nor universally welcomed. Four things more, all treated below. The scribe says "Teacher" and the next man says "Lord" (vv. 19, 21) — and that distinction runs through Matthew, where disciples say Lord while opponents, enquirers and the rich young man say Teacher, and Judas alone at the supper says Rabbi. The scribe files his own assessment in his first word. Note too that across the Gospels the people who volunteer are tested and the people who are called simply go. Matthew's word for the storm is not the word for a storm: he writes seismos megas, a great shaking — the standard Greek for an earthquake — where Mark has the ordinary term for a squall. And he uses it twice more, at the crucifixion (27:51-54) and at the tomb (28:2), each time as the setting for a declaration of who Jesus is. The sleeping is the only time the Gospels record it, and the scene is Jonah replayed and inverted: a man asleep below decks in a storm, woken by terrified sailors with almost these words (Jon. 1:5-6) — but Jonah slept fleeing God and was the cause of the storm and had to be thrown into the sea, while this sleeper is the end of it, and will himself be swallowed for three days (12:39-41). On the place name, the manuscripts genuinely divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes; Gerasa is thirty miles inland, Gadara six, and Gergesa (Kursi) is on the shore with the steep bank the story requires. And the pigs raise a question the passage does not answer — two thousand animals, somebody's business, destroyed — which is faced squarely below rather than tidied away.
verseByVerse.theology: The stilling of the storm is the Christological center of the chapter: "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?" The disciples' question is Matthew's question to the reader. Only the Creator can command his creation. The storm-still and the Gadarene exorcism together display authority over the two great threats of the ancient world — chaos (the sea) and the demonic (the Legion). Both submit instantly. The appropriate response is not comfort but worship — and the disciples begin to learn it.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadarenes' request that Jesus leave their region is one of the saddest verses in the Gospels. They preferred their pigs to their Deliverer. The economy of the region mattered more than the liberation of two men in chains. This is not ancient history; every age chooses its pigs. The question Jesus poses to every community: what do you value more than the healing he brings?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. And a scribe came up and said to him, "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus prepares to cross the lake, a scribe declares, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” Enthusiastic promises to follow Christ must be tested by what following him actually costs.

Teacher or Lord. A detail Matthew plants deliberately: the scribe calls Jesus “Teacher”; the next man calls him “Lord.” Throughout Matthew, disciples call Jesus Lord, while outsiders and opponents call him Teacher — Pharisees, Sadducees, the rich young man. At the Last Supper the others say “Lord,” and Judas says “Rabbi” (26:22, 25). So the scribe’s opening word reveals his assessment: he wants to attach himself to a rabbi, a move he understands.

Volunteers are tested. His offer is unlimited — “wherever you go” — the boldest promise in the chapter. And a pattern holds across the Gospels: those who volunteer are tested; those who are called simply go. Peter and Andrew offered nothing; they were told to follow and did. Jesus neither accepts nor refuses the scribe; he tells him one fact about what he proposes to join, and Matthew never says what the man did. The story is left open because the reader must answer it. A test: is your commitment to Christ based on what you imagine following him will be, or on what he says it costs?

parallels.desc: “Let us go across to the other side”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Another of the disciples said to him, "Lord, let me first go and bury my father." And Jesus said to him, "Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the scribe that foxes have holes and birds nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; to another who asks first to bury his father, he says, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” Following Christ offers no earthly security and allows no postponement; his call comes before every other claim.

Nowhere to lay his head. Jesus offers the scribe no home, no fixed address, no earthly security. Following means sharing that.

Why does Jesus call himself the Son of Man? It was his favourite name for himself, and almost no one else used it. It draws on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom. Yet it also speaks of his true humanity and lowliness, as here, where the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Jesus chose a title that held both his glory and his suffering.

Burying his father. Burying a parent was among the most sacred duties. But consider the situation. Jewish burial took place within a day of death; a man whose father had just died would be at home among mourners, not on a roadside listening to a teacher. The request is more likely the familiar idiom: let me stay until my father’s life is over and my duty discharged — which might mean years. Not a plea to attend a funeral, but a request for indefinite postponement dressed as duty. “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” means: let the spiritually dead, who haven’t responded to the kingdom, handle what can wait.

Not neglect of family. This must be guarded, because it has been misused. Nothing here licenses neglecting your family. Jesus attacked exactly that abuse, where religious vows excused neglect of aging parents: “for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God” (15:6). Paul says anyone who doesn’t provide for his household “has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8), and Jesus provided for his mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). Caring for family is part of following Christ. Where the collision is real — a family that will cut you off for following him — Jesus tells the truth in advance: he comes first, and he knows the cost.

Later. For most of us the application is quieter. The man isn’t refusing Jesus; he is saying “later,” for an excellent reason. That is our shape too: I’ll get serious when the children are older, when work settles, when I retire. The reasons are good, which is what makes them effective. But there will never be a convenient window; there is only today (cf. Luke 9:61–62). A test: what are you postponing in following Christ until “later”?
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died. Jesus’ call outranks even that.

parallels.desc: no one who looks back is fit for the kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. And they went and woke him, saying, "Save us, Lord; we are perishing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gets into a boat with his disciples; a great storm arises and the boat is being swamped while he sleeps, and they wake him: “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” Following Jesus can lead straight into storms, and in them the right response is to cry to him.

Following into the storm. The disciples who do follow get into the boat and immediately meet the storm. Following Jesus leads into difficulty; he never promised otherwise.

A great shaking. Matthew’s word for the storm is the word for an earthquake, “a great shaking.” He uses it again at the cross, where “the earth shook” and the centurion confessed him (27:51–54), and at the tomb, “there was a great earthquake” (28:2). Three convulsions of creation, each the setting for a revelation of who Jesus is.

The lake. The Sea of Galilee lies about seven hundred feet below sea level, ringed by hills. Cold air rushing down the ravines meets warm air over the water, and the surface can turn dangerous within minutes. Professional fishermen were in that boat, and they concluded they would drown — which tells you what kind of night it was.

He was asleep. It is the only time the Gospels record Jesus sleeping, and it is in a boat filling with water — real human exhaustion. And one other man in Scripture slept through a storm at sea. Jonah went down into the ship and “fell fast asleep,” and the sailors woke him: “What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! … that we may not perish” (Jonah 1:5–6). Jesus later points to the sign of Jonah (12:39–41). Every element is reversed: Jonah slept running from God; Jesus sleeps resting in him. Jonah caused the storm; Jesus ends it. The sailors threw Jonah into the sea to save themselves; the disciples wake a man who speaks to the water and it stops.

“Save us, Lord.” The cry is panicked, but it is prayer: they ran to Jesus, not away from him. Fear isn’t the opposite of faith; indifference is. A test: in your storm, are you running to Christ or away from him?
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?" Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. And the men marveled, saying, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks why they are afraid, “O you of little faith,” then rebukes the winds and sea, and there is a great calm; the men marvel, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” Jesus commands creation as only God can, and he is present with his people in every storm, even when he seems asleep.

Disciples first. Jesus rebukes the disciples before the storm; the order is deliberate. Their fear was the bigger problem. “O you of little faith” — they believe, but their faith is too small for the crisis. Notice what he doesn’t rebuke: not their waking him, not the panic in the prayer. The rebuke is for fear that crowded out trust, not for crying out.

Only God does this. Then he rises and speaks to the storm as to a servant, and it obeys. The psalm had said of God: “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). “What sort of man is this?” is the right question, the one Matthew’s Gospel answers. Only the Creator commands creation.

When he seems asleep. Mark records what they said waking him: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38). Anyone who has prayed through a night when nothing moved has said something like it. His sleeping didn’t mean indifference — he did what they asked and more — nor absence: he was in the boat. Whatever reached them had to come through him first. And notice how they got into the storm: they were out there because they had obeyed him. Obedience doesn’t guarantee calm water; it can put you in the weather. A storm isn’t automatic proof you took a wrong turn.

Not always calm. Sometimes he doesn’t still the storm. Paul asked three times and kept the thorn, given grace to carry it (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What is promised isn’t always a change of weather, but that he is in the boat, that he isn’t indifferent though he seems so, and that there is a far shore — because he said, “let us go across,” and he has never failed to land anyone he set out with. A test: can you trust him while the storm still rages?

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. And behold, they cried out, "What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other side, in Gadarene country, two violently demon-possessed men come out of the tombs and cry, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” Jesus has authority over the powers of darkness, which know who he is and know their judgment is certain.

Chaos on land. After authority over chaos at sea comes authority over chaos on land. Two men so fierce no one could pass, living among tombs — unclean places, outside society, beyond human help. The demons know Jesus at once: “Son of God.” They have no confusion about who he is. Their theology is accurate; their allegiance is catastrophically wrong (James 2:19).

Two men or one? Mark and Luke describe only one man, “Legion” (Mark 5:1–20; Luke 8:26–39). That isn’t a contradiction. Saying one doesn’t deny a second; Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent of the two, while Matthew notes there were two. He does the same at Jericho, with two blind men where Mark names only Bartimaeus (20:30; Mark 10:46).

Which place? Manuscripts of all three Gospels vary between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes. Gerasa was a city some thirty miles from the lake; Gadara about six miles off, its territory perhaps reaching the shore; Gergesa, probably modern Kursi on the eastern bank, lies on the water with a steep slope into it. The district was likely named by different nearby towns. What the story requires exists: a steep bank on the eastern shore, in Gentile country, with tombs above it.

Was this really demon possession, or mental illness misunderstood? The Gospels distinguish the two (4:24), and these men’s demons speak, recognise Jesus as the Son of God and know the time of their judgment, which no illness does. But that gives no reason to treat mental illness today as demonic. Those who suffer should be given medical care and pastoral love, and every believer can know that he belongs to Christ, not to any other power.

“Before the time.” They don’t dispute the outcome. They know there is a fixed day and it goes against them; only the calendar is in doubt. That is the demonic predicament: settled certainty about the future, with no intention of changing course. Knowing the truth about Jesus without submitting to him saves no one. A test: do you only know who Jesus is, or have you bowed to him?
verseByVerse.note: Gadara was a Gentile city of the Decapolis, south-east of the lake; Mark and Luke say “Gerasenes” and mention only one man. Tombs were unclean places.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A herd of pigs is feeding nearby, and the demons beg Jesus, if he casts them out, to send them into the pigs. The powers of evil can do nothing without Christ’s permission, and their nature is to destroy whatever they inhabit.

Begging for a destination. The demons don’t dispute Jesus’ authority to cast them out; they beg only about where to go. Even their request must be submitted to him. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and a large herd shows this was Gentile country. Jesus permits it without explanation.

What about the owner? A thoughtful reader will ask. Mark says there were about two thousand pigs (Mark 5:13) — someone’s substantial living, destroyed in an afternoon. Several things can be said honestly. The destruction is the demons’ work: they ask, he permits, and they do to the herd within a minute what they had done to two men for years. The pigs are a demonstration of what demons do, not of what Jesus does. The owners were almost certainly Gentiles in the Decapolis, breaking no law of their own, so this wasn’t a judgment on Jews keeping pigs. And Jesus states the valuation in this Gospel: “Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!” (12:12). Two men living in tombs, self-harming, beyond reach, were given back their minds; against that, a herd is a real cost and a small one. The town that made the opposite calculation is the villain of the story, not its victim.

The honest silence. Jesus never explains, and the Gospels don’t apologise. Matthew records the loss and the town’s response and moves on. The text doesn’t treat the objection as unanswerable or as trivial. It mattered to someone, and Scripture lets that stand. A test: do you value people restored by Christ above your own losses?
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a large herd shows this was Gentile country.

parallels.desc: the pig is unclean to you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus says, “Go,” and the demons enter the pigs, which rush down the steep bank into the sea and drown; the herdsmen flee to the city and report everything, including what happened to the possessed men. Christ’s single word overpowers a legion of demons, and the evil that destroyed the pigs shows what it would have done to the men.

One word. “Go.” Throughout the chapter everything turns on a word: to the leper, “be clean”; to the centurion, “let it be done”; to the wind and sea, a rebuke; and now to a legion of demons no chain could hold: “Go.” No formula, ritual or invocation of a higher name. Jewish exorcists of the time used elaborate procedures — incantations, roots, rings; Josephus describes one at length. Jesus speaks one word and doesn’t raise his voice.

What the demons would have done. The herd’s rush into the sea shows what would have happened to the men if the demons had stayed. The demonic destroys whatever it inhabits.

Honest witnesses. The herdsmen fled and “told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men.” They had just watched their employer’s herd go over a cliff and had every reason to say nothing or to shade the story. Instead they reported all of it, including the healing. The first news of Jesus in the Decapolis came from frightened pig-keepers whose report was mostly about their own catastrophe — and was accurate. A test: when telling what God has done, do you tell the whole truth, even when it costs you?

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole city comes out to meet Jesus and, seeing him, begs him to leave their region. People who value their possessions above Christ may ask him to go — and he may grant it, so we must not harden our hearts while he is near.

Begging like the demons. “They begged him to leave their region” — the same verb used of the demons in verse 31. The city begs as the demons begged. Two neighbours set free, a stronghold of terror broken, and the response is to ask the healer to leave. The lost pigs matter more than the liberation of two men. It isn’t only ancient callousness; it is our tendency to resist grace that costs us something.

He went. Don’t rush past how sobering this is. We love the Jesus who pursues every sinner, and the seeking Shepherd is real. But when people settle their hearts against him and say “depart,” he can take them at their word. Paul says three times of those who rejected God, “God gave them up” (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). The most fearful answer God gives to a prayer is to grant the request, “Leave us alone.” Scripture sounds the warning repeatedly: “My Spirit shall not abide in man forever” (Genesis 6:3); “I gave them over to their stubborn hearts” (Psalm 81:12); “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone” (Hosea 4:17). Jesus wept over Jerusalem: “How often would I have gathered your children together… and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate” (23:37–38). He grieves to leave, but he leaves.

The open door. Yet there is mercy inside the warning: today he hasn’t left. He still knocks (Revelation 3:20). “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15); “Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). The terror is real, and so, right now, is the open door. A test: is there anything you value so much that you would rather Christ left you alone?

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 is a sustained meditation on the authority of the Son of God. He has authority over disease (leper, fever), over distance (servant healed at a word), over demons (v. 16), and over creation (storm). Reformed theology insists that this authority is not delegated but inherent: Jesus is not a prophet with God’s power on loan but the eternal Son in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same — both accomplish what they declare. The centurion’s faith grasps this: faith is resting on the word of One who has absolute authority to perform what he promises.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, trained in chains of command, recognized the absolute authority of Jesus. His faith put to shame those who had grown up with the Scriptures but had domesticated their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that regards faith as a psychological coping mechanism. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it is epistemically grounded in the nature of the One trusted. We trust Christ not because belief makes us feel better but because he is the Lord of heaven and earth whose word does not return void. When we pray, we address the One who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he then said to the paralytic—“Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>14</sup>Then the disciples of John came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>15</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. <sup>16</sup>No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. <sup>17</sup>Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.” <sup>18</sup>While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. <sup>20</sup>And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, <sup>21</sup>for she said to herself, “If I only touch his garment, I will be made well.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And instantly the woman was made well. <sup>23</sup>And when Jesus came to the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, <sup>24</sup>he said, “Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. <sup>25</sup>But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. <sup>26</sup>And the report of this went through all that district. <sup>27</sup>And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” <sup>28</sup>When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” <sup>29</sup>Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith let it be done to you.” <sup>30</sup>And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about it.” <sup>31</sup>But they went away and spread his fame through all that district. <sup>32</sup>As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. <sup>33</sup>And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, “Never was anything like this seen in Israel.” <sup>34</sup>But the Pharisees said, “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 begins with the most audacious claim in Jesus’ ministry: “Your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately see the implication — only God can forgive sins — and charge blasphemy. Jesus responds by healing the paralytic as evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance. This is Matthew’s thesis: Jesus has come not primarily to heal bodies but to heal souls, not primarily to liberate from Roman occupation but to liberate from the bondage of sin and guilt.

The call of Matthew himself is a microcosm of the gospel. A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a social and religious outcast — is called with a two-word summons. He rises and follows. The banquet that follows is a picture of the kingdom: Jesus eating with the unworthy, the Pharisees scandalized, Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”). The chapter closes with Jesus surveying the harassed crowds with compassion and calling for labourers. The mission of the King now extends through his people.

Read straight through, the chapter reveals a second pattern woven beneath the miracles: in story after story faith stands beside unbelief, and the two are sifted apart. The paralytic comes carried by friends whose faith Jesus sees (v. 2) — while the scribes silently cry blasphemy. Matthew rises at a word — while the Pharisees mutter at the table. The ruler kneels and the unclean woman reaches, both in bold faith — while the hired mourners laugh him to scorn. The blind men confess “Yes, Lord” — while the watching Pharisees, at the chapter’s climax, sneer that he casts out demons “by the prince of demons” (v. 34). The same Jesus, the same works — and they divide every heart that meets them: some come empty-handed and receive everything, while others, certain they need nothing, receive nothing and only harden. This is the dividing line the whole Gospel will trace, and it is why the chapter closes not in triumph but in compassion for the harassed and helpless crowds (vv. 36–38) — the harvest is plentiful, and this faith must be carried to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins — triggering the first direct conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, outraging the Pharisees. When John's disciples ask why Jesus's disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with three images: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth, and the new wine. The old forms cannot contain the new reality that has arrived. The scribes never spoke — Matthew says they said it "to themselves" (v. 3), and Jesus answers the unspoken charge, which is itself a claim as large as the one being disputed (Jer. 17:10; 1 Kgs. 8:39). And their theology is correct: only the offended party can waive an offence, and no priest in Israel ever forgave anybody — he declared a forgiveness God had granted. So the alternatives really are God or blasphemer, and they could see it. Jesus does not call their conclusion mistaken but evil (poneros) — the indictment is of a heart that settled the question before weighing it. On the title: Son of Man does two contradictory things at once, which is why he chose it. In Hebrew idiom it means simply "a human being" (God calls Ezekiel that ninety times), and in Daniel 7:13-14 it is the highest title in the Old Testament — dominion, glory, an everlasting kingdom. Innocuous enough to say in public, loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel knew. And the two decisive words in v. 6 are on earth: everyone believed sins were forgiven in heaven; the disputed point is that the transaction can be completed here, by a voice, without temple, priest or sacrifice. Note also that the crowd's "authority to men" is plural (v. 8) — Matthew alone has it, and this is the Gospel that will record the keys given to Peter (16:19) and binding and loosing given to the church (18:18). On Matthew's booth: it was a customs post on the Via Maris at the frontier between Antipas's and Philip's territory, and the point most often missed is that Peter could go back to fishing and Matthew could not — a tax franchise was a purchased concession with men queuing for it. He burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. And Hosea 6:6 is Matthew's own verse: he quotes it twice (9:13; 12:7) and no other New Testament writer quotes it at all, both times against men who are technically correct and pastorally monstrous.
verseByVerse.theology: The paralytic episode is the theological pivot: Jesus claims authority to forgive sins, which belongs to God alone. The scribes are theologically right that only God forgives sins; they are catastrophically wrong in their conclusion that Jesus is therefore blaspheming. The miracle of healing is offered as proof of the greater miracle of forgiveness — the visible confirms the invisible. Matthew's call and the meal with sinners then demonstrate what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick, not the healthy.
verseByVerse.examples: The three images of newness — bridegroom, cloth, wineskins — announce that Jesus is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfillment and transformation. The joy of the bridegroom's presence cannot be contained in old mourning forms. The new covenant is not a patch on the old but its completion. The Pharisees' question about fasting reveals that they are still thinking in terms of the old forms; Jesus is announcing that the age of the bridegroom has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back in Capernaum, people bring Jesus a paralysed man on a bed, and seeing their faith, Jesus says, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” Jesus goes first to our deepest need, forgiveness, and he responds to faith that carries the helpless to him.

The deeper need. The man came for his legs; Jesus goes first to his soul. “Take heart, my son” — tender words before any healing. Then, to everyone’s shock, “Your sins are forgiven.” The paralysis is real and will be dealt with, but the deeper need comes first.

A verdict. Notice the grammar. He doesn’t say, “God will forgive you if…” or “Seek God and perhaps…” He says, “Your sins are forgiven” — a verdict pronounced over a man who has done nothing but be carried through a door. That is justification: not a process by which a sinner slowly becomes good enough, but a declaration in which the Judge pronounces the guilty righteous. The man left with his legs mended, which everyone saw, and his record cleared, which no one saw and which mattered infinitely more. And the pardon isn’t cheap: the Judge who pronounces it will pay for it himself outside a city wall, so that it is just as well as merciful.

Their faith. Jesus saw “their faith” — the friends’, whose effort carried him; Mark says they dug through the roof (Mark 2:4). If you are carrying someone — a husband who won’t come, a son who has walked away, a friend too depressed to pray — you can’t believe for them; Jesus still speaks to the man himself and pardons him personally. But you can carry them to where Jesus is: pray for them by name for years, keep the relationship open so there is still a stretcher when they need one, don’t make your love conditional, and be willing to look foolish. Keep carrying. A test: whom are you carrying to Jesus in prayer?

For the one carried. And if you suspect you are the paralytic — your faith too thin to count — look at what this man contributes: nothing. He doesn’t argue his case or say a word. He is carried in helpless, and the first thing he hears is “Take heart, my son.” That is what the church is for on the days you can’t hold yourself up. You aren’t required to arrive under your own power.

Was the man paralysed because of his own sin? The text does not say so, and Jesus elsewhere rejects a simple link between a person’s suffering and his particular sins (John 9:3; Luke 13:1–5). Sickness belongs to a fallen world (Romans 8:20–23), though Scripture does speak of illness as discipline in some cases (1 Corinthians 11:30). Jesus deals with forgiveness first because it is the deeper need, not because the paralysis was a punishment. No one who is ill should be told that it proves some hidden sin.
verseByVerse.note: “His own city” is Capernaum, his base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some scribes say to themselves, “This man is blaspheming,” but Jesus, knowing their thoughts, asks why they think evil in their hearts. Jesus claims what belongs to God alone — to forgive sins and to read hearts — and a heart closed in advance cannot see it.

Said silently, answered aloud. The scribes didn’t speak; they said it “to themselves.” And Jesus answers out loud. Before the paralytic moves, a claim as large as the one disputed has been made: the man they object to has read their minds. God says, “I the LORD search the heart and test the mind” (Jeremiah 17:10), and Solomon prayed, “you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind” (1 Kings 8:39). The evidence for the disputed claim is in the manner of the reply.

Their theology was right. These men aren’t fools. God says, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake” (Isaiah 43:25). Sin is an offence against God, and only the one offended can waive it; no priest ever forgave anyone, but only declared the forgiveness God granted through sacrifice. So their logic is correct: if this man isn’t God, he is blaspheming (cf. Leviticus 24:16). There is no third option. “Your sins are forgiven” could in principle mean “God has forgiven you,” but the scribes didn’t hear it that way — “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7) — and Jesus doesn’t correct them. He proves the claim they think he made.

Evil hearts. His question is sharp: not “Why do you think this?” but “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” He calls their reasoning wicked — not the conclusion so much as the closed heart beneath it. They had settled the question before weighing it, against a man who had done them no harm. A test: have you settled what you think of Jesus before honestly weighing what he claims?
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks which is easier, to say “Your sins are forgiven” or “Rise and walk,” and to show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he tells the paralytic to rise, take his bed and go home. Jesus proves his invisible authority to forgive sins by a visible miracle; he has God’s own authority over sin here and now.

The argument. Which is easier to say? The forgiveness, obviously, because no one can check it; any charlatan can pronounce absolution and walk away. “Rise and walk” can be tested at once. So Jesus stakes the unverifiable claim on the verifiable one, in public, with a paralysed man as the test. If the mat doesn’t move, everything he said about sins is exposed within the minute. It is an argument only one kind of person can afford to make. Both require the same divine authority; the healing isn’t a distraction from the theology but its proof.

Son of Man. It was Jesus’ own preferred title, almost always on his lips, and it does two things at once. On its face it is the most modest title there is; in Hebrew “son of man” simply means a human being, as God addresses Ezekiel. And in Daniel it is the highest title in the Old Testament: “there came one like a son of man… And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away” (Daniel 7:13–14). A phrase innocent enough to say in public, loaded enough that anyone who knew Daniel would see the claim — and when he used it plainly before the high priest, they condemned him (26:64–65).

On earth. Everyone believed sins were forgiven in heaven. The disputed point is the place: this man says forgiveness can be given here, in a crowded house, by his voice — without temple, priest, sacrifice or waiting. A test: have you received Christ’s forgiveness here and now, or are you waiting to earn it?
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man rises and goes home, and the crowds, afraid, glorify God for giving such authority to men. Fitting awe at God’s power leads to worship, and the authority to forgive belongs to Christ, while the announcing of it is entrusted to his people.

Fear and glory. The man simply rises and goes home. The crowd is afraid — the right response when God acts close at hand — and the fear turns to worship. That is healthier than the enthusiasm often produced today. A test: does God’s power ever make you afraid in a way that leads you to worship?

“To men.” They glorified God “who had given such authority to men” — plural, not “to this man.” The crowd may simply be speaking loosely, awed that God had entrusted such authority to someone in human form, without yet understanding who he is; their words are imprecise and their instinct sound. But Matthew may keep the plural because he sees where it goes. This Gospel records Jesus giving Peter the keys (16:19) and telling the church, “whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (18:18); and the risen Christ said, “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them” (John 20:23). The authority to forgive is Christ’s alone. But the announcing of it would be given to ordinary men, like those in that room — and Matthew lets a crowd say more than it knew.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees Matthew at his tax booth and says, “Follow me,” and Matthew rises and follows; then many tax collectors and sinners come and eat with Jesus and his disciples. Christ calls even despised sinners, they leave everything for him, and he welcomes them to his table.

Matthew. Called with the same two words as the fishermen: “Follow me.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome and known for overcharging. Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27); he bore two names, as many Jews did, and “Matthew” means “gift of God.” And when he lists the apostles, he alone writes “Matthew the tax collector” (10:3), pinning the old label to his own name. Someone truly forgiven doesn’t hide what he was saved from; he makes it a monument to grace.

The booth. Capernaum lay on a trade road at the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and his brother Philip. The booth was a customs post, assessing duty on goods crossing — fish, oil, produce. Collectors bought the right and lived on the margin, which is why the whole class was hated: the system paid them to overcharge.

No way back. The fishermen left their nets, but the nets were still there; later Peter said, “I am going fishing,” and the trade was waiting (John 21:3). Matthew’s booth wasn’t waiting. A tax concession was purchased and coveted; the moment he walked away, someone else had it. Peter could go back; Matthew couldn’t. Luke says he “left everything” and then threw a great feast (Luke 5:28–29). A test: is there a bridge you need to burn to follow Christ wholly?

The guest list. Reclining at table meant fellowship and acceptance. Jesus accepts sinners at table; this is the shape of the kingdom. And Matthew doesn’t even say it was his house or his feast. He lets the guest list speak, because the point isn’t what it cost him but who was invited.

Are there limits to this? Jesus went to tax collectors’ tables as a physician, not as one of the party, and his call was always “Follow me.” Christians are free to eat with unbelievers to love and reach them (1 Corinthians 5:9–10; 10:27). What Paul forbids is treating an unrepentant professing brother as if nothing were wrong (1 Corinthians 5:11). And wisdom adds a personal rule: go with a purpose, and do not walk into the places where you are weakest.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke call this tax collector Levi. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees ask why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners, and he answers that the sick need a physician, not the well; they should learn what “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” means, for he came to call sinners, not the righteous. Christ came for those who know they are sick with sin, and self-righteousness is the one condition that refuses the cure.

The physician. The Pharisees ask the disciples rather than Jesus — undermining a teacher through his followers. Jesus answers anyway. A doctor goes to the sick. If Jesus is the physician of souls, his place is among those who know they are ill. The Pharisees’ implied claim to be healthy is the most dangerous misdiagnosis in the chapter. The sick person who knows it can receive the physician; the “healthy” person who has never admitted need can’t. A test: do you come to Jesus as someone sick, or as someone basically well?

“Sinners.” In these disputes “sinners” was nearly a technical term: not simply bad people, but those who didn’t keep the purity code — people whose trade, poverty or ignorance kept them outside the observant class. Some were immoral; many were just poor. The Pharisees divided people into clean and unclean, and Jesus accepts the division and reverses the conclusion: yes, there are two groups, and I came for the other one.

Go and learn. “Go and learn” was a teacher’s formula for a pupil who hadn’t done the reading, used here on the professional interpreters of the very text. Matthew alone quotes Hosea 6:6, twice (here and 12:7), both times against religious men technically correct and pastorally heartless. In Hosea, Israel’s religion was plentiful but its love “like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away” (Hosea 6:4). The word for mercy is steadfast covenant love. The sentence doesn’t abolish sacrifice, which God commanded; it is a Hebrew way of stating priority — this before that, and that worthless without this (cf. 1 Samuel 15:22). The charge isn’t that the Pharisees are too religious, but that their religion has come loose from what it was for.

No righteous. “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” The irony bites: there are no truly righteous, only those who know they are sinners and those who don’t (cf. Luke 19:10).

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice
to seek and to save the lost

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s disciples ask why Jesus’ disciples don’t fast, and Jesus answers that wedding guests don’t mourn while the bridegroom is with them, though they will fast when he is taken away; no one patches an old garment with unshrunk cloth or puts new wine in old wineskins. Jesus is the Bridegroom whose presence brings joy, and the new life he brings can’t be forced into old religious forms.

Their fasting. John’s disciples ask sincerely. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). Other fasts were added by tradition: after the exile, fasts mourning Jerusalem’s fall (Zechariah 8:19), and by Jesus’ day the devout fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Behind it lay real longing — grief over sin, repentance, and yearning for God to send his Messiah. It was the posture of a people still waiting.

The waiting is over. That is why Jesus’ disciples weren’t fasting: “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?” Jesus is the promised Bridegroom (cf. Isaiah 62:5; John 3:29), and his presence makes it a wedding feast. Fasting belongs to absence; feasting to his presence. But a shadow falls: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them” — the first veiled hint of the cross in Matthew. After that, his people will fast again, longing for his return, as the early church did (Acts 13:2–3).

New wine. The two little parables make the same point. Unshrunk cloth on an old garment tears away and makes the rip worse; new, fermenting wine bursts old, brittle skins. Jesus brings the new — the kingdom arrived — and it can’t be crammed into the forms of mourning and waiting that belonged to the age before the King. This isn’t an attack on the Old Testament, which comes to its maturity in him; it is a warning against forcing kingdom life into a religious system too rigid to hold it. A test: are you trying to fit Christ into your old way of life, rather than letting him make you new?

Should Christians fast? Jesus assumes we will (“then they will fast”; “when you fast,” 6:16), and the early church did at prayer and weighty decisions (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet the letters lay down no command or required days. Fasting is a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: a way to humble ourselves and hunger for God, never a badge to earn his favour (see 6:16–18).
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine still ferments and expands; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew compresses four more miracles into a rapid sequence: a ruler's dead daughter raised, a hemorrhaging woman healed on the way, two blind men given sight, a mute demoniac freed. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus's teaching and healing throughout all the cities and villages, and the saying about the plentiful harvest and the few laborers. The pace is breathless — Matthew is showing the sheer scope of Jesus's ministry, the range of human need he addresses, and the consistency of his compassion. Three things more. This is the tenth miracle of a set Matthew has gathered into two chapters, arranged by design rather than chronology — leper, centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, storm, demoniacs, paralytic, ruler's daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, two blind men, mute man. In a Gospel that has already drawn Jesus as the new Moses (a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, water, forty days, a mountain, a law), ten mighty works after a mountain of teaching is the shape of the Exodus — with the difference that Moses' ten were plagues that destroyed, and these ten fall on disease, death, storm and the demonic. Verse 34 is the first Beelzebul charge, and it is worth seeing why they had to reach for it: nobody in the New Testament ever denies the miracles, so having ruled out God there was one explanation left. Its position is what chills — the same day and the same evidence produce "never was anything like this seen in Israel" from one group and "he casts out demons by the prince of demons" from the other. (A few early manuscripts omit the verse; the evidence for keeping it is good.) and the closing summary has three words stronger than any English can afford: "harassed and helpless" is eskylmenoi (flayed, mangled — the verb for skinning) and errimmenoi (thrown down, left lying where it fell); "compassion" is splagchnizomai, the churning of the inward organs, the strongest word for pity the language had; and "send out labourers" is ekballo, the very verb Matthew has used all chapter for casting out demons — beg the owner of the field to thrust workers into it. Note too that harvest in the prophets is nearly always judgement (Joel 3:13); Jesus takes the sickle out of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The two miracles of verses 18-26 are intertwined: the ruler's daughter dies while Jesus is on the way to heal her, and the hemorrhaging woman receives healing by touching his garment. Both cases involve women (a girl and a woman), both involve twelve years (the woman's illness, the girl's age in Mark's account), and both require faith that presses past social convention. Jesus stops for the bleeding woman even while the child lies dying — he does not hurry past need in order to reach crisis. Both receive exactly what they need.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37-38) is the theological conclusion of the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the laborers few, and the solution is prayer — not human strategy, not program development, but asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often responded to the harvest by increasing activity; Jesus commands increasing prayer. The two are not incompatible, but prayer is the first and foundational response.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler begs Jesus to raise his dead daughter; on the way, a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his garment and is healed, and then Jesus enters the house, takes the girl by the hand, and she rises. Jesus is Lord over chronic disease and death itself, he cleanses rather than being defiled, and his delays serve a greater purpose.

The ruler. A synagogue leader, a man of rank, kneels before Jesus with faith beyond anything he has yet seen: “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” Jesus rises and follows at once. Mark and Luke name him Jairus and say she was dying, with messengers bringing news of her death while Jesus is delayed (Mark 5:22–23, 35). That isn’t a discrepancy but Matthew’s habit: he tells in nine verses what Mark takes twenty-three to tell, giving the request in its final form. He compresses the miracle stories and expands the teaching. Brevity isn’t denial.

The woman. On the way, a woman bleeding for twelve years comes up behind him. Under the law her discharge made her continually unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27): barred from worship, unable to touch anyone without defiling them, cut off for twelve years from ordinary human touch. Pressing through the crowd meant defiling everyone she brushed — sheer desperation. She reaches for the fringe, the tassel the law required (Numbers 15:38–39) — reaching past the law that excluded her to the One who fulfils it. “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.” Her faith didn’t heal her; it joined her to the One who did. And she is the one woman in Matthew whom Jesus calls “daughter.” If your affliction has outlasted your patience and everyone else’s interest, notice that he stopped for the long, unglamorous, chronic thing — and gave her a place in his family.

Not dead but sleeping. At the house the flute players and mourners are already at work. “The girl is not dead but sleeping,” he says — the word he will use of Lazarus (John 11:11). To the Lord of life, death is a sleep he can break. They laugh. He puts them out, takes her by the hand, and she rises.

Bound together. The woman had suffered twelve years; the girl was twelve years old (Mark 5:42). Both stories are about uncleanness and death: the woman ritually unclean, the girl a corpse, the height of uncleanness (Numbers 19:11). By the law both should have defiled him; instead his holiness cleanses and his life raises. And while he stops for the woman, the girl dies — stretching the father’s faith from “heal her” to “raise her.” A synagogue ruler and a nameless, penniless, unclean woman: he has time and tenderness for both.

When he delays. Stand where the father stands: Jesus has agreed to come, and then he stops for someone who could, on any reckoning, have waited. In the delay the child dies. Anyone who has watched a clock while heaven was silent knows the feeling. The delay wasn’t neglect. It changed what the father received: he set out asking for recovery and went home with a resurrection. God’s delays are often the distance between what we asked and what he intended to give. A test: can you trust Christ when his help seems late?

Not every child. But not everyone gets the child back. Many have prayed this same prayer and buried their child, and this passage must never be preached as though the outcome were the promise. What is promised is what Jesus said: to him death is sleep, and he can break it when he chooses. This raising was a sign — the girl later died again — a window onto what he will do for all his own on the last day. “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25) is the promise; Jairus’s daughter is the preview.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke name the ruler Jairus, a synagogue leader. A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch. Hired flute players and mourners were customary at a death. The “fringe” was the tassel the law required on garments.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, "Have mercy on us, Son of David." When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" They said to him, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith let it be done to you." And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, "See that no one knows about it." But they went away and spread his fame through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two blind men follow Jesus crying, “Have mercy on us, Son of David”; he asks whether they believe he can do it, they say, “Yes, Lord,” and he touches their eyes and heals them, warning them to tell no one, though they spread his fame. Those who cannot see may recognise Jesus as the promised King, and he answers their faith; his call for silence guarded his mission until the cross revealed what kind of Messiah he is.

Seeing without eyes. They can’t see him, yet they see him more clearly than the Pharisees: “Son of David,” the promised King (2 Samuel 7:12–13). “Have mercy on us” echoes the psalm of eyes lifted to God (Psalm 123), and the church has prayed it ever since: “Lord, have mercy.”

“Do you believe?” Jesus waits until they are inside and asks, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” Faith must be spoken, not assumed. “Yes, Lord” — simple and complete. “According to your faith let it be done to you” doesn’t mean great faith earns great healing; faith is the channel through which his free gift reaches the one who asks. And their eyes are opened, as Isaiah foretold (Isaiah 35:5). A test: if Jesus asked you, “Do you believe I am able?”, what would you answer?

Why silence? Jesus sternly warns them to tell no one, and they spread the news at once. Matthew records it without condemnation; the healed can hardly keep silent. But the command had reasons. Timing: Jesus moved on his Father’s schedule toward the cross, and wildfire publicity could force a premature collision. The danger of a sign-only faith: “you are seeking me… because you ate your fill of the loaves” (John 6:26). And deepest, the title couldn’t be rightly understood until the cross defined it; “Son of David” without Calvary meant a political deliverer the crowds would crown by force (John 6:15). So even after Peter’s confession Jesus charged silence (16:20) and at once spoke of his death (16:21).

Provisional silence. Matthew sees in this reticence Isaiah’s gentle Servant: “He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets” (12:19). And the silence wasn’t absolute: in Gentile country Jesus told the freed demoniac to go and tell what the Lord had done (Mark 5:19). Once the cross and empty tomb defined who the Messiah is, the command is reversed: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (28:19). What was hushed before Calvary is shouted from the rooftops after it.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah, the king of David’s line.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, "Never was anything like this seen in Israel." But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mute, demon-oppressed man is brought to Jesus; the demon is cast out and he speaks, and the crowds marvel that nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel, but the Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of demons. The same evidence produces worship in some and hostility in others; the difference is in the heart, not the facts.

Brought. He can’t ask for himself; he is brought. Matthew tells the healing in two strokes: the demon cast out, the mute man speaks (cf. Isaiah 35:6).

The tenth. This is the tenth miracle in chapters 8–9: the leper, the centurion’s servant, Peter’s mother-in-law, the storm, the demoniacs, the paralytic, the ruler’s daughter, the bleeding woman, the two blind men, and this man. Matthew arranges them by theme, not strict chronology.
