And the verb for the healing is worth having. The hand was restored — apokathistemi, put back to its former condition. It is the word the disciples use when they ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), and the cognate noun Peter uses for the time for restoring all the things (Acts 3:21).

So a small and unmistakable sample of the last day happened in a synagogue on a Sabbath morning, in one man's hand, in front of people who responded by arranging his death.

One further note on the command. Stretch out your hand is worth pausing on because Jesus asks the man to do in public the one thing he had presumably spent his life not doing.

A withered hand is a thing you keep in your sleeve. Whatever the man's condition was — the word suggests it had dried and shrunk — he had had years of practice at keeping it out of sight, and he is told to hold it out in the middle of a synagogue with every eye in the building on him.

The healing did not come first. He had to extend the ruined thing before there was anything to see.

parallels.desc: seeking to kill him over the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all and ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus withdraws — not in defeat but in the deliberate avoidance of a premature confrontation. His "hour" has not yet come (John 2:4); the cross will happen on the Father's timetable, not the Pharisees'. The withdrawal is strategic, not fearful. Yet the healing does not stop: he healed them all. The instruction not to make him known reflects the same concern as 9:30 — preventing the premature inflaming of messianic expectations before the cross has accomplished its work. Matthew then reaches for Isaiah to explain what he is witnessing: this withdrawal is not failure but fulfillment of the Servant's pattern.

The verb is Matthew's, and by now it is a pattern worth tracking: he withdrew — anachoreo.

Joseph withdrew to Egypt with the child, and then withdrew to Galilee (2:14, 22). Jesus withdrew when John was arrested (4:12). He withdraws here. He will withdraw when he hears John has been beheaded (14:13), and again to Tyre and Sidon (15:21).

Six times, always away from danger, and never once presented as cowardice. It is a man keeping to a timetable that his enemies are not setting — and Matthew is careful to note, every time, that the withdrawal is followed by more ministry rather than less. Here: and many followed him, and he healed them all.

Which is the sentence to stop on. He healed them all.

He has just been forbidden, in effect, to heal on a Sabbath; he has been reported to a committee; a plot is under way to kill him. And he leaves the district and goes on healing everybody who comes, which is a considerable answer to the suggestion that the withdrawal was fear.

What he stops is not the work but the publicity — ordered them not to make him known. And Matthew is about to explain why, at greater length than he explains almost anything else in the Gospel: because this is what the Servant was always going to be like.

The reason matters, because a man being hunted has an obvious reason to keep quiet and Matthew explicitly declines that explanation. He does not say he kept it quiet so that they would not find him. He says it happened to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah, and then quotes four verses about a servant who does not shout in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 42:1-4 — the first Servant Song — is the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew. The Servant is God's chosen, beloved, Spirit-anointed agent who will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. The same words spoken at Jesus's baptism (3:17 — "my beloved, with whom I am well pleased") are here applied to his public ministry: the Servant who was declared beloved at the Jordan is the one now quietly healing and withdrawing from Pharisaic plots. The Spirit given at baptism is the Spirit by which he operates. And justice to the Gentiles — the universal scope of the Servant's mission — anticipates the Great Commission. The one the Pharisees plot to destroy is the one the Father has appointed to reach every nation.

Three things about this quotation, and the first is its sheer size.

It is the longest Old Testament citation in Matthew — four verses of Isaiah, running from here to verse 21. Matthew quotes Scripture constantly, usually in a line or two. This is the one place he stops the narrative and lets a prophet speak at length, and he does it to explain not a miracle or a claim but a man's decision to avoid a confrontation and ask people to keep quiet.

That is a remarkable use of a fulfilment formula. The thing being explained is not spectacular. It is the absence of spectacle.

Second, the wording at the baptism. My beloved with whom my soul is well pleased — the voice from the open heaven at the Jordan said almost exactly that (3:17), and Matthew has waited nine chapters to show the reader which text it came from.

So the Father's declaration over his Son at the beginning of the ministry echoed the first Servant Song (with Psalm 2:7). From the outset, the identity being announced was not simply the Messiah but the Servant — and every Jew who followed the reference would have known that the songs run on to Isaiah 53, and a man despised and rejected, and wounded for transgressions not his own.

Third, an honest note on the text. Matthew's Greek here matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly, and appears to be his own rendering — closer to the Hebrew in places, closer to the Greek in others, and independent in a few. That is not a defect. He is a Jewish writer working from a Hebrew Bible for readers who use Greek, and he translates as he goes, as anyone in that position does.

What he does not do is bend the sense. The Servant of Isaiah 42 is chosen, Spirit-anointed, quiet, gentle with the damaged, and destined for the nations — and that is precisely the man Matthew has been describing for eleven chapters, most recently walking away from an argument he could have won.

parallels.desc: my chosen servant, with my Spirit upon him
the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The portrait of the Servant's gentleness is the counterpoint to the Pharisees' aggression. They quarrel, plot, and cry aloud with accusations; the Servant does not quarrel. He does not seek public confrontation for its own sake. "A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench" — the most fragile and nearly extinguished forms of human need are exactly what the Servant handles with care. He does not finish off the nearly-destroyed; he tends them toward restoration. This is the pastoral heart of Jesus: the one who could silence his opponents by force chooses gentleness with the weak. He reserves his power for the final bringing of justice to victory, not for the crushing of those who are already bruised.

But that is written about somebody, and it should be said to somebody. Picture the two things Isaiah chose. A reed is a hollow stalk from the riverbank, used for a pen or a simple pipe; once it is cracked and bent it will not write and it will not play, and the ordinary thing to do with it is snap it and throw it away. A wick with no flame left is a thread of smoke and a smell in the room; you pinch it out. Both images are of things a reasonable person discards, because they have stopped being useful and are now merely untidy. That is the picture. And the promise is that he will not do it.

So if your faith is currently down to a flicker; if your praying has shrunk to a sentence or two, and not good ones; if you turn up to church out of habit rather than hunger and feel a fraud for being there; if you have failed at the same thing so many times that you have stopped making promises about it — this verse has your name on it. He is not standing over you with his fingers ready to pinch. Notice also where Matthew has placed this quotation: immediately after the Pharisees walk out and start planning a murder (v. 14). The world around him was as hard as it gets, and this is the sentence Matthew reaches for to describe how he treats the weak in the middle of it.

One guard, so the comfort does not go soft. He will not break the reed, but the sentence ends until he brings justice to victory — the tending has a destination. He is not indifferent to your ruin; he is patient with it, and he intends to finish the repair. Gentleness here is not the absence of purpose but the manner of it.

And there is one more thing, which Matthew will show you if you read to the end of his book. When the soldiers dressed Jesus up as a mock king, they put a reed in his right hand for a sceptre, and then took the reed and struck him on the head with it (27:29-30). The bruised reed was handled the way bruised reeds are always handled — snapped, mocked, and used to hit somebody. He went through that so that he would never have to do it to you.
verseByVerse.note: A bruised reed and a smouldering lamp-wick are pictures of the weak and failing, easily finished off.

parallels.desc: he will not cry aloud, nor break a bruised reed

verseByVerse.quote: and in his name the Gentiles will hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Servant Song's closing line is the chapter's quiet climax: in this gentle, bruised-reed-tending, non-quarreling Servant, the nations will place their hope. Not in the Pharisees' aggressive religiosity, not in Rome's military power, not in Israel's ethnic privilege — in his name. The name of Jesus is the name in which the Gentiles hope, which means it is the name in which all human hope ultimately rests. The one the religious establishment is conspiring to destroy is the one in whom the nations will trust. The cross that they plan will not end his name; it will make it the name above every name (Phil. 2:9-11). This is the sovereign irony at the heart of the passion narrative: their murder becomes his throne.

There is a link back one chapter that deserves to be seen, because Matthew has put two reeds a chapter apart.

In chapter 11, Jesus asked the crowd what they had gone into the wilderness to see: a reed shaken by the wind? (11:7) — the emblem on Herod's coinage, the image of the man who bends whichever way the weather is going.

Here, the Servant is described as one of whom it is said, a bruised reed he will not break (v. 20).

The same plant, and two entirely different things done with it. There is the reed a man can become, blown about, worth nothing, printed on a tyrant's money. And there is the reed a person can be reduced to — already crushed, bent over, no use to anybody, the sort of thing you would snap and throw away without thinking.

Jesus has no patience with the first and will not lay a finger on the second.

And the companion image is if anything gentler. A smouldering wick he will not quench — a lamp that has gone out and is producing nothing but smoke and a smell. The obvious thing is to pinch it. He shields it instead.

Then the honest textual note, since the last line differs from the Hebrew. Isaiah 42:4 in the Hebrew reads the coastlands wait for his law; Matthew has in his name the Gentiles will hope, following the Greek tradition. The two are not far apart — the coastlands are the Gentile lands, and waiting for his instruction is close kin to hoping in his name — but the difference is real and a reader comparing the passages should know it is there rather than wonder.

What is not in doubt is the direction. The Servant Song ends by reaching past Israel to everybody else, and Matthew puts that sentence at the exact point where Israel's leadership has begun plotting to kill him.

The nations get their hope in the same paragraph in which his own people decide he must die.

parallels.desc: the coastlands wait for his law
in him will the Gentiles hope

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–50 — The Unforgivable Sin, the Sign of Jonah, and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's second half escalates the conflict. Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac; the Pharisees attribute it to Beelzebul. Jesus dismantles the accusation with three arguments, then pronounces the solemn warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The scribes and Pharisees demand a sign; Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends with a redefinition of family: those who do the will of the Father are Jesus's true mother and brothers. Four things more. The crowd's question in v. 23 expects the answer no — closer to "this can't be the Son of David, can it?" They are edging toward a confession and flinching. And the title fits this miracle exactly: Solomon, David's son, had a reputation as master of spirits, and Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist working "according to the methods of Solomon" — with a ring and a root. Jesus says "go". Luke records v. 28 with one word different — "by the finger of God" (Lk. 11:20), which is a quotation: it is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they could no longer reproduce the plagues (Exod. 8:19). The exorcisms are a new exodus, and the Pharisees are standing where the magicians stood. "come upon you" is ephthasen — arrived, overtaken; not an offer drawing near but a thing that has landed. "every careless word" is argos, literally not-working: the unemployed remark that achieved nothing and was forgotten within the hour — and the guard that "by your words you will be justified" is forensic, evidence rather than payment. Both witnesses at the judgement are Gentiles: Nineveh, capital of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, which had one reluctant preacher; and the queen of Sheba, who had a rumour and a long journey. Neither had Scripture, temple, covenant or promise. The returning Spirit finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order" — three approving words, and the first is fatal. It is not a passage about losing salvation; there is no indwelling in the story, which is the whole problem. And v. 50 names brother, sister and mother — but not father, because the Father is already in the sentence (cf. 23:9). Mark tells us why the family came: they thought he was out of his mind (Mk. 3:21); John notes his brothers did not believe (Jn. 7:5); and Mary is in the upper room in Acts 1:14. She did not stay outside.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — attributing the Spirit's work to Satan — is the one sin Jesus calls unforgivable. It is not unforgivable because it exceeds God's mercy but because it closes the door through which mercy enters: it calls the Spirit of conviction a demon, and the person who has hardened to that degree has no remaining capacity to receive the grace they are calling evil. The Pharisees are approaching this condition, if they have not already reached it. The warning is pastoral, not vindictive: it is the warning of a doctor who sees a patient choosing death.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign of Jonah — three days and three nights in the earth — is the only sign Jesus offers to an evil and adulterous generation. The resurrection is the final and definitive sign, the one that vindicates all his claims. No amount of healing, no accumulation of miracles, will convince those whose hearts are already set against him; only the empty tomb is sufficient — and even that will not convince those determined not to believe (28:13-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The miracle is threefold: demonized, blind, and mute — all three conditions removed at once. The crowd's response is the right question framed cautiously: "Can this be the Son of David?" They sense the messianic significance without yet being able to affirm it. The Son of David was the expected Messiah who would restore Israel's glory; they are wondering if the evidence before them crosses that threshold. The question is the one Matthew's entire Gospel is answering. The Pharisees will answer it in the only way their hardened hearts can — by attributing the miracle to demonic power. The same evidence produces open-hearted wonder in the crowd and hard-hearted accusation in the leaders.

The crowd's question is more hesitant in Greek than in English, and the hesitation is the point.

Matthew uses a construction that expects the answer no. It is closer to: This can't be the Son of David — can it? The crowd is not making a confession; it is edging toward one and flinching. They have seen enough to raise the question and not enough to want to own it.

Which is very often how faith begins, and it is worth saying so, because the sentence is usually read as enthusiasm and it is not. It is the sound of people saying something they are not ready to have overheard.

And the title they reach for is exactly the right one for this particular miracle, for a reason that is easy to miss.

Son of David means the Messiah. But in Jewish tradition it also meant something more specific: Solomon, David's son, had acquired a considerable reputation as a master of spirits. Josephus records the tradition at length and describes seeing a Jewish exorcist named Eleazar drawing a demon out of a man in front of Vespasian, using a ring and a root, according to the methods of Solomon.

So a man who casts out demons with a word is not merely doing something impressive. He is doing the thing the son of David was famous for — and doing it without the ring, the root, or the incantation.

The crowd puts those together and reaches, tentatively, for the title. And the Pharisees, hearing the same crowd say it, produce their explanation within a verse.

Note also the three-fold ruin of the man. Possessed, blind, and mute. He could not see who had come to him, could not ask for anything, and had no power to resist what was in him. There is no record of his faith, because there could not be: a blind mute cannot approach and cannot request.

Matthew says only that he was brought. Somebody else carried the whole transaction — which is worth knowing for anyone praying about a person who is past asking for themselves.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons." Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Beelzebul" — the name of a Philistine god adapted as a Jewish term for Satan. The accusation: Jesus operates by satanic power. Jesus does not respond with outrage but with logic. The kingdom-divided argument is among his most elegant: if Satan is empowering Jesus to cast out Satan's own agents, Satan is at war with himself. Self-destructive civil war is not a viable military strategy. The accusation is not only false; it is internally incoherent. "Knowing their thoughts" — Jesus sees the thoughts behind what they had said. His knowledge of the human heart is another implicit claim to divine knowledge. He answers the thought beneath their words.

The most important thing in this verse is what the Pharisees do not say.

They do not say it did not happen.

A blind, mute, possessed man is standing there seeing and talking, and the official response is not that the crowd is mistaken, or that the man was faking, or that there had been no affliction to begin with. It is an explanation of the mechanism.

That pattern holds throughout the Gospels and it is worth registering, because it is a considerable piece of evidence. His enemies had every motive to deny the works and never once do. The council later says this man performs many signs and treats it as the problem (Jn. 11:47). The charge at his trial is blasphemy, not fraud. Even the story circulated after the resurrection concedes the empty tomb and disputes only how it got that way (28:13).

The argument in the first century was never about whether he did these things. It was about whose power he did them by — which is a much narrower question, and it is the one the Pharisees answer here as badly as it can be answered.

On the name itself, the note at 10:25 sets out the wordplay: Beelzebul contains an element meaning an exalted dwelling, so the title is something like lord of the house — which is why Jesus there contrasts the master of the house with those of his household. He does not repeat the joke here; he goes to the logic.

And the logic descends in three steps: kingdom, city, house.

That is not decoration. He starts at the largest scale and narrows, and the last word is the one he needs — because in four verses he will describe Satan as a strong man whose house is being robbed (v. 29). The illustration about a divided house is already reaching toward the picture he intends to end with.

The reductio is simple enough that a child could follow it, and that is deliberate. If the accusation were true, the devil is dismantling his own operation, one prisoner at a time, in public, on request. No power in history has ever run that way.

Then the clause Matthew slips in without comment: knowing their thoughts.

They had spoken; the verse says so. But he answers what was underneath the sentence rather than the sentence itself — and Matthew, who has just recorded a man reading a crowd's mind, does not pause over it at all.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan, probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second counter-argument: Jewish exorcists also cast out demons — by what power do they do it? If the Pharisees are willing to credit Jewish exorcists with divine authority, why do they attribute the same act to Beelzebul when Jesus performs it? Their own approved practitioners will stand as witnesses against their inconsistency. The double standard is exposed: the same miracle attributed differently based not on the evidence but on prior theological hostility. The "sons" who cast out demons may be disciples of the Pharisees' own movement — the accusation is an own-goal. Their condemnation of Jesus implicates their own tradition.

The argument needs one fact to land properly: Jewish exorcism was a real and respected practice, not a rhetorical invention.

Josephus describes it in detail and treats it as an ancient national skill. The book of Acts records seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva going about Ephesus attempting it — badly, in that instance, but the practice is assumed rather than explained (Acts 19:13-16). Magical papyri from the period preserve Jewish formulas that pagans borrowed because they were thought to work.

So when Jesus says by whom do your sons cast them out?, he is not scoring a debating point off a hypothetical. He is pointing at practitioners the Pharisees knew, and possibly at men in their own circle.

The trap closes neatly. If exorcism as such is Satanic, their own people stand condemned. If it is not, then their explanation of his exorcisms was manufactured for the occasion — which is precisely the charge: therefore they will be your judges.

And there is a difference between his exorcisms and theirs that the Pharisees have not accounted for. Every practitioner of the period worked with apparatus — names, rings, roots, formulas, the invocation of a higher authority. The whole art consisted in knowing what to say and what to hold.

Jesus says go, and it is over.

That difference is the thing they cannot fit anywhere. A man operating with borrowed authority has to name his source; a man who never names one is either a fraud, in which case the demons would not leave, or he is not borrowing.

They have grasped that he is not borrowing. Their only remaining move is to name the wrong owner.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” probably means Jewish exorcists of their own circle.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can someone enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If it is by the Spirit of God" — the third and decisive counter-argument: if the exorcisms are by the Spirit (which they are), then the kingdom of God has arrived. The arrival of the kingdom is the binding of the strong man. Satan is the strong man who holds humanity captive; the exorcisms are acts of plundering his house — freeing those he holds. The binding of Satan requires someone stronger, which is precisely what the Pharisees are denying: that Jesus is stronger than Satan. Every exorcism is a small victory in the decisive battle; the cross and resurrection will be the binding and ultimate defeat of the strong man. The healings are not magic tricks; they are acts of eschatological warfare.

Luke records this same sentence with one word different, and the difference is worth the detour.

Where Matthew has by the Spirit of God, Luke has by the finger of God (Lk. 11:20).

And the finger of God is a quotation. It occurs at one memorable moment in Israel's story: Egypt, the third plague, when Pharaoh's magicians — who had matched Moses trick for trick until then — could not produce the gnats and went to their king and said, this is the finger of God (Exod. 8:19).

That is the sentence in which the professional opposition concedes.

So the exorcisms are being cast as a new exodus: a stronger power arriving in enemy territory, prisoners being taken out of a house that had held them, and the resident experts unable to reproduce it. Which puts the Pharisees, in the analogy, exactly where Pharaoh's magicians stood — watching something they cannot do and cannot explain, and choosing the other answer.

Then the strong man, and the picture is a burglary.

Nobody walks into an occupied house and starts carrying out the furniture while the owner is standing there. The goods come out only after the owner is on the floor. So every demon that leaves is not a negotiation; it is evidence that somebody has already been dealt with in the next room.

The image is Isaiah's before it is his. Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? For thus says the LORD: Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued (Isa. 49:24-25). The prophet raises it as an impossibility and then says God will do it anyway.

And the verb in verse 28 is stronger than has come. Ephthasen means to arrive, to reach, to overtake — to get somewhere before you expected. The kingdom has not drawn near; it has landed on them.

Is Satan bound now? In this sense, yes: Christ has bound the strong man so that he can no longer hold the nations and his captives against the gospel (Luke 10:18; Col 2:15). Satan is still active and dangerous (1 Pet 5:8), but restrained. Many amillennial readers see the same binding in Revelation 20:1–3; premillennial readers take that passage as a future binding during a thousand-year reign. The first is the more likely, and it fits what Jesus says here.

Which is the sting in the sentence. He does not say the kingdom has come to you, as an offer. He says it has come upon you — and the men it has overtaken are the ones explaining it away.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty
he disarmed the rulers and authorities

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Whoever is not with me is against me" — Jesus rules out the middle position. Neutrality toward Jesus is not neutrality; it is de facto opposition. In the gathering of the kingdom's harvest, those who do not gather are scattering. Then the solemn declaration: every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven — the scope of forgiveness is as wide as human sin. Every sin, every blasphemy. Except one: blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The exorcisms are the Spirit's work; calling the Spirit's work demonic is the one sin that forecloses forgiveness not by divine limitation but by human self-exclusion from the only channel of grace.

A reader who knows the other Gospels may pause over that first sentence, because Jesus appears to say the exact opposite elsewhere: the one who is not against us is for us (Mk 9:40; Lk 9:50). Both are his words, and both are true, because they answer different questions. Here he is speaking about a man's own standing before Christ, and on that there is no neutral ground: you are either gathering with him or scattering, and indifference is a verdict. There he was speaking about someone else — an outsider casting out demons in his name, whom the disciples wanted to stop because he was not of their company — and the rule for judging other people's work is the opposite of the rule for judging yourself. Be strict with your own allegiance and generous about somebody else's. Most of our trouble comes from getting those two the wrong way round.

And do not let the warning at the end of verse 31 swallow the promise at the beginning of it, because the sentence contains the widest offer in the Gospel and the single exception to it, in that order, and most readers only ever hear the second half. Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people.

Weigh the word every, and weigh the company he was keeping when he said it. This is the Gospel in which a tax collector gets up from his booth and is made an apostle; and the same Lord defends a woman with a reputation in a Pharisee's house and promises a thief on a cross paradise the same afternoon (Lk 7:36-50; 23:43). And blasphemy is the strongest word available — not weakness, not failure, but speech against God himself. The man writing these words down had collaborated with an occupying power against his own people; the man who would carry them across the empire had held the coats at a stoning and described himself afterwards as a blasphemer and a violent man who was shown mercy (1 Tim 1:13).

So whatever a reader is carrying — the thing not said aloud to anyone, the thing said about God in a hospital corridor at the worst hour of a life, the years spent arguing against him — this verse was drafted wide enough on purpose. There is exactly one sin named here as beyond forgiveness, and the next entry sets out at length why the person who fears he has committed it is, by that very fear, demonstrating that he has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast between speaking against the Son of Man (forgivable — Peter does this and is restored) and speaking against the Holy Spirit (unforgivable) has puzzled interpreters. The key is the specific act of attributing the Spirit's visible work of conviction and liberation to Satan — the deliberate, sustained hardening of the heart against the Spirit's testimony. The Pharisees are doing this in this very scene. The tree-and-fruit analogy restates the chapter 7 principle: the accusation against Jesus reveals what the accusers are made of. Good fruit does not come from a bad tree. Their slander of Jesus is the evidence of a corrupt root.

Two things must be said plainly here, because no verse in Scripture has frightened tender souls more than this one. First, the pastoral word: if you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, that very fear is the surest proof you have not. This sin is a settled, defiant, clear-eyed hatred of the light — the heart so hardened that it looks straight at the work of God and calls it the work of the devil, and feels no grief at doing so. The person who commits it has no desire for Christ and no fear of having offended him. But a trembling conscience, a longing to be right with God, a dread of having sinned against him — these are the Spirit's own work in a soul, and the Spirit does not grieve over a heart he has abandoned. As the old pastors said: the very tears you weep over this question are water the unpardonable sin never sheds. Come to Christ; he has never yet cast out one who came (Jn 6:37).

Can this sin still be committed? Some think it was possible only for those who saw Christ’s own miracles and called them Satan’s. Others think it recurs wherever someone knowingly and finally rejects the Spirit’s witness to Christ (cf. Heb 10:26–29). The second is the more likely. Either way, the person who fears he has committed it shows by that fear that he has not; the hardened heart does not grieve.

Second, a smaller puzzle: "either in this age or in the age to come." Some have read this to mean certain sins can be forgiven after death — the seed of the later doctrine of purgatory. But Jesus is not teaching a second chance beyond the grave; the phrase is simply a Hebrew way of saying "never, in all the ages" (as we might say "not now, not ever"). Its force is total finality, not a hint of postponed pardon. The whole Bible knows only one place of forgiveness, and it is here, in this life, at the foot of the cross (Heb 9:27).

verseByVerse.quote: You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Brood of vipers" — the same accusation John leveled at the Pharisees at the Jordan (3:7). They have not changed. "Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" — the Beelzebul accusation is not a slip of the tongue; it is the disclosure of what fills the Pharisees' hearts. The heart is the treasury from which the mouth draws; what comes out reveals what is stored within. The good person draws from good treasure; the evil from evil. This is not fatalism — the heart can be transformed by grace. But untransformed hearts reveal themselves through their speech, especially under pressure. The Pharisees' accusation, made in the heat of confrontation, is their own self-portrait.

Two things about the insult, because Jesus did not invent it and did not use it often.

Brood of vipers occurs three times in Matthew. John the Baptist said it first, at the Jordan, to Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism (3:7). Jesus says it here, and once more in the last week, in the temple, at the climax of the seven woes (23:33).

Three times, all aimed at the same people. And the first man to say it was beheaded, and the second was crucified.

The picture is of a nest of small poisonous snakes — not a single obvious danger but a mass of them, hard to see, and lethal by accident as much as by intent. And in a chapter about what comes out of a mouth, the choice of animal is exact: the viper's mouth is the whole of the problem.

Then the principle, which is the most useful diagnostic in the chapter.

Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The word is perisseuma — the overflow, the surplus, what spills when a container is full.

So speech is not primarily a decision. It is a leak. What comes out under pressure is not what a person has chosen to say but what there was too much of to keep in.

Which explains why the test is so reliable and so unwelcome. A man can control his words while he is thinking about them; nobody controls what he says when he is startled, or tired, or contradicted in front of others. That is when the level shows.

And there is a guard needed, because this can be turned into despair. The passage does not say the treasury cannot be changed — the whole of the New Testament is about hearts being given new contents. It says the mouth reports the current stock honestly.

But Jesus forbade calling a brother a fool (5:22). Here he speaks as prophet and judge to hardened teachers who had just blasphemed the Spirit. His disciples are not licensed to copy the words as personal abuse (Jas 3:9–10; Titus 3:2), though there are times when false teaching must be named sharply (Gal 1:9; Titus 1:13).

The right response to hearing something ugly come out of oneself is therefore not to resolve to say less. It is to ask what has been going in.

parallels.desc: what comes out of the mouth

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eschatological seriousness of speech: every careless (argos — idle, thoughtless, unprepared) word will give account on the day of judgment. This is not a threat designed to produce verbal paralysis but a disclosure of the moral weight of ordinary speech. Words are not inconsequential; they reveal and shape character. "By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned" — not because verbal perfection earns justification, but because the words that flow from a mouth reveal whether the heart has been transformed by grace. The justified person speaks differently — not perfectly, but from a different treasury — than the condemned person. Speech is character made audible.

The adjective is precise and unusual, and it is not the one a reader expects.

Argos is a compound of a- and ergon: literally not-working, unemployed, idle. It is the word used of the labourers standing in the marketplace with nothing to do (20:3, 6), and of younger widows who learn to be idlers going about from house to house (1 Tim. 5:13).

So the words in view are not primarily the wicked ones. They are the unemployed ones — the remarks that were doing no job at all. Not the calculated lie or the deliberate cruelty, both of which any conscience flags, but the throwaway: the comment that cost nothing, meant nothing, achieved nothing, and was forgotten within the hour by everybody except the person it was about.

That is what will be given account for.

Which sounds intolerable until the setting is remembered. This is said in the middle of an argument in which men have just called the Holy Spirit a demon. It is not a general anxiety about small talk; it is the conclusion of a paragraph about a mouth revealing a heart, and the point is that nothing is exempt from the disclosure — not even the material we discount ourselves.

And the guard is essential, because the last sentence can be made to say what Scripture denies everywhere else.

By your words you will be justified cannot mean that speech earns acquittal; the man who said it will shortly die to secure that acquittal on entirely different grounds, and Paul spends most of Romans establishing the point.

The language is forensic. In a courtroom, evidence does not create a fact; it establishes one. The words are exhibits, not payment. What they demonstrate is what was in the treasury — and the treasury is what grace changes and nothing else does.

So the verse is terrifying to a man who thinks his words are trivial, and it is not terrifying to a man whose heart has new contents and whose tongue keeps embarrassing him. Those are two different situations and this sentence distinguishes them.

parallels.desc: death and life are in the power of the tongue

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." But he answered them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After witnessing the healing of the blind-mute and hearing Jesus's extended response, the scribes and Pharisees demand "a sign" — as if the healing were not a sign. This is the demand of those who have decided not to believe: no available evidence is sufficient; the request is a pretense for continued rejection. "An evil and adulterous generation" — adultery here is the Old Testament metaphor for covenant unfaithfulness: a people pledged to God who have given their loyalty to other powers. The refusal of a sign is not withholding evidence from genuine seekers; it is refusing to play the game of the hardened heart that will require ever more evidence as a pretext for never believing.

Note how they address him, because Matthew has been keeping score.

Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.

In this Gospel, disciples say Lord and outsiders say Teacher. The scribe who volunteered to follow said Teacher (8:19). The rich young man said Teacher. The Pharisees say Teacher, the Sadducees say Teacher, the Herodians say Teacher — and Judas, alone among the twelve at the last supper, says Rabbi while the rest say Lord.

The address is the assessment. These men have come to test a religious lecturer, and their opening word says so before the request does.

And the request is astonishing in its position. They have just watched a man who was blind, mute and possessed walk away seeing, speaking and free. That is the sign. It had just happened in front of them, and it is the reason for the whole argument that followed.

What they mean by a sign is therefore something other than evidence. They want a demonstration on demand, of their choosing, on their terms — the thing the devil had proposed in the wilderness and Jesus had refused there too (4:5-7).

On adulterous, the metaphor is not casual abuse. Israel's covenant with God is described throughout the prophets as a marriage, which is why unfaithfulness is adultery — Hosea was told to marry a faithless woman so that the nation could see itself. To call a generation adulterous is to say that it is not a stranger to God but a spouse who has gone elsewhere.

Which is why the demand for a sign is so galling. A wife does not require her husband to prove his identity.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign of Jonah is the resurrection — the only sign that will be given, and the one that makes all other signs unnecessary. Three days and three nights in the earth: Jesus applies the Jonah type to his burial and resurrection with precision. He is greater than Jonah: Jonah was swallowed unwillingly; Jesus lays down his life voluntarily. Jonah preached reluctantly to a foreign city; Jesus preaches willingly to his own people. The Ninevites repented at Jonah's preaching — a Gentile city responding to a reluctant Jewish prophet. This generation has heard something greater and remains unmoved. The pagan Ninevites will rise in judgment against them. Again: greater privilege, greater accountability.

But how do we get 'three days and three nights' from a Friday afternoon burial to a Sunday morning resurrection — which looks like only two nights? The answer is the Jewish way of counting time: any part of a day was reckoned as a whole day and night. So Friday (day one), Saturday (day two), and Sunday (day three) were counted as 'three days and three nights,' even though only part of Friday and part of Sunday were involved. Scripture counts this way elsewhere: Esther calls a fast for 'three days, night or day' and then acts 'on the third day' (Esther 4:16; 5:1); the same idiom appears in 1 Samuel 30:12-13 and 2 Chronicles 10:5,12. A few have proposed a Wednesday crucifixion to fit a literal 72 hours, but the Gospels' own timing (Jesus rose 'on the third day,' not the fourth) fits the ordinary Jewish reckoning best.

One thing more, and it is the phrase Jesus chooses for the tomb.

Not in the grave, but in the heart of the earth — which is a strange and deliberate expression, answering Jonah's own "heart of the seas" and "belly of Sheol". Jonah, inside the fish, prays a psalm: out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice… the waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me… I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me for ever (Jon. 2:2-6).

That is not the language of a man in an awkward situation. It is the language of a man describing his own death, from underneath.

So the sign Jesus offers is not merely a three-day interval. It is the whole of what Jonah's prayer describes: going down into the place from which nobody negotiates a return, and being brought up out of it — and being brought up specifically so that a city of Gentiles could be preached to.

Was Jonah a real person? Many critics treat the book as a parable. But Jesus sets Jonah beside his own death and resurrection and says the men of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment (cf. Luke 11:30). That makes best sense if the events happened, and the more likely reading is that Jesus believed they did.

Which is the last irony of the comparison. Jonah went into the deep because he was running from the commission to preach to pagans. Jesus goes into the earth in order to fulfil it.
verseByVerse.note: “Three days and three nights” was a way of counting any part of a day as a day. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

parallels.desc: three days and three nights in the fish

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of Sheba traveled from "the ends of the earth" to hear Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 10). She will rise in judgment against this generation, which has heard the wisdom of the one greater than Solomon and turned away. The Gentile queen sought wisdom more earnestly than those with it in their midst. Then the parable of the returning spirit: a person from whom a demon has been expelled is not automatically safe. If the spirit returns and finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order" — morally reformed but spiritually vacant, not occupied by the Spirit of God — the spirit returns with seven worse companions. Mere moral reformation without the indwelling Spirit is insufficient; the empty house invites worse occupation.

One thing about the two witnesses at the judgement, and it would have been unbearable to hear.

Jesus names two figures who will stand up and condemn this generation. The men of Nineveh (v. 41). And the queen of the South (v. 42).

Both are Gentiles.

Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom and carried ten tribes away for ever — the cruellest power in Israel's memory, whose kings boasted in inscriptions about the men they flayed. And the queen came from Sheba, at the far southern end of the known world, a pagan monarch on a trade mission.

Neither had the Scriptures. Neither had the temple, the covenant, the prophets, or the promises. Nineveh had one reluctant preacher who did not want to be there and gave them a single sentence of warning; Sheba had a rumour about a clever king and a long journey.

Both responded. And Jesus says they will be on their feet at the last day as witnesses for the prosecution against people who had everything and watched him heal a blind mute and called it Beelzebul.

And notice how the two comparisons are constructed. Jonah was a prophet, and a poor one — he ran away, sulked, and wanted the city destroyed. Solomon was a king, and ended badly. These are not Israel's finest; they are simply the two who reached the Gentiles.

Set against them: something greater than Jonah is here, something greater than Solomon is here. Both neuter, both the same construction as verse 6 — greater than the temple, greater than the prophet, greater than the king.

The temple was the place, the prophet was the voice, the king was the throne. All three are named in one chapter, and the same word is used of what has arrived to replace them.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, in south-west Arabia.

parallels.desc: the queen of Sheba visits Solomon

verseByVerse.quote: Then it says, "I will return to my house from which I came." And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable applies to "this evil generation" — the generation that received John's preaching, was morally stirred, and then rejected the kingdom when it arrived in Jesus. They swept the house but left it empty; the reformation of John's revival was not followed by the indwelling of the Spirit that comes with genuine faith. The seven spirits worse than the first represent the depths to which apostasy can fall when initial stirring is followed by final rejection. The last state is worse than the first: not unchanged but actively more corrupt. The generation that heard the greatest preaching in history and finally crucified its Messiah illustrates this pattern with terrible precision.

The three participles in verse 44 are the whole parable, and they are all approving words.

The returning spirit finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Nothing is dirty. Somebody has been at work: the place has been cleaned out, the floor has been swept, the furniture has been arranged. On any inspection it would pass.

And the first of the three is the fatal one. Empty.

The house is not reoccupied. It is in excellent condition and there is nobody in it — which is exactly the state a life is left in by a reformation that goes no further than removal. The habit was given up, the company was dropped, the language cleaned. Nothing has moved in.

Which is what makes the ending so bleak, and the guard has to be set carefully here.

This is not a passage about a Christian losing his salvation, and it should not be used that way. There is no indwelling in the story — that is the entire problem. A house with an occupant is not vacant, and the New Testament's word for a believer is precisely that God has taken up residence.

What the parable describes is moral improvement without new birth: the very thing that looks most like progress and is most vulnerable, because it produces a clean space and no defender.

And the application is stated outright, which is unusual for a parable: so also will it be with this evil generation.

He means the one in front of him. They had had a genuine national awakening — enormous crowds going out to the Jordan, confessing sins, being baptised. The house had been swept. And then the one who was to fill it arrived, and they said he had a demon.

Within forty years the temple was rubble and the nation was scattered, and the last state was worse than the first.

Which is worth saying plainly to any reader who has had a clear-out and stopped there. An emptied life is not a safe life. It is a vacant one, and the previous tenant knows the address.

parallels.desc: the last state worse than the first

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Someone told him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The interruption is deliberate and public: his mother and brothers (presumably James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas — 13:55) stand outside asking to speak with him. Mark's account adds that they thought he had lost his mind (Mark 3:21) — they came to restrain him. The family's arrival is the occasion for one of Jesus's most searching redefinitions. The interruption mid-teaching, the public setting, the unnamed messenger who reports it — all are part of the drama Matthew constructs for the declaration that follows. The natural family, which is the most powerful social unit in the ancient world, is about to be relativized by a deeper bond.

Two notes, and the second is one readers ask about constantly.

On the text. Verse 47 — the messenger's report — is missing from several of the earliest and best manuscripts, and most modern Bibles either bracket it or footnote it. It is very likely original and was lost by an easy copying slip, since verses 46 and 47 end with almost the same words and a scribe's eye could skip from one to the other. Nothing whatever turns on it; the sense is identical either way.

On the brothers. Matthew names four of them two chapters later — James, Joseph, Simon and Judas — and mentions sisters as well (13:55-56). Christians have read this in three ways, and it is worth knowing them without heat.

The oldest Eastern view takes them as Joseph's children by a previous marriage, and therefore stepbrothers. The Western Catholic view, from Jerome onwards, takes them as cousins, since the Greek word for brother can stretch that far in Semitic usage. The Protestant view takes them at face value as later children of Joseph and Mary — and points to Matthew's own wording that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth (1:25), and to Luke calling Jesus her firstborn.

The plain reading favours the third, and it is followed here. But the doctrine of the virgin birth, which is the thing that actually matters and which all three views affirm, is untouched by the question — and it would be a poor use of a chapter about family to be uncharitable about a point on which sincere Christians differ.

What is not in doubt is why they came. Mark tells us plainly: his family… went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind" (Mk. 3:21).

They were not paying a visit. They had come to take him home, and the reason they gave was that he had lost his reason.

Which should be held beside John's flat observation about the same men: for not even his brothers believed in him (Jn. 7:5). One of them, James, would later lead the church in Jerusalem and write a letter, and would open it by calling himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ.

It took a resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 47: “Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.’”

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to the man who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Stretching out his hand toward his disciples" — the gesture is the declaration. Not his biological family outside, but his disciples gathered around him: these are his mother and brothers. The family of Jesus is constituted not by blood but by discipleship. This is a radical redefinition in a culture where family bonds were the primary social reality. Jesus is not dishonoring his mother (he will care for her from the cross, John 19:26-27) but revealing that the kingdom creates a family deeper than biology. The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is a family — with all the obligations, intimacies, and mutual responsibilities that family implies.

The gesture echoes verse 13, and Matthew uses the identical verb.

Stretching out his hand — ekteinas. It is what he told the man with the withered hand to do (v. 13), and what that man did before anything was healed.

So the chapter has two outstretched hands in it. A ruined one, held out on command in front of a hostile congregation and restored. And this one, held out over a circle of ordinary men to say: here is my family.

And it is worth being honest about how hard the saying is. His mother is outside. She had carried him, and had been told by an angel who he was, and had watched shepherds arrive, and had kept all these things in her heart. She is standing in the street unable to get in, and he does not go out.

The Gospel does not soften that and neither should a commentary. It is not a warm redefinition of family; it is a public preference exercised in front of a crowd, at his mother's expense, in a moment when she had come to take him away for his own good.

But note where she ends up. Mary is in the upper room after the ascension, named among those devoting themselves to prayer with the apostles (Acts 1:14). She did not stay outside.

The circle he pointed at that day was the one she joined. She got in — not as his mother, which had never been in doubt, but by the door he was describing, which was open to her on the same terms as everybody else.

Which is the answer to the discomfort of the scene. He is not disowning her. He is telling her, in the hearing of the whole room, that the relationship she is about to need is not the one she already had.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The criterion of membership in Jesus's true family is "doing the will of my Father in heaven" — the same standard given in 7:21 for entering the kingdom. This is not a works-righteousness test but a relational description: those who belong to Jesus are those who are being shaped by his Father's will, who are learning from him (11:29), who are taking up their cross (10:38). The sister is added in verse 50, not in verse 49 — Matthew includes women explicitly in the definition of Jesus's family. In a culture that routinely excluded women from significant religious community, this inclusion is itself a kingdom statement. The family of God is constituted by grace received and obedience offered — open to all who enter.

Count the relations he names, and then count the one he does not.

Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.

Brother. Sister. Mother. Three.

He does not say father.

The omission cannot be accidental, because the missing word is standing in the sentence already: the will of my Father in heaven. There is a father in the verse, and the place is taken.

He will say it outright in the last week, in the temple: call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven (23:9). In a household there is one father, and the family being described has one, and he is not in the room.

Which quietly settles what this new family actually is. It is not an association of like-minded people, and it is not a replacement for the household. It is a household — with siblings, and a mother's place in it, and one Father, and everybody else at the same level under him.

That is why the obligations are what they are. Christians are not asked to be fond of each other, which is beyond arranging. They are told what they are: people with the same Father, which is a fact about the arrangement rather than a description of the feeling.

He was standing in a house, with his own mother outside and his brothers convinced he had lost his mind, when he said it. It cost him something to define the family that way, and it is the definition under which the church has lived ever since — held together not by temperament, or nation, or blood, but by one Father in heaven and a will that everybody in the room was learning to do badly.

The men he stretched his hand over would all abandon him within a year, and not one of them was struck off the list.

parallels.desc: you are my friends if you do what I command

12.theology: Christ as the fulfilment of the Sabbath. The Sabbath controversy of chapter 12 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the antitype of every Old Testament type. The Sabbath rest of creation (Gen 2) and covenant (Exod 20) pointed forward to the final rest that God’s people would enjoy in the new creation. Hebrews 4 draws this line explicitly: the rest that Joshua could not give, the rest that the weekly Sabbath symbolised, is found in Christ. When Jesus says “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath,” he is claiming to be both the giver and the substance of that rest. The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a weekly proclamation that the rest has arrived in Christ and will be consummated at his return.
12.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ religion had become a burden rather than a delight. Rules multiplied around the Sabbath until the day of rest was a day of anxiety. Jesus exposed the inversion: when religious observance crushes the people it was meant to bless, something has gone terribly wrong.

Now: The temptation of every religious tradition is to mistake the form for the substance, the sign for the thing signified. The Sabbath becomes a test case: are we worshipping the living God who gives rest, or performing compliance with a schedule? The Lord’s Day is meant to be a foretaste of heaven, a weekly resurrection celebration, not a legal obligation. Christ is Lord of it — and he gives it as a gift.

13.title: The Kingdom in Parables
13.text: <sup>1</sup>That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. <sup>2</sup>And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. <sup>3</sup>And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. <sup>5</sup>Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, <sup>6</sup>but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. <sup>8</sup>Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <sup>9</sup>He who has ears, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” <sup>11</sup>And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. <sup>12</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>13</sup>This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. <sup>14</sup>Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: ”’“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” <sup>15</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>16</sup>But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. <sup>17</sup>For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <sup>18</sup>“Hear then the parable of the sower: <sup>19</sup>When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. <sup>20</sup>As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, <sup>21</sup>yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. <sup>22</sup>As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>23</sup>As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” <sup>24</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, <sup>25</sup>but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. <sup>26</sup>So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. <sup>27</sup>And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ <sup>28</sup>He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ <sup>29</sup>But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. <sup>30</sup>Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” <sup>31</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. <sup>32</sup>It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” <sup>33</sup>He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” <sup>34</sup>All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. <sup>35</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” <sup>36</sup>Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” <sup>37</sup>He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, <sup>39</sup>and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. <sup>40</sup>Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. <sup>41</sup>The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, <sup>42</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>43</sup>Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. <sup>44</sup>“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. <sup>45</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, <sup>46</sup>who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. <sup>47</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. <sup>48</sup>When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. <sup>49</sup>So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous <sup>50</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>51</sup>“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” <sup>52</sup>And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” <sup>53</sup>And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, <sup>54</sup>and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? <sup>55</sup>Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? <sup>56</sup>And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” <sup>57</sup>And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” <sup>58</sup>And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the third great discourse of Matthew — a collection of seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Jesus shifts to parables at a moment of escalating opposition (chapters 11–12), and explains to his disciples that parables reveal to the insiders and conceal from the hardened outsiders. This is not capricious; it is the judicial hardening of those who have repeatedly refused the light (v. 15, quoting Isa 6:9–10).

The parables themselves paint a picture of a kingdom that is present but not yet consummate, growing but not yet glorious, mixed but not yet purified. The mustard seed and leaven speak of unexpected, hidden growth from small beginnings. The wheat and tares speak of a kingdom growing alongside counterfeit until the final harvest. The treasure and pearl speak of the surpassing value of the kingdom that makes all sacrifice worthwhile. Together they answer the perennial question: why is the kingdom not more obvious? Because this is the age of seed-sowing, not harvest. The harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Parable of the Sower and the Mystery of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to the seashore and teaches in parables for the first time in Matthew. The parable of the sower describes four kinds of reception of the kingdom's word — the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil. When the disciples ask why he teaches in parables, Jesus answers that parables reveal the kingdom to those with ears to hear and conceal it from those whose hearts are hardened. He then interprets the parable of the sower in detail. What the summary cannot hold. First-century sowing came before ploughing, not after: a man broadcast seed across the whole field as it stood and then turned the soil to cover it. So the sower is not careless — the path, the rock shelf and the thorn roots are all ground he is about to plough, and the parable is about ground rather than about a fool with a bag. "rocky ground" is not soil with stones in it but a shelf of limestone a few inches down, extremely common in Galilee — and thin soil over rock warms faster, which is exactly why that seed comes up first. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground. The yields are the point and are usually skimmed: a normal harvest returned seven to tenfold, so thirty is triple a good year and a hundredfold is what Genesis records of Isaac as a Mark of extraordinary blessing (Gen. 26:12). One patch of good ground repays the whole sowing many times over — the parable is not pessimistic arithmetic. On the hardening, Matthew and Mark genuinely differ: Matthew has "because (hoti) seeing they do not see"; Mark has "so that (hina)... lest they should turn and be forgiven" (Mk. 4:12). Consequence and purpose. Both are in the Isaiah passage both writers quote — "their eyes they have closed" is active and theirs, and "lest they should turn, and I would heal them" is purpose and God's. Anybody who resolves that has dropped one half. Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts; it is the settled apostolic explanation for Israel's unbelief. And "grown dull" is epachynthe, thickened — the language of a callus, which is formed by repetition rather than by one injury.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils — the sower and the seed are constant; the variable is the heart that receives the word. The four soils are not four types of people as if fixed in their category, but four ways the same heart can receive or resist the word. The parable is both diagnostic (what kind of soil am I?) and eschatological (the harvest will reveal what was real). The interpretation makes explicit that the word of the kingdom is the seed and the devil, persecution, worldly care, and the deceitfulness of riches are the enemies of fruitfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The mystery of the kingdom — given to the disciples, hidden from others — is not arbitrary divine caprice but the consistent pattern of revelation-and-response: those who have ears to hear receive more; those who have closed their ears lose even what they have. The disciple's responsibility is to cultivate the good soil of an open, honest, persevering heart — "hear the word and understand it" (v. 23) — so that the seed which is sown can bear its appointed fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shift in setting is deliberate: from the house (the intimate space of discipleship, 12:46-50) to the open shore (the public arena). The crowd is so large that Jesus uses a boat as a floating pulpit, the sea as an amphitheater. This is the great teaching discourse — seven parables of the kingdom in one chapter — and Matthew gives it the stage setting it deserves. The beach crowd is the mixed audience of chapter 13's concern: within that crowd are all four soils. The same word will be sown on all of them; what happens next depends not on the word but on the heart that receives it. The boat-and-beach arrangement separates teacher from crowd in a way that makes the parable of hidden and revealed word immediately concrete.

Two details are worth having, and the first is a link Matthew has built across the chapter break.

That same day Jesus went out of the house. Which house? The one he was in at the end of chapter 12, when his mother and brothers were standing outside unable to reach him, and he stretched out his hand over his disciples and said here are my mother and my brothers (12:46-50).

He leaves that house and goes and sits by the sea, and the crowd that gathers is so large he has to get into a boat. Matthew has put a scene about who really belongs to him immediately before a discourse about who really receives his word, and the join is the same day.

And the boat is not merely picturesque. The north-west shore of the lake near Capernaum has a small natural bay, and its shape has long been noticed: the ground rises from the water in a curve, and a voice from a boat a few yards out carries remarkably well up the slope. Visitors have tested it and been surprised.

Whether or not this is the exact spot, the arrangement is sound. A man standing on a beach is heard by the first three rows. A man sitting in a boat pushed out a little, with water in front of him and a natural amphitheatre behind, can be heard by thousands.

He did not have a building, so he used the shape of the ground.

And he sat. Twice in two verses. That was the posture of authoritative teaching — a rabbi stood to read the Scripture and sat down to expound it, which is exactly what he did in the synagogue at Nazareth (Lk. 4:20) and what Matthew records on the mountain before the great sermon (5:1).

Nothing about this is casual. The crowd stands; the teacher sits.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach; the boat let the crowd on the shore hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them many things in parables, saying: "A sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sower goes out to sow without visible selectivity — the seed is scattered broadly, on all kinds of ground. This is the pattern of the gospel proclamation: indiscriminate, generous, uncalculating. The first soil is the beaten path running through the field: compacted earth that cannot receive seed. The birds come immediately and take the seed away. In the interpretation (v. 19), the birds are the evil one. The hardened path represents a heart so packed down by constant traffic — the busyness, the distractions, the accumulated resistance — that the word cannot penetrate. It lies on the surface long enough to be taken. The sower is not blamed for sowing on the path; the problem is the path itself.

One fact about first-century farming removes a misreading that has troubled a great many readers, and it should be given early.

The usual complaint about this parable is that the sower seems incompetent. Three-quarters of his seed lands where no farmer would put it. Why scatter good grain on a footpath, a rock shelf, and a thorn patch?

The answer is that in Palestine the ploughing very largely came after the sowing, not before. A man broadcast the seed across the whole field as it stood — stubble, path, and all — and then turned the soil over to cover it. So what looks like carelessness is standard practice: he is sowing the ground he is about to plough.

The path is a right of way that villagers had beaten across the field, and it will be ploughed up with everything else. The thorns have been cut back and their roots are still there. He is not being wasteful; he is sowing a field, and a field in that country has all of this in it.

Which changes the tone of the parable considerably. It is not a story about a fool with a bag of seed. It is a story about ground.

And the birds are the detail that gives the game away about the path.

On every other soil the seed at least goes in. Here it does not — it lies on top, in plain sight, on ground packed so hard by feet that nothing penetrates. The birds do not have to dig.

The interpretation names them: the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart (v. 19). And the verb is the violent one — harpazo, to seize, the word used of a wolf carrying off a sheep and of the crowd trying to take Jesus by force.

It is worth noticing how little time there is in that picture. No struggle, no gradual erosion, no argument. The word arrives, does not go in, and is gone before the man has walked home.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
