The question matters, because the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, have taken them to be either cousins (so Jerome) or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). The words themselves, however, most naturally mean what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, the younger half-brothers and half-sisters of Jesus — born, unlike him, in the ordinary way. Matthew has already hinted as much, saying Joseph "knew her not until she had given birth to a son" (1:25), and calling Jesus her "firstborn," a word that quietly expects others to follow. There is no need to protect Mary's honour by keeping her a perpetual virgin; her honour is that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then was a mother to his brothers. And there is gospel gold here. These brothers did not believe in him during his ministry — "not even his brothers believed in him" (Jn 7:5) — yet after the resurrection we find them in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14), and two of them, James and Jude, wrote letters that stand in our New Testament, James becoming a pillar of the Jerusalem church. What turns a skeptical younger brother into a man who calls his own brother "the Lord"? Only an empty tomb. The conversion of the brothers of Jesus is one of the quiet, powerful evidences that he rose.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They took offense at him" — the same word skandalon used in 11:6 for those offended by the form of Jesus's coming. The townspeople stumble over his ordinariness: they cannot reconcile the wisdom with the workshop, the miracles with the carpenter's hands. The proverb about the prophet without honor in his hometown reflects the consistent biblical pattern: God's spokesmen are received everywhere except home. Familiarity breeds contempt; proximity without faith produces offense rather than worship. The tragedy of Nazareth is the personal tragedy of Jesus: the people who watched him grow up, who saw him daily, refused to worship him. He was rejected not by strangers but by neighbors.

The questions the neighbours ask are worth reading as a group, because they are not stupid and they are not hostile at the start.

Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? That is the right question. Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?

Every one of those is accurate. They have the family right, the trade right, the names right. Nobody in Nazareth is mistaken about a single fact.

And then: where then did this man get all these things? — which is the same question they opened with, asked the second time as an objection rather than an enquiry.

That is the whole tragedy of the passage in one paragraph. They began by asking where it came from, assembled a complete and correct account of everything they knew about him, found that it did not explain what they were looking at — and concluded that the problem was with him.

The evidence had raised a question their information could not answer. The right response was to widen the information. They narrowed the evidence instead.

And the word for their reaction is the chapter's own. They took offence at him — eskandalizonto, the trap-word. It has run all through this material: the message to John (11:6), the rocky-ground hearer who falls away (13:21), the causes of sin gathered out at the harvest (13:41), and now his own village.

They did not argue him down. They tripped over him — over the very thing that should have made him easiest to believe, which was that they had known him all his life.

One detail worth having: his sisters are with us. Present tense, still living in the village, presumably married locally. His brothers are named; his sisters are not, but they were there, and their neighbours could point to their houses.

Nothing about this family was mysterious, and that was the difficulty.

parallels.desc: his own people did not receive him

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The connection between unbelief and the absence of miracles is striking and sobering. Jesus is not powerless; he is choosing not to perform miracles where they would be rejected as further evidence of ordinary presumption. The miracles are acts of grace responding to faith; where faith is absent, the miracles would only deepen the condemnation of those who saw and refused. Mark adds that "he could do no mighty work there" (Mark 6:5) — the "could not" is not inability but the consistent pattern of Jesus: he does not force grace on those who have already made their decision. Unbelief does not limit God's power; it limits the channel through which his mercy flows. The closed heart receives nothing — not because God withholds, but because it cannot receive.

That sentence must be handled carefully, though, because it is one verse away from a cruelty that has done a great deal of damage. Read carelessly it says: miracles run on faith, so if God has not acted in your situation, the fault is the thinness of your believing. Some have been told exactly that over a hospital bed. It is not what the verse means.

Look at what it actually reports. He did not do many mighty works there — and Mark, telling the same visit, says he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them (Mk 6:5). Even in that atmosphere, some were healed. So this is plainly not a mechanism in which a quantity of faith buys a quantity of power. And set it beside the rest of the Gospel: he heals a paralysed man on the strength of his friends' faith and not his own (9:2), he raises the dead, who by definition contribute nothing, and he restores people who do not yet know who he is. Faith is the open hand, never the currency.

What Nazareth's unbelief actually prevented was simpler and sadder. They did not bring their sick to him, because they had already settled who he was — the carpenter's boy, whose family lived down the road. You cannot receive what you have decided not to come for. The verse describes a town that had made up its mind, not a formula governing answered prayer. If you have prayed and not received, this passage is not an accusation against you; the note at 8:16-17 sets out what may and may not be expected, and Paul, whose faith was equal to anything, asked three times and kept his thorn.

But do take the warning that is genuinely here, because it is aimed at exactly the sort of person who reads commentaries. The people who got least from Jesus in his whole ministry were the ones who had been nearest to him longest. They were not hostile; they were familiar. They had him filed. A lifetime of church can do the same thing to a soul — the sermons heard before, the passage you already know, the quiet assumption that there is nothing here you have not met. Nazareth is what happens when knowing about him has replaced knowing him, and this chapter has already told you what that ground is called.

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. The parables of Matthew 13 develop a theology of the kingdom that runs against both triumphalism and despair. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows secretly, like leaven, not by worldly power or coercion. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes the largest tree; the handful of leavened dough leavens the whole batch. The kingdom’s smallness is not its failure but its method. Reformed theology has always insisted that the church advances through the ordinary means of grace — word, sacrament, prayer — not through political power or cultural dominance. The harvest will be glorious; the sowing is patient.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living through the mustard-seed phase of the kingdom. From their vantage point, a small band of Galileans following a rabbi who was being plotted against by the religious establishment, the kingdom’s glory was not obvious. Jesus tells them: do not judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Every era of church history has felt like the mustard-seed phase. Persecution, secularisation, nominalism — all seem to contradict the kingdom’s advance. The parables of Matthew 13 are the antidote to both despair and triumphalism. The Sower keeps sowing. The leaven keeps working. The net keeps gathering. The harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>4</sup>because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” <sup>5</sup>And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. <sup>6</sup>But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, <sup>7</sup>so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. <sup>8</sup>Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” <sup>9</sup>And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>22</sup>Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. <sup>23</sup>And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, <sup>24</sup>but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. <sup>25</sup>And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. <sup>26</sup>But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. <sup>27</sup>But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” <sup>32</sup>And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <sup>33</sup>And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” <sup>34</sup>And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. <sup>35</sup>And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick <sup>36</sup>and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death (John’s head on a platter) to Jesus’ banquet of life (five thousand fed in the wilderness). The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity, and the murder of a prophet. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer, and the creative power of the Creator multiplying what is surrendered to him. John’s death is the herald’s fate; Jesus will face his own; but the meals he gives point beyond death to the resurrection feast.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (besides the resurrection). Matthew frames it with Exodus typology: a desolate place (wilderness), manna-like provision, the Shepherd feeding his people. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the same fourfold action he will perform at the Last Supper. Every Lord’s Supper echoes this meal. The chapter closes with Peter walking on water — and sinking. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. Matthew then narrates the death of John the Baptist — arrested for condemning Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, beheaded to fulfill a rash oath at a banquet. Jesus withdraws on hearing the news, but the crowds follow him. He heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish. The feeding is the great Eucharistic sign, anticipating the Last Supper and the heavenly banquet. What the summary cannot hold. Herod is a tetrarch, not a king — Herod the Great's realm was quartered at his death and this son got Galilee and Perea. He wanted the higher title, went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled for his trouble. He came to power soon after the nativity and was still in power at the crucifixion, and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him during the trial (Lk. 23:12). His explanation is theologically bizarre: nobody in Judaism expected an individual to be raised in the middle of history, so "this is John, he has been raised" is not a belief he is reaching for — he has invented it on the spot, and said it to his servants, the people who had watched the platter come in. On the geography, Josephus names the prison: Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea with luxurious apartments above and cells below — so the banquet and the dungeon were in the same building. He also names the girl: Salome. And Matthew calls her a korasion, the diminutive, the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old (9:24-25) — a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say. The oath is a quotation: Mark gives it in full, "up to half my kingdom" (6:23), which is what Ahasuerus says to Esther three times, at her banquets (Est. 5:3, 6; 7:2). A drunken king, a rash promise, a woman with a prepared request, a man's life in the balance — and every element inverts. Esther's request saved a people from a murderer; this one murders a prophet. Note too that Herod and the chief priests are restrained by the same calculation, in almost identical words: both fear the crowd "because they held him to be a prophet" (14:5; 21:46). And verse 12 is the quietest sentence in the chapter — John's disciples walked into a royal fortress to ask for the body, buried what there was, and then went to the one man who had told them who John was. Matthew records no reply. The next thing Jesus does is withdraw; the next thing after that is to feed five thousand men, besides women and children. On the day he heard.
verseByVerse.theology: John's death is the dark center of the chapter: the fate of the forerunner anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod's fear that Jesus is John raised from the dead is simultaneously wrong (Jesus is not John) and prophetically ironic (the resurrection John could not achieve, Jesus will). The feeding of the five thousand is the messianic act par excellence: the shepherd-king who provides bread for his people in the wilderness, echoing the manna of the Exodus. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives — the fourfold action of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' protest — "we have only five loaves here and two fish" — is the protest of faith that has not yet learned what it is living with. They are calculating from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. "Bring them here to me" is the word for every situation where human resources fall desperately short of human need. The miracle occurs not in the disciples' hands but in his: he takes, blesses, breaks, gives — and twelve baskets remain. Twelve: one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod Antipas — ruler of Galilee, puppet of Rome, murderer of John — hears the reports of Jesus and his guilt-ridden conscience supplies the explanation: this must be John, resurrected. The resurrection of John the Baptist was not a Jewish expectation; Herod has constructed it from his own terror. He knows what he did to John, and the report of miraculous powers working through a Galilean teacher brings it all back. Guilt is theologically productive: it confirms that John was innocent and that Herod's deed was murder. The man who silenced the prophet cannot silence the memory of the prophet's voice. Herod's fear of a resurrected John is the beginning of what should have been repentance but remains only dread.

Two things about the man, because Matthew assumes a reader who knows the family and most of us do not.

He is called the tetrarch, and the title is precise. Herod the Great's kingdom was carved up at his death, and this son got a quarter of it — Galilee and Perea — with the rank of tetrarch rather than king. He wanted the higher title badly, and eventually went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled to Gaul for his trouble. Mark calls him king, informally, the way people did.

So the man is a client ruler with a grievance about his own status, ruling the district where Jesus grew up, for almost all of Jesus' life. Antipas came to power soon after the nativity, when his father died, and was still in power at the crucifixion — Luke records Pilate sending Jesus to him during the trial, and the two of them becoming friends that day (Lk. 23:12).

And his explanation is worth weighing, because it is theologically bizarre.

Nobody in Judaism expected a single individual to be raised in the middle of history. Resurrection was a doctrine about the last day and the whole people. What Herod says — This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead — is not an available belief he is reaching for. He has invented it on the spot.

Which is what a guilty conscience does. He is not reasoning from the evidence; he is being visited. And the detail Matthew records is that he said it to his servants — the people who had been in the palace, who had seen the platter come in, and who now had to stand there while their master worked out loud through what he had done.

Luke adds the sequel: Herod sought to see him (Lk. 9:9). He got his wish at the very end, and when he finally had Jesus in front of him he asked for a conjuring trick and got silence.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a divided kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John in prison because he told the truth to power: "It is not lawful for you to have her." Herodias was Herod's niece whom he had married after she divorced his half-brother Philip — a union the Mosaic law prohibited (Lev. 18:16; 20:21). John did not qualify his condemnation for the sake of safety or soften it for political convenience. He said to the king's face what was true, and he paid with his freedom and eventually his life. This is the prophetic calling: to speak the word of God without regard for the consequences, to the powerful as to the powerless. John's imprisonment is not a tragedy of mismanagement; it is the faithful prophet's expected fate in a world that prefers comfortable lies.

The name in this verse has drawn fire, and a reader who has met the objection deserves the answer. Matthew calls Herodias the wife of Herod's brother Philip. Josephus, writing his history of the period, names her first husband as Herod — another son of Herod the Great — and says that Philip the tetrarch married Salome, who was Herodias's daughter. Critics have made a good deal of this: the Gospels, it is said, have muddled the family.

They have not, and the tangle is of Herod's own making. Herod the Great had at least ten wives and a swarm of sons, and he named a remarkable number of them after himself; there are several men called Herod in this family and more than one called Philip. Josephus himself gives some of them two names. In such a household a son known formally as Herod and familiarly as Philip is quite possible — and Matthew's readers, living close enough to the events to know the family gossip, would have needed the second name precisely to tell one brother from another. We meet the same convention in the Gospels with the man who wrote this one, called Matthew here (9:9) and Levi in Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27.

It is worth saying plainly why this matters and why it does not. It does not touch the point of the passage in the slightest: whichever brother she left, the marriage was unlawful and John said so and died for saying it. But it is worth knowing that where the Gospels can be checked against an independent historian they hold up under checking — and that an apparent collision, patiently examined, usually turns out to be a detail we were missing rather than an error the writer made.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

parallels.desc: the nakedness of your brother’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod wants John dead but fears the crowd's opinion — the tyrant who rules by calculation of popular response, not by conviction. This is the portrait of power without principle: he can imprison the prophet but cannot execute him without calculating the political cost. The birthday banquet opens the window of opportunity that Herodias has been waiting for: her daughter dances, pleases Herod, and the rash oath follows. The dance was designed by Herodias to extract the promise she wanted. The powerful man who yielded to popular fear now yields to sexual gratification: two forms of weakness that will seal John's fate.

A note on the geography, because it makes the banquet scene concrete.

Josephus tells us where John was held: Machaerus, a fortress-palace Herod the Great had built on a ridge east of the Dead Sea, in the bleakest country in the region. It was a stronghold with luxurious apartments — a place a ruler could entertain in and hold prisoners under at the same time.

So the birthday feast and the cell were in the same building. The music was audible from the dungeon.

And Josephus supplies the other detail Matthew leaves out. The girl was called Salome, daughter of Herodias by her first husband, and she later married her great-uncle Philip the tetrarch. She was probably in her teens.

Which is worth stating plainly, because the scene is often painted as seduction by a grown woman and the text does not say that. Matthew calls her a korasion — the diminutive, a little girl, and it is the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old daughter (9:24-25).

She is a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say.

Then the fear, and it is worth setting the two rulers side by side.

Herod wants John dead and does not dare, because he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. And in seven chapters the chief priests will want Jesus dead and hesitate for exactly the same reason — they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet (21:46).

Matthew uses almost identical words. The tyrant and the temple establishment are governed by the same calculation, and neither of them is restrained by conscience for a moment. What restrains them is a headcount, and in both cases it only postpones matters.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

verseByVerse.quote: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise with an oath — a rash vow that Herod is too proud to retract — and the daughter's request, prompted by Herodias: the murder of the prophet is accomplished through a chain of human weakness, vanity, and malice. Herodias had tried to kill John before (Mark 6:19) and been prevented by Herod's fear of the crowd. Now she finds her moment: the oath, the banquet, the daughter, the guests who will witness Herod's honor if he fulfills the vow or his humiliation if he breaks it. The head of John the Baptist on a platter: a request so grotesque that it reveals the depth of Herodias's hatred. The one who preached repentance is murdered by the sins he named.

There is an Old Testament scene standing behind this banquet, and once seen it will not go away.

Mark records the full wording of the oath: whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom (Mk. 6:23).

That is a quotation. King Ahasuerus says it to Esther three times, at her banquets: What is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled (Est. 5:6; 7:2; cf. 5:3).

The elements line up exactly. A drunken king at a feast. A rash and enormous promise. A woman with a request she has prepared. And a man's life hanging on what she asks for.

And then everything inverts. Esther used her request to save a people from a murderer. This one is used to murder a prophet. Esther risked her life going in unbidden; this girl is sent in. In Esther the villain ends on his own gallows; here the villain gets what she wants and walks away.

The Persian court behaved better than the Jewish one.

Then the mother, who is the actual agent throughout.

Prompted by her mother — Matthew's word suggests she was pushed forward, instructed. Mark fills in the gap: the girl went out and asked For what should I ask?, and came back in haste with the answer and one addition of her own — at once (Mk. 6:24-25).

Herodias had wanted this for months and had been blocked (Mk. 6:19). She does not appear at the feast, does not make the request, and never speaks in the scene. She simply arranged the conditions and waited, and used her daughter as the instrument.

And the request has one word in it that is pure cruelty: here.

Not have him executed. Here, on a dish, now, while the guests are still at the table. It is designed to make retreat impossible and to turn a murder into the evening's entertainment.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The king was sorry" — Matthew records the sorrow, which makes the capitulation worse. Herod knew it was wrong. He was sorry. And he did it anyway, because the social pressure of his oath and his guests outweighed his conscience. This is sin at its most nakedly human: not ignorance, not compulsion, but the choice of pride over what is right. "Because of his oaths and his guests" — the opinion of dinner guests determined the fate of the greatest prophet born of woman. The frivolous social calculus of a birthday banquet, the vanity of a man who cares more about his reputation among his friends than about justice: this is the condition of the powerful who are also cowards.

Notice, too, the word "king." Back in verse 1 Matthew called this man "the tetrarch" — the accurate title, for Herod Antipas ruled only a quarter of his father's realm and was never granted the crown. Here he is "the king," the courtesy his court and his own vanity gave him. And there is a bitter providence buried in that word. The title Antipas did not have, he ached to have — and it was Herodias, the very woman who had just used him to murder John, who drove that ambition. A few years later she pressed him to sail to Rome and beg the emperor for the royal title; instead he was accused, stripped of even the tetrarchy, and exiled to die in Gaul (so Josephus). The woman for whom he broke God's law and shed a prophet's blood was the same woman who steered him to his ruin. Sin keeps its promises exactly backwards: he grasped for a crown and lost the little he had. "The one who loves his life loses it" (Jn 12:25) is written across Herod's whole story.

One phrase deserves isolating, because it is the exact anatomy of how a decent impulse gets overruled.

The king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given.

He was sorry. Matthew grants him that, and Mark goes further — Herod had been in the habit of sending for John and listening to him, and heard him gladly, and was greatly perplexed by what he heard (Mk. 6:20). This is not a man who hated the prophet. He was fascinated by him, protected him from his wife, and kept going back for more.

And he killed him anyway, for two reasons, and both are worth naming.

His oaths. A rash promise made to a dancing girl, which no court on earth would have held him to, and which any decent man breaks. Herod treated it as binding because breaking it would have cost him something.

His guests. That is the real one. The room was full of his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee (Mk. 6:21) — the people whose opinion of him constituted his standing.

So a man who privately admired John, and had gone to some trouble to keep him alive, had him beheaded before the pudding, because of what a roomful of officials would think if he did not.

Nothing in this story requires Herod to have wanted it. That is what makes it so recognisable. He did not lose an argument with his conscience; he simply valued the opinion of people in the room above the life of a man in the cellar, and the mechanism took about a minute.
verseByVerse.note: Antipas was only a tetrarch, but was popularly called king.

verseByVerse.quote: and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The head on a platter given to the girl, who brings it to her mother: Matthew narrates it without comment, because no comment is adequate. John's disciples bury him — the last act of love available to them — and then do the most important thing: they go and tell Jesus. They are the only people in the Gospel who bring news of a death to Jesus and receive no word back — Matthew does not record Jesus's response. The response comes in action: he withdraws to a desolate place (v. 13). The grief of Jesus at the death of his forerunner, his cousin, the one who baptized him — Matthew leaves it to the reader's imagination and points only to the action that grief produced.

Verse 12 is one of the quietest sentences in the Gospel and it deserves to be read slowly.

And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.

They came. That took courage. These are the followers of a man executed for criticising the ruler, walking into a royal fortress to ask for the corpse — which is precisely what Joseph of Arimathea will do at another execution, and Mark says he took courage to do it (Mk. 15:43).

They took the body. Not the head; the head had gone to Herodias, and there is no record of it being returned. They buried what there was.

And then, having done the last thing that could be done for their master, they walked to the one man in the country who had told them who John was.

They had been his rivals, in a sense. These are the disciples who came earlier to complain that Jesus' followers did not fast (9:14), and who had been sent with John's question from prison (11:2-3). There had been a certain awkwardness between the two groups all along, and John himself had settled it — he must increase, but I must decrease.

And when their teacher was dead, they knew where to go.

Matthew records no reply. The next verse is now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself.

He said nothing that anybody wrote down. He went away to be alone — which, for the man who had called John the greatest born of women, and who was his kinsman, and who had stood in the Jordan and been baptised by him, is a more eloquent record than any sentence would have been.

And the crowds followed him on foot round the lake and would not leave him alone, and he came ashore and had compassion on them and healed their sick, and then fed all of them. On the day he heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The withdrawal is the response to grief: Jesus needs to be alone. But the crowds follow — they need him too much to honor his solitude. The response of Jesus when he sees them is not irritation at the intrusion but compassion: the same splagchnizomai of 9:36, the churning of his whole being in pity for the needy. He came to be alone; he finds a great crowd. And he heals them. This is the shape of servant-ministry: the one who gave himself to the crowds all day and needed solitude finds the solitude interrupted, and gives himself again. The compassion does not run out. The healer who is also grieving still heals. His mercy is not contingent on his personal comfort.

Slow down over this, because three things sit in these two verses that a tired or grieving reader needs, and one guard that keeps them from being turned into a whip.

The first: he grieved. Told that his cousin and forerunner had been beheaded to amuse a dinner party, the Son of God went away by himself. That ought to settle a question that torments sincere Christians — whether sorrow is a failure of faith. It is not. It is what love does when it loses something, and here it is done by the only person who never sinned. If you have been made to feel that your grief is unspiritual, or that you should have processed it by now, this verse is your answer.

The second: he withdrew deliberately, and he did it more than once in this chapter. Solitude was not an indulgence he permitted himself when nothing else was pressing; it was a necessity he arranged. Anyone who thinks stepping back from demand is weakness or selfishness should notice who is doing it here. You are not more robust than he was.

The third, and the hard one: he did not get it. The crowds went round the lake on foot and were standing there when the boat came in, and instead of the solitude he had gone looking for he found several thousand people wanting things from him. And he did not send them away.

Now the guard, because this is exactly where the passage gets misused into a theology of burnout — as though the Christian ideal were a person who never rests and always serves. Read the whole chapter. He withdraws here in verse 13; and after the feeding, he makes the disciples get into the boat, dismisses the crowds himself, and goes up the mountain alone to pray (v. 23). He got his solitude. It came later that night, but it came, and he took it. The pattern is not the abolition of rest but its postponement, once, under a particular pressure — followed by actually taking it.

So for the reader in a season of relentless demand — the parent of small children, the one nursing a dying relative, the pastor, the carer who cannot see the end of it — take all four together. Grief needs room and is allowed. Withdrawal has to be planned, because it will never happen by accident. Interruptions will come, and compassion rather than resentment is only possible for someone who is not treating exhaustion as a permanent policy. And what is taken from you now must be taken back later, as he took it. Notice where the day's resources actually came from: he fed fifteen thousand people from a boy's lunch, and the one place he went for supply was up a mountain by himself with his Father. That is still where it comes from.
verseByVerse.note: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said, "They need not go away; you give them something to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' proposal is practically reasonable: it's late, there's no food, send them to the villages. Jesus refuses with a counter-command: "you give them something to eat." He is not asking them what they have; he is telling them what to do. The disciples are to be the solution, not the problem-managers. This is the pattern of kingdom service: Jesus does not manage the crisis from a distance; he places his disciples in the middle of it and tells them to act. Their protest ("we have only five loaves and two fish") is the honest acknowledgment of the gap between what is required and what is available. Jesus accepts the acknowledgment and then supersedes the limitation: "bring them here to me."

The command is stronger in Greek than it looks, because of where the emphasis falls.

You give them something to eat — and the pronoun is emphatic. It is closer to: you yourselves, give them to eat. He is not making a suggestion; he is putting the crowd's dinner on their account.

Which is a startling thing to do to twelve men whose entire commissariat is a boy's lunch, and John tells us why he did it: he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do (Jn. 6:6).

So the impossibility was deliberate. He asked them for something he knew they could not produce, in order to find out what they would say.

And their proposal was sensible. That deserves saying, because they are usually treated as faithless here and the plan was perfectly reasonable: it is late, there is nothing here, send them off in time to reach the villages before dark and buy their own.

Nobody would be harmed by it. It is the responsible, adult, administratively sound answer, and it has exactly one defect — it gets the crowd off their hands.

They need not go away. That is the sentence to hold. The disciples' solution was dispersal; his was provision. And the difference between those two instincts has divided Christian ministry ever since, because sending people somewhere else to be dealt with is always available and always looks like good sense.

One further note on the timing. This is the same day John's disciples brought the news. He had gone to a lonely place to be by himself, and the crowd had walked round the shore and found him, and he had healed all their sick — and now, at evening, on the worst day of his life, the twelve want him to send them away and he will not.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "We have only five loaves here and two fish." And he said, "Bring them here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Bring them here to me" is the word for every moment of inadequacy in kingdom service. The disciples have assessed their resources and found them laughably insufficient — five loaves, two fish, five thousand men plus women and children. Jesus does not ask them to stretch the loaves further; he asks them to bring what they have to him. The miracle does not happen in the disciples' hands; it happens in his. But the disciples' obedience in bringing what seems useless is the necessary first step. This is the consistent pattern: human insufficiency surrendered to divine sufficiency is the precondition for the kingdom's abundance. The miracle of the feeding is not a reward for human effort but the fruit of obedient surrender.

John's account adds the detail Matthew omits, and it changes the arithmetic from small to comical.

The five loaves and two fish were not the disciples' rations. Andrew found them: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish (Jn. 6:9).

Barley loaves — the cheap grain, the poor man's bread, half the price of wheat. And the word for the fish is a diminutive: little fish, the pickled or salted sort eaten as a relish with bread rather than as a meal.

So what is brought to Jesus is a child's packed lunch: five small barley rolls and a couple of dried fish. Against a crowd of perhaps fifteen thousand.

Andrew's own comment on it is the honest one — but what are they for so many?

And that is the point at which the sentence lands. Bring them here to me.

Four words, and they do not ask for more. He does not say find more, or see what else you can raise, or we shall have to make a collection. He asks for the ridiculous thing they have already assessed and dismissed.

Which is worth turning into a test, because the passage invites it.

Most of us do the disciples' arithmetic instinctively: measure the need, measure the resource, conclude that the gap is unbridgeable, and start looking for a way to reduce the need. That calculation is almost always correct, and it is the reason a great deal never gets attempted.

What the passage adds is one term the arithmetic leaves out. The five loaves were genuinely inadequate. They were also genuinely all that was required, because the multiplication did not happen in the boy's basket or in Andrew's hands.

The instruction is not to pretend the loaves are enough. It is to hand them over anyway.
verseByVerse.note: John adds that the loaves were barley loaves, the bread of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourfold action — took, blessed, broke, gave — is identical to the institution of the Lord's Supper (26:26). Matthew writes the feeding with Eucharistic language, pointing forward to the meal that will interpret this one. The crowds sit on green grass (the Psalm 23 setting — the shepherd making his sheep lie down in green pastures). Jesus looks up to heaven before blessing — prayer as the context of all miracle. The blessing is the Jewish berakah, thanking God who provides. The breaking and giving through the disciples: they are the servants of the table. All ate and were satisfied — not merely sufficient, but full. And twelve baskets remained — a number that may recall the tribes or the twelve disciples, the abundance of the kingdom always exceeding the need. Do not miss where this meal is happening. It is a desolate place, bread is coming from heaven's hand to a hungry crowd, and there is more left over than anyone began with. Israel had eaten a meal like that before, in a wilderness, under Moses, gathered fresh every morning (Exod. 16). Jesus is doing openly what the manna only sketched — and John, recording the same day, tells us what Jesus said the morning after: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). The manna kept a nation alive for forty years and then it stopped, and everyone who ate it died anyway. This bread does not run out and neither do those who feed on it. What the crowd received in their hands that evening was a picture of what they were being offered in him.

Four verbs in verse 19 are worth counting, because Matthew's readers would have recognised them instantly.

He took the loaves, and blessed, and broke, and gave them to the disciples.

Take, bless, break, give. That is the sequence Matthew will record again, in the same order and almost the same words, in an upper room on the last night: Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples (26:26).

The identical four verbs. And Luke records them a third time, at a table in Emmaus, where two men who had walked seven miles with a stranger recognised him at the moment he did this — he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened (Lk. 24:30-31).

Three meals: a hillside, an upper room, an inn. The same four movements each time, and on the third occasion they were enough to identify him without a word being spoken.

And note the middle step in this one. He gave the bread to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

He could have distributed it himself. What actually happened is that twelve men who had just said the thing was impossible spent the next hour walking up and down a hillside handing out food that would not stop coming out of their own hands.

Some have suggested that the crowd simply shared food they had hidden. But they were in a desolate place, the disciples had only five loaves and two fish, twelve baskets were left over, and the crowd wanted to make Jesus king because of what they had seen (John 6:14–15). That is a response to a sign, not to a picnic.

Whatever they understood about him before that evening, they had a new fact by the end of it: the supply ran through them and did not come from them.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with some left over
he took bread, blessed and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five thousand men, plus women and children: the crowd was likely ten to fifteen thousand people. Matthew's "besides women and children" is a characteristic precision — he is not minimizing the women and children but giving an accurate total by the conventional Jewish counting method (men were the legally significant unit for assemblies). The enormity of the miracle scales with the specificity of the count: this was not a small gathering that shared modest rations; it was a multitude miraculously fed from a child's lunch. The numerical precision is Matthew's way of insisting on the factual reality of the miracle — this happened, these many people, twelve baskets of surplus. The evidence was counted and verified.

Matthew alone adds those four words, and they are worth noticing precisely because they can be misread.

Besides women and children. Mark, Luke and John also give five thousand men. Matthew alone adds that women and children were there too, and that there were others.

Read carelessly it sounds dismissive — as though the women and children did not count. It is the opposite. The other three leave a reader with the impression that five thousand people were fed. Matthew is the one who tells us the real number was considerably higher, and that the reported figure had left people out.

He is correcting an undercount, not making one.

And the resulting scale is worth holding. A crowd of ten to fifteen thousand in first-century Galilee is not a large meeting; it is a city. Capernaum held perhaps fifteen hundred people. Tiberias, Herod's new capital, may have held eight or ten thousand.

So the number of people sitting on that hillside was greater than the population of any town on the lake — assembled with no notice, on foot, in a place with no food, because they had heard where he had gone.

And every one of them ate.

Not a token distribution, not a sample, not enough to take the edge off. Matthew says at verse 20 that they all ate and were satisfied — and the verb is the animal-feeding word, filled up, eaten to the point of stopping.

Then twelve baskets were collected from what was left over.

Which means the surplus at the end was very much larger than the supply at the beginning. He did not stretch five loaves across fifteen thousand people. He produced a meal for a city and had more left than he started with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Walking on Water and Healings at Gennesaret
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain alone to pray. In the early morning hours the disciples are struggling against the wind; Jesus walks to them on the sea. Peter walks on the water toward Jesus, sinks when he doubts, is rescued, and worship breaks out in the boat. They land at Gennesaret, and Jesus heals all who touch the fringe of his garment. Four things more. "he made the disciples get into the boat" is anankazo, to compel — the word for forcing someone to do what they do not want. They did not want to go, and John supplies the reason: the crowd was about to seize him and make him king (Jn. 6:15). Thousands of people on a Galilean hillside who have just watched dinner appear out of nothing is a political event, and the country had seen risings before. He got the twelve off the beach before it could form. The boat is "beaten" by the waves — basanizomenon, a word for torture, used of the demons begging not to be tormented (8:29). And "the fourth watch" is Roman reckoning, three to six in the morning: they had been rowing since evening, roughly nine hours, and had covered three or four miles of a lake they could normally cross in two (Jn. 6:19). Note that they were exactly where he had sent them — this was not a wrong turning, and Mark says he saw them from the mountain (6:48). Mark preserves one clause Matthew omits and it is the strangest in the account: "he meant to pass by them" (6:48). Read flatly that is baffling; but passing by is technical Old Testament language for a theophany — what God does for Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exod. 33:19-22) and for Elijah at Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:11). The intention was to be seen. He does not ask for ability; he asks to be commanded, having just watched a word do this to five loaves. The record stands that one man got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence. Finally, "the fringe of his garment" is the kraspedon, the tzitzit commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 — and the Hebrew for the corner of a garment, kanaph, also means wing. Malachi's last page promises that "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings" (Mal. 4:2). They were reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi described, and finding that it was there.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus walking on the water is another creation-sovereignty miracle: the same one who stilled the storm (8:26) now walks on it. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Ps. 77:19). Jesus is doing what God does. Peter's walking on the water is the only time anyone but his Master is recorded doing this, and it happens not by Peter's power but by Jesus's command: "Come." The sinking and rescue express the pattern of every disciple's faith: bold initial response, fear when looking at the circumstances, cry for help, rescue by the one who is always within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' worship in the boat — "Truly you are the Son of God" — is the first time in Matthew that the disciples make this full confession. The storm-stilling produced "What sort of man is this?" (8:27); the water-walking produces "Truly you are the Son of God." The miracles are cumulative revelation. Each display of his authority over creation moves the disciples closer to the full confession that Peter will make at Caesarea Philippi (16:16). Faith grows through the accumulation of evidence seen with open eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He made the disciples get into the boat" — the verb is strong, even coercive. Jesus insisted on their departure. After the great feeding miracle, the crowd's messianic enthusiasm would have been at its peak — John 6:15 records that they wanted to take him by force and make him king. Jesus dismisses the crowds and sends the disciples away before the political situation can develop. He will not be made king by popular acclamation; the crown he will wear is of thorns. Then he goes alone to pray. This is the rhythm of Jesus's life: massive expenditure of himself in ministry, followed by solitary prayer. The feeding of fifteen thousand people does not replace his need for communion with the Father; it increases it.

The verb is worth pressing, because it is not merely strong — it is the word for force.

He made the disciples get into the boat — anankazo, to compel, to constrain. It is the word Paul uses of trying to force people to blaspheme (Acts 26:11) and of Peter compelling Gentiles to live like Jews (Gal. 2:14).

So they did not want to go, and he overrode them.

John supplies the reason: perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself (Jn. 6:15). And the verb there is harpazo, to seize.

A crowd of fifteen thousand, on a hillside, in Galilee, having just watched a man produce dinner out of nothing, is a political event. That is the raw material of a rising, and the country had seen several. What is being averted is not embarrassment; it is a messianic revolt with Jesus at the head of it, and twelve very willing lieutenants.

He got the disciples off the beach before the crowd could reach them.

And then the sentence Matthew ends on. When evening came, he was there alone.

Consider what that day had held. It opened with the news that John had been beheaded. He tried to get away by boat and was followed on foot round the lake by thousands. He healed their sick. He fed all of them. He broke up a movement that wanted to crown him. He sent his friends away over the water.

And then, at last, he got what he had set out for that morning — and used it to pray.

The Gospels record him going off alone to pray only a handful of times, and this is one of them: after the largest public success of his ministry, on the day he heard his kinsman had been murdered.
verseByVerse.note: John says the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

verseByVerse.quote: but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth watch is three to six in the morning — the darkest hours, the hours of deepest sleep and lowest human resilience. The disciples have been struggling against the wind for most of the night. Experienced Galilean fishermen know the sea; they know when the situation is serious. The wind is against them — a detail that will matter for the interpretation: they are going in the right direction (the direction Jesus sent them) but everything is working against it. Then Jesus comes to them, walking on the sea. Job 9:8 says God "alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea." Jesus is doing what Job said only God does. The fourth-watch timing: he waits until they are at the end of their resources before he comes.

Two details are sharper in the Greek, and one of them is unexpectedly cruel.

The boat is beaten by the waves — basanizomenon, and that is a word for torture. It is used of the demons pleading not to be tormented (8:29), of the paralysed servant suffering terribly (8:6), and of torment in judgement.

Matthew has chosen a word for what is done to a person under interrogation and applied it to a boat.

And the fourth watch tells us how long it had gone on. Jews divided the night into three watches; Romans into four. Matthew uses the Roman reckoning, so this is between three and six in the morning.

They had got into the boat at evening. That is somewhere around nine hours of rowing into a headwind, in the dark, on a lake they knew, going nowhere. Mark says they were making headway painfully (Mk. 6:48), and that after all of it they had covered perhaps three or four miles (Jn. 6:19) — roughly halfway across the lake.

Now the detail that will not be improved on: they were where he had sent them.

This is not a storm they sailed into by poor judgement. He put them in that boat, over their objection, and pointed them at the far shore. The wind was against them in the middle of an errand they had been compelled to undertake.

Others have suggested that Jesus walked along the shore or on a sandbar. But the boat was a long way from the land (v. 24), Peter also walked and sank (v. 30), and the disciples worshipped (v. 33). Nothing in the account can be explained away.

Which is worth holding beside the more comfortable idea that difficulty means a wrong turning. On this occasion the head wind was blowing against men who were exactly where they had been told to be, and it blew for nine hours, and the one who sent them was on a hill watching — Mark says he saw them (Mk. 6:48), which in the dark, from a mountain, three or four miles offshore, is its own kind of statement.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch of the night ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.

parallels.desc: who alone trampled the waves of the sea
your way was through the sea

verseByVerse.quote: But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' terror at the sight of Jesus is understandable: a figure walking on water in the dark, in a storm, has no natural explanation. "It is a ghost!" — the supernatural correctly perceived, incorrectly attributed. "Take heart; it is I" — the Greek ego eimi, which can also echo the divine name of Exodus 3:14. Jesus reveals himself using the name by which God revealed himself at the burning bush. "Do not be afraid" is the word God often speaks when he appears to a human being who is undone by the encounter: to Abraham (Gen. 15:1), to Joshua (Josh. 1:9), to Israel (Isa. 41:10), to the disciples. The word of reassurance precedes the miracle of arrival: first the voice, then the hand.

Mark records one clause here that Matthew leaves out, and it is among the strangest sentences in the Gospels.

He came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them (Mk. 6:48).

Read as ordinary narrative that is baffling — a man walking past a boat in distress. But passing by is technical language in the Old Testament, and it belongs to one particular kind of scene.

Moses asks to see God's glory, and is told: I will make all my goodness pass before you… while my glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock (Exod. 33:19-22). Elijah at Horeb is told to stand on the mountain, and behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11).

That is what the phrase means. It is not indifference; it is the vocabulary of a theophany — God making himself visible by going past.

So the intention was to be seen. He came out on the water in order that they should look up and see who was walking on it.

Which they did, and concluded it was a ghost.

The word is phantasma, and their reaction is not scepticism but terror — the text says they cried out in fear. It is worth noticing that men who had spent the night fighting a hopeless sea were more frightened by the sight of him than by the wind.

And then three short sentences, in this order.

Take heart. It is I. Do not be afraid.

The middle one is ego eimi — the two words from the burning bush, and the words that will get him arrested and stoned at in John's Gospel. In English it reads as an identification: it's me. In Greek it is that, and it is also the Name.

He does not begin by stopping the wind. The wind blows for the whole of the next four verses. What arrives first is a voice across black water saying who it is.
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

parallels.desc: when you pass through the waters

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's request is often criticized as impulsive or attention-seeking. But it is also faith: he does not trust himself to walk on water but trusts the command of Jesus to carry him. "If it is you, command me" — the condition is appropriate, and Jesus honors it with a simple "Come." Peter steps out of the boat. This is the most extraordinary act of faith in the Gospels outside the resurrection appearances. He is walking on water — genuinely, physically — because Jesus commanded it. The command created the ability to obey it, as always. For a brief moment, Peter is doing what Jesus does, where Jesus does it, by Jesus's word alone. This is the shape of all genuine discipleship.

The condition Peter attaches is not a doubt, and the Greek settles it.

Lord, if it is you — and the construction is the one that assumes the thing is true. It is closer to since it is you, or if it is you, as it is. He is not testing whether the figure is a ghost; he has heard the voice and believed it.

What he asks for is a command: command me to come to you on the water.

And that is the theologically careful part of an otherwise reckless request. He does not ask for the ability, or announce that he will try. He asks Jesus to order him — because he has grasped that a word from this man is what makes a thing possible, which is exactly what he has just watched happen to five loaves.

One word comes back. Come.

And then the sentence that ought to stop every reader: so Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.

He walked on water. Not far, and not for long, and it ends badly enough that the failure is what everybody remembers. But the record stands: one man in the history of the world got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence without any commentary at all.

He is usually treated as the cautionary tale of this passage. It is worth noticing that the other eleven are still in the boat, and that nothing whatever is said about them.

And the direction matters. Came to Jesus. He does not walk about on the water, or walk to the shore, or demonstrate anything. He goes toward the person who called him, which is the only thing the water was ever going to be crossed for.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records Peter walking on the water.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter walks on the water until he looks at the wind — until he lets the circumstances displace the word of Jesus as the center of his attention. The sinking is immediate: fear replaces faith and the physics reassert themselves. His prayer is the briefest and most urgent in the New Testament: "Lord, save me." Three words. It is enough. Jesus "immediately" reaches out his hand — there is no pause for a lesson about what Peter should have done. The rescue precedes the rebuke. "O you of little faith" — Peter walked on water and is called little-faith! Because the faith, though genuine, was not sustained. He trusted the command until he looked away from the commander. The question "why did you doubt?" presses at the moment of departure from trust. What was more real to him — the wind or the word?

This is the passage for anyone who has stepped out at Christ's word and gone under — the ministry that did not flourish, the move that went wrong, the costly obedience that has so far produced nothing but water round the ankles. Four things are worth taking from it.

First, notice who sinks. Peter is the only man other than his Master ever to have walked on water, and he is the only man in that boat who failed at it. The other eleven had a dry night and no story. This particular humiliation is only available to people who attempted something, and there is a kind of safety that is really just refusal.

Second, notice what actually went wrong, because it was not the getting out. Jesus had said Come. And it was not the wind either — the wind was already blowing when he climbed over the side; nothing changed in the weather. What changed was where he was looking. He sank at the moment the storm became more real to him than the word that had sent him into it. Sinking is not evidence that the step was presumption; before you conclude that, check where your eyes have been.

Third, notice the prayer. Three words, from a man with his mouth full of water, and no time to make it respectable — Lord, save me. It was enough. Do not wait until you can compose something better; you will drown politely. Cry out now, in the shape the panic actually takes.

Fourth, and best, notice the order of what Jesus does. Immediately he reached out his hand and took hold of him — and only then said O you of little faith, why did you doubt? The rebuke is real, but it is spoken by someone whose grip is already on him, above the water, with the sinking over. That is the tone to hear it in. It is not contempt from the shore; it is the question of a man holding you up.

One guard, though, because this passage has launched a good deal of foolishness. Peter did not leap. He asked — if it is you, command me to come — and he did not move an inch until Jesus said Come. Wanting an adventure is not the same thing as being sent, and the desire to do something dramatic for God is not itself a call. Test the word first, as he did; then get out of the boat, and keep your eyes where they belong.

parallels.desc: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck
he drew me out of many waters

verseByVerse.quote: And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly, you are the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wind ceases at the same moment Jesus enters the boat — not by rebuke this time (as in 8:26) but by his mere presence. The storm-stiller of chapter 8 stills this storm simply by arriving. The worship of the disciples is the right response to the accumulation of evidence they have now witnessed: the feeding of the thousands, the walking on water, the rescue of Peter, the ceasing of the wind. "Truly, you are the Son of God" — the "truly" marks this as a considered confession, not a momentary exclamation. It is the first full Christological confession in Matthew's Gospel, coming from those who have seen enough to know. The miracles do not create faith; they confirm it in those whose hearts are already open.

Note what stops the wind.

In chapter 8, on this same lake, he was woken in a swamped boat and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (8:26). He spoke to it.

Here he says nothing at all. When they got into the boat, the wind ceased. No command is recorded. He steps over the side and it stops.

Nine hours of headwind end without a word being spoken to it.

And then the confession, which is the first of its kind in this Gospel.

Compare what the same men said after the earlier storm: What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? (8:27). A question.

Now: Truly you are the Son of God. A statement, with truly in front of it, offered as worship — Matthew says they worshipped him, and the word is the one for prostration.

Two storms, two responses, and between them the disciples have moved from asking what sort of being he is to telling him what he is, on their faces, in a wet boat, at dawn.

One thing worth being clear about, since Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is usually called the turning point. That is right in the sense that Jesus receives it there formally and builds on it. But it is not the first time the words are said. They are said here, two chapters earlier, by the whole crew — and the ground of them is not an insight into his identity but a night of being terrified and then rescued.

The theology at Caesarea Philippi came out of a conversation. This came out of the water.

Twelve men who had spent the night convinced they were going to drown, and who had watched one of their number sink and be caught by Jesus's hand, were the first in this Gospel to get the sentence right.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gennesaret is a fertile plain on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee — densely populated. The men of the region "recognized him" and immediately sent word through the whole surrounding region. The network of word-of-mouth that spread Jesus's fame is the ancient social media of the first century: messenger to messenger, household to household, village to village. "All who were sick" were brought. The response of Gennesaret contrasts with the response of Nazareth (13:58) and Chorazin and Bethsaida (11:20-24): the same Jesus, different reception. Faith brings the sick; unbelief stays home. The physical location of healing is wherever faith carries its need to Jesus.

The plain of Gennesaret is worth a moment, because it explains the scale of what follows.

It is a crescent of land on the north-west shore, about three miles long and a mile deep, and it was famous. Josephus describes it at some length and calls its fertility extraordinary — walnuts, palms, figs and olives growing side by side, which normally require different climates, and grapes and figs available for ten months of the year. He says the region could be thought of as the ambition of nature.

So this is not open country. It is the most productive and most densely settled ground on the lake, and the boat has come ashore in the middle of it.

Which is why the sentence runs the way it does. The men of the place recognised him — and the verb suggests identification, working out who this is — and then sent around to all that region.

Messengers went out. Whole villages were told. And what came back was all who were sick, carried on mats along the paths of a fertile plain, from every direction, to a beach.

And the contrast is worth sharpening with a name.

Nazareth had asked Where then did this man get all these things? and taken offence, and Matthew's verdict was that he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief (13:58).

Gennesaret asked nothing. It sent runners.

The difference between the two places is not information — Nazareth had more of it, and thirty years of it. The difference is what each did in the first hour after finding out he was there.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Only touch the fringe of his garment" — the hemorrhaging woman's act (9:20-21) has apparently spread through the region as testimony. Now whole crowds reach for what she reached for: the fringe of his prayer shawl, the symbol of Torah-keeping that he wears. The faith that reaches for the edge of his garment and finds healing is faith in the least requiring form — not a full theological confession, not a face-to-face encounter, just the outstretched hand of someone who believes that even the hem of his cloak carries the power of the Son of God. "As many as touched it were made well" — none were turned away, none were excluded because their faith was expressed in reaching rather than speaking. The kingdom's mercy is not selective about its channel.

The word for what they reach for is not hem in the vague sense, and knowing what it was opens something remarkable.

Kraspedon is the tassel — the tzitzit that God commanded every Israelite to wear on the four corners of his outer garment, with a blue cord in it, a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD (Num. 15:38-39; cf. Deut. 22:12).

So Jesus wore them. He kept that law like any observant Jew, and the sick of Gennesaret were reaching for a tassel on the corner of his cloak.

And now the thing that makes this more than a detail of dress.

The Hebrew word for the corner of a garment is kanaph — and kanaph also means wing. It is the ordinary word for a bird's wing, and the same word is used of the corners of a robe throughout the Old Testament. Boaz is asked to spread his kanaph over Ruth; God says he spread his kanaph over Israel.

And the last page of the Old Testament contains this promise: for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Mal. 4:2).

Healing in his kanaph. In his wings — or in the corners of his garment.

Whether or not the crowds at Gennesaret had worked that out, that is what they were doing: reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi said would rise with healing in them, and finding that it was there.

And the last clause is the one to end on: as many as touched it were made well.

Not most. Not those who touched it in the right frame of mind, or who had understood the prophecy, or who could say afterwards what they had believed. As many as touched it — every single one, including whoever was last in the queue and whoever got there by being carried.
verseByVerse.note: The fringe was the tassel the law required on the corners of a garment.

parallels.desc: the woman who touched the fringe

14.theology: Christ as the true bread from heaven. John 6 makes explicit what Matthew implies: the feeding of the five thousand points to Christ as the bread of life. He is the antitype of the manna — not merely a physical provision for the body but the living bread who gives eternal life to all who feed on him by faith. The Lord’s Supper is the sacramental extension of this meal: in it, we receive not merely bread and wine but Christ himself, the bread of heaven, by faith. The wilderness feeding thus stands at the intersection of Exodus typology, Eucharistic anticipation, and kingdom eschatology: we are fed by Christ in the wilderness of this age until the great feast of the new creation.
14.examples:
Then: Five loaves and two fish were laughably inadequate for five thousand people. The disciples knew it. Jesus knew it. He asked for them anyway. What he asks for is never the measure of what he can do with it.

Now: Every pastor, teacher, parent, and missionary knows the feeling of inadequate resources — not enough time, energy, money, or skill. Matthew 14 is not a promise that resources will always multiply visibly, but it is a call to bring what we have to Jesus and trust him with the rest. The twelve baskets of leftovers are the testimony: what is given to Christ is never wasted, and rarely runs out.

15.title: What Defiles a Person
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, <sup>2</sup>“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? <sup>4</sup>For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>5</sup>But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” <sup>6</sup>he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. <sup>7</sup>You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: <sup>8</sup>“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>9</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” <sup>10</sup>And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: <sup>11</sup>it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” <sup>12</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” <sup>13</sup>He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. <sup>14</sup>Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” <sup>15</sup>But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” <sup>16</sup>And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? <sup>17</sup>Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? <sup>18</sup>But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. <sup>19</sup>For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. <sup>20</sup>These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. <sup>22</sup>And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” <sup>23</sup>But he did not answer her a word.
