And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” <sup>24</sup>He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” <sup>25</sup>But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” <sup>26</sup>And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>27</sup>She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” <sup>28</sup>Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. <sup>29</sup>Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. <sup>30</sup>And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, <sup>31</sup>so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. <sup>32</sup>Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” <sup>33</sup>And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” <sup>35</sup>And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, <sup>36</sup>he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>37</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>38</sup>Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>39</sup>And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 confronts the deepest corruption in religion: the substitution of human tradition for the word of God. The Pharisees have constructed an elaborate system of ritual purity — washings, dietary rules, oral traditions — that they treat as divinely binding. Jesus cuts through it all with a single theological move: defilement is not external but internal. The heart is the problem. No ceremony can cleanse it; only the blood of the covenant can reach it.

Then, in a jarring turn, Jesus goes to Gentile territory and encounters a Canaanite woman whose persistence in faith stands in shaming contrast to the Pharisees' hypocrisy. She is the wrong ethnicity, the wrong gender, the wrong religion — and Jesus commends her as having “great faith.” She is the second Gentile in Matthew to receive this commendation (after the centurion in chapter 8). The kingdom breaks every ethnic and ritual boundary. The chapter closes with a second feeding miracle — four thousand this time, in Gentile territory — extending the bread of the messianic banquet to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — What Defiles a Person: Tradition and the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharisees from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples eating without washing hands. Jesus counters by exposing how their tradition nullifies the command to honor parents, then teaches the crowd that defilement comes from within, not without. He explains privately to the disciples: it is what comes out of the heart that defiles a person — evil thoughts, murder, adultery, all the rest. What the summary cannot hold. The handwashing was not about dirt. It is netilat yadayim, a ritual pouring in prescribed quantity and order to remove ceremonial uncleanness — a man with filthy hands who performed it was clean, and a man who had scrubbed and not performed it was not. And the Torah requires it of priests, before the altar, on pain of death (Exod. 30:19-21); the tradition had extended priestly purity to everybody at every meal. The impulse is not contemptible — if Israel is a kingdom of priests, why not treat the table like the altar? — but it had become the thing a delegation walked ninety miles from Jerusalem to complain about. Watch the structure of the reply: they ask why his disciples break the tradition; he asks why they break the commandment for the sake of their tradition. Same verb, nouns exchanged, and it puts them on trial in one sentence. Note also that he says "your tradition" twice, where they had said "the tradition of the elders" — a phrase that gives it distance and belongs to nobody. And the two texts he cites are the fifth commandment and its capital sanction (Exod. 21:17), so nobody can claim a small matter is being inflated. "hypocrite" is the Greek theatre word for the masked actor — and the mask was not a disguise but a device for projecting a character to people too far off to see a face. Matthew uses it thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together. On the quotation, Matthew follows the Greek of Isaiah 29:13, which sharpens the Hebrew rather than altering it. "in vain" is maten — not wrongly, not insincerely: useless, which is a colder verdict than hypocrisy about men who fasted twice a week and tithed their herb garden. And note what he does at v. 10: he stops answering the delegation, calls the crowd, and gives the answer to them directly.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy exposes the Pharisees' deepest error: they have allowed their oral tradition to override the written word of God. The corban rule (declaring assets dedicated to God, thereby relieving oneself of the duty to support parents) is the example Jesus uses — a legal fiction that honored the letter of piety while violating the command to honor father and mother. Isaiah's word stands: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." External religion without heart-transformation is hypocrisy by definition.
verseByVerse.examples: The list of defiling things in verses 19-20 is a heart-audit: from the inside come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are not random vices; they map onto the second table of the Decalogue. Jesus is saying: the law you claim to keep is being broken from the inside out. Clean hands matter less than clean hearts — and clean hearts are precisely what the Pharisees have not addressed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delegation from Jerusalem signals that official opposition to Jesus has now reached the highest levels. The washing of hands before eating was not a biblical command but a rabbinic extension of the priests' washing before temple service — extended to all Jews as an act of piety. The tradition of the elders (the oral law) had elevated this practice to near-mandatory status. The Pharisees frame the absence of handwashing as the disciples "breaking tradition" — the highest possible charge in their framework. Jesus will reframe the entire discussion: the question is not about the disciples' practice but about the Pharisees' own violation of God's explicit command.

Two facts about this handwashing make the confrontation sharper than it looks, and the first is the one most readers do not know.

It was not about hygiene, and it was not about dirt. The washing in question is netilat yadayim — a ritual pouring of water over the hands, in a prescribed quantity and order, to remove ceremonial uncleanness. A man with visibly filthy hands who had performed it was clean; a man who had scrubbed them and not performed it was not.

So nobody is accusing the disciples of eating with dirty hands. They are accusing them of eating without a rite.

And the rite was for priests. The Torah commands the washing of hands and feet — of Aaron and his sons, before they approach the altar, on pain of death (Exod. 30:19-21). That is the whole of the biblical requirement, and it applies to men on duty in the sanctuary.

What the tradition had done was extend priestly purity to everybody, at every meal, for ever.

The impulse behind that is not contemptible, and it should be said. If Israel is a kingdom of priests (Exod. 19:6), why should the table not be treated like the altar? It is a serious idea, seriously held, by devout men.

And it had become the thing they came from Jerusalem to complain about.

Which is the second fact: this is a delegation. Matthew says they came from Jerusalem — ninety miles on foot, four or five days' walk, to a lakeside district in Galilee.

Nobody makes that journey to raise a question about hand hygiene. The centre has sent a deputation north, and the opening charge is that his men eat wrong.
verseByVerse.note: The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law. The washing was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?" — Jesus moves immediately from accusation to counter-accusation, and his charge is far more serious. He cites two explicit biblical commands: the fifth commandment (Ex. 20:12) and its capital sanction (Ex. 21:17). Both are among the most foundational of the Torah. The contrast he is building: handwashing is tradition; honoring parents is commandment. When tradition overrides commandment, the tradition must go. The Pharisees have inverted the hierarchy of obligations, placing their oral elaboration above the written word that was always meant to govern it.

Watch the exchange as a piece of argument, because the structure is exact and it is devastating.

They ask: why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders?

He answers: and why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

The same verb — break — thrown straight back, with the two nouns exchanged. They accused him of breaking the tradition; he accuses them of breaking the commandment, by means of the tradition. It is not a change of subject and it is not evasion. It is the same charge at a higher level, and it puts them on trial in one sentence.

And the two texts he cites are chosen with care.

The first is the fifth commandment — honour your father and your mother — which Paul calls the first commandment with a promise attached (Eph 6:2), and the first of those that govern how people treat each other.

The second is its sanction: whoever reviles father or mother must surely die (v. 4, citing Exod. 21:17). That is a capital statute.

He does not select a peripheral regulation to make his point. He goes to the Decalogue, and then to the death penalty behind it — so that when he shows in the next two verses what their rule does to it, nobody can suggest a small matter is being blown up.

Note also the possessive, which he uses three times in this passage: your tradition.

They had called it the tradition of the elders — a phrase that gives it weight and distance, as though it descended from Moses through the generations and belonged to nobody in particular.

Does that death penalty still apply? Jesus cites it to show how seriously God takes the fifth commandment, and how guilty the Pharisees were in evading it. The civil penalty belonged to Israel’s law as a nation; the moral duty to honour parents still stands for Christians (Eph 6:1–3).

He calls it theirs. Whatever its pedigree, the men in front of him are the ones enforcing it, and they will answer for it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, "If anyone tells his father or his mother, 'What you would have gained from me is given to God,' he need not honor his father." So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The corban practice (here presented as "given to God") allowed a person to declare their assets dedicated to the temple, thereby claiming that supporting parents from those assets was impossible — even if no actual temple donation ever occurred. It was a legal fiction that prioritized institutional religion over family obligation. "For the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God" — the charge is the gravest possible: nullifying Scripture. The tradition has not merely supplemented the command; it has abolished it in practice. This is the perennial danger of institutional religion: the elaboration meant to honor the text ends by displacing it.

But name the manoeuvre itself, because the shape of it long outlived the practice. A man owed his parents support. He could not simply refuse — that would be plainly wrong, and everyone would say so. So he found a religious way of being unavailable: the money was dedicated, his hands were tied by piety, and the duty was not neglected but outranked. Nobody has ever needed to be taught that move.

It survives wherever a religious activity is used to excuse a moral one. I am too committed at church to visit my mother. I give generously, so my brother's situation is someone else's problem. I am busy with the Lord's work, which is why my children see so little of me. Each sentence is true on its face, and each is corban. The tell never changes: the thing being done for God happens to be precisely the thing that lets you off something costly, unglamorous and explicitly commanded.

So the test is not whether the religious activity is good — corban was good, and dedicating property to God was honourable. The test is what it is being used to avoid. Put it to your own week: is there a duty I am dodging, and is my reason for dodging it a spiritual one? Jesus does not call this a lapse or an imbalance. He calls it making void the word of God, which is about as strong as language gets, and he says it to the most devout men of their generation, who would have been genuinely shocked to hear it.
verseByVerse.note: Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, Corban — “given to God.” Property declared dedicated could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 29:13 was spoken against the Israel of Isaiah's day but finds its fullest application in the Pharisees Jesus confronts: a people whose religion has become entirely external — formal prayer, exact tithing, ritual washing — while the heart remains unchanged and far from God. "Hypocrites" — the Greek word for stage actors, those who wear a mask. The Pharisees wear the mask of piety while the heart is absent. The word applies wherever religious performance substitutes for transformed desire. Jesus does not use "hypocrite" lightly; he uses it here because the evidence is specific and systematic: they have constructed an elaborate system that looks righteous while nullifying righteous action.

The word is worth having exactly, because English has borrowed it and worn it down.

Hypokrites was a technical term of the Greek theatre: the man who answers, the actor who speaks from behind a mask. It carried no moral charge at all — it was simply a job.

What gives it its edge in the Gospels is what the mask is for. In a Greek theatre the mask was not a disguise; it was how a character was presented, at scale, to a crowd who could not see a face at that distance. The mask projected.

So the accusation is not primarily that they are lying about themselves, though they are. It is that what an audience sees is a constructed exterior designed to be read from a long way off — and that behind it there is a man whose own face is doing something else.

Matthew uses the word thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together, and almost always of these men.

Then the quotation, and there is an honest textual note to make.

Matthew follows the Greek version of Isaiah 29:13, which reads in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The Hebrew runs slightly differently — their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.

The Greek sharpens what the Hebrew implies. Isaiah's complaint is that reverence for God had become a matter of learned human procedure, and the Greek states outright what that makes of the worship. Nothing is invented; the emphasis moves.

And Isaiah's own setting deserves a moment, because it is not what one would expect.

Isaiah 29 is addressed to Jerusalem — to Ariel, the city where David encamped — in a chapter about a people who cannot read a sealed book. The complaint is not that they had abandoned religion. It is that they were performing it accurately and had gone somewhere else while doing so.

Does this condemn all church tradition? No. Paul told believers to hold to the traditions he had taught (2 Thess 2:15), and creeds and orders of worship can serve the church well. Traditions become wrong when they are bound on the conscience as if they were God’s commands, or when they override what God has plainly commanded. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches give tradition authority alongside Scripture; Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final rule, and that tradition must always answer to it.

Seven hundred years later, a deputation from that same city walks ninety miles to complain about hand washing, and gets read its own mail.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." And he called the people to him and said to them, "Hear and understand:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In vain" — worship that God does not accept, prayer that does not ascend. The seriousness of the charge cannot be overstated: the Pharisees are the most devout people in Israel, and their worship is vain. This is not because they lack sincerity but because sincerity of the wrong kind is worthless before God. Teaching human commandments as divine doctrine is the error that makes their worship void: when tradition displaces Scripture, the worship constructed on that tradition worships a god of human construction, not the God who gave the law. Jesus then turns from the Pharisees to the crowd: what he is about to say applies to all, not only to religious professionals.

Two words in this pair of verses do a great deal of work.

The first is in vain — maten, meaning to no purpose, without effect, uselessly. Not wrongly, and not insincerely. Useless.

That is a colder verdict than hypocrisy, and it should be felt as one. These men prayed at fixed hours, fasted twice a week, tithed their herb garden, and kept a purity code more demanding than the Torah required. And the assessment is not that it was inadequate but that it accomplished nothing whatever.

The second is teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.

Notice the mechanism, because it is not what people usually imagine happening. Nobody in this story has thrown Scripture out. The Pharisees revered it, memorised it, and would have died for it — and several of their descendants did.

What went wrong is that human material had been promoted into the same category. Once a tradition is taught as doctrine, it acquires the authority of the thing it was built to protect, and from that moment it can overrule it — which is precisely what verses 5 and 6 describe happening to the fifth commandment.

The danger is not irreverence. It is reverence attached to the wrong object, by people who cannot any longer tell which of their convictions came from God.

Then the turn in verse 10, and it is a deliberate public act.

He called the people to him. He has been answering a delegation from Jerusalem; he stops, summons the crowd, and says the next thing to them.

Which means the ordinary people standing about — who had been told all their lives that these were the men who understood — are made witnesses to the argument, and are then given the answer directly rather than through the usual channel.

Hear and understand. The second verb is the one that has been running since chapter 13, and it is now being asked of the crowd rather than the experts.

verseByVerse.quote: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person." Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Not what goes into the mouth but what comes out" — a summary that would have sounded revolutionary to Jewish ears trained to think of defilement as primarily ritual and dietary. Jesus is not abolishing the food laws (that debate belongs to Acts 10 and Rom. 14-15) but addressing the deeper issue: the Pharisees' entire defilement theology is oriented outward when defilement is fundamentally an inward problem. The disciples report that the Pharisees were offended — the inevitable response of those whose framework has been exposed as insufficient. Jesus's response to the report of offense is not apology but intensification.

That said, the claim that he is not touching the food laws needs qualifying, because Mark — telling this same scene — adds a sentence Matthew does not: Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). That is not a small addition. Mark is telling us that the saying carried an implication which reached all the way to the dietary code, and a reader who has both Gospels open will notice that the two accounts seem to be pulling in different directions.

They are not. What Jesus says here is the principle; Mark supplies the conclusion the principle was always going to force. And notice that the conclusion was not obvious even to the men in the room. If Peter had understood on that afternoon that all foods were clean, he would not have needed a sheet let down from heaven three times, years later, before he would eat with a Gentile — and he still argued with the voice that told him to (Acts 10:9-16). The disciples heard the words and did not draw the inference. The church would take years, a vision, a council, and a good deal of correspondence to work it through.

So both writers are right, and the difference between them is the difference between a seed and its fruit. Matthew, writing for Jewish readers, records what Jesus said. Mark, writing later and for Gentiles among whom the question had become urgent, tells his readers where it led. This is the same pattern noticed at 9:18 — Matthew gives the thing itself and leaves the working out to others. The ceremonial laws were never abolished by being broken; they were fulfilled by the arrival of what they pointed to, and this sentence in a Galilean courtyard is the moment the shadow began to give way.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up" — the Pharisaic tradition, however ancient and elaborate, does not have divine origin and will not stand. "Let them alone" — the most chilling instruction: stop arguing with them, stop trying to convince them; they are beyond the teachable moment and on their way to judgment. "Blind guides" — a devastating assessment of those who claim to lead others in the way of God while themselves being unable to see. The double blindness of leaders and followers produces a common fate: both fall into the pit. This is the pastoral consequence of false teaching: it does not merely leave the teacher unchanged; it destroys those who follow.

Two things, and the first is the sentence that ought to stop a reader: let them alone.

It is startling in the mouth of Jesus. He has just been told that the Pharisees were offended by what he said (v. 12), and this is his response to it — not an explanation, not another attempt, not go and put it right with them.

Aphete autous. Leave them. Let them go.

That has to be held with care, because it is not a general licence to give up on people. The man saying it wept over Jerusalem, and went on preaching to these same men until the last week of his life, and prayed for the people driving nails into him.

But it is in the text, and it means something. There is a point at which further argument is not owed — where a man has seen enough, decided, and hardened, and the loving thing is not to keep supplying material. Paul reaches the same conclusion twice, and each time after a considerable effort: after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him (Tit. 3:10).

It is a permission, not an instruction. And it is given about religious leaders rather than about the lost.

The second is the image, and it is grimly funny before it is serious.

Blind guides. The two words do not go together. A guide is a man hired precisely because he can see the road — and this one cannot, and has not mentioned it, and is taking money for it.

Matthew will use the phrase again in chapter 23, where it becomes a refrain: blind guides (23:16, 24).

And the consequence is put with no cruelty at all: both will fall into a pit. Not the guide only. The tragedy of bad teaching is that the teacher is rarely the only casualty, and in this picture he is not even the one who most deserves to be in the hole.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "Explain the parable to us." And he said, "Are you also still without understanding?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter asks for explanation of the "defiles from within" saying — calling it a "parable" because it feels enigmatic. Jesus's response is a gentle rebuke: "Are you also still without understanding?" The "also" — like the Pharisees, like the crowd — suggests that the disciples should be further along. Their privileged access to Jesus's teaching, their experience of his miracles, the investment he has made in them — all of this should have produced more capacity for understanding. The rebuke is loving but pointed. The disciples are not yet where they need to be, and Jesus will not pretend otherwise. He explains anyway — because patient teacher-love continues past the point of apparent failure.

The word in the rebuke is the chapter-13 word, and its recurrence here is the point.

Are you also still without understanding? — asynetoi, the negative of syniemi, which ran six times through the parable discourse: they do not understand, never understand, understand with the heart, hears and understands, and at the end, have you understood all these things? — to which the disciples had answered yes (13:51).

That was two chapters ago. Here the same men are told they are still without understanding, and the adverb is doing the work.

Their yes had been honest and it had been thin, and this is the first place Matthew shows it being tested. It will not be the last.

And the little word also is worth its weight.

Are you also still without understanding? — placing them, for a moment, in the same column as the crowd and the Pharisees. The privilege of the inner circle has not produced a different result yet.

Which is a mercy to record, and Matthew records it repeatedly. These men are not presented as spiritual naturals who grasped things the rest of us would not. They were slow, they asked for basic things to be explained twice, and one of the two whose names we know best is the one asking here.

Note also what Peter calls it: explain the parable to us.

It was not a parable. Verse 11 is a plain declarative sentence — it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth — with no story, no image, and nothing hidden.

Peter files it as a riddle because it cannot mean what it appears to mean. He has been raised on food laws that God himself gave, and the sentence he has just heard sounds like it dismantles them, so he assumes there must be a second level.

He is wrong about the form and right about the size of it. Mark, writing the same scene, adds the clause Matthew leaves out: thus he declared all foods clean (Mk. 7:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The physiological explanation is remarkably direct: food enters the body and passes through it. It does not reach the heart. Only what comes from the heart — speech, which expresses thought, desire, and intention — reaches into the moral dimension. The heart is the center of the biblical person: not the organ but the seat of will, desire, and the whole inner life. What the heart is determines what comes out. External food, however ritually classified, cannot corrupt the heart; the already-corrupt heart corrupts the mouth that expresses it. This is the radical inwardness of Jesus's ethics: morality is not managed from the outside but flows from the inside, and only transformed hearts produce transformed speech and behavior.

Mark's parenthesis on this saying is the most consequential four words in his Gospel, and Matthew does not have them.

Mark writes: Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled? — and then adds, in his own voice: (Thus he declared all foods clean) (Mk. 7:18-19).

Matthew records the argument and omits the conclusion.

That is not an accident, and the likeliest explanation tells us something about who each man was writing for. Mark writes for Gentiles in Rome, for whom the question is settled and the implication is welcome. Matthew writes for Jewish Christians, for whom the food laws were their grandmothers' whole practice, and for whom this was the most painful issue in the early church — the one that split Peter and Paul at Antioch (Gal. 2:11-14) and required a council in Jerusalem.

He gives them the words of Jesus and lets them draw it out themselves.

And the physiology is deliberately crude. Food goes into the stomach and is expelled — the Greek is blunter than most translations, and there is no delicacy about it.

He is not being coarse for effect. The argument requires the route to be traced: in at the mouth, through the gut, out of the body. At no point does it pass through the heart. Whatever a food is, it never touches the part of a person where defilement happens.

Which is why the heart is the word to define, since it does not mean what it means in English.

In Scripture the heart is not the seat of the emotions as against the head. It is the whole interior control room — thinking, willing, deciding, loving, remembering. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (Prov. 4:23).

So out of the heart is not out of the feelings. It is out of the place where a person is actually operating from — and the mouth, on this account, is simply the outlet where that becomes audible.
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.”

parallels.desc: out of the abundance of the heart

verseByVerse.quote: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list maps the heart's corruption onto the second table of the law: evil thoughts (the root of all), murder (sixth commandment), adultery and sexual immorality (seventh), theft (eighth), false witness (ninth), slander (the general corruption of speech). The commandments are broken first in the heart, then in action. The Pharisees had policed the outside while the inside remained unexamined. "But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person" — the closing line returns to the original charge and dismisses it. The whole elaborate handwashing tradition cannot address the actual problem of human defilement, because it addresses the wrong organ. Clean hands, dirty heart: defiled. Unwashed hands, transformed heart: not defiled. But that leaves the honest reader with the hardest question in the chapter, and it must not be left hanging: if the trouble is my heart, and my heart is the very thing doing the wanting, how is it ever going to be transformed? Jeremiah put the diagnosis at its bleakest — the heart is "deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jer. 17:9). This is what the older theologians meant by total depravity, and the word is often misheard. It does not mean every person is as wicked as they could possibly be; it means there is no part of us — mind, will, affections — that the corruption has not reached, so there is no clean corner left to start the repairs from. Scrub the outside of that and you have washed a cup that was never dirty on the outside.

So the cure cannot be a better tradition, a stricter rule, or a firmer resolution. It has to be a replacement. And God promised exactly that, centuries before this argument in the courtyard: "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezek. 36:26). That is not reform; it is transplant. It is the Spirit's work, purchased at the cross toward which this whole Gospel is walking. Jesus is not standing here to tell you to try harder at the impossible. He is telling you where the disease actually is, so that you will stop treating your hands and bring him your heart — which is the one thing he came to make new.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–39 — The Canaanite Woman and the Feeding of the Four Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for her demon-oppressed daughter. After testing her faith through apparent reluctance, he heals the daughter and commends her great faith. Jesus then returns to Galilee, heals many on a mountain, and feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few fish. More to notice. This is the one time in his ministry that Jesus goes into Phoenicia — he had already crossed to the Gentile east bank at 8:28 and will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi at 16:13, but Tyre and Sidon are foreign soil. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician cities outside Israel, outside Herod's jurisdiction — and in the Old Testament they are bywords, with Ezekiel devoting three chapters to Tyre's fall and Jezebel a Sidonian princess. That is the address he withdraws to after Jerusalem sends a deputation about hand washing. And Matthew's word for her is deliberately archaic: Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, the ordinary current term; Matthew calls her a Canaanite — the Old Testament name for the nations Israel was to drive out, rarely heard in his day. He has reached back for maximum freight, and then has her say "Son of David". On the dogs, Greek has two words: kyon is the street scavenger and the word used when "dogs" is an insult (7:6; Phil. 3:2), and Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion, the diminutive — the animal that lives in the house, belongs there, and is fed there. The saying is about order, not worth. But the shock should not be dissolved: he ignored her, the disciples asked him to send her away, and he answered her kneeling with a proverb about dogs. What resolves it is the outcome rather than the vocabulary. Her reply begins "yes, LORD" — she agrees, disputes nothing, and adds only "for even", staying inside his picture and finding that it contains her. And Jesus commends faith of this order in only two people: this woman (great is your faith) and the centurion (with no one in Israel have I found such faith, 8:10) — both Gentiles, both asking for somebody else, and neither present when the healing happens. The crowd at vv. 29-31 is Gentile, and Matthew signals it by how they worship: they glorified "the God of Israel", which is what an outsider says. Which explains the second feeding — and the two are not one story twice. The basket words differ consistently: kophinos at the five thousand (a small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in) and spyris at the four thousand (a hamper big enough to hold a man — the one Paul was lowered down the Damascus wall in, Acts 9:25). Jesus himself distinguishes the two events at 16:9-10.
verseByVerse.theology: The Canaanite woman episode is one of the most theologically dense in Matthew. Jesus's apparent reluctance — "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and the difficult "dogs" saying — is best understood as testing her faith rather than expressing genuine exclusion. Her response — "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table" — is the model of faith that does not demand, does not argue, does not claim rights, but presses through apparent rejection on the strength of the Savior's character. Jesus pronounces her faith "great" — the only time this word is used of any individual's faith in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: The second feeding (four thousand) parallels the first (five thousand) but occurs in Gentile territory — the region of the Decapolis. Where the first feeding fed a Jewish crowd (twelve baskets, echoing the twelve tribes), the second feeds a largely Gentile crowd (seven baskets, echoing the seven Gentile nations of Canaan). The Messiah who first came to the lost sheep of Israel is already extending his table to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tyre and Sidon are Gentile territory — the furthest Jesus has traveled from the center of Jewish life. The Canaanite woman who approaches him is identified by her ethnic heritage: Canaanite, the most foreign possible category in Jewish consciousness. Yet she cries out with a Jewish messianic title: "Son of David." She knows the right words — perhaps from border-region contact with Jewish communities — and she knows the right need: "my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon." Her faith begins with the character of Jesus, not with any claim of her own. She does not argue about whether she deserves help; she simply identifies him and states the need. This is always the starting point of prayer.

Two things about this scene are more remarkable than they appear, and the first is simply where it takes place.

This is the only occasion in the Gospels on which Jesus goes outside the borders of Israel altogether. He had crossed to the Gentile east bank before, among the Gadarenes and their pig herds (8:28), and he will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi (16:13); but Tyre and Sidon are Phoenicia, foreign soil, off the map of the promised land. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast, outside Israel, outside Herod's jurisdiction, outside anything that could be called the land of promise. He had been to the Decapolis, which was mixed; this is foreign soil.

And in the Old Testament these two cities are bywords. Ezekiel devotes three chapters to the fall of Tyre; Isaiah and Joel and Amos all pronounce against them. Jezebel was a Sidonian princess, and it was her marriage that brought Baal into Israel.

That is the address he withdraws to after a delegation from Jerusalem comes north to complain about hand washing.

The second is the word Matthew chooses for her, and it is deliberately archaic.

Mark, telling the same story, calls her a Syrophoenician by birth (Mk. 7:26) — the ordinary, current, geographical description a first-century writer would use.

Matthew calls her a Canaanite.

It is the Old Testament word — the name of the nations Israel was commanded to drive out of the land, the people of Jericho and Ai, the ones whose religion the whole law was designed to fence against.

It is roughly as if a modern writer described someone as a Philistine. Matthew has reached back over five hundred years for a term with maximum freight, and it can only be on purpose: he wants the reader to feel the full distance between this woman and the covenant before she opens her mouth.

And then she opens her mouth and says: Son of David.

A Canaanite, using Israel's messianic title, correctly, in Gentile country — while back in Galilee the scribes who owned that title were arguing about whether his men had washed properly.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician; Matthew uses the old name Canaanite, Israel’s ancient enemies.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The silence of Jesus is the hardest moment in the episode. He does not answer — not a refusal, not an explanation, but silence. The disciples' request to send her away reveals their impatience with persistent need that complicates the journey. Jesus's response to the disciples clarifies his mission's current scope: the lost sheep of Israel are his primary assignment at this moment. But this is not the final word. The woman presses past both the silence and the scope-statement. The silence is a test, not a rejection; the mission-statement is a context, not a ceiling. Every subsequent word of Jesus will demonstrate that the Gentile woman who presses through the silence will receive what she seeks.

Her position is harder than the storm at 8:26 or the delay on the road to Jairus's house at 9:18-26. This is not sleep and it is not lateness. She asks and receives nothing at all; she asks again and gets what sounds like a closed door.

Watch what she does with it, because it is the most instructive thing in the chapter. She does not withdraw offended, which most of us would call self-respect. She does not argue that the framework is unfair. She takes the very words that seem to shut her out and finds the opening inside them — Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs. She accepts his terms and appeals within them, and that is what he calls great faith.

Notice too that she never once rests her case on herself. There is no protest that she deserves better, no account of how long she has waited, no résumé at all. Her entire argument is about what he is like: that enough falls from that table to heal her daughter.

Did Jesus come only for the Jews? His earthly ministry was directed to Israel, as he told the Twelve (10:5–6), because God’s promises came first to them (Rom 1:16; 15:8–9). The mission to all nations came after the resurrection (28:19). Yet even here he blesses a Gentile woman, a foretaste of the gathering of other sheep (John 10:16).

If you are praying into silence, that is the shape to copy — not louder, and not a better case for your own deserving, but persistence with the plea fastened to his character rather than your merit. And take the ending with you. The silence was never a refusal. It was the last thing standing between her and a sentence she would otherwise never have heard, and a daughter healed that hour. He was not withholding from her. He was drawing something out of her that she did not know was there.

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel
a servant to the circumcised, that the Gentiles might glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: But she came and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, help me." And he answered, "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Lord, help me" — the briefest and most urgent prayer, stripped of all argument and claim. She does not dispute his mission-statement; she simply maintains her need. The "dogs" saying is the most difficult in this passage. In Jewish usage "dogs" was a derogatory term for Gentiles; Jesus uses the diminutive (little dogs, house dogs — kunaria) which softens it. He is presenting the order of salvation: Israel first, then the nations. He is not insulting her; he is setting up her response, which will be the definitive statement of faith that transcends the apparent boundary. The test reveals what the woman already knows: she is not claiming the children's place; she is asking for something much smaller.

The diminutive has to be pressed, because it is the difference between a slur and a household.

Greek has two words. Kyon is the dog of the streets and the rubbish heaps — a scavenger, unclean, dangerous, and that is the word used when dogs is an insult. It is the word in do not give what is holy to the dogs (7:6) and in Paul's look out for the dogs (Phil. 3:2).

Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion — the diminutive, the little dog, the one that lives in the house.

And the picture changes entirely. This is not a pack outside the gate; it is a family at a meal with an animal under the table. The dog belongs there. It is fed there. What is being said is not you are vermin but the children eat first — which is a statement about order, not about worth.

The woman hears that instantly, which is why her reply works.

But the difficulty should not be dissolved entirely, and it is worth being honest about how the scene reads.

He ignored her (v. 23). The disciples asked him to send her away. He told her his commission did not extend to her. And then, when she knelt and said Lord, help me, he answered with a proverb about dogs.

No amount of philology makes that gentle, and readers who feel the shock of it are reading correctly. What resolves it is not the vocabulary but the outcome: within two verses he calls her faith great, grants her request without qualification, and heals the girl at a distance in that hour.

Whatever he was doing, it was not refusing her. He was drawing something out of her — and what came out is the finest reply anybody gives him in the Gospel.

One more thing about her posture. She came and knelt before him — the verb is the worship word, proskyneo. A Canaanite woman on her knees in Phoenicia, doing what the Pharisees of Jerusalem had never done.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table.

verseByVerse.quote: She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yes, Lord" — she accepts the framework. She does not argue against his metaphor; she uses it. Even within the metaphor of dogs and children, there is room for her: the dogs eat the crumbs that fall. She is not claiming the children's place at the table; she is asking for what overflows from the children's feast. The crumbs of the Messiah's blessing are sufficient to heal her daughter. This is one of the most theologically luminous moments in the Gospels: a Gentile woman out-argues Jesus on his own terms, by accepting his terms rather than challenging them. "Great is your faith" — the only individual so described in the Synoptics. Her faith is great because it does not require a place at the table; it trusts in the overflow of grace.

Her reply is a single word longer in Greek than the English suggests, and everything turns on it.

Nai, kyrie — Yes, Lord. She agrees. That is the whole of her argument's foundation: she does not dispute the order he has described, does not claim it is unfair, does not point out that her daughter is suffering, does not appeal to her own decency.

She says yes, and then adds one word: kai gar — for even.

Yes, Lord — for even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.

She has taken the picture he offered and stayed inside it, and found that the picture itself contains her. If the household is as he says, then there is a floor under the table, and things fall onto it, and the animal that lives there eats them. Nothing has to be taken from the children. Nothing has to be rearranged. She is asking for what drops.

And it is worth saying plainly what has just happened.

Twice in this Gospel somebody argues with Jesus and wins. Both times it is a Gentile. Neither of them wins by disputing him — the centurion accepts that he is unworthy to have Jesus under his roof, and this woman accepts that she is not a child of the house — and both press through on the strength of what they have grasped about him rather than about themselves.

Then the commendation, and the statistic is worth having.

In all four Gospels, Jesus says great is your faith to exactly two people. This woman, here. And the centurion, of whom he said not even in Israel have I found such faith (8:10).

Two commendations of great faith in the entire record, and both are Gentiles, and both are about somebody else's child or servant rather than themselves, and neither of them ever sees Jesus perform the healing.

He went north to Phoenicia to find the second one.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mountain where Jesus sits recalls the Sermon on the Mount — but now the context is Gentile territory (the eastern shore, the Decapolis). The crowds bring "the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute" — the four categories of Isaiah's eschatological restoration (Isa. 35:5-6). The Canaanite woman's healing was an individual sign; this is the collective demonstration: the Messiah's healing ministry extends beyond Israel's borders. "They put them at his feet" — the posture of those who have come to the end of human resources and place their need before the only one who can address it. Every one of them received what they came for.

The four categories are a quotation, and Matthew lists them in an unusual order for a reason.

The lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute — and Isaiah had written: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5-6).

That is the passage Jesus quoted back to John in prison as evidence that the age had begun (11:5). Here Matthew simply reports it happening, in bulk, on a hillside — and the location is the thing to notice, because Isaiah 35 is about the desert blossoming and a highway called the Way of Holiness on which the redeemed come home to Zion.

It is happening on the wrong side of the lake.

And he went up on the mountain and sat down. Matthew has used that pairing once before, at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount (5:1) — the same two verbs, the same posture of authoritative teaching.

On that mountain he taught. On this one he heals, and does not say a word that Matthew records.

Then the detail that carries the most: they put them at his feet.

Not brought them to him, which is what Matthew usually writes. They were set down — which tells you these were people who could not stand, carried some distance by others, and laid on the ground in front of a seated man.

The crowd is described as great, and the list has four categories in it, and the word for what happened to them is one syllable in the Greek and one clause in the English: he healed them.

No preaching is recorded, no dialogue, no faith is examined, and nobody is asked anything. They were put down at his feet, and picked up again working.
verseByVerse.note: Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake.

parallels.desc: the lame leap and the mute sing

verseByVerse.quote: so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, "I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They glorified the God of Israel" — the Gentile crowd giving glory to Israel's God. This is the moment Isaiah foresaw: the nations praising the God of Abraham when they see his Messiah at work. The compassion Jesus feels for the crowd after three days is the same splagchnizomai of 9:36 and 14:14 — the physical churning of profound pity. "I am not willing to send them away hungry" — the same insistence as before the first feeding (14:16). Jesus does not manage scarcity; he addresses need. The disciples' protest ("where could we get enough bread in this desolate place?") shows they have not yet fully learned the lesson of the five thousand. Faith remembers what grace has done; unbelief recalculates the available resources.

Four words suggest who this crowd was, and they are easy to read past: they glorified the God of Israel.

The qualifier of Israel may well be what an outsider adds, distinguishing this God from the ones he grew up with.

So the people on that mountain were Gentiles, and Matthew signals it in the way they worship rather than by stating it.

Which settles a good deal about the meal that follows, and about why there are two feedings in this Gospel at all.

Then the compassion, and the word is physical.

Splanchnizomai comes from the noun for the inward organs — the guts. It is not a word for pity considered at a distance; it describes something that happens in the body, and Greek writers used it of the churn a person feels when they see something they cannot bear.

The Gospels use it almost exclusively of Jesus. Matthew has it of the shepherdless crowds (9:36), of the sick at the first feeding (14:14), of two blind men on a road (20:34), and here.

And the reason given is unusually specific. They have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat.

Three days. That is not an afternoon's crowd; these people have camped on a hillside in Gentile country for three days, and whatever food they brought ran out. Some of them, he adds, have come from far away (Mk. 8:3).

The concern is not spiritual and he does not dress it up as such: lest they faint on the way. He is thinking about people collapsing on the walk home.

Which is worth noticing about the order of his priorities. He has spent three days healing them. The healing is over, the teaching is done, and the last thing on his mind before they disperse is whether they will get back without falling over.
verseByVerse.note: “The God of Israel” may suggest a largely Gentile crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples said to him, "Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?" And Jesus said to them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven, and a few small fish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' question — "where are we to get enough bread?" — should not come from men who watched five loaves feed five thousand. The failure to transfer the lesson of one miracle to the next similar situation is the characteristic failure of human faith: we believe after the miracle; we doubt before the next one. Each new need is experienced as if there were no previous provision. Jesus asks, as Mark records at the first feeding (Mark 6:38): "How many loaves do you have?" He begins with what they have, not what they lack. Seven loaves and a few fish: more than before (five and two), but still laughably insufficient for four thousand men plus women and children.

The disciples' question is the most astonishing sentence in the chapter, and it should not be smoothed over.

Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?

These are the same men. Not their successors, not a different group — the same twelve who, a few weeks earlier, had each carried a basket of leftovers away from a hillside where five loaves had fed a crowd of much the same size.

And they ask the question as though it had never happened.

Commentators have found this so implausible that some have argued the two feedings must be one story told twice. It is worth saying plainly that Jesus himself settles that: a chapter later he asks them, do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? (16:9-10). He treats them as two events, and rebukes the disciples for failing to learn from either.

So the implausibility is real, and it is in the men rather than in the record.

Which is one of the quiet arguments for the Gospels' honesty. A writer inventing a movement's founding generation does not make them look like this. Matthew is one of the twelve; he is describing his own memory lapse and putting his name on the book.

And the answer he gets is the question Mark records at the first feeding (Mark 6:38): how many loaves do you have?

No rebuke is recorded here — that comes later, at 16:8-11, and it is sharp. In the moment he simply asks what is in the bag.

They have seven loaves and a few small fish, which is more than they had at the first feeding for a smaller crowd. They have improved slightly on the arithmetic and not at all on the conclusion.

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourfold action — took, gave thanks, broke, gave — again anticipates the Last Supper. The thanksgiving (eucharistesas — giving thanks) is the word from which "Eucharist" is derived. The meal in the wilderness, the disciples distributing, the crowd fed: every element points forward and backward simultaneously — backward to the manna in the Exodus, forward to the table of the Lord. The disciples are again the servants at the table; they distribute what they cannot produce. This is the shape of all ministry: we distribute what we have received from him. The minister is not the source but the channel; the source is always the one who took, gave thanks, broke, and gave.

The two feedings differ in a way that is invisible in English and decisive in Greek, and it is the answer to anyone who says this is the same story twice.

At the five thousand, twelve baskets of fragments were taken up. The word is kophinos — a small stiff wicker basket, the sort a Jew carried his own food in when travelling so as to avoid Gentile provisions. Roman satirists mocked Jews for going about with one.

Here, seven baskets are filled. The word is spyris — a large hamper, big enough to hold a man. It is the basket Paul was let down the Damascus wall in (Acts 9:25).

Two different objects, consistently used: kophinos every time the five thousand is mentioned, spyris every time the four thousand is, in Matthew and in Mark, and in Jesus' own recollection at 16:9-10.

That is not how a duplicated story behaves.

And the numbers are doing something too. Twelve may recall Israel's tribes. Seven may suggest completeness, or the seven Canaanite nations Israel displaced (Deut. 7:1), and the number of deacons later appointed to serve the Greek-speaking widows.

Twelve baskets on the Jewish shore. Seven on the Gentile one.

Then the sequence, which is the same as before and will be the same twice more.

He took, gave thanks, broke, and gave — and the second verb here is eucharisteo rather than the eulogeo of chapter 14. The two are interchangeable in this formula, and both appear in the accounts of the Last Supper.

And again the disciples distribute. The men who had just asked where bread could possibly come from spent the next hour handing it out.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven baskets — spyridas, large wicker baskets (different from the twelve kophinos of 14:20) — of surplus bread. Seven: the number of completion, and possibly evoking the seven nations of Canaan that Israel was to displace (Deut. 7:1). The Gentile feeding overflows with Gentile-symbolic abundance. Four thousand men plus women and children: the second feeding is smaller than the first but no less miraculous. Matthew's precision about the numbers is the insistence of an eyewitness tradition that these things actually happened: these specific quantities, these specific leftovers, these specific numbers counted and remembered. The miracle of abundance in desolate places — Exodus manna, the five thousand, the four thousand — is God's signature of covenant faithfulness across both Testaments.

A fair question arises here, and skeptics have pressed it hard: is this really a second feeding, or just the story of the five thousand told over again — a "doublet" that betrays a garbled tradition? The answer is that the two are plainly distinct, and Jesus himself treats them so. Not long after, he reminds the disciples of both in one breath, carefully keeping the numbers apart: the five loaves for the five thousand and how many baskets (twelve) you gathered, and the seven loaves for the four thousand and how many baskets (seven) you gathered (16:9-10). The details differ throughout: five thousand on the Jewish shore versus four thousand in Gentile Decapolis; five loaves versus seven; twelve small personal baskets (kophinos) versus seven large hampers (spyris); a crowd there for an evening versus one that had been with him three days. Even the disciples' baffling forgetfulness — "where would we get bread?" after they had just seen it done — is not the seam of a clumsy editor but the very thing the text is exposing: the slowness of the human heart to carry yesterday's grace into today's need, which is exactly what Jesus will rebuke them for (16:8). Two feedings, two peoples, one Lord who is bread enough for Jew and Gentile alike.

One number in verse 38 repays a second look, because Matthew adds the same four words he added at the first feeding.

Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

He did it at 14:21 and he does it again here, and both times he is spelling out what the round number leaves out. The reported figure counted men; the actual crowd on that hillside was very likely eight or ten thousand people.

Which means the two feedings were closer in size than the round numbers suggest, and that the smaller of the two — the Gentile one — was still larger than any town on the eastern shore.

And the fragments are worth one last thought.

Seven hampers of surplus, gathered after everybody had eaten to satiety, from seven loaves. The supply at the end exceeded the supply at the start, in a desolate place, in a desolate place, among foreigners.

Nothing is said about what happened to it. Twelve baskets went somewhere after the first feeding and seven hampers went somewhere after this one, and no Gospel writer thought to record it.

They were interested in the arithmetic of the miracle. Somebody, presumably, ate the leftovers on the road home — and that, in a story about a man who did not want people fainting on the way, is very likely the whole point of gathering them.
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand, and could mean a large hamper.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is dismissed and Jesus crosses by boat to Magadan — a location not otherwise identified with certainty, possibly the same as Magdala on the western shore of Galilee. The movement is constant in these chapters: across the sea, into Gentile territory, back again. Jesus is not confined to any one region or constituency. The Canaanite woman's healing and the Gentile feeding have extended the kingdom's table; now Jesus returns to the Jewish side. The boundary between Jew and Gentile that the Pharisees guarded so carefully is already being blurred by the Messiah whose compassion has no ethnic terminus. The Great Commission is not a new idea in chapter 28; it is the theological conclusion of what chapters 8-15 have been demonstrating.

An honest note on the place name, since a reader with two Bibles open will find two different words.

Matthew has Magadan; Mark has Dalmanutha (Mk. 8:10); and some manuscripts of Matthew read Magdala. None of the three can be identified with certainty, and there is no obvious way to reconcile them.

The likeliest account is the ordinary one: a stretch of shoreline with more than one landmark on it, named differently by different people, exactly as a modern traveller might say he landed at Dover or in Kent. Magdala — the home town of Mary Magdalene — sat on that western shore, and a small harbour there has been excavated.

Nothing hangs on it, and it is worth knowing that Matthew's geography is not usually vague. He names Capernaum, Bethsaida, Chorazin, Gennesaret, Caesarea Philippi, Bethany and Bethphage without difficulty. This is one obscure landing place on a lake, in a Gospel written a generation later.

What the verse does mark is the end of a long arc, and it is worth tracing.

He left Jewish territory at verse 21 and has not been back since. In between: a Canaanite woman commended for great faith, a mountain of Gentile sick healed without a word, a crowd praising the God of Israel as outsiders do, and four thousand people fed in seven hampers.

Now he gets into a boat and crosses back — and the very first thing that happens on the other side is that the Pharisees and Sadducees come and ask him for a sign (16:1).

Matthew has put those two paragraphs side by side without comment. Gentiles who had nothing glorified the God of Israel on a hillside; the men who had everything met the boat and asked for evidence.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Magadan is uncertain; Mark names it Dalmanutha.

15.theology: Total depravity and the need for regeneration. Matthew 15:18–19 is one of the clearest statements of the doctrine of the heart’s corruption in the Gospels. The evil that defiles comes not from outside but from within — from the heart that Jeremiah described as “deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9). Reformed theology insists that this corruption is total in extent (reaching every faculty) though not infinite in degree (common grace restrains it). The implication is that the solution must be equally radical: not education, not ceremony, not moral effort, but the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26 — “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” That is the work of regeneration by the Spirit, purchased by the cross of Christ.
15.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ tradition had become a way of performing piety while avoiding its cost. The Corban ruling let a man appear devout while dishonoring his parents. Religion had become a loophole system. Jesus shut it down.

Now: Every generation finds ways to honour God with the lips while protecting the heart from real submission. Theological correctness without personal holiness, church attendance without costly love, tithing without generosity of spirit — all are versions of the Pharisaic trap. The Canaanite woman is the antidote: no credentials, no performance, just desperate faith in the mercy of Christ. That is always enough.

16.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. <sup>2</sup>He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ <sup>3</sup>And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. <sup>4</sup>An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. <sup>5</sup>When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. <sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>7</sup>And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” <sup>8</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said, “O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? <sup>9</sup>Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>10</sup>Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>11</sup>How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>12</sup>Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” <sup>14</sup>And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” <sup>15</sup>He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” <sup>16</sup>Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. <sup>18</sup>And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <sup>19</sup>I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” <sup>20</sup>Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. <sup>21</sup>From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. <sup>22</sup>And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” <sup>23</sup>But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>24</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>25</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>26</sup>For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? <sup>27</sup>For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. <sup>28</sup>Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Peter’s confession — “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” — is the summit of the disciples’ journey of recognition. Jesus affirms it as divinely revealed, not humanly deduced, and builds the future of his church on this confession. But he immediately turns to the cross: the Christ, the Son of the living God, must go to Jerusalem and die. Peter, who has just made the highest confession of faith in the Gospel, immediately becomes “Satan” — a stumbling block — by refusing the necessity of the cross.

The pairing is deliberate and profound. You cannot confess Jesus as Christ without receiving the cross. Caesarea Philippi was a pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon, a centre of Roman imperial cult and pagan worship. Here, at the edge of empire and paganism, Jesus declares that he will build his church — and the gates of hell will not prevail. The church is built on the confession, and on Peter only as the first man to make it; and it advances not by cultural power but by the cruciform mission of a cruciform King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Sign of Jonah, Peter's Confession, and the Keys of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. At Caesarea Philippi he asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter confesses: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus pronounces a blessing on Peter, declares he will build his church on this rock, and gives him the keys of the kingdom. Then, having accepted the confession, he forbids them to repeat it (v. 20): the title is true, but it is sealed until the cross can say what kind of Christ he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Peter's confession is the christological climax of the first half of Matthew's Gospel. The question Jesus asks — "But who do you say that I am?" — is addressed to the disciples after they have lived with him through chapters 4-15. Peter's answer is the only possible answer for those who have truly seen: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus responds with the foundational promise of the church's existence: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." The church does not build itself; it is built by Christ on the confession of who he is. The first half of the section is a study in reading. Men who can forecast weather cannot read the moment they are standing in (vv. 1-4), and the only sign they will get is a grave and an empty tomb. The leaven warning that follows (vv. 5-12) names the two ways a faith is brought under human management: the Pharisees added to God's word until their tradition outranked it, the Sadducees subtracted from it until nothing supernatural was left, and verse 12 calls the two of them one teaching. And the section closes on a deliberate silence (v. 20). The confession is true and the definition in the hearers' heads is false, so the title goes under guard until Jerusalem explains it — and the ban is lifted only when the risen Christ commands the nations to be told (28:19).
verseByVerse.examples: "Who do you say that I am?" is the question every person must answer. The crowds reach for the biggest names they have — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah — and every one of them belongs to the past and is a forerunner, a signpost rather than a destination. Peter offers the only category that fits the evidence: Messiah, Son of the living God. The confession is the door through which everything else follows — the keys of the kingdom, the binding and loosing, the promise that the church will stand against the gates of hell. The church is not a human institution that may or may not endure; it is Christ's building, constructed on the indestructible foundation of the confession that he is Lord. Two practical edges run through the same section. The leaven warning is spoken to the Twelve about themselves, with no opponent present — it is not a licence to hunt heresy in other people but a question about which way your own faith drifts when nobody is checking: toward a list of things you are careful about, or toward a quiet removal of everything in the Bible that would be awkward to say out loud at work. And the silence of verse 20 is a warning to anyone impatient for results: it is entirely possible to get a man to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees and Sadducees — theological opponents who have united against Jesus — demand a sign from heaven, something unmistakably divine and beyond natural explanation. The signs Jesus has already given (the healings, the feedings, the exorcisms) are apparently insufficient — or rather, are being dismissed as potentially demonic (12:24). Jesus begins with weather prediction: you read the sky and make accurate forecasts from natural signs. The point is that the capacity for sign-reading exists; what is missing is the willingness to apply it to the spiritual situation unfolding before them.

A reader with an open Bible will notice something here before he notices anything else. The ESV puts brackets around the weather saying — from "When it is evening" in this verse to "the signs of the times" at the end of verse 3 — with a footnote saying that some manuscripts omit the words altogether. So he is being taught from a passage his own Bible has marked as uncertain, and nobody has told him what to make of that. The facts are these. Two of the oldest and best copies of Matthew we possess, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, do not have these words; neither do several early translations; and Jerome, working in the fourth century, remarked that most of the copies in front of him lacked them. Many later manuscripts do have them. The likeliest explanation is the one we meet elsewhere in this Gospel: Luke records Jesus saying almost exactly this — you know how to read the sky, why can you not read the present time (Luke 12:54-56) — and a copyist who knew the saying from Luke would very naturally have filled in what looked to him like a gap in Matthew. It is the same movement of a scribe's hand that put Luke 19:10 into Matthew 18:11 and Mark 9:29 into Matthew 17:21 (see on both). Others argue the other way round — that copyists in Egypt, where a red morning sky does not forecast a storm as it does in Palestine, dropped a line of weather lore that made no sense where they sat. The honest verdict is that we cannot be certain, which is precisely why your Bible uses brackets rather than either deleting the words or printing them plain.

And now notice how little is at stake, which is the usual outcome of these questions and worth feeling. Every word of the exchange that carries the weight stands in undisputed text: they came to test him, they demanded a sign from heaven, and he answered that an evil and adulterous generation would be given none but the sign of Jonah. Matthew has already given us the same refusal in full at 12:38-39, and the rebuke about reading the sky is beyond dispute in Luke. Whether Matthew wrote these two sentences here, or a later hand carried them over from Luke because they belonged so obviously to the scene, not one thing taught in this chapter depends on the answer. The bracket marks a question about a copyist. It does not mark a doubt about the Lord's words.
