Genesis 2:24 — the first word about marriage in Scripture — establishes the three movements: leaving (the previous primary bond of parents), cleaving (the exclusive covenant of husband and wife), and becoming one flesh (the physical union that expresses and seals the covenant). "The two shall become one flesh" is not merely physical union but the merging of two lives into a shared existence — social, economic, emotional, spiritual, physical. "What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" — the divine agency in marriage ("God has joined") makes human dissolution not merely ill-advised but a violation of what God has done. This is not law external to persons; it is the structure of what marriage actually is.

Take one flesh literally enough to feel it, because the phrase has been worn smooth. It does not mean the couple are close, or well suited, or committed. It means that something which was two has become one thing — and the consequence is that they can no longer be separated, only torn. That is why the ending of a marriage does not feel like the ending of any other relationship, and why people are so often shocked by the depth of it. A partnership can be dissolved and both partners walk away whole. A friendship can end and leave two friends. Cutting one flesh in two does not produce two people; it produces two halves, and they bleed for years. Anyone who has been through it, or watched a friend go through it, already knows this and has usually been told he should be over it by now.

The other word to slow down on is the one behind joined together: sunezeuxen, yoked. The picture is not a knot but a harness — two animals under one beam, pulling the same load in the same direction, unable to turn without the other turning. And the subject of the verb is God. Which settles something a great many people quietly wonder about: whether a marriage begun badly is really a marriage at all. Two unbelievers in a registry office with no prayer said over them and no thought of God in the room are, on the authority of this sentence, joined by God. He does the yoking whether or not he was invited to the wedding. There is no such thing as a merely civil marriage in heaven's records.

Notice also who is forbidden to separate them. Let not man is not addressed only to the husband and wife. It reaches the judge who grants it lightly, the friend who has been advising for months that she deserves better, the parent who never accepted the marriage and has been waiting, the colleague who makes the affair easy. There are usually more hands on a broken marriage than the two belonging to the couple.

And there is a practical command here that the church almost never preaches, because the verse is nearly always quoted from hold fast onward. Genesis puts leave first. A man shall leave his father and his mother, and then hold fast to his wife. The order is not decorative. A very great deal of trouble in the early years of a marriage is a leaving problem rather than a cleaving problem: a man who still runs decisions past his mother, a woman whose father remains the final court of appeal on her husband, a couple whose Christmases are still arranged by somebody else. And the word for holding fast, proskollao, is the word for gluing. You cannot glue something that is still attached to what it was fixed to before.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?" He said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Moses allowed" — not commanded. The Pharisees misquote the tradition: Deuteronomy 24:1 regulates an existing practice; it does not mandate divorce. Jesus corrects the category: the certificate of divorce was a concession to the hardness of the human heart in a fallen world, a regulation of something God never intended but permitted because of the reality of sin. "From the beginning it was not so" — the creation norm is the standard against which the Mosaic permission is measured, not the other way around. Jesus does not abolish the Mosaic permission; he locates it correctly as a concession, and restores the creation design as the positive ideal toward which kingdom citizens are called.

Watch the verb change hands, because the whole exchange turns on one word. They said Moses commanded. He answered that Moses allowed. That is the argument over. They had taken a permission and promoted it to a duty, which is exactly what a hard heart always does with a concession: what is tolerated becomes what is normal, what is normal becomes what is expected, and within a generation somebody is citing the concession as though it were the command.

And Deuteronomy 24 will not carry what they wanted it to carry, as anyone can see by reading it slowly. The whole passage is one long sentence, and divorce appears only in the opening conditions — if a man divorces her, and if she leaves and marries another, and if the second husband also divorces her or dies. The actual command does not arrive until verse 4, and it is this: her first husband may not take her back. Moses is not legislating divorce at all. He is regulating a remarriage, and mentioning divorce only as the miserable background everybody already knew about. The Pharisees had built a licence out of a subordinate clause.

There is a further irony in their choice of text, and it is worth recovering, because the certificate they cite as a man's right was in fact a woman's protection. A wife discarded without documents was in an impossible position: she could not prove she was free, no man would risk marrying her, and she was exposed to the charge of adultery if she tried. The written certificate was the one thing standing between her and destitution. So the very provision quoted here as evidence that a man may send his wife away was designed to restrain the man and to shield her. They had turned her shield into his sword.

Then because of your hardness of heart — and mark the pronoun. He does not say because of their hardness of heart, referring to a generation dead a thousand years. He says your, to the men standing in front of him, who had come with a question designed to get somebody killed. Sklerokardia is a hard word: not weakness, not confusion, but a heart gone stiff, unable to bend where it should. The concession was not made because the situation was complicated. It was made because men were like that, and are.

Which raises a question a thoughtful reader should ask: if divorce law is a concession to sin, is it wrong for a country to have any? No — and notice that Jesus does not abolish the provision he has just put in its place. This is one of the most useful principles in Scripture for living in a world that is not going to be Christianised by legislation: God legislates for the world as it is without ever lowering what he made it for. A merciful provision for a broken situation is neither an endorsement of the breaking nor a recommendation to use it. That the law permits a thing settles nothing whatever about whether you should do it, and it is possible to be entirely within your legal rights and standing exactly where Jesus says the hardness of heart is.

verseByVerse.quote: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery." The disciples said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exception for porneia (sexual immorality, likely including adultery) acknowledges that the covenant can be broken by one party, releasing the other. But apart from that exception, remarriage after divorce is adultery — the ongoing violation of the prior covenant. The disciples' response is understandable: if marriage is this binding, it is a serious risk. Their conclusion — "better not to marry" — misses the point but captures the weight of Jesus's teaching. Marriage is not merely a preference or a social convenience; it is a covenant with the permanence that God's own covenants have. The disciples are beginning to sense this, even if their response is flight rather than faithfulness.

Because this touches real and painful lives, two things should be added plainly. First, Matthew's single exception is not the whole of Scripture's teaching. Paul gives a second ground: when an unbelieving spouse deserts a believer, "the brother or sister is not enslaved" (1 Cor 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long held, with the Westminster Confession, that there are two grounds on which the marriage bond may be broken and the innocent party freed to remarry — adultery and desertion — and no others; those who took a stricter line (no remarriage ever) or a looser one (Hillel's "any cause") both miss the balance of the whole. Second, and more importantly: none of this is a loophole to be worked but a fence around something holy. Jesus's aim is not to license divorce but to guard the one-flesh covenant against the hardness of heart that treats it lightly. And to any reader whose own marriage has already broken — through your sin, or another's, or a tangle of both — hear this: there is no sin here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no past so broken that grace cannot make something new of what remains. The gospel meets us not in the marriage we should have had but in the life we actually have.

One last thing, for the reader with Mark or Luke open alongside. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9) — and Mark and Luke record none at all: "whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery" (Mark 10:11; cf. Luke 16:18). Critics say Matthew softened his Lord to suit his church. But this is how people have always spoken and still do. A father who says "we do not lend the car out" is not lying when he lends it to his own son in an emergency; the rule is stated as a rule, and the known qualification is not repeated every time it is uttered. Mark and Luke give the principle in its blunt form, which is where the force of it lies. Matthew, writing for Jewish readers to whom the Shammai-Hillel quarrel was a live and daily argument, records the qualification Jesus actually made — because his readers were the very people who would ask. Neither of them is saying something the other denies, and the direction of both is identical: not how little a man may keep his marriage, but that God joined it and man must not take it apart.

One question has not been asked yet, and for some readers it is the only question in the chapter. What about a marriage that is not being betrayed but is destroying somebody — the husband who is violent, the wife whose rage has made the house unsafe, the parent whose drinking has turned a home into somewhere the children brace themselves to enter? Matthew names one ground and Paul names a second, and neither of them uses the word. Does Christ require a battered woman to stay?

He does not, and it will not do to be vague about it, because vagueness here has cost real people a great deal. Three things are true, and the order matters.

First, and before any question of divorce arises at all: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden in Scripture. Paul contemplates a wife who has separated and simply tells her to remain unmarried or be reconciled (1 Cor 7:11); he lays down no conditions for the separating and attaches no shame to it. Getting out of reach of a dangerous man is not a step toward divorce. It is a step toward not being killed, and nothing in this chapter stands in its way. It is also, very often, the only thing that has ever cost him anything, and therefore the only thing that has ever made repentance a live possibility.

Second, the children are not a secondary consideration. A parent who removes them from a violent house is obeying rather than disobeying, and the man who tells her otherwise should be asked to read the previous chapter aloud — where the Lord who forbids the easy divorce says that a man who causes one of these little ones to stumble would be better off in deep water with a millstone round his neck (18:6).

Third, on the bond itself. The Reformed churches held that the marriage bond may be broken by adultery or by desertion, and the men who framed that were not innocent about cruelty. Desertion was never treated as a question of geography alone. A husband who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted the marriage as surely as one who packs a bag; he has simply arranged for his wife to do the walking. Judging desertion by its substance rather than by who physically left the house is not a modern loophole. It is what the older pastors meant, and it is why they said the innocent party is not to be held bound.

Two things follow. This is a matter to be taken to a church rather than settled alone — which is precisely why the previous chapter placed such judgments in the hands of a congregation and its elders (18:15-20), and why a wounded person needs people around her who will look at the evidence. And any church that hears such a case and answers by sending a woman home to try harder, or by weighing a man's standing in the congregation against what she has described, has not been careful with Matthew 19. It has been careless with a life, and it should be told so plainly.

Those who hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives have serious reasons: Mark and Luke record no exception (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18), Paul says a wife is bound while her husband lives (Rom 7:2–3), and many in the early church held this view. Others read the exception only of unfaithfulness during betrothal. The historic Reformed reading is the more likely, because Jesus’ exception is a real exception, and Paul shows that the bond can be released (1 Cor 7:15). Sexual immorality covers adultery and sexual sin of the same gravity. And the exception permits divorce; it does not command it. Where there is repentance, reconciliation is the better path.

What of someone who divorced without biblical grounds, or who divorced and remarried before becoming a Christian? The guilty party who repents is called to remain single or be reconciled (1 Cor 7:11), though Reformed churches differ on remarriage in that case. Those already remarried are not to break up the second marriage; it is a real marriage, and the call is to repent of how it began and to live faithfully in it. The phrase commits adultery describes how the second marriage began, not a sin repeated every day it continues.

Look last at what our Lord is actually protecting in this passage. He is not defending an institution against the people inside it. Every stroke of it — the one flesh, the yoking, the refusal of the convenient exit — is meant to make a marriage the one place on earth where a human being is safe for life. A reading of it that shuts somebody inside cruelty has taken the fence he built around a person and used it as a cage.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, "Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this, receive it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not command celibacy but acknowledges it as a gift given to some "for the sake of the kingdom." Three categories: those born without capacity for marriage, those made so by human action, and those who choose singleness for the kingdom's sake. The third category — voluntary celibacy in service of the kingdom — is presented as a legitimate and honored vocation, not a lesser alternative to marriage. Paul will develop this (1 Cor. 7:32-35): the unmarried person is undivided in attention to the Lord's affairs. Both marriage and singleness are gifts; neither is universally better; both can be lived to the glory of God in the kingdom.

That is true, and it is written from a comfortable distance. This chapter is about marriage from its first verse to its twelfth, and a great many of the people reading it are not married and did not decide that. They deserve more than a balanced sentence.

Begin with the three categories, because the middle one is nearly always skipped. Some, Jesus says, were born this way. Some were made this way by other people — that is, by circumstances entirely outside their control, and in the ancient world often by an act of cruelty. And some choose it for the kingdom. He names all three in a single breath and honours the calling in all three; the dignity of it is not reserved for those who volunteered.

Which meets the most common objection to the phrase the gift of singleness, an objection that is entirely fair. A gift is normally something you wanted and unwrapped. Many single Christians did not choose this and would exchange it tomorrow: the woman who hoped to marry and is now fifty, the widower, the person whose marriage ended and who will not remarry, the believer whose convictions about sexuality mean marriage is not open to them. Told that their situation is a gift, they may reasonably feel they are being asked to be grateful for a loss. But that is not what the word carries. In the New Testament a charisma is grace given for a purpose, not a pleasure guaranteed — Paul's thorn was no delight either, and what he was promised in it was not enjoyment but sufficient grace (2 Cor 12:9).

So what is actually promised is not that you will like it. It is that there is grace enough for it; that it is a genuine vocation rather than a waiting room for real life to begin; and that it is not a lesser existence. Notice who is speaking. The most completely human being who has ever lived was single, and so was the apostle who wrote most of the New Testament. Whatever singleness is, it cannot be a deficiency in a person's humanity or in their usefulness to God.

The third kind of eunuch is figurative: those who give up marriage for the kingdom, not those who mutilate themselves. Nor does this require ministers to be unmarried; Peter had a wife (8:14; 1 Cor 9:5), and Paul expects overseers to be husbands (1 Tim 3:2). The “eunuchs from birth” were those born unable to marry; the text is about that incapacity, not about sexual orientation.

And notice what the church owes, because Jesus says it later in this same chapter: everyone who has left houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold (v. 29), which Mark spells out as brothers, sisters, mothers and children now in this time (Mark 10:30). That is not decoration. It is a debt. A congregation that preaches marriage constantly and has no place at its tables for the unmarried has left half its members outside the promise its Lord made. If you carry this as a grief, say so plainly to God and to somebody who will not rush you; Scripture has ample room for people who wanted a good thing and did not receive it, and it never once calls that unbelief.
verseByVerse.note: A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some, like Paul, remained single to serve the kingdom.

parallels.desc: a name better than sons and daughters

verseByVerse.quote: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, but Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The children are brought for prayer and blessing — the most natural parental act. The disciples rebuke those who bring them: children are not important enough to take Jesus's time. Jesus's response is one of the most direct of the Gospel: "do not hinder them." The word (kolyo) is used elsewhere for the impediments placed before those seeking baptism (Acts 8:36; 10:47) — the disciples are placing the same kind of barrier before the children. "To such belongs the kingdom of heaven" — not "such as these will eventually be admitted" but "theirs is the kingdom." The children possess what the adult disciples are still learning to receive.

Do children who die in infancy go to heaven? This verse does not say that children are innocent; Jesus has just warned that we must become like them, not that they are sinless (18:3). But it shows his welcome to them, and Scripture gives grieving parents real hope. David said of his dead infant, I shall go to him (2 Sam 12:23), and the historic Reformed confessions teach that elect infants who die are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. Many Christians are confident that God, the Judge of all the earth, will do right by every child who dies before it can believe. We do not have a verse that says so in plain words, but we have the character of the God who said, Let the little children come to me.

And here a question presses that divides sincere Christians, and this passage sits at the centre of it: should the children of believers be baptized? Those who say yes point to this very scene — Jesus takes infants (Luke calls them brephe, babies, Luke 18:15) into his arms and says the kingdom belongs to such as these — and they set it beside the covenant sign given to Abraham's children (Gen 17:7), Peter's "the promise is for you and for your children" (Acts 2:39), and the whole households baptized in Acts. Those who say no answer that this passage says nothing about baptism at all: Jesus blesses these children, he does not baptize them, and every baptism the New Testament describes follows a profession of faith. Honesty requires admitting that the second point lands. This text does not settle the question, and a case for infant baptism has to be built from the shape of the covenant across both Testaments rather than from these three verses, and that wider case is less convincing than the plain New Testament pattern of baptism after faith (see on Acts 2:39). What this text does settle is smaller and sharper, and both sides can take it home: the only people rebuked in the story are the ones who thought children were a distraction from the real work. Whatever a church concludes about the water, a church that treats its little ones as an interruption to be managed until they are old enough to matter has been told plainly, by name, to stop it. He did not tolerate them; he called for them, and he laid his hands on every one.

verseByVerse.quote: And he laid his hands on them and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He laid his hands on them — every child presented to him was blessed. Matthew does not record what he prayed or what he said; the act is sufficient. The laying on of hands was the gesture of blessing from the patriarchs onward: Jacob blessing Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48), the priests blessing the people. Jesus blesses children not as future adults who may one day be important but as present recipients of kingdom grace. The brevity of verse 15 — no words quoted, just the act and the departure — suggests that the blessing of children needs no commentary. It simply is what it is: the King welcoming the least.

Read the verse against what had just happened, because the sequence is the point. The apostles had just been turning these families away. Now the last recorded act of Jesus in that place, before he leaves the district altogether, is that he put his hands on their children — and hands laid on a group of children is not a gesture made in a moment. And the parents who had been told off by the inner circle stood there and watched it happen.

Which raises the question of who brought them. Somebody thought it worth the walk, in the heat, with small children, on the chance of getting near. And when the men closest to Jesus told them they were wasting his time — and being corrected by the inner circle is an intimidating thing, then and now — they did not take the children home. The people who received the blessing in this story are the ones who declined to be embarrassed out of the queue.

So the instruction to a parent or a grandparent is not complicated, and it is not sentimental. Bring them. Put them where Christ is, week after week, when it is inconvenient and when they are difficult and when they are old enough to say they would rather not. Pray with your hand on them, out loud, using their name — which is, as nearly as we can manage it, the thing that is happening in this verse. And do not be argued out of it by anyone who implies that the serious work of the church is going on elsewhere; that argument has been made once already in this passage, by better men than will make it to you, and it was publicly overruled.

But a guard is needed here, because this verse is quietly used to wound. It is not a promise that every child of a believing home will come to faith. Scripture is honest about godly parents whose children went their own way, and so is every congregation that has been going long enough. A mother or father grieving over a grown son who wants nothing to do with any of it must not read these verses as a verdict on their parenting or as a promise that failed. What is here is a picture of Christ's disposition toward children — warm, unhurried, and personally administered — and an instruction about the church's. That disposition has not altered for a man of forty who was once carried up to him.

And notice the last four words. And he laid his hands on them and went away. He blessed them, and left. Every one of those children grew up in a country that would crucify him inside the year, and Matthew does not tell us what became of a single one of them. The blessing was not a promise of a smooth life. It was a real thing, done by real hands, on an ordinary afternoon, by a man on his way to Jerusalem — and it was the last thing he did before he went.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Rich Young Man and the Great Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man asks what good deed will earn eternal life. Jesus directs him to the commandments; he claims to have kept them all. Jesus says: sell your possessions, give to the poor, and follow me. The man goes away sorrowful, for he has great wealth. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are astonished. Jesus promises rewards for those who have left everything to follow him, and closes with the great reversal: the first shall be last and the last first. Two exchanges inside the section carry more weight than their length. Jesus meets the opening question with one of his own — why do you ask me about what is good, when there is only one who is good (v. 17)? And after the camel and the needle, Peter asks what the Twelve, who did leave everything, will have for it (v. 27); the promise of thrones and a hundredfold is his answer, and verse 30 is the warning attached to it.
verseByVerse.theology: The rich young man's failure reveals the nature of the commandment he thought he kept: "love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 19) was the final commandment in Jesus's list, and the sell-everything command is the test of whether it is actually operative. One cannot love one's neighbor as oneself while sitting on wealth that could address their need. The commandment was kept in its visible form (no theft, no fraud) but not in its spirit (genuine love that costs something). Jesus's diagnosis is precise: the man's wealth is not neutral; it is the specific obstacle between him and eternal life. Verse 17 is regularly produced as proof that Jesus denied being God — he pointed away from himself, so he cannot have thought himself divine. But he does not say I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a deed you can perform and me a teacher who knows the trick, and there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking and whom you are asking. The rest of the Gospel will not let the denial stand — this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2-6), who says the Lord of the Sabbath is standing here (12:8), and who claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' astonishment at the camel-and-needle saying reflects their assumption that wealth is a sign of divine blessing — the standard view. Jesus upends the assumption: wealth is a spiritual obstacle, not an advantage. The camel through the needle's eye is not a metaphor for difficulty but for impossibility — making the way of salvation clear. "With God all things are possible" is the only resolution: the rich man cannot save himself; only God can accomplish the transformation that makes a rich man enter the kingdom. Guard that promise, since it has been lifted off the page and attached to whatever a reader happens to want. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man; it is not a general assurance that anything is obtainable with enough belief. And Matthew has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the crucifixion is over, a man comes to Pilate for the body — and Matthew alone tells us he was rich, plousios, the same word used here of the man who cannot get in (27:57). The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink. God did the thing he said only God could do.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man came up to him, saying, "Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" And he said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"What good deed must I do?" — the question frames eternal life as a transaction: what action can I perform to secure it? Jesus redirects: "Why do you ask me about what is good?" implicitly pressing the question of who Jesus himself is. "There is only one who is good" — God alone is the standard of goodness, the source of all that is good. The answer to "what must I do?" is not a new requirement but the standard that has always been there: keep the commandments. The young man will claim he has. Jesus will reveal that the commandments, rightly understood, require something he is not prepared to give.

But we must stop on "there is only one who is good," because it is regularly produced as proof that Jesus denied being God — he pointed away from himself to God, so he cannot have thought himself divine. Read the sentence again and see what it actually does. Jesus does not say I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a thing you can do and me a teacher who can tell you the trick; there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking and about whom you are asking it of. He is not refusing the title. He is telling a man who used it casually that he has no idea what he has just said. And the rest of the Gospel refuses to let the denial stand: this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2-6), who says the Sabbath's Lord is here (12:8), who receives worship without ever once waving it away, and who at the end of the book claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). A man building a case against his own deity does not talk like that.

Does this teach salvation by works? No. Perfect obedience would bring life, but no sinner can offer it (Rom 3:20; Gal 3:10–12). Jesus uses the law here to expose the young man’s need, which is why he goes on to say that salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (v. 26).

The reader with Mark open will notice something further. There Jesus says, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19) — the sharper form, aimed at the adjective the man used. Matthew has him ask instead about what is good. It is often said that Matthew tidied the wording to protect his Christology. More likely he is doing what he has done all along: giving the exchange in a compressed form that keeps its point (cf. 9:18). The man came asking what good deed he must do; Matthew's wording holds the question and the answer together, and the reply is the same reply in both — goodness is not a deed in your hand, it is a property of God, and you have come to the one place where the two meet without knowing it.
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke record the question as “Good Teacher.” Luke calls him a ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus lists commandments from the second table of the Decalogue — human-to-human relationships — plus the summary command from Leviticus 19:18: love your neighbor as yourself. The list is not random; it is the set of commandments most easily performed at the level of external compliance. One can refrain from murder, adultery, theft, and perjury while remaining fundamentally self-centered. The neighbor-love command is the one that bites, because genuine neighbor-love — love that gives as freely as one would give to oneself — cannot be achieved by not doing things; it requires positive, costly action. This is the commandment that the young man's wealth will test.

Begin with his question, because it gives him away before he says anything else. Which ones? A man who asks which commandments has already turned the law into a syllabus and is asking what is on the examination. He is not asking how to love God; he is asking which items he will be marked on, so that he can check them off and know where he stands. That is not an unusual way to hold a religion. It is the most common way there is, and it is comfortable precisely because a list can be finished.

Now look very carefully at what Jesus leaves out, because the omissions are the whole diagnosis. He recites from the second table of the Decalogue — murder, adultery, theft, false witness, honour your parents — and he stops. He does not say you shall not covet. And he does not touch the first table at all: not one of the commandments about God, about idols, about having no other. Between them, those two omissions are exactly this man's problem. He has another god and he is holding it in both hands. Jesus recites a list with the man's own sin carefully removed, lets him answer all these I have kept, and then in the very next breath asks him for the one thing the missing commandments were about. It is the method Nathan used on David, who angrily passed sentence on a man who stole a lamb.

The addition is as pointed as the omission. Jesus ends the list with a sentence that is not in the Ten Commandments at all: you shall love your neighbour as yourself, from Leviticus 19:18 — the same command he will name at 22:39 as the second on which everything hangs. And notice what kind of command it is. Every other item on his list can be obeyed by sitting still. A man asleep is keeping five of them. This one cannot be kept by not doing something, and it has no upper limit, which is why it is the only one on the list the young man cannot tick.

That is worth turning on the reader, because the young man's instinct is everybody's. If somebody asked you what you got wrong last week, you would almost certainly answer with things you did — a temper lost, a sharp reply, an hour wasted, a lie about why you were late. Very few of us would think to answer with the person we did not go and see, the money we did not give, the conversation we avoided because it would have cost an evening. A conscience built entirely out of prohibitions can be satisfied by half past ten in the morning, and that is exactly what recommends it.

One more thing, in his defence. All these I have kept may not have been a lie. By the standard he had been given, it may have been perfectly true — and that is the most frightening thing about him. He is not a hypocrite caught out. He is a decent, careful, religious man who had done everything he understood himself to have been asked, and who nevertheless knew that something was missing, and had the honesty to say so out loud to the only person who could tell him what it was.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour and adds Leviticus 19:18.

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: The young man said to him, "All these I have kept. What do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"What do I still lack?" — the young man senses his insufficiency even while claiming full compliance. His honest question is the most hopeful thing about him. Jesus answers with precision: not a general principle but a specific command tailored to this specific person's specific obstacle. "Sell what you possess and give to the poor" — this is not a universal command requiring all Christians to sell all possessions (Zacchaeus gives half, Luke 19:8; the Jerusalem church holds property, Acts 5:4). It is the surgical identification of what stands between this man and the kingdom: his wealth. The treasure in heaven is the trade offered. Then "come, follow me" — the same call given to fishermen who left their nets immediately.

If it is not a universal command, though, the obvious question follows: then what does it require of me? Watch how the diagnosis actually works, because that is where the answer is.

Jesus gives no rule about percentages and no general exhortation to moderation. He puts a finger on one thing — the specific object that had this specific man — and asks for exactly that. Which means the question to bring away is not how much is enough but what is mine.

And here is the uncomfortable part: the man already knew. Nobody asks what do I still lack unless something has been nagging at him. He did not need information; he needed to hear it said out loud by someone with the authority to say it. That is usually how this works. Most people, sitting still for a minute, can name the thing they would least like Christ to ask them for. It is not always money. It may be a relationship you know is pulling you away, a career you have quietly made the point of your life, your reputation, a plan for your children, an addiction you manage rather than end, a grudge you have decided to keep (see on 18:29-30), or simply the fear of what people would say. The tell is the flinch.

Notice too what the test is not. It is not would I be willing in principle, because everyone is willing in principle; principle costs nothing. The test is the one run in this passage: what happens when the thing is actually named, out loud, and asked for.

Two things keep that from becoming morbid self-inspection. The first is that Jesus is not confiscating. Read the whole sentence: sell, give, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. The removal exists for the sake of the last clause. He is not impoverishing the man; he is prising his fingers off something small so that his hands are free for something enormous. And the young man's sorrow is the proof that he understood the offer and knew Jesus was right.

Does if you would be perfect mean there is a higher class of Christian, as some teach of vows of poverty and celibacy? No. Jesus means complete, wholehearted devotion, the same word he used in 5:48, and he calls this man to it because wealth was his rival god. The call is to every disciple; what it costs varies from person to person.

The second is the chapter's own answer, six verses later, to the disciples' panic. When they ask who then can be saved, Jesus does not say those with the strength to let go. He says that with men it is impossible, and with God all things are possible (v. 26). So if you have identified your one thing and find you cannot open your hand, you have not failed the test — you have arrived at the point where the gospel starts. That inability is precisely what to bring him.

verseByVerse.quote: When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went away sorrowful — the saddest departure in the Gospels. He came with a question; he leaves with an answer he cannot accept. The sorrow itself reveals something: he knows the command is right; he knows what he is choosing. He is not dismissive or angry; he is grieved. But he goes. The grief does not change the direction. "He had great possessions" — they had him. The possessions were not his property; they were his prison, and he chose to stay in it. Jesus's verdict on the rich is blunt: "only with difficulty." The difficulty is not economic but spiritual: wealth creates illusions of self-sufficiency and security that are the precise opposite of the childlike dependence the kingdom requires.

Weigh what has just happened, because it is unique in this Gospel. Jesus personally invites this man to follow him — come, follow me, the same words that emptied a fishing boat and a tax booth — and he is the one man in Matthew who receives that invitation and declines it. Fishermen left nets. A tax collector left a table with money on it. This man went home. Matthew records the invitation and the refusal in a single sentence and never tells us his name.

And he was not scornful about it. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew Jesus was right. That is the disturbing thing about him: he felt everything a man ought to feel, and did nothing. Grief is not repentance. A person can be moved almost to tears by a sermon on a Sunday, and know while it is happening that the thing being described is his own life, and have altered nothing at all by Wednesday — and can then mistake the being moved for the change. The most dangerous condition in this passage is not the hard heart. It is the softened one that goes home anyway.

Now the guard, because this passage is preached as though money were damnation, and by any measure the world would recognise, most people reading a commentary in English are the rich man in this story. So say the honest thing rather than letting them off or crushing them. Jesus does not say a rich man cannot be saved. He says only with difficulty, and three verses later he says that with God all things are possible. And Scripture is full of wealthy believers: Abraham with his herds, Job at both ends of his book, and the women who paid for this very ministry out of their own means and stayed to the end when the men had gone (27:55-56). What we have here is a warning about a specific danger and an honest statement of the odds. It is not a sentence.

So name the danger precisely, because vague warnings about materialism change nobody. The trouble with money is not that it is evil; it is that it quietly removes the daily experience of dependence. A man who can solve most of his problems by paying for them will, across twenty years, gradually stop asking anyone for anything — and he will never notice it happening, because every individual decision along the way was sensible. He did not rebel against God. He simply stopped needing him for anything specific, and a faith with nothing specific left in it goes thin without ever being renounced.

Which gives a test that takes about ten seconds and is unusually hard to fool. When did you last pray about something that money could not also have fixed? For most people in a comfortable country the honest answer is: about health, and about people I love. That is precisely why illness and bereavement so often turn out to be where God is finally met. They are the two remaining rooms in a wealthy life where a cheque does absolutely nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, "Who then can be saved?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The camel through the needle's eye is not softened by the "small gate" interpretation (the "Needle's Gate" in Jerusalem is a later legend with no ancient support). It is impossible: the largest animal commonly seen in Palestine cannot pass through the smallest common opening. The impossibility is the point. "Who then can be saved?" — the disciples' astonishment is the right response: if not the wealthy man who keeps the commandments, who? Their question assumes that wealth is a sign of blessing; Jesus has revealed it as an obstacle. If wealth cannot save, and wealth was thought to indicate divine favor, then on what basis can anyone enter?

There is a second attempt at softening it, less well known than the gate but with the same motive. A handful of late manuscripts read kamilos, a rope or ship's cable, in place of kamelos, a camel — one letter's difference, and a much more manageable picture, since a rope at least belongs to the same world as a needle. It is a scribe's improvement, not Matthew's word. And the giveaway is that both softenings pull in exactly the same direction: they are attempts to make the sentence survivable. The rabbis had their own form of the proverb, in which an elephant passes through the eye of a needle, and they used it for the plainly impossible. In Palestine the largest animal to hand was a camel; in Babylon it was an elephant. Everyone who first heard this knew it was a joke about impossibility, and they were not laughing.

The disciples' question only lands if their assumption is stated out loud, and it is not the assumption we bring. They believed, on what looks like a plain reading of Deuteronomy 28, that prosperity was the visible sign of God's favour. A rich man was therefore not merely a man with resources; he was a man whose life displayed that God was pleased with him. And this particular rich man was also young, morally serious, scrupulous about the commandments, and willing to walk up to a travelling rabbi in public and ask what he still lacked. He was the strongest candidate any of them had ever seen. So their question is not who among the wealthy can be saved. It is who at all. They had just watched the front-runner walk away down the road.

Almost nobody asks that question honestly, because almost everybody keeps a private category of people who obviously qualify — the missionary, the pastor's wife, the old woman in the third row who has prayed for forty years and never said a sharp word to anyone. As long as that category exists, salvation remains comfortably plausible and somebody else's problem. What Jesus has just done is abolish the category. Not one name survives it.

And that is not cruelty; it is the necessary clearing of the ground. Nobody has ever heard the next verse — that with God all things are possible — until he has first stopped believing that with men some things are. The astonishment of verse 25 is not a failure of faith on the disciples' part. It is the first correct reaction anybody in this chapter has had.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Then Peter said in reply, "See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"With God all things are possible" — including the salvation of rich people, as the subsequent story of Zacchaeus (Luke 19) will demonstrate. The impossibility is human impossibility: no human effort, no amount of commandment-keeping, no management of wealth can produce the transformation required. Only God can transform the heart that is captive to its possessions. Peter's follow-up question is honest and not entirely mercenary: they have done what the rich young man refused to do. They left everything. What is the accounting? The question could be pure calculation or genuine desire to understand the kingdom's economy. Jesus answers both readings.

Matthew keeps the detail that he looked at them — emblepsas, a straight, deliberate look — before he said anything. He did not reply immediately. The look was part of the answer, and Matthew thought it worth recording that a dozen frightened men were held in his eye for a second before they were told the thing that would settle them.

Then the sentence that turns the whole chapter over. Everything up to this point has been about what a man must do — keep the commandments, which ones, sell what you have, come and follow. And now: with man this is impossible. The chapter has spent twenty-five verses building a staircase, and this sentence removes it. Notice the shape of what has happened. The young man arrived asking what good deed must I do to have eternal life, and the final answer to his question is that there is no deed. He asked exactly the right person, and he went home six verses before the answer came.

Guard the promise, though, because it has been lifted off this page and printed on more posters than any other sentence in Matthew, and attached to whatever the reader happens to be hoping for. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man. It is not a general assurance that anything you want is obtainable if you believe hard enough. It is the specific promise that the one thing which genuinely cannot be done — the unfastening of a heart welded to its possessions — is precisely the thing God does. And the phrase has an old home. When Sarah laughed behind the tent door at the promise of a son, the LORD asked, is anything too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14). The impossibility there was a settled biological fact too, and the answer to it was a baby.

And Matthew, who never wastes a word, has left the proof at the far end of his book for anyone still reading. When the crucifixion is over and the disciples have scattered, a man comes to Pilate and asks for the body. Mark calls him a respected member of the council. Luke calls him good and righteous. Matthew, and only Matthew, tells us that he was rich — plousios, the same word used twice in this passage of the man who cannot get in (27:57). Eight chapters after saying that it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom, the same writer, using the same word, shows us a rich man who is a disciple, spending his money and his position and his new tomb on a corpse that nobody else would claim. Matthew does not point it out. He does not need to. The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink; God did the thing he had said only God could do, and Matthew simply waited until the end of the story to let us watch it happen.

Which leaves Peter's question, and the most striking thing about it is that it is not rebuked. What then will we have? is honest and faintly grubby at the same time, and Jesus does not tell him to stop thinking that way. He answers it, and at length. Christianity is not indifferent to reward, and a piety that claims to want nothing at all is not more spiritual than Peter but less truthful than he is; this same Gospel has already told these men to lay up treasure in heaven (6:19-21), which is an instruction to want something. The trouble in Peter's sentence is not the wanting. It is the small word we. He has just watched another man fail the test, and he has begun to compare. Three verses later the Lord will put his finger on exactly that.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The "new world" (palingenesia — regeneration, renewal of all things) is the eschatological restoration of creation: the new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65-66 and Revelation 21-22. The twelve thrones for the twelve apostles reflects the role of foundational authority in the church that will be built on their witness. The hundredfold promise for everything surrendered is not primarily material (though the family of the church is a real present community of belonging) but the abundance of kingdom life that exceeds anything surrendered. The community of believers becomes the new family, now and in the new world.

Read the promise about the thrones with the room in mind, because Judas Iscariot is standing in it. You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones is said, with no qualification and no glance sideways, to a group of twelve men one of whom will sell him for silver before the Passover. Jesus is neither mistaken nor being kind at the expense of the truth. He is addressing the apostolic company as a body, and the Acts of the Apostles shows the vacant seat being filled by another when the man who forfeited it had gone to his own place. But do not hurry past what it means that the sentence could be spoken at all. It is possible to stand inside the circle to whom the promise is made, to hear it addressed to you personally, and not to be in it.

Two words need their sense restored. The new world is palingenesia — literally a being born again — and Matthew uses of the creation the word the New Testament elsewhere uses of a person. Whatever happens to a Christian is going to happen to the world. And judging is not primarily a courtroom word. Israel's judges were her rulers and deliverers, men who governed and rescued rather than men who passed sentence; the promise to the Twelve is closer to governing than to condemning.

The hundredfold now needs a firm hand, because it has been made to fund a great deal of nonsense about God repaying generosity a hundred times over in cash. Read what is actually on the list of things surrendered: houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, lands. Then read what the hundredfold is made of — the same items. It is not a promise that a man who gives up one house receives a hundred houses. It is a promise that a man who loses a family receives a family a hundred times its size, which is a plain and unmystical description of what the church is whenever it is working properly. Four relatives lost; four hundred gained.

And that promise is not theoretical, though it is theoretical to most readers in a comfortable country, who have left nothing at all for Christ and know it. Somebody is paying this cost today. The convert out of Islam whose family holds a funeral for him while he is still alive and never speaks his name again. The young woman in a Hindu village whose marriage, inheritance and place at the table all go on the day she is baptised. The believer who loses the land because the village will not sell to a Christian. For them verse 29 is not a figure of speech; it is the promise they staked everything on. And it is worth being extremely clear about who has been made responsible for keeping it. Christ did not say they would feel a hundredfold. He said they would receive a hundredfold (Mark spells it out: brothers, sisters, mothers, children), and the only place on earth where that can be handed over is a congregation. As with the unmarried (see on vv. 11-12), this is not a sentiment. It is a debt.

Who are the twelve tribes of Israel, and when will this happen? Premillennial readers take it of ethnic Israel in a future earthly kingdom. The more likely reading is that it describes the renewal of all things at Christ’s return (the new world), and that the twelve tribes stand for the whole people of God, as the twelve gates and twelve foundations of the new Jerusalem suggest (Rev 21:12–14).

This does not license a believer to neglect his family; Jesus condemned that (15:3–6), and Paul says it denies the faith (1 Tim 5:8). It describes the cost when loyalty to Christ and loyalty to family conflict.

Which turns the verse round on the reader who has surrendered nothing. The honest question is not what you have left for Christ. It is whether anybody, anywhere, is receiving their hundredfold through you.
verseByVerse.note: “The new world” is the renewal of all things at Christ’s return.

parallels.desc: I am making all things new

verseByVerse.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great reversal principle closes the chapter and opens chapter 20's parable: the kingdom inverts the world's calculations of worth and reward. The rich young man who was "first" by every human measure — wealth, youth, moral earnestness — ends up last. The disciples who left everything and appear to have lost by any worldly accounting will be first. This is not a simple reversal that makes poverty virtuous or wealth sinful; it is the announcement that the kingdom operates by different values than the world's economy. Those who are first in their own estimation, first by social consensus, first by economic position — these are often the last to enter the kingdom that requires them to be last.

Notice first the word many, which is doing careful work. He does not say that all who are first will be last. A mechanical inversion, in which being at the front automatically damns and being at the back automatically saves, would only be the same league table turned upside down — and people enjoy that arrangement rather too much, as anyone knows who has met the Christian who is quietly proud of having nothing to be proud of. Many, not all. It is a warning, not a formula.

Then see where it falls, because that is the sting and it is easy to miss. This sentence does not follow the rich man's departure; he left eight verses ago. It follows Peter's what then will we have? and the enormous answer he was given — thrones, a hundredfold, eternal life. The men most in danger of finishing last, on the Lord's own reckoning, are the men who have this moment been promised that they will be first. He hands them the throne and, without so much as a pause between sentences, warns them what being handed a throne does to a man.

And Matthew tells us plainly how he means it to be read, by what he sets next. Verse 30 is not a closing flourish; it is a hinge. Chapter 20 opens at once with the parable of the labourers in the vineyard and closes it at 20:16 with this same sentence turned around — so the last will be first, and the first last. The saying is a pair of brackets, and what stands between them is a story about men who worked the whole day in the heat and could not be glad about the wage given to men who worked an hour.

Which is where it lands, and it lands on the long-serving rather than the newcomer. The man who has given thirty years and cannot rejoice when the convert of six months is asked to do the thing he had always assumed would come to him. The unwritten order of seniority that no church admits to having and every member could recite. The faithful couple who say that nobody knows what this congregation has cost them — who are telling the truth, and are in more danger for it than the newcomer who has cost it nothing. Length of service is a real thing and God does not forget it (v. 29 has just said so). It simply does not establish a position in the queue, and the moment a man begins to think it does, this verse has his name on it.

It cuts the other way too, and that is the comfort in it. The reader who came in late, who wasted the years everyone else was building on, who contributes little and is privately certain he belongs at the back — he is the one this sentence was spoken to encourage. He is not being told that his lateness does not matter. He is being told who decides the order.

Look at who has walked through this chapter, and the shape of it is unmistakable. Men arguing about the legal minimum a husband may keep. Children with nothing to contribute, nearly turned away at the door. A young man with everything, who went home. And twelve who had left everything, and were already, within the hour, counting what it was worth. The chapter opened with a question about how much a man is permitted to keep. It closes with a warning about how much a man can lose by being sure he is near the front.

parallels.desc: the same saying ends the next parable

19.theology: Monergism and the impossibility of self-salvation. Matthew 19:26 is the clearest statement in this Gospel of the Reformed doctrine of monergism: God alone works the miracle of salvation; unaided human will cannot accomplish it. The rich young man is not an extreme case; he represents every human being before the grace of God. His idolatry is more visible than most, but every person has a god that competes with Christ. The new birth — God’s sovereign act of grace that overcomes the resistance of the sinful will — is what makes it possible for anyone to sell all, follow Christ, and inherit eternal life. This is the good news hidden inside the severe word: with God, even this is possible.
19.examples:
Then: The rich young man came running (Mark 10:17) — he was eager, sincere, morally serious. He went away sorrowful. Sincerity and moral seriousness are not sufficient for salvation. Only the miracle of grace is sufficient.

Now: Every generation has its version of the young man’s idol — wealth, reputation, career, family, comfort, security. Jesus’ question to every person is the same: what is the one thing you are not willing to surrender? That is the idol that must go. The command is not an obstacle to grace; it is the exposure of where grace needs to go.

20.title: First and Last
20.text: <sup>1</sup>“For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. <sup>2</sup>After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, <sup>4</sup>and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.’ <sup>5</sup>So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. <sup>6</sup>And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ <sup>7</sup>They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’ <sup>8</sup>And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first.’ <sup>9</sup>And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. <sup>10</sup>Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. <sup>11</sup>And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, <sup>12</sup>saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ <sup>13</sup>But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? <sup>14</sup>Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. <sup>15</sup>Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?’ <sup>16</sup>So the last will be first, and the first last.” <sup>17</sup>And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, <sup>18</sup>“See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death <sup>19</sup>and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” <sup>20</sup>Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. <sup>21</sup>And he said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” <sup>24</sup>And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. <sup>25</sup>But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>26</sup>It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>27</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, <sup>28</sup>even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>29</sup>And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. <sup>30</sup>And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>31</sup>The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>32</sup>And stopping, Jesus called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>33</sup>They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is structured around the inversion of worldly values. The parable of the workers in the vineyard opens with the same reversal that closed chapter 19: “the last will be first, and the first last.” Those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day. The vineyard owner’s generosity is not unfair to the all-day workers (he pays exactly what was agreed) but it offends their sense of merit-based distribution. The parable is not about labour economics but about grace: God owes nothing to anyone; every denarius of salvation is sheer mercy.

The third passion prediction follows (vv. 17–19), and immediately James and John’s mother requests the seats of honour. Jesus responds with the kingdom’s law of greatness: the leader is the servant, the first is the slave. He grounds it in his own mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This is the only place in Matthew where Jesus explicitly calls his death a ransom. The chapter closes with two blind men healed on the Jericho road — men who call him “Son of David” and, having received their sight, follow him on the road to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The parable of the workers hired at different hours — dawn, nine, noon, three, and five — all receiving the same denarius wage at day's end. Those hired first complain; the owner insists he has done them no wrong and is free to be generous with his own resources. "So the last will be first, and the first last." The parable illustrates the preceding reversal saying and the nature of God's grace: it is not a reward calculated by duration of service but a gift determined by sovereign generosity. Two mechanics inside the story carry it. Only the dawn workers negotiate a figure; everyone hired later goes into the vineyard on the owner's character alone, with no number (vv. 3-4, 7). And the owner instructs that the last be paid first (v. 8) — he could have paid in the obvious order and bought the dawn men's contentment for nothing, and instead he arranges for them to watch.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable's offense is intentional: the all-day workers' complaint is understandable by any standard of fairness. They worked more; they should receive more. The owner's response demolishes the complaint: he paid exactly what was agreed; his generosity to others does not diminish what they received. The problem is not injustice but envy — "is your eye evil because I am good?" The evil eye (stinginess, grudging spirit) cannot tolerate grace extended to others. The parable indicts the spirit of religious entitlement that calculates reward rather than receiving grace. Two further things the parable does deliberately. It sets the wage by need rather than by output: a denarius was a day's keep for a household, and an hour's honest pay would have sent the last man home with enough for nobody. There is only one wage in the story because there is only one thing God has to give, and eternal life does not come in grades. And the men who grumble are the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads — a man holding a contract can be disappointed, while a man trusting a person cannot, since the promise was kept. Note too that the eleventh-hour men are not blamed for their idleness: because no one has hired us (v. 7) stands without qualification.
verseByVerse.examples: The owner of the vineyard represents God, whose generosity is not constrained by human calculations of desert. Those hired last — with no track record, no extended service, no obvious claim — receive the same gift as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. This is the gospel: the deathbed convert and the lifelong believer receive the same eternal life, because eternal life is not a wage proportional to service but a gift given by the one who owns the vineyard. The men left standing have a name in every congregation: the long-term unemployed, the believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic and concludes he has nothing to bring, the chronically ill Christian who cannot do the things his church visibly counts. And notice the direction of travel in every scene — not one labourer in the parable finds his own way to the vineyard. Each is there because the owner came down to the market and found him standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand in the marketplace at first light before reading a word of the theology. A day-labourer in that country owned nothing but his hands. He had no contract, no notice period and no savings; he came down to the square before dawn and stood where he could be seen, and if a landowner picked him he ate that night and his children ate, and if nobody picked him they did not. The law itself assumed the knife-edge he lived on: a hired man's wage had to be paid before sundown, for he is poor and counts on it (Deut 24:15). That is why everybody in this parable is paid at evening, and it is why standing unhired at five in the afternoon is not an inconvenience. It is a disaster with a family attached to it.

A denarius was the going rate for a day, and it is worth being clear that there is nothing generous about it yet. The master pays the market price, agrees it openly, and sends them off. No one is being done a favour in verse 2. The story opens as an entirely ordinary piece of business, which is exactly why what happens at the end lands as hard as it does.

But notice the detail the parable will repeat until it cannot be missed: he went out. This man has a foreman — verse 8 tells us so — and he does not send him. He walks down to the market himself at dawn, and then again at nine, and at noon, and at three, and again at five in the afternoon when there is barely an hour of daylight left and no sane employer is still hiring. Five times in one day the owner of the vineyard comes out to the square where the unwanted men are standing. Whatever else this parable is about, it is not chiefly about the workers. Every scene in it turns on a man going out again.

Nor is the vineyard a neutral setting. Israel had been God's vineyard since Isaiah sang over it and found wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7), and every hearer knew it. So the field in this story is the covenant people, and the labour in it is the work God gives his own to do. That matters when the grumbling starts. The men who complain are not outsiders resenting the church from a distance. They are inside the vineyard, and they have been working in it since dawn.

Is a deathbed conversion real? Yes. The thief on the cross received the whole of salvation in his last hours (Luke 23:43), and the parable says the eleventh-hour workers received the same wage. But nothing here licenses delay. The late workers were hired the moment they were called, and now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

One thing to fix before the story runs. Jesus does not say the kingdom of heaven is like a wage system, or like a day's labour, or like a vineyard. He says it is like a master of a house — a person. Every question the parable raises about fairness is going to be answered not with a principle but with a man, and by the end the only question left on the table will be what sort of man he is.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset.

parallels.desc: do not hold back a hired worker’s wages overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, "You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you." So they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something changes at nine in the morning that the parable never draws attention to, and everything later depends on it. The dawn men had negotiated: a denarius, agreed, settled before a foot went into the vineyard. These men are offered no figure at all. Whatever is right I will give you — dikaion, whatever is just — and that is the whole of it. They have a promise and a person, and no number.

And they go. That is a considerable thing for a man with nothing in the house to do on a stranger's word, and the parable simply records it: so they went. Every group after the first goes into that vineyard on the character of the owner rather than on terms. Only one group in the story has a contract.

Which turns out to be the difference between the men who end the day content and the men who end it bitter, and it is worth stating as plainly as the parable does. A man holding a contract can be disappointed. A man trusting a person cannot — he has nothing to measure the outcome against except the one who promised, and the promise was kept. The dawn workers were not cheated of a penny. They were simply the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads to compare things to, and by evening the figure had become a grievance.

There is a test in that, and it goes deeper than it first appears. Most Christians could not say out loud that they deal with God on terms, and most of us do it anyway. The tell is not what you say when things go well; it is what rises in you when they go badly. A man on a contract feels cheated — after all these years, after all I have given up, after the way I have kept myself. A man who is trusting a person is bewildered and frightened and goes on trusting, because his confidence was never in the arithmetic. Ask which of those two sentences was closer to your own the last time God did not do what you expected. (A related question, about whether you believe your debt was cancelled or merely deferred, is at 18:25-26; this one is about whether the relationship has terms at all.)

One guard, because the parable is not against agreements. The dawn men did nothing wrong in accepting a denarius, and the master never once suggests they did; he will call the agreement binding and honour it to the penny. Contracts are not sin. The trouble comes when a man carries a contract into a relationship that was never contractual, and then reads every kindness God shows to somebody else as a clause he has been denied.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m.

verseByVerse.quote: Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, "Why do you stand here idle all day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noon, and then three, and the master is still coming out. Then the eleventh hour, which is five in the afternoon with the working day ending at six, and he finds men still standing there.

Sit with what that standing had been like. They had been in that square since before dawn, in the same place, for eleven hours. Four separate times they had watched an employer walk in, look along the line, choose other men, and walk out again with them. Four times they had straightened up and been passed over. By the middle of the afternoon a man in that line has stopped arranging his face. He is not hoping any more; he is simply standing there because going home is worse, and because his wife will ask.

So read the master's question in the tone the next verse requires, not in the tone we expect. Why do you stand here idle all day? sounds like an accusation and is nothing of the kind — their answer will satisfy him completely and he will hire them on the spot. It is the question of a man who has walked up to people nobody else has spoken to all day and asked them what happened.

These men have a name in every congregation. The one who has been out of work long enough that the sympathy has run out and people have started to theorise about him. The believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic on the years and concludes he has nothing to bring. The disabled or chronically ill Christian who cannot do any of the things his church visibly counts, and sits through another meeting hearing about the workers who can. The person who has never in his life been picked first for anything, and has quietly built a whole theology out of it. If you have ever thought that the useful part of your life is behind you and you arrived too late to matter, this is the hour you were hired in.

And notice the direction of travel, because it is the same in every scene and it is the opposite of what religion usually describes. Not one man in this parable finds his way to the vineyard. Nobody knocks at the estate, nobody applies, nobody hears there is work going and walks out to ask for it. Every single labourer in the story is in that vineyard because the owner came down to the market and found him standing there.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., the eleventh about 5 p.m. — an hour before the day ended.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Because no one has hired us." He said to them, "You go into the vineyard too." And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, "Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because no one has hired us. That is the whole answer, and the parable lets it stand without a word of qualification. They were not lazy and they were not hiding. They had been available since dawn and the market had looked at them and chosen somebody else, over and over, until the day was nearly gone. The reason they had done no work was that no one had given them any.
