Do not over-soften it either. The parable is not sentimental about idleness, and it does not say that standing about is the same as working. What it does is refuse to blame these men for a condition that was done to them, and then it puts them in the vineyard for the last hour of the light. You go into the vineyard too — no interview, no explanation of terms, not even the whatever is right the nine o'clock men were given. Just go. There is an hour left; go and have it.

Then comes the instruction that makes the rest of the story possible, and it is the most deliberate sentence in the parable: beginning with the last, up to the first. Think about what it would have cost the master to do it the other way round. Pay the dawn men first, and they take their agreed denarius, and they walk home perfectly satisfied, and they never learn what happened at the far end of the queue. Not one word of complaint is ever spoken. The master could have bought their contentment for nothing, simply by paying in the obvious order.

He arranges for them to watch instead. He has the last men paid first, in full view, while the men who have been there since dawn stand in the line and do the arithmetic. That is not carelessness and it is not cruelty; it is diagnosis. God does not conceal his kindness to other people in order to keep us comfortable, and this parable says so on purpose. He lets us see what he has given somebody else, because what rises in us when we see it is the truest thing anyone could tell us about ourselves — and until it rises, it cannot be dealt with.

Which is worth remembering the next time you find out what somebody else was given. The information did not reach you by accident, and it was not sent to make you miserable. It was sent the way a doctor sends a man for a scan.

parallels.desc: give him his wages on the same day

verseByVerse.quote: And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do the arithmetic the dawn men did, because their reasoning is not stupid; it is excellent. One hour has just been paid a denarius. Twelve hours at that rate comes to twelve denarii, and they had worked twelve hours. Any accountant in the world would have signed off the expectation. They were not being greedy. They were being consistent.

But look at what the master was actually doing with that coin, because it is not what they assumed. A denarius was not a lavish sum; it was a day's keep — bread, oil, whatever a family of that size needed to get to tomorrow. The eleventh-hour man had earned, strictly, about a twelfth of it. If he had been paid a twelfth of it he would have gone home with enough for nobody. So the master does not pay him what his hour was worth. He pays him what his household needs. The wage in this parable is not set by output at all; it is set by need, and once you have seen that, the shape of the whole gospel is standing there in a coin.

Which also explains why the dawn men cannot be given twelve. There is only one wage in this story, and it is the whole of what the master has to give. Eternal life does not come in grades. There is no larger portion of God available to a man who has been at it longer, because God is not a quantity you accumulate. The first workers were not given less than they deserved; they were given everything there is, which is precisely what the last men were given, and the reason it feels like an insult is that they had been thinking of it as pay.

Now the verb Matthew chooses, which is the quiet accusation in the sentence: they thought they would receive more — enomisan, they supposed, they assumed. Nobody had told them anything of the kind. The master had made them one promise and kept it exactly. The extra eleven denarii existed nowhere but in their own heads, and they had spent the walk up the line building it.

That is a test most of us fail regularly and quietly. A great deal of the disappointment Christians carry with God is disappointment over things he never said. He did not promise that the marriage would be easy because you waited. He did not promise that the child raised in the faith would keep it, or that the years of service would be recognised, or that the diagnosis would go the other way. Somewhere in the walking, an arrangement got built that he was never party to, and when it did not arrive it felt exactly like a broken promise. It is worth going back through the grievance sometime and asking, item by item, which of these did he actually say. The list is usually shorter than the grievance, and the difference between them is the size of the bitterness.

verseByVerse.quote: And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, saying, "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The complaint is articulate and, by human standards, fair: twelve hours of summer work in a Palestinian vineyard versus one hour in the cool of the evening — and the same pay? The dawn workers' resentment is the resentment of every religious person who has "done the right thing" for decades and then watches a late convert receive the same grace, the same standing before God, the same eternal life. The Pharisee at the feast watching the prostitute receive forgiveness (Luke 7:44-47). The elder son watching the fatted calf be killed for the prodigal (Luke 15:25-30). The dawn workers' complaint is one of the most human moments in the parables.

Look closely at what had actually happened to those men, because the parable is doing something precise. Nothing had happened to them. Their wage had not been cut. Their hours had not been lengthened. The sun was no hotter at six in the evening than it had been at five, and the coin in their hand was the coin they had been perfectly content to work all day for. Every fact about their own situation was exactly as agreed and exactly as they had been satisfied with an hour earlier. One thing changed: they saw somebody else's pay.

That is the whole mechanism of envy, and it is worth seeing plainly, because envy is the one sin that has never in history made anybody better off, including the person committing it. It cannot take anything from you. All it can do is alter how you feel about what you have — and it is extremely good at that. A man entirely happy at dawn is bitter by dusk with the same denarius in his pocket.

The Christian version is easy to recognise once you know the shape. Someone comes to faith at fifty and appears to have skipped the decades you spent under obedience. Someone else's ministry flourished while yours never did. Someone got the marriage, or the child, or the health, or the money, or simply the easier road — and you notice, in the place where gladness ought to be, a small persistent coldness.

The master's cure is a question, and it can be borrowed: did you not agree with me for a denarius? Go back to what you were actually given and what you actually agreed to, and say it out loud if it helps. Then do the three things that break it. Name it to God as sin rather than as a grievance, since it will always present itself as a grievance — that is its disguise, and the disguise is why it survives so long in respectable people. Thank him deliberately and specifically for your own denarius. And pray for the person by name, asking God for more of the very thing you envy them — which is close to impossible, and works.

And notice how the master speaks to the man who complains. He calls him friend. He does not sack him or throw him out; he reasons with him at the gate. Luke's elder brother is left in the same position at the end of his story, standing outside the party with his father still talking to him. That is where anyone stands who is still arguing about fairness — outside, but being spoken to kindly, with the door open behind the voice.

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to one of them, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first word out of the master's mouth is the one to stop on. Friend — and it is not the warm word we hear in English. Matthew uses hetairos exactly three times in his Gospel, and the company it keeps is chilling. Here, to the man grumbling at the pay table. At 22:12, to the guest discovered without a wedding garment, two seconds before he is thrown into the outer darkness. And at 26:50, in the dark of Gethsemane, from Jesus to Judas with the kiss still on his face: Friend, do what you came to do. Three times, and every one of them is addressed to a man in the wrong, and every one of them is courteous. It is not the word for someone you love. It is the word you use to a man you are still treating civilly when both of you know what he is doing.

Then the argument, and it is unanswerable. I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Every fact is on the master's side. The wage was named before the work; the work was done; the wage was paid in full and on time. There is no case here at all. The grievance is not that the man received too little. It is that somebody else received the same.

Which is why the next sentence has an edge that is easy to miss under the courtesy. Take what belongs to you and go. He gets exactly what he bargained for, down to the coin, and then he is dismissed with it. There is nothing else coming, because he asked for terms and he has been given terms. A man who insists on strict justice from God will receive strict justice, and it is difficult to think of a more frightening thing to be granted. The eleventh-hour men went home with the same coin and something the grumbler never got near: they knew it was a gift.

I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you — and the verb is thelo, I will it, I want to. Not I am obliged, not the accounts require it. He wanted to. That is the only reason given in the entire parable for the eleventh-hour denarius, and no other reason is ever offered anywhere in Scripture for why God saves anybody.

One guard, because this scene can be read as God turning cold. Look again at how he handles the man. He does not have him removed. He does not answer him through the foreman. He comes to him personally, calls him by a courteous name, sets out the reasoning step by step, and asks him two questions — which is more than the man's complaint deserved and a good deal more patience than most of us would have shown. Whatever else is happening at that pay table, the master is standing there talking to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" So the last will be first, and the first last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second question is the one that goes through the ribs, and the English hides it. Do you begrudge my generosity? is, word for word, is your eye evil because I am good? That is a Hebrew idiom with a long history: a man with a good eye is open-handed, and a man with an evil eye is the grudging one who cannot bear to give or to see giving (Deut 15:9; Prov 23:6; 28:22). And Matthew's readers had met it already in this Gospel, in the Sermon: if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness (6:22-23) — sitting, as it happens, in the middle of a passage about money and treasure. So the master's question is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a diagnosis of an organ. The problem is not the wage; it is the eye that looked down the line.

And notice which way the sentence runs, because it is not what we would write. He does not say, is your eye evil because he is undeserving. He says because I am good. The goodness of God is the thing that has provoked the reaction. That is a startling account of what is wrong with us, and it is far more searching than a charge of greed: there is something in a man that can be made bitter by God being kind where it did not expect him to be.

Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Here is the sovereignty, and it needs its guard on both sides. This is not a God who does as he likes and calls it righteousness — the master has just proved, item by item, that he has wronged nobody, and he does not appeal to his rights until after he has cleared himself on justice. Sovereign generosity is not the same as caprice. But nor is it negotiable. What is his is his, and grace is not a substance that gets thinner when it is shared. Nobody in that line was given less because somebody else was given something.

Then the verse that closes the parable is the verse that opened it, turned round. So the last will be first, and the first last — and 19:30 said it the other way about, so that the whole story sits inside a pair of brackets (see on 19:30). Matthew is telling us how he wants the parable read: not as a lesson in employment practice, but as the worked example of what Jesus had just said to twelve men who had been promised thrones and had immediately started counting.

Does the one denarius mean there are no differences of reward in heaven? The wage everyone receives is eternal life, God himself, and that is the same for all. Other texts speak of different rewards and responsibilities (Luke 19:17–19; 1 Cor 3:12–15), but those rewards are themselves grace, and no one in heaven will envy another.

And there is a mercy in the arithmetic that the grumbler never saw. If the kingdom really did pay by the hour, then the man who came in at the eleventh hour would have almost nothing, and the man who came in at dawn would spend eternity knowing exactly how much of it he had earned. Both would be intolerable. What the master does instead is hand every one of them the entire day's keep and shut the ledger — and the only man who goes home unhappy is the one who kept it open.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “do you begrudge” is literally “is your eye bad” — an idiom for envy.

parallels.desc: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–34 — The Third Passion Prediction, the Mother's Request, and Two Blind Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus gives the fullest passion prediction yet: delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, crucified, raised. Immediately the mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at Jesus's right and left in his kingdom. Jesus corrects the request: greatness is service, and the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Two blind men at Jericho cry out "Son of David, have mercy on us" and receive their sight. Between the request and the healing the other ten turn on the two brothers (v. 24) — not from principle but because they wanted the same thing and were beaten to it — and Jesus answers all twelve rather than the two who asked.
verseByVerse.theology: The timing of the mother's request — immediately after the passion prediction — reveals the distance between the disciples' understanding and Jesus's reality. He has just announced crucifixion; she asks for thrones. The response of Jesus is not irritated dismissal but patient teaching: "You do not know what you are asking." The cup he must drink and the baptism he must undergo are not metaphors for achievement but for suffering. The right and left are not his to give; they are the Father's appointment. The contrast between the Gentile rulers who "lord it over" others and the Son of Man who gives his life is the most concentrated leadership theology in the Gospels. Two things guard it from becoming a slogan. Jesus does not abolish ambition: the sentence is whoever would be great among you, and only the object of the wanting is changed. And the standard is not an attitude but a cross — he does not say be like a servant, he says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The many of v. 28 is Isaiah's word for a multitude nobody could number (Isa 53:11-12), not a word that fences people out.
verseByVerse.examples: The two blind men at Jericho echo the two blind men of 9:27-31. The title "Son of David, have mercy on us" is the messianic title of chapter 9, and it elicits the same response: Jesus stops, asks, heals. Their sight is the last healing miracle before the triumphal entry — a fitting preparation for Jerusalem. Those who cry "Son of David" will soon hear the crowds cry "Hosanna to the Son of David." The blind who gain sight anticipate the seeing of what Jerusalem refuses to see. Matthew also asks the same question twice in this chapter, and the two answers are the spine of it: What do you want? to the mother of James and John (v. 21), and What do you want me to do for you? to the beggars (v. 32). One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom; the other asks for eyes. And in both Jericho scenes the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the crowd already following him — as it was with the children in the previous chapter (19:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going up to Jerusalem is not a figure of speech. Jericho sits in the Jordan rift about 250 metres below sea level; Jerusalem stands roughly 750 metres above it, and the road between them climbs the whole of that in some fifteen miles of bare rock and ravine. Every pilgrim in the country used the phrase and every pilgrim meant it literally. They are climbing, in a crowd, at Passover, and the man at the front of the column knows precisely what is waiting at the top.

So he takes the twelve aside. Picture that on a packed festival road: he pulls the twelve out of the stream of singing pilgrims to tell them, quietly and on the move, that he is going up there to be killed. He did not want them to hear it later, and he did not want them to hear it from anyone else.

This is the third time he has told them, and the thing to notice is that each telling is more exact than the last. At 16:21 it was suffering at the hands of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and being killed. At 17:22-23 it was being delivered into the hands of men, who would kill him. Now it is the chief priests and scribes condemning him, the Gentiles receiving him, mocking, flogging — and crucifixion, named for the first time in any of the predictions. He has been walking toward this for months and telling them about it in instalments, and the detail he has kept back until last is the manner of the death.

Which is worth holding beside the way most of us handle what is coming. We manage dread by not looking directly at it: by keeping the appointment vague, by not asking the consultant the second question, by leaving the letter unopened on the side. Jesus did the opposite. He named it, in detail, out loud, three times, months in advance, to people who did not want to hear it — and then he set his face to the hill and kept climbing. Whatever strength he had for Jerusalem, he did not get it by refusing to look at Jerusalem.

And read the verb in the middle of it: the Son of Man will be delivered over. Delivered by whom? Judas will do it, and the Sanhedrin will do it, and Pilate will do it, and every one of them will be fully answerable for it. But the passive sits there unexplained, the way it does all through Isaiah 53, and Peter will eventually say the quiet part out loud at Pentecost: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and crucified by lawless men (Acts 2:23). Both halves of that sentence are true at once. Nobody took him up that road.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verbs, and then a fifth that changes everything. Mocked. Flogged. Crucified. Raised on the third day.

Take them at their weight, since familiarity has worn them smooth. Mocked is not teasing; Matthew will show us what it means — a scarlet robe thrown over a flayed back, a circle of thorns pressed down, a reed put in his hand for a sceptre, men kneeling in the dirt in front of him and calling him King of the Jews before they spat (27:28-31). Flogged is the Roman scourge, from which citizens were legally exempt and slaves were not; men were known to die under it before the cross was reached. And crucified was so far beneath a Roman citizen's dignity that Cicero said the very word should be kept away from Roman ears. It was the death kept for slaves and rebels — which is a detail worth carrying nine verses forward, where the same man tells his friends that whoever would be first among them must be a slave, and then says what he came to do.

Notice also who does what. The chief priests and scribes condemn; the Gentiles mock and flog and crucify. Jew and Gentile, the covenant people and the nations, each contributing their own portion to the same crucifixion. Nobody in the story gets to stand outside it, which is precisely the point when the ransom is named in verse 28.

And then the fifth verb, which he has never once left out. Three predictions, three times the resurrection attached to the end of the sentence — and the disciples remember none of it. When the women come to the tomb, the angel does not break news to them; he reminds them, he is not here, for he has risen, as he said (28:6). It had been said, plainly, three times, on an open road.

That is a strange comfort, and it is worth taking personally. The men closest to him, who heard all three predictions from his own mouth, retained nothing useful from them and fell apart entirely when it happened. Their failure to take it in did not derail a single detail of it. He was not depending on their comprehension to get it done, and he is not depending on yours.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the first to name crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mother's kneeling before Jesus is the posture of petition (cf. 2:11; 8:2; 9:18), but the petition itself is a request for her sons' privilege, not for their formation. The right and left of a king are the positions of greatest honor — the first and second ministers. The request comes immediately after the most specific passion prediction: Jesus has just announced crucifixion, and the family of Zebedee responds with a throne request. The ambition is the same: positions of privilege in the kingdom they are beginning to believe is imminent.

But a reader with Mark open will stop here, because there it is not the mother at all: "James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him" and made the request themselves (Mark 10:35). Which was it? It is often said that Matthew moved the words onto their mother to spare the two apostles. That explanation is worth resisting, for two reasons. The first is that Matthew is not a man who spares people: he is the one who records Peter called Satan (16:23), the disciples fleeing (26:56), and his own name in the list as Matthew the tax collector (10:3). A writer covering for the Twelve does not write like that. The second reason is decisive, and it is sitting in the very next verse. Jesus does not answer the mother. He turns and says, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup?" — and in the Greek every one of those is plural, addressed to the sons; it is the sons who reply, "We are able." Three verses later the ten are indignant, and not with her: they are indignant "at the two brothers" (v. 24). Matthew's own account, read to the end, has James and John behind the request exactly as Mark says. So both are true, and anyone who has watched a family do this will recognise it at once: the sons wanted the thrones, and they sent their mother to ask. Matthew tells you who spoke; Mark tells you whose ambition it was. The manoeuvre fooled nobody in the story, and it has not fooled anyone since.
verseByVerse.note: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. Comparing the women at the cross, their mother may be Salome.

parallels.desc: the mother of the sons of Zebedee at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?" They said to him, "We are able." He said to them, "You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You do not know what you are asking — and the pronouns have already shifted. She asked; he answers you, plural, and it is the two sons who reply. Everyone in the scene knows whose request this really was (see on vv. 20-21).

Then the cup, and it has to be understood or the answer is unintelligible. In the prophets the cup is not an image of hardship in general; it is a very specific vessel. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine… and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it (Ps 75:8). Isaiah calls it the cup of his wrath and describes Jerusalem staggering after drinking it (Isa 51:17). Jeremiah is handed it and made to take it round the nations (Jer 25:15-17). So when Jesus asks two ambitious young men whether they are able to drink the cup he is about to drink, he is not asking whether they can cope with a hard road. He is telling them what he is going up to Jerusalem to receive, and it is not chiefly nails. It is the wrath of God against sin, poured out and drained to the bottom by somebody who never earned a drop of it.

We are able. Brave, entirely sincere, and spoken by men with no idea what they had just volunteered for. And he does not call them liars. He says they will indeed drink his cup — and they did, in two shapes so different that nobody would have guessed they were the same drink. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, cut down with a sword by Herod Agrippa about a dozen years later (Acts 12:2). John outlived every one of them and died old, having watched all his friends killed, an exile on a small island. A short violent one and a long lonely one. The cup is not one flavour, and a Christian who has been given the slow version should not conclude he was given the easy one.

Then the hardest sentence: to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant. Guard this carefully, because it is not Jesus disclaiming authority — this is the man who ends the book saying all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (28:18). It is the Son declining to act outside the Father's arrangement, which is the pattern of his whole earthly life. And the practical edge of it is sharper than it looks: position in the kingdom is not open to lobbying. There is no queue to join and no case to put, and the sooner a Christian believes that the sooner he is free of a great deal of exhausting comparison.

It cuts the other way too, and that is the comfort in it. If your place cannot be secured by asking, it cannot be lost by somebody else asking either. Nobody can manoeuvre you out of what the Father has prepared, because it was never in the gift of anyone who could be manoeuvred. That is a settled thing, decided elsewhere, by someone who is not taking applications.

And there is one more turn in it that the two brothers could not have seen. On the day Jesus finally entered his kingdom there were in fact a man on his right hand and a man on his left. They were both criminals, and they were both on crosses (27:38). James and John had asked for the two places nobody would have wanted if they had understood what was being requested.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is an Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten's indignation at James and John is not moral superiority — they are angry because two of them tried to get ahead. The competitive dynamics within the Twelve are laid bare: they all want the positions of honor, and they resent the ones who asked first. Jesus does not let anyone off the hook; he addresses all twelve. The Gentile rulers who "lord it over" their subjects are the model of power that the kingdom explicitly rejects. Both verbs he uses carry the same prefix, kata, meaning down upon: katakyrieuousin, they lord it down over them, and katexousiazousin, they bring their authority down on them. Crushing the people beneath you with the sheer weight of your position is the world's pattern, and Jesus describes it without a flicker of admiration. The kingdom inverts it entirely.

Since "servant leadership" has become a phrase people put on conference brochures, it is worth pinning down what Jesus actually says, because the words in the next verse have content and the slogan often has none.

Start with something he does not do: he does not abolish ambition. The sentence is whoever would be great among you — the wanting is allowed to stand, and only its object is changed. James and John are not rebuked for wishing to matter. They are told they have misunderstood what mattering is. A Christian is not required to want nothing; he is required to want the right thing, which turns out to be a towel rather than a throne.

Then the two words. A diakonos is the man who waits at the table — practical, unglamorous work done for the comfort of other people. A doulos is a slave, who owns no rights at all: not his time, not his preferences, not his reputation, not his plans for the afternoon. Jesus uses both, in ascending order, which is the opposite direction from the one careers normally travel.

Which gives some usable tests, and they are uncomfortable ones. A servant is available — he does not control his own diary in the way a master does. A servant does work that nobody sees and nobody thanks him for, and keeps doing it when the thanks do not come. A servant can be interrupted. And the sharpest test of all: you can tell a servant by how he behaves when he is treated like one. Anyone can adopt the language while quietly requiring the deference; the moment of truth is when the deference is not given.

Two guards, one on each side. This is not the abolition of authority. Jesus gave commands, appointed leaders, rebuked error and made decisions; he did not run a committee, and a leader who will not lead is not being humble but is simply leaving people unshepherded. Servant leadership is authority exercised for the good of those under it rather than for the comfort of the man holding it — which is a description of how power is used, not a reason to give it up. But the other guard matters more, because it is the commoner failure: a man who wears the phrase as a title while making every decision alone, resenting every challenge, and requiring loyalty from everyone beneath him has kept the substance of what Jesus forbade and taken the vocabulary of what he commanded. That is worse than the Gentile rulers, who at least did not pretend.

And the reason none of this is mere advice is in the next breath. He does not say be like a servant; he says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom. The standard is not an attitude but a cross. Notice too that the whole conversation is addressed to all twelve, not to the two who asked — the ten were indignant precisely because they wanted the same thing. Nobody in the room got to listen to this as advice for somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: "It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave," "even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"It shall not be so among you" — the kingdom community operates by different rules than the world. Greatness is defined by service; primacy is defined by slavery. This is not merely ethical advice but ontological redefinition: what greatness actually is in the kingdom is the opposite of what the world calls great. The servant (diakonos) and the slave (doulos) are the two levels of submission — the servant who performs tasks, and the slave who has no rights of their own. Both are models of kingdom leadership. The elder is to exercise oversight "not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). Leadership in the church that looks like Gentile lordship has forgotten this saying.

"A ransom for many" (lytron anti pollon) — this is the atonement in its most concentrated Matthean form. In the first-century Roman world, the lytron was a specific legal term: the price paid to liberate a slave from bondage or to redeem a prisoner of war from captivity. The transaction was concrete and public — the lytron was brought to the slave's owner or to the magistrate's table, the sum was paid, and the captive person walked free. One person's payment produced another person's freedom. The preposition anti means "in place of" — not merely "for the benefit of" but a direct substitution: one thing given in the place of another. Jesus gives his life as the lytron in the place of the many who owe it; his death at the magistrate's table of divine justice purchases their freedom. The ransom metaphor does not specify to whom the payment is made (not to Satan, as some early theologians speculated; the debt is to the justice of God). It specifies what is paid (his life) and who benefits (the many — the same "many" of Isaiah 53:11–12, for whose transgressions the servant bore the penalty). The Son of Man who commands servant-leadership in the verses preceding this demonstrates it in the ultimate form: the cross is the supreme act of service, and it is the service that makes all other service possible.

One word in that sentence has carried more argument than any other, and the reader deserves it plainly: a ransom for many. Does many mean not all? Begin where the objection is weakest. In Hebrew and Aramaic, "the many" is not a word that shuts people out; it means the multitude, the great mass of them. Isaiah uses it exactly so of the servant who "makes many to be accounted righteous" and "bore the sin of many" (Isa 53:11-12), which is the passage Jesus is quoting, and Paul can move between "the many" and "all" in the same breath without feeling he has changed the subject (Rom 5:15-19). So the word itself is not a fence. It is the opposite: it is a word for a crowd nobody could count.

Underneath that, though, is a real question Christians have long divided over, and it is worth naming honestly rather than smoothing away. Scripture says the ransom is for many here, and elsewhere that Christ "gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Tim 2:6; cf. 1 Jn 2:2). Reformed churches have answered that the two are not in competition, and the key is what a ransom actually does. A ransom is not an offer; it is a payment. Money laid on the magistrate's table for a hundred prisoners does not make a hundred men releasable — it releases them. If Christ's death merely made salvation possible for everyone and certain for no one, then the thing Jesus calls a ransom would be the one ransom in history that might be paid and leave the captive in his cell. So the cross is held to have actually secured the freedom of those it was given for, which is why the New Testament can speak of it as purchasing a people and not merely an opportunity (Acts 20:28; Eph 5:25). Other believers who love this same Lord read the "all" texts more broadly, and they should be heard with respect and not caricatured; the disagreement is real, and it is a disagreement among brothers.

What must not be lost is the pastoral end of it, because this doctrine has been used to frighten people it was meant to comfort. Nobody is ever asked to work out first whether he is one of the many. That is not how it is discovered, and no one in Scripture is ever sent looking for it. The invitation is unrestricted — "whoever will, let him take the water of life without price" — and there is no small print under it. You find out you were among the many the way the eleventh-hour workers found out they were in the vineyard: by coming when called, and being handed the wage. The doctrine is not a gate to be checked before you approach. It is the discovery, afterwards, that the price of your freedom was paid before you ever thought to ask.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two blind men at Jericho cry "Son of David" — the messianic title that the crowds will shout at the triumphal entry two days later. They heard he was passing by and seized the moment. The crowd's rebuke mirrors the disciples' rebuke of the children (19:13) — both times Jesus overrules the gatekeepers. The blind men who cannot see him cry to him more loudly when silenced: persistence born of need, not of presumption. "All the more" — the opposition intensifies their prayer rather than silencing it. This is the faith that receives: it does not stop when the crowd says no, because the need is greater than the social pressure to be quiet.

Two small puzzles meet the reader who lays the Gospels side by side here, and both have honest answers. First, Matthew sees two blind men where Mark records only one, whom he names — Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). This is Matthew's habit, as at the Gadarene tombs (8:28): Mark and Luke fix on the one memorable, named man, while Matthew, careful of the whole, notes that there were two. "One" never denies a second. Second, and harder: Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus was leaving Jericho, but Luke sets it as he drew near (Luke 18:35) — entering, not leaving. The likeliest answer is simple once you know the ground: there were two Jerichos a mile apart — the crumbled ruin of the old Jericho of Joshua, and the gleaming new Jericho that Herod had built beside it. Jesus was leaving the one and approaching the other at the same time, so both "as he went out of Jericho" and "as he drew near to Jericho" could both be literally true, describing one moment from two sides of a single town. That is one likely explanation among several offered, and none requires a contradiction.

Now the detail in this scene that ought to make a churchgoing reader uncomfortable. It is not the town officials who tell these men to be quiet, and it is not the Romans. It is the crowd — the people who were at that moment following Jesus up the road. The men walking with him were the ones trying to shut up the men calling out to him. And Matthew has shown us this once already, in the previous chapter, when the disciples turned away the families bringing children (19:13). Twice in two chapters the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the group of people already committed to him.

That is worth taking home rather than admiring at a distance. Every congregation has a way of signalling that a particular sort of person is making the occasion difficult — the man who asks questions that hold everything up, the woman whose crisis has gone on too long, the family whose children are loud, the person whose need is chronic and will not resolve into a testimony. Nobody says be quiet. The crowd in this story probably thought it was being helpful, keeping the road clear for an important man on important business. It is worth asking, seriously, who has learned to keep their voice down in your church, and who taught them.

And see what the blind men do with the rebuke: they cried out all the more. The opposition made them louder. They had nothing to lose that they had not already lost, they knew exactly how much they needed, and they were not going to be silenced by people whose eyes worked.

One guard, because this passage is regularly turned into a technique. Their persistence is not what obtained the miracle, and shouting longer is not a lever that moves God. Jesus is not worn down here; he is not reluctant at any point in the story, and there is no suggestion that a quieter pair of men would have been left blind. Persistence in prayer is not leverage — it is what real need looks like from the outside. The reason they kept calling is not that they had a method. It is that they had no alternative, and they had worked out who was walking past.

Which is the irony the chapter has been building toward. Two men who could not see anything shouted the one title on that road that was actually true — Son of David — while a crowd with perfect eyesight told them to stop making a scene. Within days the streets of Jerusalem would be full of people shouting Hosanna to the Son of David, and then, a few days after that, something else entirely.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Mark names one of the men, Bartimaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: And stopping, Jesus called them and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him, "Lord, let our eyes be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew has put the same question twice in one chapter, and it is the spine of the whole thing. To the mother of James and John, in verse 21: What do you want? To two beggars on the Jericho road, in verse 32: What do you want me to do for you? Same questioner, same chapter, same courtesy — and two answers that could not be further apart. One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom. The other asks for eyes.

Before the answers, look at what he does. And stopping, Jesus called them. He is in a column of pilgrims going up to the Passover at which he will be executed; he has just told the twelve in detail what is waiting at the top of that road; the crowd around him is large and moving and has already tried to shut these men up. And he stops it. The whole procession waits on the roadside while the Son of David deals with two men whom everybody else had classified as an interruption. If you want to know what he is like when he is under the most pressure a human being has ever been under, this is the answer: he stops.

Now the two petitions side by side, because between them they teach a man how to pray. The mother asked for something that would put her sons above the other ten. The blind men asked for something they could not obtain anywhere else, could not manufacture, and could not pretend to have. Nobody fakes sight. That is what made it a good request — not that it was modest, because it was not modest at all; opening blind eyes was a thing reserved in the Old Testament for God himself (Ps 146:8; Isa 35:5). It was enormous. It was simply honest.

So run the question on yourself and do not tidy the answer. If he stopped, and called you, and asked what you want him to do for you, what would actually come out? Most of us would hear ourselves asking for something a good deal nearer the thrones than the eyes: for the situation to resolve in our favour, for the person who was wrong about us to be shown to be wrong, for the position, the recognition, the outcome. It is worth knowing that about yourself. It is not a reason to despair; it is a reason to ask him for better wants, which is itself a prayer of the second kind.

And notice that he asks at all. He could see they were blind. The whole road could see they were blind. He does not need the information, and he asks anyway, because he will not treat a man as a case to be processed when he can treat him as a person to be spoken to. There is nothing efficient about that question, and he asked it with Jerusalem in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew tells us what moved before he tells us what happened. In pity — splanchnistheis, the word for something turning over in a man's insides, the same word used when Jesus looked at harassed crowds like sheep without a shepherd (9:36) and at four thousand hungry people (15:32). The healing is not the first event in the verse. The compassion is.

Then: he touched their eyes. He did not have to, and this Gospel has already shown us that he did not have to. He healed a centurion's servant from the other side of a town without going near him (8:13), and a Canaanite woman's daughter at a distance on a word (15:28). Power was never the issue. So the touch was not for the miracle; it was for the men. Two beggars who had spent that morning being told by a crowd to be quiet, and the first thing that happens to them is a pair of hands on their faces. Whatever they had been in that town for years — a fixture, a noise, a thing to step around — they were not that to him.

And then the last four words, which are the point of putting the story here at all: and followed him. Followed him where? Up the road he had just finished describing in detail. Their first act as seeing men was to fall in behind somebody walking to a flogging and a cross. These are the last two people Jesus heals before Jerusalem, and what they do with their new eyes is use them to follow him into the passion.

Set that against everyone else on that road and the chapter finishes its argument without a word of comment. The twelve had been told three times where this was going and were arguing about seats. The crowd was going up for a festival. Two beggars, blind an hour earlier, saw exactly who he was, and went with him.

Which is where the whole chapter has been heading, and it is one movement from beginning to end. It opens with a landowner who does not send his foreman but walks down to the market himself before dawn, and goes back again at nine, at noon, at three, and at five in the afternoon for men that nobody had chosen. It closes with the Son of Man stopping a procession on the way to his own execution because two beggars the crowd had silenced were shouting for mercy. The parable said that is what the owner of the vineyard is like. The Jericho road shows him doing it. He is still, at the end of the chapter, going out to the people who were left standing.

20.theology: The atonement as ransom. Matthew 20:28 is Matthew’s clearest statement of substitutionary atonement. The word “ransom” (lytron) carries the weight of a payment that secures release — it is used in the Septuagint for the price paid to redeem a slave or a firstborn. Jesus applies it to his own death: he gives his life as the price that sets the many free from their captivity to sin, death, and judgment. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is primarily objective — it actually accomplishes something in the divine court (the cancellation of debt, the satisfaction of justice) — before it is subjective (inspiring us, moving us, transforming us). The ransom is paid; the captives are free.
20.examples:
Then: James and John wanted the best seats. They had left everything (19:27) and felt entitled to the premium return. Jesus redefines the currency: greatness is measured in service and suffering, not in position and honour. The Twelve would spend the rest of their lives learning this.

Now: The parable of the workers challenges every theology of spiritual merit — the idea that longer service, greater sacrifice, or more faithful obedience earns a greater share of God’s favour. Grace cannot be earned; it can only be received. The workers who grumble are those who have forgotten that any wage at all is mercy. The appropriate response to grace is gratitude, not calculation.

21.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, <sup>2</sup>saying to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.” <sup>4</sup>This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, <sup>5</sup>“Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” <sup>6</sup>The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. <sup>7</sup>They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. <sup>8</sup>Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. <sup>9</sup>And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>10</sup>And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” <sup>11</sup>And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” <sup>12</sup>And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>13</sup>He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers.” <sup>14</sup>And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. <sup>15</sup>But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant, <sup>16</sup>and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them, “Yes; have you never read, “‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” <sup>17</sup>And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. <sup>18</sup>In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. <sup>19</sup>And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once. <sup>20</sup>When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. <sup>22</sup>And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” <sup>23</sup>And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” <sup>24</sup>Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>25</sup>The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” And they discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>26</sup>But if we say, ‘From man,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.” <sup>27</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>28</sup>“What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ <sup>29</sup>And he answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went. <sup>30</sup>And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go. <sup>31</sup>Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. <sup>32</sup>For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. <sup>33</sup>“Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. <sup>34</sup>When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. <sup>35</sup>And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. <sup>36</sup>Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. <sup>37</sup>Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>38</sup>But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ <sup>39</sup>And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. <sup>40</sup>When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” <sup>41</sup>They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.” <sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: “‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? <sup>43</sup>Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. <sup>44</sup>And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>45</sup>When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. <sup>46</sup>And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the hinge between the Galilean ministry and the Passion Week. Jesus enters Jerusalem not as a military conqueror on a warhorse but as a humble king on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 with deliberate precision. The crowds shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!” — they are celebrating a political liberation that is not coming. Jesus has a different kind of liberation in mind.

The chapter is structured around three confrontational actions: the entry (vv. 1–11), the temple cleansing (vv. 12–17), and the cursing of the fig tree (vv. 18–22), sandwiched around a series of parables and controversies. The fig tree and the temple interpret each other: Israel, like the fig tree, has leaves of religious activity but no fruit. The temple establishment has turned the Father’s house of prayer into a market. Jesus’ authority is challenged (vv. 23–27); he responds with the parable of the two sons (vv. 28–32) and the parable of the tenants (vv. 33–46), both of which declare that the kingdom will be taken from the current tenants and given to a people who produce its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Triumphal Entry, Cleansing of the Temple, and the Withered Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, enters Jerusalem to the crowd's Hosannas, cleanses the temple of money-changers and dove-sellers, heals the blind and lame in the temple, and returns to Bethany. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit; it withers immediately. He teaches the disciples about faith that moves mountains. In between, children run about the temple courts shouting the same Hosanna, the chief priests object to what they are saying, and Jesus answers them out of Psalm 8 (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The triumphal entry deliberately fulfills Zechariah 9:9: the king who comes humble and mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. Jesus is not claiming the military kingship Israel wanted; he is claiming the humble-servant kingship Zechariah foresaw. The Hosanna (Hebrew: save now!) from Psalm 118:25-26 is the pilgrims' greeting to the coming king. The crowd who shouts it does not fully understand what they are saying; they are speaking more truly than they know. "Hosanna to the Son of David" is the church's cry from that day to this. Two things the section does that are easily missed. Hosanna is not a cheer but a prayer — hoshia-na, save now — and the crowd prayed it with the wrong emergency in mind, wanting Rome dealt with while he came for something they had not thought to mention. And the psalm they sang is the psalm he quotes back in the temple: the pilgrims shout Psalm 118:26 on the way in (v. 9), and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone, to the men who run the place (v. 42). Between two verses of one psalm lies the whole week.
verseByVerse.examples: The cleansing of the temple is an act of prophetic judgment: the court of the Gentiles (the only place where non-Jews could pray) has been turned into a market. The money-changers and dove-sellers served legitimate temple functions, but their location in the court of the Gentiles prevented the very prayer the temple was meant to facilitate. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 — "a house of prayer for all nations" — and Jeremiah 7:11 — "a den of robbers." He restores the temple to its purpose as a place of prayer and healing, then leaves it to be destroyed (ch. 24). The withered fig tree is a living parable of Israel's fruitlessness: outward leaves of religious activity, no fruit of genuine repentance. Three notes on that sign. It belongs to a recognised prophetic genre — Jeremiah smashing a jar, Ezekiel lying beside a brick, Ahijah tearing a cloak — and it is worth observing that in a ministry of raising the dead and healing all who came, the only thing Jesus ever destroyed was a plant, by a roadside, where nobody was hurt. The charge against the tree is precise: not barrenness but advertising, since a fig in full leaf out of season is making a claim that can be checked from the road. So the guard matters for the anxious reader — this condemns pretence, not weakness, and the same Gospel says a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). The children of vv. 15-16, meanwhile, get Psalm 8 quoted in their defence, and the rest of that verse — to still the enemy and the avenger — tells the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bethphage sat on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, and it mattered because it was the last village before the city — cross that line and you were, for legal and ritual purposes, in Jerusalem. So this is the threshold, and the first thing Jesus does on reaching it is stop the whole party and send two men for an animal.

Which is worth sitting with, because of a fact that is easy to miss and hard to forget once seen. He had walked everywhere for three years. Up and down Galilee, out to Tyre and Sidon, north to Caesarea Philippi, down the Jordan valley, up the long climb from Jericho — hundreds of miles on foot, in sandals, and Matthew never once mentions him riding. This is the only journey in the Gospels that Jesus refuses to walk. The one time he sits down and lets himself be carried is the mile and a half into his own capital, as her king.

And the mount he chose it from is not incidental either. Zechariah had said that the day would come when the LORD's feet would stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:4), and the expectation had settled in Jewish hope that this was where deliverance would arrive from. Jesus does not stumble into the fulfilment. He stops at the right hill, sends for the right animal, and then rides down it.

Guard the donkey against the reading it usually gets. This is not a story about a man too poor for a horse, and the donkey is not merely a symbol of lowliness. In Israel it was a royal mount: when David wanted the succession settled beyond argument he had Solomon put on the king's own mule and led down to Gihon, and the crowd came up after him shouting Long live King Solomon until the ground shook (1 Kgs 1:33-40). A king's son, a borrowed royal beast, a descent from a hill, a shouting crowd — the last coronation procession Israel had seen looked exactly like this one. The people lining that road knew what they were watching.

Two details finish the picture. The colt, Mark tells us, had never been ridden (Mark 11:2) — and anyone who has been near a young donkey knows what an unbroken animal does in a shouting crowd with cloaks flying under its feet. It carried him. And the instructions are exact: not a donkey, but a donkey tied, with a colt beside her, in the village in front of you, and you will find it immediately. Whether that is arrangement made earlier or knowledge given directly, Matthew does not say and we should not pretend to know. What is plain is that nothing about the next four days is happening to Jesus. He is setting it up.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, near Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord needs them. Four words to say to a stranger whose animal you are untying, and they are extraordinary in both halves.

Take the first half. The Lord — ho kyrios, with the article, absolute, no explanation attached. Jesus is not often reported using that of himself to people outside the circle, and here he sends it ahead of him as the whole of his credentials. No name, no message about who is asking, no promise to return the animal. If the owner asks, tell him the Lord needs them, and that will be sufficient. It was.

Now the second half, which is stranger. Needs. This is the only occasion in the Gospels on which Jesus says he has need of anything, and what he needs is the loan of a young donkey. The one through whom all things were made, walking toward the city where he will be crowned and killed, sends two friends to borrow transport. It is the same condescension that runs through the whole story and is easy to miss because it is so quiet: he had no house, he will borrow an upper room for the supper, he will be laid in a tomb somebody else had cut for himself, and the only thing he ever owned outright at the end was the clothes soldiers gambled over. He owns everything. He arrives owning nothing and asking for a colt.

Then Matthew steps out of the narrative to say what is going on: this took place to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet. He has used that formula a dozen times since chapter 1, and by now the reader should know what he means by it — not that a prediction has ticked over, but that a pattern long written has arrived at the thing it was always shaped for (see on 2:15). The words were on a scroll for five hundred years. Now they are hoofbeats on a road.

One thing not to over-claim, since the text does not. Matthew does not tell us whether the owner had been spoken to in advance or whether he simply released the animals because something in the request made refusal unthinkable. Both are entirely possible and the narrative is indifferent to the question. What it does report is the result: he will send them at once, and he did. Somewhere in that village is a man who lost the use of his donkey for an afternoon and never appears again in the story, and the whole entry into Jerusalem waited on his willingness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah's word for the king is praus, and Matthew's readers had met it twice already. It is the word in the Beatitudes for the meek who inherit the earth (5:5), and it is the word Jesus used of himself when he offered rest to people carrying too much: I am gentle and lowly in heart (11:29). It does not mean weak. It is the word used of a horse that has been broken — all the strength still there, and every ounce of it under control. That is the king riding down the hill.

Then read the next verse of Zechariah, because the prophet explains the donkey himself and almost nobody quotes it: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations (Zech 9:10). The animal is not a note about the king's humility. It is his policy. He is riding the thing you ride when the war horses have been abolished, and the sentence ends with the nations — the same nations whose only court in the temple he is about to clear by force within the hour.

Set it beside what a triumphal entry actually looked like in that world and the contrast goes further than a change of animal. A Roman triumph had a fixed shape: the general in a four-horse chariot with his face painted red, the spoils of the campaign carried before him, the captured enemy leaders walking in chains behind, and at the end of the route the prisoners executed and bulls sacrificed. Go down the list. This king has no chariot. He has no spoils, having accumulated nothing. He drags no prisoners, having spent three years setting them free. And at the end of his route there is indeed a sacrifice — and it is him.

Which is the thing to hold on to when this scene is preached, as it often is, as the moment Jesus finally accepted the crown. He accepted it in the one form nobody wanted. The crowd on that road was shouting for a king who would deal with Rome, and the king they were shouting at had come to deal with something they had not asked him to touch. He let them cheer. He did not correct the volume, only the meaning, and he did it by choosing his transport.

The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. Matthew keeps saying this about them, and it is worth noticing how ordinary the obedience is. They were not asked to understand the Zechariah citation or to grasp what was about to happen in the city. They were asked to walk into a village and fetch a donkey, and they did it. A great deal of obedience is that size.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Matthew mentions both the donkey and her colt.

parallels.desc: your king comes, humble and mounted on a donkey
say to the daughter of Zion

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spreading of cloaks on the road was the ancient gesture of homage to a king: the same was done for Jehu when he was anointed king of Israel (2 Kings 9:13). The palm branches from the trees add another layer of royal symbolism — palms were associated with the Maccabean victories and with the Feast of Tabernacles. The crowd is welcoming a king with the gestures appropriate to a king, even if they do not understand the full nature of his kingship. Matthew's crowd is large — "most of the crowd" — and the welcome is public and unmistakable. This is the royal entry that the whole ministry of chapters 1-20 has been moving toward.

One detail here has been mocked more than almost any other in Matthew, and it deserves a straight answer. Matthew mentions two animals — the donkey and her colt — where Mark, Luke, and John mention only the colt Jesus rode; and he writes that they put their cloaks "on them, and he sat on them." Did Jesus, the scoffers ask, ride two animals at once, straddling both? And did Matthew, misreading the Hebrew poetry of Zechariah 9:9 (which names "a donkey" and "a colt" in a single parallel line, the Hebrew way of saying one animal twice), clumsily invent a second beast? Neither charge holds. There really were two animals, and Matthew, an eyewitness, simply notices what the others pass over: the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2), and an unbroken colt is far steadier with its mother walking beside it — exactly the arrangement a careful observer would recall. As for "he sat on them," the nearest plural is the cloaks: they threw their garments over both animals, and he sat on the garments. Matthew rode nothing into confusion. And far from misunderstanding the parallelism, Matthew — a Jew steeped in the Scriptures — saw the real scene match even the doubled wording of the prophet, and rejoiced to record it. The eye that notices the mother donkey is not the eye of a careless writer but of a man who was there.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosanna is not a cheer, though it has become one. It is hoshia-na, and it means save now — an imperative addressed to God, a cry for help. The crowd on that road was not applauding. It was praying, at the top of its voice, in the words of the psalm every pilgrim sang coming up to the feast: Save us, we pray, O LORD… Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD (Ps 118:25-26).

And they were praying the right prayer with the wrong emergency in mind. Ask that crowd what they wanted saving from and they would have said Rome — the garrison in the Antonia, the taxes, the eagles on the standards, the whole humiliation of being occupied in the land God gave them. It was a real grievance and he did nothing about it. He had come to deal with something they had not thought to mention, and the rescue they asked for was smaller than the one he was carrying up that hill. They were more right than they knew and less right than they thought, which is the usual condition of anybody praying.

Now watch which psalm it is, because Matthew is building something. The crowd shouts Psalm 118:26 on the way into the city. Before the chapter is over Jesus will stand in the temple and quote Psalm 118:22 at the men who run it: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (v. 42). Two verses of one psalm, four verses apart on the page — and between them, in the events, lies the rejection, the trial and the cross. The pilgrims sang the welcome. The Lord supplied the verse about what would be done with him.

The whole city was stirred up — and the verb is eseisthe, from the root that gives us seismic. The city quaked. Matthew has used that root before and will use it twice more, and the sequence is worth having: Jerusalem shakes when he enters it; the earth shakes when he dies and the curtain tears (27:51); the ground shakes again at dawn on the third day when the stone is rolled back (28:2). Three tremors, and the city's is the only one caused by people.

The question it shakes out is the right one — Who is this? — and the answer the crowd gives is true and much too small: the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee. It is exactly the answer the villages had been giving all along (16:14), and it is the honour of a great category that is still the wrong one. Note too what they have handed his enemies without meaning to: Nazareth, Galilee. The provincial address will be used against him.

One correction, because it is preached almost every year and it is not accurate. It is commonly said that the same crowd which shouted Hosanna on Sunday shouted Crucify on Friday, and the sermon usually turns on how fickle people are. The text will not support it. These are pilgrims coming up the Jericho road with him, largely Galileans who had followed him for months. The crowd at the trial is a different gathering altogether — assembled early in the morning inside the city, at the praetorium, and Matthew tells us plainly that the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). The truth is less tidy than the sermon and worse: it was not that everyone turned. It was that when it mattered, the people who had cheered him were nowhere to be found, and a smaller crowd that had been worked on all night was.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple cleansing follows immediately — the entry and the cleansing are the same act of messianic authority extended into the holy place. The money-changers converted Roman coins (bearing the emperor's image, unacceptable for the temple tax and offerings) to acceptable currency; the dove-sellers provided the offering of the poor. Both services were legitimate; their location in the court of the Gentiles was the problem. Jesus drives out the commerce to restore the space to prayer.

Isaiah 56:7 promises that the temple will be "a house of prayer for all peoples" — including the Gentiles, for whom the outer court was the only available space. Jeremiah 7:11 condemns those who use the temple as a refuge for injustice — a "den of robbers" who retreat to religious performance while exploiting the vulnerable. Jesus applies both texts simultaneously: the court has been turned from prayer-space into market-space, and the market has displaced the Gentiles and the poor who needed it for prayer. Then immediately the blind and lame come to Jesus in the temple and are healed — the space is restored to its purpose: prayer and healing. What the temple was meant to be, Jesus makes it be, in his own person. And that last phrase is worth slowing down over, because it is where this scene is finally pointing. Ask what the temple was actually for, and three answers come back: it was the place where God dwelt among his people, the place where sacrifice was offered for sin, and the place through which prayer went up. Now look at the man standing in the middle of the wreckage of the money tables. He is Immanuel, God with us, so the dwelling is no longer a building (1:23). He is days away from offering the sacrifice that will end the need for every other one. And he is the mediator through whom prayer now reaches the Father (John 14:13-14). John records him saying it outright after a cleansing like this one: destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up — and John adds, "he was speaking about the temple of his body" (John 2:19-21).

So this is not merely a reformer tidying up an institution he intends to keep. It is the reality walking into the shadow and standing there. Within a lifetime the building would be rubble, in AD 70, and the loss — devastating as it was — took nothing away from the people of God that they had not already been given in Christ. The type had handed everything over to the antitype. The house of prayer for all nations turned out to be a Person, and the Gentiles those traders had crowded out would find room in him.

A word is owed on something just slipped past above. John records a temple cleansing too — the tables overturned, the cord of whips, the same words about his body as the temple — but he places it at the very beginning of Jesus's ministry, some two or three years before this one (John 2:13-22), while Matthew, Mark and Luke all place it in the last week. So which is it: did one of them move it? There are two honest answers, and Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness hold both. Some say there was one cleansing, and John has arranged his Gospel by theme rather than by calendar, putting it early because he wants the temple question raised at the outset. That is not a charge against him; John openly organises his material around signs and feasts rather than a diary. But the simpler answer is that it happened twice, and the details rather suggest it. In John it is oxen and sheep and a whip of cords; here it is the dove-sellers and the money-changers. In John the leaders ask for a sign and get the saying about the temple of his body; here they ask by what authority he acts and get the parable of the tenants. Even the charge at his trial preserves a memory of the earlier saying (26:61) — which is easiest to explain if the words were spoken years before and remembered against him.

And there is nothing strange in the repetition. The trade grew back, as trades do; what a man clears out at the start of three years of ministry will be standing again by the end. Nor is it surprising that Jesus, who came to this temple as its Lord, should have confronted it both when he began and when he finished — an opening statement and a closing verdict, with everything in between as the argument. Either way, and this is the point to carry off, nothing hangs on the answer that touches the meaning of what he did here. The court of the Gentiles had been turned into a market, and the Lord of the house came in and said so.

One further word is owed here, because no passage in the Gospels is quoted more often to justify behaviour. Jesus flipped the tables has become the standing defence of the furious tweet, the walk-out, the scorching email, the man who is rude to his elders and calls it prophetic. So it is worth asking what this scene actually licenses.

Notice first who is acting and in whose house. The whole force of the passage is that the owner has arrived — the Lord of the temple, exercising an authority that belongs to him and to nobody else, over abuses in his own courts. This is not a worshipper losing his temper about the state of the church. It is the proprietor closing a market that had set itself up in his front room. Whatever else may be drawn from it, the one thing it is not is a general permission for angry men to act like the owner.

Notice next what the anger is about. Not a slight to himself. He had been mocked, doubted and plotted against for three chapters without overturning anything.
