If they say, ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. <sup>27</sup>For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>28</sup>Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. <sup>29</sup>“Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>30</sup>Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. <sup>31</sup>And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. <sup>32</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>33</sup>So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>34</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>35</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>36</sup>“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only. <sup>37</sup>For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, <sup>39</sup>and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. <sup>40</sup>Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left. <sup>41</sup>Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left. <sup>42</sup>Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. <sup>43</sup>But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into. <sup>44</sup>Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. <sup>45</sup>“Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his master has set over his household, to give them their food at the proper time? <sup>46</sup>Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>47</sup>Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>48</sup>But if that wicked servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’ <sup>49</sup>and begins to beat his fellow servants and eats and drinks with drunkards, <sup>50</sup>the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know <sup>51</sup>and will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
24.overview:
The Olivet Discourse (chapters 24–25) is Jesus’ extended teaching on the end of the age, delivered on the Mount of Olives overlooking the temple. It is the most complex and debated passage in Matthew, weaving together two horizons: the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 and the final coming of the Son of Man at the end of history. Jesus deliberately leaves the two horizons blurred, because the near event (Jerusalem’s fall) is the type and foretaste of the far event (the final judgment).

The chapter resists every system that charts the future with calendar precision. “No one knows the day or the hour” (v. 36) is not a temporary limitation but a theological statement: the appropriate posture before the end is not calculation but watchfulness, not a schedule but readiness. The gospel of the kingdom must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 14) — the mission is the church’s present calling. The Son of Man will come as lightning, suddenly and unmistakably. Until then: stay awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — Signs of the End and the Great Tribulation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus walks out of the temple and tells the disciples that not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives they ask three questions as though they were one: when will this happen, what will be the sign of your coming, and when is the end of the age. His answer runs through false messiahs, wars and famines that are expressly not the end, betrayal inside the church and love growing cold, the promise that endurance marks the saved and the gospel will reach all nations, the abomination of desolation and the order to run for the hills, a tribulation cut short for the elect, and a final warning that his coming will be as unmistakable as lightning.
verseByVerse.theology: The discourse answers a compound question and therefore has a compound shape, in the manner of Old Testament prophecy, which repeatedly sees a near horizon and a far one in one view. Everything to v. 35 is hedged with signs and set inside a generation; from v. 36 there are no signs at all. The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 is both a real event and a type of the last one. Two doctrinal loads are carried in this half. Endurance to the end is the mark of genuine salvation rather than a feat the anxious must manage, kept by the God who promises to keep. And the days are cut short for the sake of the elect: the duration of the worst years in that nation's history was measured with reference to people whose names appear in no chronicle. History bends around them, not around Titus.
verseByVerse.examples: The most ignored clause in the chapter is the end is not yet (v. 6). Every generation has read its wars into the timetable and every one has been wrong, which is exactly what this verse said would happen. The usable test is not prophetic but personal: when the headlines are bad, does your confidence in God's government move? Two other verses land closer to home than the tribulation does. Verse 12, love growing cold, is the commonest condition in a mature congregation and almost nobody names it: prayer as a duty discharged, Scripture familiar, other people's troubles mildly tiresome. The remedy is the one given to Ephesus: remember, repent, and do the works you did at first, because feeling follows the feet. And the response to the sign in v. 15 is startlingly practical: not gather, not interpret, but leave the district. The Christians of Jerusalem did, and lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus left the temple and was going away, when his disciples came to point out to him the buildings of the temple. But he answered them, "You see all these, do you not? Truly, I say to you, there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two movements happen in this verse and the first is the one to notice. Jesus left the temple and was going away. He has spent three days in those courts teaching, and he walks out, and he does not go back. Any Jewish reader with Ezekiel in his memory felt the shape of that, because Ezekiel had watched the glory of the LORD rise from the threshold, move to the east gate, and go up from the city to the mountain on its east side — the Mount of Olives (Ezek 10:18-19; 11:23), which is exactly where Jesus is about to sit down. The last time God left that building, the building came down.

Then the disciples point at the stonework, and they were not being naive. Herod's temple was the most impressive structure in the Jewish world. Building had begun almost fifty years before (forty-six at the start of his ministry, Jn 2:20) and was still going on; the platform was faced with masonry on a scale that is difficult to take in even now, since some of the surviving blocks in the retaining wall weigh several hundred tonnes. Josephus says the whole thing was clad so that at sunrise a man approaching had to look away. Pointing at it was the natural thing for a Galilean to do.

There will not be left here one stone upon another. Forty years later Titus's legions took the city after a siege, the sanctuary burned, and soldiers levered the stones apart to get at the gold that had melted and run into the joints. The ground was afterwards cleared so thoroughly that Josephus, who had known the place, says a visitor would not believe it had been inhabited.

And notice how exact the prophecy turns out to be, which is worth knowing because it is often reported carelessly. What survives today, and what pilgrims pray at, is a retaining wall of the platform. The temple itself — the building the disciples were pointing at — has not one stone standing on another. He did not say the mountain would be flattened. He said the house would not have two stones left in contact, and that is precisely what happened.

Does Scripture predict a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem? Dispensational Christians expect one, pointing to Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11. The more likely reading is that Christ has replaced the temple once for all: his body is the true temple (John 2:19–21), and his people are now God’s dwelling (1 Cor 3:16; Eph 2:19–22). Hebrews shows that the sacrifices are finished (Heb 10:11–14). Nothing in Jesus’ words here looks for the building to rise again.

Two men looking at one wall and seeing entirely different things is the whole of this verse, and it puts a question worth carrying. The disciples saw permanence: God's house, in God's city, built to last, evidently approved. Jesus saw a building whose purpose had already been fulfilled elsewhere and which was therefore forty years from rubble. It is very easy to read the solidity of religious infrastructure as evidence of God's pleasure — the full building, the institution with a history, the denomination that has always been here. Stone is not evidence of anything. This particular stone was the most God-approved masonry on earth, and he walked out of it and told them to watch it fall.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt and enlarged the temple on a vast scale; work was still going on. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the end of the age?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask three things, and the whole chapter turns on the fact that they thought they were asking one. When will these things be? — the temple. What will be the sign of your coming? And the end of the age? To them these were three faces of a single event, and it is not hard to see why: if the house of God comes down, what could possibly follow but the end of everything?

The word for coming is parousia, and it is worth knowing because it does not mean return. In ordinary Greek it was the word for a royal visit — the formal arrival of a king or governor at a city, with the reception and the escort and the honours that went with it. Cities minted coins for a parousia. Matthew uses the word four times, all of them in this chapter (vv. 3, 27, 37, 39), and nowhere else in his Gospel. The disciples are asking about a state visit.

Because they have asked a compound question, the answer is a compound answer, and that is the single most useful thing to know before reading the rest. Christians who love this Gospel read the discourse in three main ways. Some take nearly all of it as fulfilled in AD 70, with the language of cosmic collapse being the ordinary prophetic idiom for the fall of a nation. Others take nearly all of it as still future, the tribulation and the signs belonging to the end. And many take it as answering both questions in turn, in the manner of Old Testament prophecy, which repeatedly sees a near horizon and a far one in a single view — a mountain range that looks like one ridge from a distance.

The third is followed here, for a reason lying in the text rather than in a system: the discourse has a visible seam. Everything down to verse 35 is hedged about with signs and told to a generation that will see them; and then verse 36 begins but concerning that day and hour no one knows, and from there on there are no signs at all, no timetable, and a coming compared to a thief in the night and a flood nobody expected. Signs and no signs cannot describe the same event. The seam is where the second question begins to be answered, and the full case for reading it that way is set out at verses 34-35.

One thing to settle before going further, because it saves a great deal of frustration. Jesus does not answer the question they asked in the form they asked it, and he never once gives them a date. He gives them, instead, four commands repeated throughout the chapter: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, endure, stay awake. The disciples wanted a schedule and were handed a way to live. That is not evasion; it is the answer, and every generation since has wanted the schedule instead.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "See that no one leads you astray. For many will come in my name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing out of his mouth is not catastrophe but deception, and the pronoun is worth noticing. See that no one leads you astray — you, the men sitting on this hillside. He is not briefing them on world affairs. He is warning them about their own footing.

And the claimants were not hypothetical. Josephus catalogues them: Theudas, who gathered a crowd at the Jordan and promised to part the river — a man of the same name as the Theudas Gamaliel cites to the Sanhedrin in Acts (Acts 5:36); an Egyptian who led thousands out to the Mount of Olives expecting the walls of Jerusalem to fall at his word; men who took people into the wilderness promising signs of deliverance. Within a century Simon bar Kokhba would be hailed as messiah by one of the most respected rabbis of the age, and would lead the nation into a catastrophe worse than the first. Every one of those movements ended with the followers dead.

Note the precise form of the danger: many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ. Not denying him — using him. That is a considerably harder thing to detect than open opposition, and it has always been the church's chief hazard from within rather than without. The wolves in this Gospel do not arrive announcing themselves; they arrive in sheep's clothing (7:15).

The modern form of this is rarely a man claiming to be Jesus — that variety appears occasionally, is easily identified, and gathers very few. The dangerous version is a man who functions as though he were, without ever making the claim: whose pronouncements cannot be questioned, whose approval has become the measure of standing in a community, who mediates access to God for people who have stopped going directly. Nobody in such a movement believes their leader is the Christ. They simply behave as though he were, and the seat has been quietly occupied (see on 23:9-10).

One guard, because this warning can be turned into a habit of suspicion that does its own damage. Jesus is not telling his disciples to spend their lives auditing other Christians. The safeguard he gives everywhere else is positive and specific: know the real thing well enough that the counterfeit does not persuade you. A man who knows his Bible and is known by a congregation is very hard to lead astray. A man who is impressed by confidence, and has nobody with the standing to disagree with him, is exactly the person these movements were built for.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that you are not alarmed. It is a command, in the imperative, and it is addressed to men who will live through the fall of their own capital. The Greek me throeisthe means do not be thrown into confusion or panic. Christians are ordered not to panic about the news, which means panic is not a neutral reaction to be excused but a thing to be resisted with effort.

Then the clause that has been ignored more thoroughly than almost any other in the New Testament: but the end is not yet. Wars, rumours of wars, nation against nation, famines, earthquakes — and his verdict on all of it is that this is not the sign. He is not saying such things are unimportant, or that they carry no message. He is saying they are the ordinary texture of the age and must not be read as a countdown.

Which is worth stating plainly, because the church has ignored it in every century. The fall of Rome, the Black Death, the Turks at Vienna, Napoleon, 1914, the rise of Hitler, the atom bomb, the founding of the state of Israel, the Cuban missile crisis, Chernobyl — because the name was taken to mean wormwood — and a dozen dates confidently published and quietly forgotten. In every case sincere Christians read the headlines as the timetable, and in every case they were wrong, and in every case this verse had already told them they would be. It is a remarkable thing to be warned so precisely and to keep doing it.

The reason it keeps happening is not stupidity. It is that reading the news eschatologically feels like faith. It produces urgency, it makes the world legible, and it flatters the reader with the sense of being one of the few who understand. Jesus offers something less exciting and considerably more useful: expect all of this, refuse to be shaken by it, and get on with what you were given to do.

There is a test in it that can be run without reference to any prophecy chart. When the headlines are bad, does your confidence in God's government of the world move? If a war or an election or a market can alter your sense of whether he is in control, then you are being alarmed in the precise sense he forbids — and the remedy is not better information about the end but a firmer grip on the one who told you in advance that all this would happen and that it would not be the end.

verseByVerse.quote: "All these are but the beginning of the birth pains. Then they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the metaphor seriously, because it is doing precise work. Birth pains — odines — are not the pains of dying, and that is the whole point of choosing them. They increase rather than fade. They come in waves with intervals that shorten. They are purposeful, they cannot be stopped once they have properly begun, and they end not in death but in a person. Anyone who has been in the room knows that the pains are the worst part and also the sign that the thing everyone is waiting for is close.

So the wars and famines and earthquakes are not evidence that the world is winding down. Paul uses the same image of the whole creation groaning as in the pains of childbirth (Rom 8:22), and it is the most hopeful thing said about history anywhere. The world is not decaying. It is in labour.

Then the pains become personal: they will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death. The verb paradosousin is the word used of Judas handing Jesus over and of Jesus being handed over to Pilate. His followers will go through what he went through, in the same vocabulary. That is not incidental to the age between his comings; it is the shape of it.

Hated by all nations for my name's sake. Two things in that. The scope is total — not one nation, all of them — and the cause is exact. Not for their politics, not for being difficult, not for their culture: for the name. Whatever hostility a Christian meets that has nothing to do with Christ is not this, and should not be dignified with the label.

Which is where a comfortable reader needs a word of honesty in both directions. If you live somewhere the faith is merely unfashionable, do not manufacture persecution out of social awkwardness or an argument at work; treating an eye-roll as martyrdom trivialises the real thing and makes the church look self-pitying. But do not conclude from your own comfort that the verse has expired. Most Christians alive today are not in your position. There are believers this morning in prison for a Bible, families who lost a house for a baptism, and congregations meeting where a knock at the door would end it. This verse is their daily weather, and one of the things the comfortable part of the church owes the rest of it is to stop reading these words as metaphor.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

parallels.desc: the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth

verseByVerse.quote: "And then many will fall away and betray one another and hate one another. And many false prophets will arise and lead many astray."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs, and they get worse: many will fall away, and betray one another, and hate one another. Notice that all three describe damage done inside the church. The previous verse had the world doing the hating; this one has the brothers doing it.

The middle verb is the sharpest. Betray is paradosousin again — the same word used two verses earlier of the world handing Christians over, and the same word used of Judas. So the sentence means: they will do to each other what Judas did to me. And it was not hypothetical. When Pliny was governor of Bithynia early in the second century he wrote to the emperor describing how he dealt with Christians brought before him, and the machinery of the thing depended on denunciation — somebody had to give the names. Under pressure, some of them were given by people who had sat in the same room to break bread.

Then hate one another, which is the most disturbing clause of the three, because persecution is doing something here beyond thinning the visible church. It is turning it on itself. That is worth understanding rather than merely deploring: sustained fear makes people suspicious, and suspicion in a small frightened group looks for somewhere to land. The ones who held out despise the ones who cracked; the ones who cracked cannot bear the sight of the ones who held out; and everybody has a theory about who talked.

And the low-grade version of this does not require a persecutor. Any congregation under real strain — a financial crisis, a scandal, a split, a long illness in a leader — will discover the same instinct at a lower temperature. Positions harden, factions form around men rather than around truth, motives get assigned, and people who prayed together last year cannot be in the same room. Nobody involved thinks of it as apostasy. It presents itself as conviction.

Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. This is the second of three warnings about deception in this chapter, and the placing tells you why: it comes immediately after the betrayal and the hatred. A frightened, divided, exhausted church is exactly the market for a confident new voice with a simpler explanation. The damage such men do is not usually measured in the people they take from a strong church. It is measured in the people they take from a wounded one.

verseByVerse.quote: "And because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of everything in this discourse, this is the verse most likely to describe the reader, and it is the quietest sentence in it. Not apostasy. Not scandal. Not betrayal under interrogation. The love of many will grow cold.

The verb occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Psygesetai comes from the word for breathing or blowing, and it means to be cooled — the picture is not a fire put out but a fire no longer fed, going grey at the edges while nobody notices. There is no dramatic moment in it. That is precisely what makes it dangerous, because a man can watch for the sins he has been warned about and never once check the temperature.

And the mechanism Jesus names is exposure: because lawlessness will be increased. Anomia is the same word he used of the whitewashed tombs a chapter earlier (23:28). The logic is not that wicked people force Christians to stop loving; it is that living for years in an environment where God's order is ignored has an effect on the person living there. You stop being shocked. Then you stop being grieved. Then you stop noticing that you stopped, and the whole adjustment feels like maturity.

So it is worth naming what cooling actually looks like, because it never announces itself as a spiritual problem. Prayer becomes a duty discharged rather than an appointment kept. Scripture is familiar — you know the passage, you have heard the sermon, there is nothing new here. Other Christians' troubles become mildly tiresome; you help, but you time it. Worship is assessed rather than entered. The gospel is information you possess rather than news you still cannot quite believe. None of that will get a man disciplined by any church on earth, and it is the most common condition in a mature congregation, and almost nobody says it out loud.

Notice also the words of many — ton pollon, not of all. It is not inevitable, and it is not a description of what age does to everybody. There are people at eighty who are warmer than they were at thirty, and everybody who has been in a church long enough has met one and been slightly unnerved by them.

The remedy is not to try to feel more, which never works, and the apostolic prescription is unexpectedly concrete. To a church whose first love had cooled the risen Christ said three things in one breath: remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first (Rev 2:4-5). Remember: think back to when it was warm and be specific about what was different. Repent: call the coldness sin rather than a season, which is the step everybody skips. And do the first works — not feel the first feelings, but resume the actions, the ones you did when it was easy, before the feeling has returned. Feeling follows the feet, and it will not be argued into place.

parallels.desc: you have abandoned the love you had at first

verseByVerse.quote: "But the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two anchoring promises amid the tribulation warnings. First, endurance to the end is the mark of genuine salvation — not earning salvation by persisting, but the perseverance of the saints as evidence of genuine new birth (cf. 1 John 2:19; Phil. 1:6). Second, the mission will be completed before the end: every nation will hear the gospel. This is the church's task and the precondition for the parousia. Together the two verses describe the shape of Christian life between the comings: personal endurance and global mission, each sustaining the other, and both sustained by the certainty that the King is coming.

The doctrine is right, and it leaves a fear sitting in the room. It is one of the commonest fears among people who have believed a long time, and it is rarely said out loud: I believe today — but will I still believe at the end? Anyone who has watched someone fall away knows the question is not imaginary. People do depart, sometimes people who once seemed further on than we are.

So begin by noticing what the verse does not say. It does not say the one who is strong enough to hold on. Endurance is described here as the mark of the saved, not prescribed as a feat to be managed by the anxious. And notice who is said to do the keeping everywhere else. The same Lord promises that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (Jn 10:28-29). Paul is confident that he who began a good work will bring it to completion (Phil 1:6). Peter says believers are guarded by God's power through faith (1 Pet 1:5). Jude closes by blessing him who is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24). Perseverance is a promise before it is ever a duty — though it is genuinely a duty, and both halves have to stand.

Which means the question will I endure? is unanswerable in advance, and sitting with it produces nothing but paralysis. It is rather like standing at a wedding asking whether you will still be married in forty years. That is not settled by introspection; it is settled by tomorrow, and the tomorrow after that.

And here is the useful part, because endurance is not a heroic quality that some people were issued with. It is an accumulation of very ordinary actions. Almost nobody falls away in a single dramatic crisis; they drift, over years, out of the means God gave to hold them — Scripture, prayer, the Lord's Table, the honest confession of sin, and the company of other believers. Those are the ordinary machinery of perseverance, and they are unglamorous on purpose. Stay inside them and the question largely answers itself.

Note especially the last of those, because it is the one most under your control and the one most easily lost. Hebrews tells the church to exhort one another every day, so that none may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). God's normal method of keeping his people is other Christians. Which makes isolation the single largest risk factor in the whole business — and a Christian who has quietly stopped being known by anybody has removed the very instrument God usually uses.

Has this happened? In one sense, yes: before AD 70 Paul could say that the gospel was bearing fruit in the whole world (Col 1:6; cf. Rom 16:26). In its fullest sense the gospel goes on reaching the nations until the end, and Revelation sees people from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages before the throne (Rev 7:9). But Christ’s return is not triggered by our success. Its day is fixed by the Father (v. 36); our part is to be faithful in the task.

And if you have already had a season away — a stretch you are ashamed of, a period when you stopped altogether — read the fact that it troubles you. The genuine apostate does not come back uneasy; he leaves and does not miss it. Peter denied his Lord with oaths in a courtyard and was eating breakfast with him on a beach a few weeks later. Falling is not the same as falling away, and the God who intends to finish this has dealt with worse than your worst month.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The abomination of desolation is a phrase with a history, and Daniel's readers knew what it had already meant once. In 167 BC Antiochus IV, ruling Judea from Syria and determined to hellenise it, had an altar to Olympian Zeus set up in the temple and pigs sacrificed on it, banned circumcision and the Scriptures, and turned the sanctuary into a pagan shrine. That is the desecration Daniel's phrase had described (Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11), and it had provoked the Maccabean revolt. So when Jesus uses the phrase of something still future, everyone listening had a template: a pagan thing standing where it must not stand.

Then a remarkable aside: let the reader understand. That is not spoken to the disciples on the hillside; it is addressed to the person holding the scroll — a note from the page to whoever is reading it, and the only one of its kind in Matthew. Whatever else it means, it means: this is not decoration, work it out, and when you see it, act on it.

Candidates for the fulfilment are not in short supply, and the honest position is that Christians differ. The Roman standards carried into the temple precincts bore the emperor's image and were objects of military veneration. Earlier, in AD 40, Caligula had ordered a statue of himself erected in the sanctuary, and Judea came within a hair of open revolt before he died and the order lapsed — an episode inside the lifetime of these disciples that made the prophecy feel entirely live. Others take the desecration as still future. Luke’s parallel points to the first: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). What is not in doubt is the response required.

And the response is the striking thing. Given a sign of cosmic significance, Jesus tells them to leave the district. Not to gather, not to fast, not to organise a defence of the holy place, not to interpret. Flee to the hills. It is the most practical instruction in the whole discourse, and it is the pattern for how prophecy is supposed to work on people: it produces action, and the action is usually mundane.

What is the abomination of desolation? Luke gives Jesus’ words in a form his Gentile readers could understand: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). That points to AD 70, when Roman armies with their idolatrous standards surrounded the city and the temple was desecrated and destroyed. Many Christians, especially dispensationalists, expect a future antichrist to set himself up in a rebuilt temple (2 Thess 2:3–4; Rev 13). The AD 70 reading is the more likely for this verse, though Paul’s man of lawlessness shows that a final rebellion against God is still to come.

Which is worth holding against the two failures this passage most often produces. One is fatalism — if it is written, nothing can be done, so we wait. The other is the endless identification of the sign in the newspaper, which produces excitement and no action whatever. Jesus gave a sign and a route out. The people who obeyed him packed.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple. It was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take what is in his house, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instructions are so domestic that they can only have come from someone picturing the actual streets. Houses in that country had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, and the roof was living space — where you slept in hot weather, dried figs, prayed. In a packed town the roofs adjoined, so that a man could go along the tops of the houses and out at the edge of the village without ever coming down into the street. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down means: do not go back inside for anything. Go across the roofs.

The second picture is sharper than it looks. A man working in a field left his outer cloak at the boundary and worked in his tunic. That cloak was not a spare coat; it was his blanket, and the Law itself protected it on exactly that ground — a creditor holding a poor man's cloak in pledge had to return it before sundown, for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? (Ex 22:26-27). So the command is: leave behind the one possession you will genuinely need tonight, and do not walk the two hundred yards to fetch it.

They took him at his word, and there is a footnote in church history worth having. Eusebius records that before the siege closed on Jerusalem the Christians of that city, warned by prophecy, left and settled at Pella across the Jordan. While the rest of the population was still arguing about whether to trust the walls, the church walked out of the city on the strength of a sermon preached forty years earlier on a hillside. They kept the roofs and the cloaks instruction, and they lived.

The principle underneath is not that possessions are wicked. It is that they have a grip which only shows up under time pressure. Nobody discovers what he is attached to while sitting comfortably; he discovers it in the four seconds when he has to choose between the thing and the door. This is why Jesus attaches the warning to a crisis rather than to a sermon on contentment: the crisis is the only reliable diagnostic.

Which gives a test that requires no crisis to run, only honesty. If you had two minutes and one bag, you would take the passports and the photographs. Everybody knows that list. The more revealing question is the other one: what would you be quietly grieving over three weeks later? That is the thing with the grip on it, and knowing its name now is a considerable advantage over discovering it on the stairs.
verseByVerse.note: Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: "And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has just told them to run, and now he thinks about who will not be able to. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days. The word is ouai — the same word that opened each of the seven woes a chapter earlier, and here it is not an indictment but a lament. Somebody is doing arithmetic about the people at the back of the column.

Then two specific prayers, both practical. Not in winter: the rains come between November and March, the wadis fill and become impassable within an hour, the tracks turn to mud, and a night in the open on the Judean hills in February can kill a child. Not on a Sabbath: the city gates were shut, no supplies could be bought, no animal hired, and a population trained from infancy in the Sabbath limit would hesitate at exactly the moment hesitation was fatal. He is not being sentimental. He is thinking about roads and weather and what people will actually do.

But the striking thing is that he tells them to pray about it — and that raises a difficulty worth meeting head on, because it is the difficulty most people have with prayer generally. He has just declared, with absolute certainty, that this catastrophe is coming. What is the use of praying about the timing of a thing God has decreed?

Two answers, and the second is the one that helps. The first is that God's decree includes the prayers of his people; they are not an attempt to get around his purpose but part of the way it is carried out, which is why Scripture can hold both without embarrassment. The second is simpler and more useful: he told them to. The man who knew with complete certainty what was coming instructed frightened people to pray about the weather on the day, and that settles the question of whether such prayers are worth praying rather better than any argument about mechanism.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? No. Jesus is speaking of practical danger in Judea: on the Sabbath, city gates were shut, travel was restricted and many would hesitate to flee. It is a word about the circumstances of AD 70, not a command to the church, for whom the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17; Rom 14:5–6).

Which is precisely the shape of a great deal of Christian praying, and it is worth saying so to anyone who has felt foolish doing it. The scan has already been done and the result is already on a screen somewhere. The letter is written. The decision was taken at a meeting last week. The thing is, in every practical sense, fixed — and you are told to pray about it anyway, and about the details, and about the timing, by someone who was never once in any doubt about how it would go. Pray about winter. He did not think it was a foolish request.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard; Sabbath rules restricted travel.

verseByVerse.quote: "For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, and never will be. And if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The language is superlative and it needs no exaggeration to fit what happened. Josephus was an eyewitness to the siege and no friend of the rebels, and his account is very difficult reading: the famine inside the walls, families fighting over scraps, the bodies thrown from the gates in numbers nobody could count, the city taken street by street, and the sanctuary burning while Titus — by Josephus's telling — tried and failed to stop it. Whatever else it was, it was the end of a world. The temple has never been rebuilt, and the sacrificial system that had defined the worship of God for a thousand years stopped that summer and has never restarted.

Then a sentence that changes the way a person reads history: if those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short.

Take the two halves in order. The first is a statement about how bad it would otherwise get — no flesh would survive it. And the second says who set the limit and why. Not the exhaustion of the aggressor, not the intervention of a treaty, not the collapse of a supply line. The days are shortened for the sake of the elect, and that is the stated reason and the only one given.

Sit with the size of that, because it reorganises the whole picture of who matters in history. Empires keep records of themselves; the annals are full of emperors and legions and the dates of campaigns, and the people God has chosen appear in none of them. And Jesus says the duration of the catastrophe was set with reference to them. The calendar of the worst years in that nation's life was adjusted for the benefit of a group whose names occur in no chronicle and whose existence the men prosecuting the war never once considered. History does not bend around Titus. It bends around people nobody was counting.

Is this great tribulation the siege of AD 70, or a future seven-year tribulation? Dispensational Christians take it as future, pointing to Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 7:14. The more likely reading is that it describes the horror of AD 70, since Jesus tells those in Judea to flee from it (vv. 16–20), and flight would not help in a worldwide judgment. The words such as has not been are a familiar way of describing an overwhelming disaster (cf. Exod 11:6). That siege was a foretaste of the final judgment, but it was not the end itself.

Which is a comfort of a particular kind, and it is not the comfort of being spared. Nothing here says the elect avoid the tribulation; they are plainly in it, and shortening the days would be pointless if they were not. What it says is that the thing has a measured end, and that the measuring was done with them in view. That is worth knowing in any hard stretch. You may not be taken out of it. It has been shortened for you.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: "Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third warning about deception, and this time with a detail that should unsettle anyone who assumes the supernatural settles arguments: the false christs and false prophets will perform great signs and wonders. Not conjuring tricks. Signs and wonders — the phrase used of Moses in Egypt and of the apostles in Acts.

This is not a new problem in Scripture, and the Law had already addressed it in terms so blunt that they are rarely quoted. If a prophet arises and gives you a sign, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass, and he then says let us go after other gods — do not listen to him, for the LORD your God is testing you (Deut 13:1-3). Read that slowly. God does not say the sign will fail. He allows that it may come true and instructs Israel to disobey the man anyway. Power was never the test.

So the criterion is doctrinal and it always has been. What does the man say about Christ? Paul puts it with a bluntness that has offended every generation since: even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed (Gal 1:8). An angel, with the full apparatus of the supernatural, ranks below the message. Which means the church's defence against a powerful counterfeit is not discernment about power — nobody can assess that — but familiarity with the gospel. You cannot tell a false miracle from a true one by looking. You can tell a false gospel from a true one by reading.

Then so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. The two halves of that clause both have to stand, and the balance is exactly right. If possible concedes that it is not — the same construction, and the same reassurance, met earlier in this Gospel (see on 19:14). And even the elect concedes that the pressure is real and aimed directly at them. So the security is genuine and it is not a reason to relax, and the way those two fit together is visible in the sentence itself.

Notice how, in fact, the elect are kept. Not by being lifted above the danger, but by being warned about it in advance by their Lord, three times in one chapter, with the specifics included. This warning is not a caveat on the promise of preservation. It is the machinery of it. God keeps his people through means, and the chief of them is that he tells them the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: "See, I have told you beforehand. So, if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out. If they say, 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, I have told you beforehand. The purpose of the warning is stated: not to satisfy curiosity but to remove surprise. Prophecy in Scripture very rarely exists so that people can work out a schedule; it exists so that when the thing arrives, God's people are not thrown by it. Jesus does the same for the disciples about his own death, three times, in detail, and they still fell apart — but they had it to remember afterwards, and the remembering is what put them back together.

Then the two false locations, and they are chosen with care because they are the only two available. He is in the wilderness — out beyond the settlements, austere, radical, away from the compromised institutions, where a hard prophet gathers a following. That is exactly where the messianic movements of that century did gather; Josephus's claimants took their crowds out to the desert and the Jordan. And he is in the inner rooms — the private chambers, the hidden circle, knowledge available to those admitted. One movement says the truth is out on the edge; the other says it is in the back room. Both are false and both are still trading.

What they have in common is worth naming, because it is the family likeness of every counterfeit: each offers access that other people do not have. The wilderness version flatters you with radicalism — the ordinary churches have sold out, and you have seen through them. The inner-room version flatters you with initiation — there is more to this than what is preached on Sundays, and you are among the few who have been let in. Both make the hearer feel distinguished, and both require him to leave the ordinary company of God's people to get what is on offer.

Which is the reason the instruction is so flat: do not go out; do not believe it. No debate, no investigation, no going to hear him once to see. Jesus does not tell them to assess the claim. He tells them not to travel.

And the reason it can be that simple is the next verse. If the real thing will be visible from horizon to horizon, then any claim that requires directions is self-refuting. You will not need to be told where he is. That single test disposes of every secret coming, private revelation and exclusive circle that has ever asked a Christian for his address.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two verses telling them where he will not be, the image that says where he will be. As the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west — and every feature of that comparison is doing work. Lightning is not local; it is seen across a whole sky at once. It is not gradual; there is no moment when a man is halfway to noticing it. It comes from outside, not from any movement on the ground. And nobody has ever had to be told that it happened.

Which settles the question the previous verses raised, and settles it permanently. If his coming is like that, then any announcement of it is disproved by the fact that it needed announcing. News of the return of Christ is a contradiction in terms. He will not be reported. He will be seen.

The second image is harder, and honesty is better than confidence here: wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. Two readings have real weight. The first takes it as a grim proverb about inevitability — carrion draws the birds without fail and without delay, and judgment finds its object with the same certainty. Nobody has to summon vultures; they arrive because the thing is dead.

The second is more pointed, and it turns on the Greek word aetoi, which means eagles as readily as vultures. The Roman legions carried the eagle as their standard, a silver bird on a pole that was the object of near-religious devotion in the army, and it was those standards that would be planted in the ruins of Jerusalem within the lifetime of the men listening. Read so, the sentence is a veiled and terrible piece of specificity: the eagles gather where the body is, and the body is the city. Given that half of this discourse concerns AD 70, this reading fits the context uncomfortably well.

The two are not rivals so much as a near and a far view of the same principle, which is the pattern of the whole chapter. What the sentence establishes either way is that judgment does not need to be arranged. There is no summons to be issued and no case to be brought. Where there is death, the birds come — and the interval between the two is never long enough for anybody to make arrangements.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “eagles” for “vultures.”

parallels.desc: where the slain are, there is he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–51 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The discourse turns to the coming itself: the heavens shaken, the Son of Man on the clouds, the tribes of the earth mourning, and angels gathering the elect from one end of heaven to the other. The fig tree teaches the season without the date. This generation will not pass until all these things take place, and then comes the hinge at v. 36, where no one knows the day or the hour, not the angels, not the Son, only the Father. From there the teaching is all readiness: the days of Noah, two in a field and two at a mill, the thief in the night, and two servants left in charge of a household, one of whom decides his master is delayed.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 36 is the seam of the discourse. Before it, signs and a generation; after it, no signs, no timetable, and a coming likened to a burglary and a flood. Signs and no signs cannot describe one event, which is the text's own answer to the charge that Jesus predicted his return within his hearers' lifetime and was wrong. Nor the Son raises the question of how the Son of God can be ignorant of anything, answered from the two natures: according to his deity he knows all things, and the human mind he genuinely took grew and learned. Note that in the same sentence he ranks himself above the whole angelic host and names himself absolutely as the Son. The gathering of the elect from the four winds is the pastoral weight of the section: believers buried at sea, in unmarked ground, under wrong names. Nobody is mislaid.
verseByVerse.examples: Stay awake has been made to mean two things Jesus did not mean. It is not reading the news apocalyptically, since six verses earlier he said no one knows the day; and it is not living in dread, since see that you are not alarmed is a command in this same discourse. Wherever the New Testament describes the church's own attitude to that day the emotion is longing, not terror. What it does mean is testable tonight: is there anything in your week you would need to stop or start if you knew he were coming on Thursday? The picture Jesus himself reaches for is not a watchman scanning the horizon but a steward handing out food at the proper time, which is catering, and which is how the most exalted prophetic discourse in the Gospels chooses to define faithfulness. And the wicked servant's ruin begins in one sentence never said aloud: my master is delayed. He does not deny the master. He postpones him, and the postponement does all the damage the denial would have done.

verseByVerse.quote: "Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sun darkened, moon giving no light, stars falling, the powers of the heavens shaken. Before deciding what this describes, it is worth knowing that the vocabulary is not new. It is quarried wholesale from the prophets, and in every case there is something instructive about what it originally described.

Isaiah says the stars will not give their light and the sun will be dark at its rising — and the oracle is about the fall of Babylon (Isa 13:1, 10). He says the heavens will roll up like a scroll and all their host fall like leaves — and that is about Edom (Isa 34:4-5). Ezekiel says God will cover the heavens and darken their stars, put out the sun with a cloud and stop the moon giving light — about Egypt (Ezek 32:7-8). Joel says the sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great day of the LORD — and Peter stands up at Pentecost and says this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel, of a morning in Jerusalem when nothing happened to the sun at all (Acts 2:16-20).

So the idiom is established and it is consistent: in the prophets, the collapse of the sky is how you say that a world is ending — a kingdom, an order, a settled arrangement of things that everybody assumed was permanent. It is not primarily astronomical language. It is the language of an order coming down.

That does not by itself settle the verse, and Christians who love the Bible read it both ways. Some take it, on the strength of that idiom and the immediately after, of the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the temple order — an event that genuinely was the end of a world. Others take it of the last day, and point out that Peter elsewhere describes the heavenly bodies themselves dissolving. The reading followed here gives the discourse a near horizon and a far one, which allows the words their full weight in both directions without forcing either.

What is not in question is the point the imagery exists to make, and it is the same point on any reading. When he appears, creation does not carry on in the background. The sun and moon are the two great fixed certainties by which every human being has ever told the time, and the prophets keep reaching for them because there is nothing steadier available. At his coming they are described as failing — not because the universe is fragile, but because it is his, and in his presence there is nothing left that can be treated as the background.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light
the host of heaven rotted away

verseByVerse.quote: "Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is drawn almost entirely from Daniel 7, and the detail that matters most is the one easiest to read past. Coming on the clouds of heaven. In the Old Testament, riding the clouds is not something a man does; it is what God does. He makes the clouds his chariot (Ps 104:3); he rides on a swift cloud into Egypt (Isa 19:1). Daniel sees one like a son of man come with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receive dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away (Dan 7:13-14). Jesus takes that vision, applies it to himself, and will repeat it under oath at his trial — which is the moment the high priest tears his robe, because everyone in that room knew exactly what had been claimed.

Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, which is usually read as sheer terror and may be something better. The phrase is Zechariah's, and in Zechariah the mourning is repentance: they look on the one they have pierced, and mourn for him as one mourns for an only child, family by family, each apart (Zech 12:10-12). Matthew has drawn on Zechariah before (21:5). If the allusion is deliberate — and the wording is very close — then the mourning at his appearing is not only the panic of the condemned. It includes the grief of people finally seeing what they did to him.

The sign of the Son of Man has been debated since the second century: some take it as the cross blazing in the sky, others as a standard or an ensign raised for the nations, others simply as the Son of Man himself being the sign. The text does not say, and it is better to admit that than to decorate it.

Then the trumpet, which is a homecoming instrument rather than a military one. Isaiah promised a great trumpet blown so that those who were lost in Assyria and driven out to Egypt would come and worship (Isa 27:13). It is the sound that gathers exiles.

Do these verses describe AD 70 or the final coming? Some read the coming on the clouds as Christ’s vindication in the judgment on Jerusalem, Daniel’s Son of Man coming to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom. The more likely reading is that here the far horizon breaks through. The darkened heavens, the coming seen by all the tribes of the earth, and the gathering of the elect from the whole world go beyond anything that happened in AD 70, and Jesus speaks of his final return in the same terms elsewhere (16:27; 25:31). The seam at verse 36 marks where Jesus turns from the timing of the temple’s fall to the unknown day; but as in the prophets, the two horizons can appear in one view, and these verses are where the far one shows.

And the last clause is the pastoral weight of the whole passage: the angels gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. Consider what that sentence covers. Believers buried at sea, and in unmarked ground, and in war graves with the wrong name on them, or no name. Children whose parents never got a grave to visit. Christians who died alone in places where nobody knew what they were. The scattering has been total, across every continent and every century, and much of it is unrecorded by anybody now living. He sends out angels, and the gathering runs from one end of heaven to the other, and the sentence has no exceptions in it. Nobody is mislaid.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small horticultural point makes the parable work. Most trees in that country are evergreen — the olive, the pine, the cypress hold their leaves through winter and tell you nothing about the season. The fig is bare all winter and among the last to come into leaf, so when a fig puts out its tender shoots there is no ambiguity left: summer really is close. Jesus has chosen the one tree in the landscape whose leafing is a reliable signal.

And there is a quiet irony in it, given where they have just come from. The last fig tree in this Gospel was the one he cursed on the road into the city two days earlier, all leaves and no fruit, withered to the root as a sign against a religion that looked alive (21:19). The same tree that served as the emblem of judgment now serves as the emblem of hope. It is the same tree, read the same way — by its leaves — and it tells the truth both times.

What the parable licenses, and what it forbids, both matter. It licenses reading the signs: when you see all these things, you know that he is near, at the very gates. Eschatological awareness is not a sign of an unbalanced mind; the disciples are expected to watch and to draw a conclusion. But notice what conclusion a fig tree actually supports. Buds tell you the season. They do not tell you the date, or the week, or even reliably the month. No gardener has ever looked at a branch and named a Tuesday.

That is the exact line the church has spent twenty centuries failing to hold. The difference is easy to state and unpopular to keep: the season is late, and the date is unknown. A Christian may say the first with confidence and every generation has been right to. The moment he says the second he has left the parable, contradicted verse 36, and joined a long procession of sincere men whose confident dates are now footnotes.

Is the fig tree Israel, so that the founding of the modern state in 1948 is the sign? Many have been taught so, but Jesus does not say it. He explains his own parable: when you see all these things, the season is near. And every attempt to count from 1948 to a date runs straight into verse 36.

And it is worth asking why the pull toward dates is so strong, because it is not really about prophecy. A date would make the waiting finite. Watching indefinitely for something certain but unscheduled is one of the hardest things a person can be asked to do, and a timetable would convert it into something manageable. Jesus withholds it — not to tantalise, but because the readiness he wants cannot be produced by a deadline. A man who prepares because the date is close is not watchful. He is punctual.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"This generation" is among the most disputed phrases in the chapter. Three main interpretations: (1) the generation alive in Jesus' day — meaning all the signs were fulfilled in AD 70; (2) the race of Israel, which will not cease until these things are fulfilled; (3) the final generation alive at the end. The permanence of Jesus' words — more enduring than heaven and earth — is the bedrock of all prophecy. Whatever the precise referent of "this generation," Jesus' authority over time itself is the ultimate claim. His word does not expire; it outlasts the universe it describes.

But the phrase must be faced more squarely than this, because skeptics have made it their prize exhibit: here, they say, Jesus flatly predicted his second coming within his hearers' lifetime — and the lifetime passed, and he did not come. If that were the meaning, it would be a failed prophecy. But look closely at what "all these things" actually names. Back at verse 3 the disciples asked two questions — when will the temple fall, and what will be the sign of your coming? Most of the discourse to this point has answered the first: the wars and rumours, the false messiahs, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, the unequalled distress. Every one of those "things" did happen within that generation, in the horror of AD 70, roughly forty years later, exactly as he said. That is why the fig-tree parable just before speaks of knowing the season is "near, at the very gates" — the temple's fall was near, and it came. Then notice the hinge at verse 36: "But concerning that day and hour no one knows." The word "but" turns a corner. From here Jesus speaks of his final coming — and of it he says the very opposite: no signs, no timetable, no one knows the day, it breaks in like a thief and like Noah's flood. So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgment on Jerusalem, hedged with signs and set inside that generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way — and it is the reading that best fits the text's own seams — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He told them the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did; he told them his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so. (Some godly interpreters instead take "this generation" as the final generation that sees the end-signs begin; but the simplest answer to the skeptic is the one the text itself supplies at verse 36.)

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unknown day and hour is God's deliberate reserve. Even the Son in his incarnate state of humiliation did not access this knowledge — a window into the genuine limitation of the incarnation (cf. Phil. 2:7). This verse decisively condemns all date-setting: if the angels do not know and the Son in his earthly ministry did not know, no human calculation can determine it. And the reserve is itself the pattern for discipleship: we do not need to know the day, because we are to be ready on all of them. Readiness makes date-knowing unnecessary.

Two things about "nor the Son" deserve more than a passing clause. The first is textual: a reader with a King James Bible will find no such words here at all — "of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." Some manuscripts of Matthew omit the phrase, which is why the older translation does. Nothing whatever is at stake, because the same words stand undisputed in Mark's account of this moment (Mark 13:32), so the saying is certainly the Lord's either way. And the direction of the change is easy to guess: a copyist troubled by the words might quietly drop them, but no copyist ever invented a sentence that made Scripture harder to explain. That is a rule worth carrying — the more difficult reading is usually the original one, because nobody ever made the Bible harder on purpose.

The second is the question the words raise: how can the Son of God not know something? This book has already given the answer at the manger (see on 1:22-23): two natures, one Person — remaining what he was, he became what he was not. According to his deity the Son knows all things, for he is God and knows the Father's mind as his own. According to the true human nature he took, he grew and learned like any of us; Luke says he "increased in wisdom and in stature" (Luke 2:52), and the same man got tired at a well, slept in a boat, and asked who touched him. The not-knowing is real, not a performance — he was not pretending ignorance while secretly consulting his divinity. He had genuinely taken a human mind, and lived within it, for us.

And notice, before anyone uses this verse to demote him, what he is actually doing in the sentence. He names a rising scale of those who do not know: not men, not the angels of heaven, not even the Son — but the Father. He has just placed himself above the entire angelic host and named himself in the same breath as the Father, absolutely, as the Son. That is not the language of a prophet reporting the limits of his information. The verse the skeptic reaches for to make Jesus less than God is a verse in which he calmly ranks himself above every created thing in heaven. But his purpose in saying it was never Christology. He told them what he did not know in order to stop them asking — and to send them back to the only thing that was ever their business, which is the next verse but six: stay awake.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “nor the Son.”

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: "For as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the list of what Noah's generation was doing when the water came, because it is not the list anybody expects. Eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage. Not one sin among them. Four ordinary human goods — meals, drink, weddings, families — the very things Scripture elsewhere commands and blesses.

Genesis does say the earth was filled with violence, and it would have been easy to reach for that. Jesus does not. He selects the domestic items deliberately, because his point is not that they were monsters. It is that they were busy. The thing that destroyed them was not wickedness so much as absorption: a world entirely full of ordinary business, with no room left over for the one announcement that mattered.

And the announcement had been running a long time. Noah built for years, in public, on dry ground, and Peter calls him a herald of righteousness, so there was preaching to go with the hammering. Nobody can say the generation was ambushed. They had the warning, they had the visual aid, they had the eccentric neighbour on the hill, and they had a very long time to think about it. What they also had was a Tuesday that looked exactly like Monday, and that turned out to be enough.

Which puts a question worth answering honestly. What is the strongest argument in your own mind against taking the return of Christ seriously — not as doctrine, which you would affirm, but as something that could interrupt this week? For most people it is not an argument at all. It is the sheer weight of the ordinary: the school run, the deadline, the appointment on Thursday, the fact that nothing like that has ever happened in living memory and today looks very like yesterday. That is precisely the case Noah's neighbours made, and it was the best case available right up until it was not.

Note too that normality is a far more effective anaesthetic than vice. A man in open rebellion against God at least knows the subject exists; he has a position on it. The generation of the flood had no position. They were not opposing the ark. They were planning a wedding, and it was a perfectly good wedding, and the rain began during the reception.

verseByVerse.quote: "and they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two men will be in the field; one will be taken and one left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Unaware until" — the catastrophe of Noah's flood was its surprise to the unprepared, not its violence. The two men in the field present the great division of the parousia: same location, same occupation, radically different destinies. The taking and leaving has been interpreted in opposite directions (taken in judgment, left in mercy; or taken to be with Christ, left in judgment). In the Noahic context, the flood "took" the wicked while Noah was "left" — suggesting the taken may be those taken in judgment. Either reading underscores that the parousia produces ultimate separation where the present age produces apparent equality.

It is worth saying plainly what is at stake here, because almost every modern reader arrives at this verse carrying something: this is the text behind the rapture — the belief that Christ will quietly remove his church from the earth before the tribulation, leaving clothes on car seats and the world to wonder. Many warm-hearted believers hold it, and it is held with real love for Christ and real longing for his appearing. But the verse will not carry it, and the reason is sitting in the sentence immediately before.

Jesus has just said, "as were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man," and then: "they were unaware until the flood came and swept them all away." So ask the obvious question of the analogy Jesus himself supplies. In Noah's day, who was taken? The flood took the wicked. Noah was the one left. If the days of Noah govern this picture — and Jesus says twice that they do — then to be taken is not rescue but judgment, and the popular reading has the verse exactly backwards. Then set it beside what this same chapter has already insisted three times: the coming is like lightning blazing from east to west (v. 27), every tribe on earth sees him (v. 30), and there is a trumpet loud enough to gather the elect from the four winds (v. 31). Whatever else that is, it is not quiet, and it is not secret. A silent disappearance is the one thing Matthew 24 has gone out of its way to rule out.

What of 1 Thessalonians 4, where the living are "caught up… to meet the Lord in the air"? That passage is gloriously true, and it is not secret either — it has a cry of command, an archangel's voice, and the trumpet of God, with the dead rising first. The word Paul uses for that meeting is the ordinary one for a civic welcome: when a king or governor approached a city, the citizens went out to meet him on the road and escorted him back in (it is the same word used when the Roman brothers came out to meet Paul and walked with him into the city, Acts 28:15). That is the picture — not the church evacuated away from the earth, but the church going out to meet her returning King and coming back with him. Read so, Paul and Matthew describe one event, not two, and the church has no need of a secret preliminary coming to make sense of either.

And the pastoral difference is worth naming, because it is not academic. A rapture before the trouble promises that Christians will be spared the worst. Jesus promises something else, and it is sturdier: "the one who endures to the end will be saved" (v. 13), and "for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short" (v. 22). He does not tell his people they will miss the storm. He tells them the storm has been measured, that it has been shortened for their sake, and that he himself will be there at the end of it. That is a harder comfort and a much better one, because it has held for every generation of martyrs who were not spared and were never once abandoned.

verseByVerse.quote: "Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second example is domestic and it is closer than the first. Grinding was women's work done at a hand mill: two circular stones, the upper turned by a wooden handle, and for anything more than a household portion it took two people sitting opposite each other, each reaching for the handle as it came round, for hours at a stretch. So the picture is not merely two people doing the same job. It is two people at the same stone, facing each other, close enough to talk all morning — and at the end of it one is taken and one is left.

Matthew pairs the examples deliberately: two men in a field, two women at a mill. Outdoors and indoors, men and women, farming and food. Between them they cover the working day of an ordinary village, which is the point — no occupation is too obscure for this reckoning and none is exempt from it. Whatever the division at his coming turns on, it does not track any of the categories human beings use to sort each other.

(On whether being taken is rescue or judgment, and what this pair of verses does and does not teach about a rapture, see on vv. 39-40. The point being pressed here is the indistinguishability, not the direction of the taking.)

And that is the thing to sit with. These two women were not a believer and an atheist. They were, so far as anybody watching could tell, the same: same village, same work, same conversation, probably the same synagogue and the same family connections. Nothing visible separated them, and something did. The present age produces apparent equality; his coming produces the real division, and the second bears no reliable relation to the first.

Which cuts in two directions and both are needed. It forbids confidence about anybody else — you cannot read the state of the person beside you at the mill, and a great deal of religious conversation consists of pretending otherwise. And it forbids confidence about yourself on the grounds of proximity. Sitting at the same stone as a believing woman, for years, sharing her work and her talk and her table, did not make the second woman what the first one was. Nearness to the faithful is not the same as faith, and it is the most comfortable substitute there is.
verseByVerse.note: Grinding grain with a hand mill was daily work, often done by two women together.

parallels.desc: the slave girl behind the handmill

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming. But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what part of the night the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake and would not have let his house be broken into."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Stay awake" is the imperative the entire discourse is building toward. The thief illustration shows that the unknown hour is itself the reason for constant readiness: if the hour were known, targeted preparation would be possible; since it is unknown, perpetual watchfulness is the only appropriate posture. This does not mean eschatological anxiety but faithful, present-tense discipleship. So the question the chapter presses is not when is Christ coming, but whether a man is living in a way that would make his arrival welcome rather than terrifying.

Which is the right question, and it deserves a concrete answer, because stay awake has been made to mean several things Jesus plainly did not mean.

It does not mean reading the news apocalyptically. Every generation has believed itself the last, and the ones most certain of it have been most reliably wrong — and Jesus has just said, six verses back, that no one knows the day, not the angels, not the Son in his humanity, only the Father. A Christian who is confident he has worked out the timetable has not achieved deeper insight than his Lord; he has contradicted him.

Nor does it mean living in dread. See that you are not alarmed is a command in this very discourse (v. 6), and the picture Jesus reaches for in the next paragraph is not a man scanning the horizon but a servant handing out food at the proper time — the most ordinary duty imaginable, done on schedule.

That matters for a particular reader. Some people were raised on end-times films and wall charts and can remember being frightened as children by an empty house — and the fear has never entirely gone. It should be said plainly that this is not what the chapter is for. Wherever the New Testament speaks of the church's own attitude to that day, the emotion is longing, not terror: Maranatha, our Lord, come (1 Cor 16:22); a crown laid up for all who have loved his appearing (2 Tim 4:8); the Spirit and the Bride saying Come. If the thought of his return frightens you more than it gladdens you, the remedy is not more information about the timeline.
