Six centuries later the same officials, in the same valley, buy the same kind of ground with blood money, and the city gives it a new name — and Matthew, who knew his Jeremiah, saw the shape of it and told us where to look.

Which is the point worth taking from a technical footnote. The men handling that silver thought they were tidying up an administrative problem. They were walking, step by step, through a prophecy about themselves, and the name of the field is still on the map.
verseByVerse.note: The words are closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, but Matthew names Jeremiah, who bought a field and visited the potter.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said, "You have said so." But when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge has changed. Before Caiaphas the demand was tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God; before Pilate it is are you the King of the Jews? Blasphemy would not interest a Roman governor for a moment. Sedition would end a career if it were ignored. The same man is being accused of a different crime in a different building an hour later, and everyone involved knows why.

Pilate's question has an emphatic pronoun in it — you are the King of the Jews? — and the emphasis is almost certainly contempt. He is looking at a man who has been up all night, beaten, bound, deserted by his followers and handed over by his own nation's leadership. Rome had seen pretenders before; they generally arrived with an army. This one has arrived with rope marks on his wrists.

You have said so. It is the same form of words he gave Judas at the table and Caiaphas in the night — an affirmative, but one that hands the sentence back to the speaker. Yes, and you have no idea what you have just said. Pilate means a rival to Caesar in a troublesome province. The answer is yes to something immeasurably larger, and Pilate will shortly write it on a board and nail it over his head without believing a word of it.

Then the accusations come, and he stops answering. Isaiah had said so: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). It is worth remembering what he was capable of in argument. This is the man who had silenced the Pharisees on tribute, the Sadducees on resurrection, and the lawyers on David's son, all in one afternoon, so completely that no one dared to ask him any more questions (22:46).

He could have taken this court apart. There was no case; the witnesses had already contradicted each other once. He says nothing, and the silence is not helplessness — it is the loudest thing in the room. A man who could clear himself and will not has decided something in advance.
verseByVerse.note: “King of the Jews” was the political charge that mattered to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate cannot understand it. Do you not hear how many things they testify against you? — and the astonishment in the question is genuine. He is offering the prisoner an opening. Say something. Give me one thing I can work with.

Then Matthew's verb: the governor was greatly amazed, thaumazein, the word this Gospel has used of crowds watching a paralytic walk and a storm go quiet. The man who represents the power of Rome in Judea is the one left staring.

And it is worth asking what exactly astonished him, because Pilate had presided over a great many trials. He had seen men beg, bribe, bluster, weep, and inform on their friends. What he had presumably never seen was a defendant with nothing to say — not sullen, not broken, not defiant, simply not interested in the one thing every other prisoner had wanted, which was to get out.

That is the beginning of a pattern in this chapter, and it is the saddest thing about Pilate. He is amazed at the prisoner. He is warned by his wife. He states twice that he can find no fault. He knows the charge is driven by envy. He tries three separate manoeuvres to get the man released. Nobody in the story sees more clearly than Pilate, and nobody does less with what he sees.

Which is worth naming plainly, because it is a modern position as much as an ancient one. A great many people are impressed by Jesus. They find him remarkable, unlike anyone else, impossible to dismiss; they will say so warmly and mean it. Pilate was impressed. He was amazed at him at nine in the morning and signed his death warrant before noon, and the amazement made no difference to the outcome whatever, because admiration is not the same thing as allegiance and never once has been.

One more detail in the Greek is worth having, because it sharpens the silence. Matthew does not merely say Jesus gave no answer; he writes that he did not answer him to a single charge — not one word, to not one accusation. It is emphatic and it is total. Isaiah had described exactly this: like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). What Pilate took for an inexplicable failure of self-preservation was a prophecy being kept in front of him, by a man who had decided in a garden the night before that he was not going to be talked out of this.

parallels.desc: when he suffered, he did not threaten

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The custom is not otherwise attested outside the Gospels, though the practice of a goodwill release at a festival is entirely plausible for a Roman administrator managing a restive province at its most crowded and most nationalistic moment. Pilate keeps a card to play at Passover.

And the man in the cell is described by Matthew as notorious, episemos, literally marked or distinguished — he had a reputation. Mark and Luke fill it in: he was in prison with the rebels who had committed murder in the insurrection (Mk 15:7). So Barabbas is not a burglar. He is a nationalist fighter who has killed for the cause of getting Rome out of Israel, and he is precisely the kind of messiah a great many people in that city were hoping for.

Then his name, which is a sermon by itself. Bar-Abba means son of the father. And there is a genuine textual question worth knowing about, because a number of manuscripts, and some early versions, give his full name as Jesus Barabbas — and Origen in the third century knew the reading and disliked it, thinking it improper that a criminal should share the Lord's name. That kind of squeamishness is exactly how a name gets quietly dropped from a text, which is why many scholars think the longer reading is original.

If it is, then the question Pilate is about to put to the crowd is almost unbearable: which Jesus do you want — Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? Two men with the same name, one the son of a human father and one the Son of the eternal Father, and a crowd is asked to choose.

Whatever the manuscripts finally say, the substance is not in doubt, and it is the clearest picture of substitution in the New Testament. There is one cross and two candidates. Barabbas is guilty and everyone knows it — he has no defence and expects none. He is released, and he is released for exactly one reason: the other man took his place. Every person who has ever been forgiven is standing where Barabbas stood that morning, listening through a cell door to a crowd deciding, and walking out into the sunshine while somebody else is led away to the cross that had his own name on it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “Jesus Barabbas.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate is not stupid and he is not confused. Matthew tells us flatly what he had worked out: he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.

Phthonos is a precise word and it is the right diagnosis. Not fear of blasphemy, not zeal for the law, not concern for public order — envy, the resentment of a man's standing that curdles into a wish to see it destroyed. The crowds had gone after him. The temple courts had emptied of their audience and filled with his. Whatever the theological charges said, the council's motive was that this Galilean had taken something that belonged to them, and Pilate — a professional reader of provincial politics — saw it in about five minutes.

So the offer is shrewd. Give the crowd the choice, and let the crowd's affection for Jesus override the leaders' spite. It has the enormous advantage of costing Pilate nothing: he does not have to acquit anybody or defy anybody; he merely opens a door and lets public opinion carry the prisoner out.

And that is the whole of Pilate's method. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for. He has an innocent man, he knows the accusation is malicious, and he has absolute authority in the province — and instead of releasing him he goes looking for a procedure that will release him without anybody being able to blame Pilate for it. He will try the crowd, then the custom, then a basin of water. All three are ways of arriving at justice without paying for it.

There is no such route, and this chapter exists partly to say so. Doing right when it is unpopular has a price, and the price is the whole point; anything that removes it has also removed the rightness. Pilate wanted a way to be just at no personal cost, and when he could not find one he chose the cost he could bear and let the innocent man pay the other.

And a word about the envy Pilate spotted, since it is the one sin in this chapter that most readers will have committed this month. Envy never arrives announcing itself. Not one of those priests woke up thinking he wanted the Galilean dead because the crowds preferred him; each of them had a reason, and the reasons were theological, and they would have been genuinely offended to hear the charge. That is how it works. Envy borrows the language of principle, because it cannot survive being named. The test is simple and unpleasant: when a person doing your kind of work is praised, do the objections you raise to his methods occur to you before or after the praise?

verseByVerse.quote: Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the trial, a note arrives. Somebody has to carry it through the praetorium and put it into the governor's hand while he is sitting on the judgment seat, which means his wife thought this urgent enough to interrupt a capital case in public.

Her message is short and it contains the only unambiguous verdict anyone gives in the chapter: have nothing to do with that righteous man. Not innocent of this particular charge — righteous, dikaios. The council would not say it. Pilate never quite says it. Judas said it and threw the money at the priests. A Gentile woman who has never met him says it from her own bedroom on the strength of a dream.

And Matthew, of all the evangelists, is the one who would notice. Open his Gospel at the beginning: an angel warns Joseph in a dream to take the child (1:20); the magi are warned in a dream not to go back to Herod (2:12); Joseph is warned in a dream to flee to Egypt, and again to come home (2:13, 19). Matthew's account of the birth is full of God protecting his Son by warning people in their sleep — including foreigners.

Now, at the end of the same Gospel, one last dream, one last warning, one last foreigner. The bookend is exact and the outcome is opposite. Every warning at the beginning was heeded and the child lived. This one is set aside, and the man dies.

It is worth sitting with what that arrangement says about God. He is under no obligation to warn Pilate. The trial is a formality, the outcome is fixed, the prophecies require the death — and heaven still sends word into the governor's house, at the last possible hour, through the one person who might reach him. God will not have it said that no one told him. Even in the hour of the greatest crime ever committed, the mercy is still working, still knocking, still going to the trouble of a dream at dawn for a man who will wash his hands and do it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. Only Matthew records the message from Pilate’s wife.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor again said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release for you?" And they said, "Barabbas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd. Matthew is careful here and the care matters. The crowd does not arrive with a demand; it is worked. The verb is the one for winning somebody over by argument and pressure, and it takes time and effort and people moving through a gathering having quiet conversations.

So consider who is actually standing in that courtyard at daybreak. It is not the nation of Israel, and it is not the Passover pilgrim crowd — most of Jerusalem is asleep or preparing for the feast, and the great majority of Jews alive that morning were scattered across the empire and had never heard of the case. This is a body of people assembled at short notice, at dawn, outside the governor's residence, by men with a specific outcome in mind. Rented crowds have been a standard instrument of politics in every century since.

That has to be said plainly, because this scene has been pressed into service for centuries as a charge against a whole people, and Christians have used it to do great harm. There is no doctrine of collective guilt available here. The man on trial is a Jew; his mother is a Jew; every apostle is a Jew; the women at the cross are Jews; Joseph who buries him is a Jew; the author of this Gospel is a Jew; and within weeks three thousand Jews in this same city will believe and be baptised. A managed crowd at a dawn hearing is not a people, and anyone who has read this chapter as a warrant for contempt has read it exactly backwards.

What the scene does teach is something about crowds generally, and it is not comfortable for any of us. These were not monsters. Five days earlier a crowd in this city had spread cloaks on the road for him and shouted Hosanna; some of the same people may well have been in both. What changed was not the evidence but the direction of the pressure and the identity of the men doing the talking.

Which is why a Christian should be permanently suspicious of the safety of numbers. The instinct to go with the room is the strongest social force there is, and it does not feel like cowardice while it is happening — it feels like consensus, and it feels like being sensible, and it can move a hundred ordinary people from Hosanna to Crucify inside a week.

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said, "Let him be crucified!" And he said, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Let him be crucified!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? Pilate asks it as a procedural question by a man who has run out of manoeuvres, and it is the question the whole Gospel has been driving toward. He is not asking what is true about Jesus. He is asking what he is going to do about him, which is the harder question and the only one that ever gets anybody anywhere.

Notice that the one option not available to him is the one most people assume they have. He cannot leave the prisoner in the cell and think about it. There is a man in front of him who must be either released or executed before the feast begins, and doing nothing is a decision with a body attached. Pilate would have given a great deal for a third door, and there was not one.

Then his last flicker of conscience: Why? What evil has he done? It is the right question, asked by the right official, in the right forum, and it is the only genuinely judicial sentence spoken in the entire proceeding. Nobody answers it. Matthew does not record a single charge in reply — they shouted all the more. That is the answer, and it is the answer a crowd gives when it has no answer: not a better argument but a louder one.

The escalation is worth watching because it is the ordinary physics of a mob. First a verdict — let him be crucified. Then a question they cannot meet. Then the same verdict at greater volume. No new evidence has entered the courtyard and nobody's mind has changed; the noise is doing the work that reasons cannot. Anyone who has watched a public argument in our own day, where volume and repetition settle what evidence never will, has seen this precise mechanism at work in a milder form.

And Pilate's question is still open. It cannot be handed back to a crowd, and it cannot be deferred indefinitely, and there is no neutral answer to it — because the choice is not between accepting him and leaving him alone. It is between accepting him and sending him away, and Pilate found out that morning that sending him away is also something you have done.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves." And all the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The basin is theatre, and it is borrowed theatre. Washing the hands to disclaim responsibility for blood is a Jewish rite, not a Roman one: when a body was found in open country and the killer unknown, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands over a heifer and said our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed (Deut 21:6-7). Pilate, who cares nothing for the law of Moses, performs a ceremony from it in front of a Jewish crowd, because it is the gesture they will understand.

And it settles nothing. The rite in Deuteronomy is for men who genuinely did not do it and genuinely do not know who did. Pilate knows exactly who is doing this, because he is: he holds the authority, he has heard the case, he has stated twice that he finds no fault, and in the next verse he signs the order. A judge cannot become a bystander by getting his hands wet. I am innocent of this man's blood is the only demonstrably false statement anybody makes in the trial.

Then the crowd's answer, and it must be handled with great care, because these words have been quoted over centuries to justify appalling cruelty against Jewish people — pogroms, expulsions, ghettos, and worse. That use of this verse is not a regrettable excess. It is a flat contradiction of the New Testament, and it should be said so plainly that no reader is left in any doubt.

Consider what the sentence actually is. It is a shout from a managed crowd in a courtyard at dawn (see on vv. 20-21), not a legal instrument, and no crowd on earth has the authority to bind its children, still less the unborn generations of a whole people. Scripture rules the principle out in terms: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek 18:20). And the New Testament nowhere charges the Jewish people with the death of Christ. It charges the human race, and it charges the reader. Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd they crucified him and then baptises three thousand of them the same day. Paul, a Jew, writes that the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, and that his heart's desire and prayer for his own people is their salvation.

And now the thing that turns the verse inside out, which is why a Christian should be the last person on earth to use it as a weapon. They said his blood be on us — and his blood coming down on a person is the best thing that can happen to anyone alive. Seven weeks later Peter stood up in that city and preached to people who had been in that crowd, and three thousand of them went down into the water; and the blood they had called down on their own heads landed on them exactly as they had asked, and it did not condemn them, it washed them. Nobody, shouting in a courtyard, ever asked for something better than they knew. The curse they pronounced on themselves is, word for word, the prayer of every Christian who has ever come to the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Washing the hands was a public declaration of innocence in a death.

parallels.desc: the elders wash their hands over the heifer
I wash my hands in innocence
to bring this man’s blood upon us

verseByVerse.quote: Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two clauses, and Matthew will not linger on either. He released for them Barabbas — the guilty man walks. Having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified — the innocent man is flogged and handed over. Substitution is not a doctrine imposed on this verse by later theologians; it is the shape of the sentence.

The flogging was not a beating. The Roman flagellum was a short whip of several leather thongs weighted with pieces of bone or metal, laid on a man stripped and tied to a post. Roman scourging had no fixed limit of strokes as Jewish law did. Eusebius, quoting an early account of the martyrs of Smyrna, says the victims' veins and inward organs were laid bare; the historians record that men sometimes died under it before ever reaching a cross. It was administered before crucifixion precisely to shorten the ordeal by weakening the condemned.

Matthew gives it a participle. Not a sentence, not a paragraph — a subordinate clause on the way to something else. The restraint of all four Gospels here is remarkable and it is deliberate. They are not writing to harrow the reader's feelings, and there is a kind of devotion that dwells on the physical horror until the emotion produced becomes the point. The evangelists refuse it. What they want understood is not chiefly how much it hurt but what it accomplished.

Which is where Isaiah has been waiting for seven hundred years: he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5). The older English Bibles said stripes — the marks left by a lash. Isaiah saw the scourging centuries before Pilate ordered it, and he saw whose it was, and he wrote the pronoun: our.

So keep the two clauses of this verse side by side, because they belong together and the gospel lives in the gap between them. A convicted murderer went home to his own street that afternoon a free man, and never had to explain why, and did nothing whatever to earn it. Down the corridor, the man who had taken his place was being tied to a post. That is not an illustration of the atonement. On that Friday it was the plain municipal record of what happened, and it is the reason the word gospel means news rather than advice.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They take him inside, and Matthew notes the numbers: they gathered the whole battalion — the cohort, on paper up to six hundred men, though the detachment on duty would have been smaller. Whatever the exact figure, the point stands. Word has gone round the barracks that there is something worth watching in the courtyard, and the off-duty soldiers come out to see.

This is the part of the Passion that is easiest to skip and hardest to explain. It serves no judicial purpose whatever. The verdict is given, the execution detail is forming, and nothing that happens in this courtyard advances the case by a minute. It is done because they felt like it, and because it was funny, and because he could not stop them.

They strip him — the second stripping of the day, and not the last. And then the scarlet robe, which was almost certainly a soldier's own cloak, the faded red military cape that every man in that yard was wearing. Somebody took his off and put it round the prisoner's shoulders, and the joke was that it looked near enough to imperial purple to pass.

That is worth pausing over, because of what it says about the appetite being fed. Boredom in an occupying garrison, a prisoner who will be dead by evening, an afternoon to fill, and a man available who cannot retaliate — and out of those ordinary ingredients comes a piece of cruelty that is entirely gratuitous. Nobody in that courtyard was a monster. They were soldiers with an hour free.

And the deepest irony of the Passion is running underneath the whole scene. Every single element of the mockery is true. The robe is a real coronation robe, on a real King. In a few hours a sign will be nailed over his head naming his title, in three languages, by order of the governor. They are dressing him for a throne while thinking they are dressing him for a laugh, and the only person in the courtyard who knows what is actually being enacted is the man in the cloak.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. A soldier’s red cloak served as a mock royal robe.

verseByVerse.quote: and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crown was not a costume piece. Thorn scrub grows everywhere in that country and the spines on some of it are two or three inches long; somebody went out, cut a handful, twisted it into a circle, and pressed it down. It was the last item needed to complete the outfit.

And of all the things a soldier could have grabbed for a joke, this one reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the ground was cursed for man's sake the sentence was thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Gen 3:18). Thorns are the visible signature of a world under judgment — the thing that grows where nothing was planted, in every garden anyone has ever tried to keep. The curse of the ground was gathered into a circle and pushed onto the head of the man who came to carry the curse away, by soldiers who thought they were being witty.

Then the reed in his right hand — a mock sceptre, the hand of authority given a piece of grass. And the kneeling, which is the most extraordinary detail in the scene, because genuflection before a king was a real act with a real form, and they performed it correctly in order to make it ridiculous. Hail, King of the Jews is a parody of Ave, Caesar.

They were rehearsing. One day every knee in heaven and on earth and under the earth will bend at this name, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). The first knees ever bent to the crowned Christ belonged to a Roman execution detail in a barracks yard, and they did it as a joke, and they were not wrong about the posture — only about the reason.

And then the spitting, and the reed taken back out of his hand and used to strike him on the head, which drove the thorns further in. It is worth being clear who is receiving this. The man being spat at by a bored garrison is the one who holds their hearts beating in his hand; a word from him and the courtyard would have been empty and silent. He had told Peter in the garden a few hours earlier that he could ask his Father for twelve legions of angels. The Roman cohort in that yard was a tenth of a legion at the very most, and it was playing games with the one person present who could have ended it, and who had already decided not to.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The game finishes the way such things do — abruptly, because the shift has started. They take the cloak back. Somebody folds it and returns it to its owner, and the man who was Caesar for ten minutes is put back into his own clothes.

The detail is practical: a condemned man was normally walked to execution in his own clothing so the crowd could see who was being crucified, and the garments came off again at the site. So he is dressed twice and stripped three times in a single morning — once for the scourging, once for the joke, and once at Golgotha. Whatever else the day did to him, it kept taking his clothes.

And then six words that carry the whole distance: led him away to crucify him. Matthew has been building to this since the sixteenth chapter, when Jesus first told them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things and be killed. He has said it three times. Every time, the disciples argued or misunderstood or fell asleep.

What should be held onto here is that not one step of this walk is being forced on him. He chose it in the garden, out loud, twice, with his face on the ground — not as I will, but as you will. He could have stayed in Galilee. He could have accepted the crowd's crown after the loaves. He could have answered Pilate and walked out. At every junction there was a door standing open and he did not take it.

So the little procession that leaves the praetorium is not a man being swept along by events larger than himself. It is the most deliberate walk in the history of the world, taken by the only person on the road who knew exactly where it ended and exactly why he was going — and the reason he kept walking was that the people he was doing it for could not have walked it themselves.

And keep an eye on the clothes he is wearing out of that gate, because they have four verses left. They were taken from him for the flogging and given back; put on for the walk so the crowd could see who was being executed; and at the top of the hill they will come off for the last time and be divided among the execution party, who will throw dice for the best piece. He walks to Golgotha dressed in the last thing he owns.

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in what is now Libya, with a large and long-established Jewish population. Simon may have come the best part of a thousand miles for Passover, or may have lived in Jerusalem among the Cyrenian Jews. He is walking into the city on the morning of the feast when a soldier picks him out of the crowd.

The word for what happened to him is angareuo, a technical term for the right of requisition: a Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry his kit for a distance, and the resentment it caused was universal. Matthew's readers knew the word well, and they had met it before in this Gospel — in the Sermon on the Mount, from the mouth of the man now being led up the road: if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two (5:41).

So the sentence Jesus preached about being conscripted is now applied to a stranger, in order to carry the cross Jesus can no longer carry himself. That he could not carry it is itself a piece of evidence about what the scourging had done to him; Roman practice was for the condemned to carry the crossbeam, and they only substituted a bystander when the prisoner was failing and they wanted him alive at the site.

Simon appears in three Gospels and Mark adds a detail he expects his readers to recognise: he is the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mk 15:21), naming two men as though the church already knew them. And when Paul sends greetings to Rome he includes Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Rom 16:13). It cannot be proved that this is the same family. It is a very natural reading, and if it is right, then the woman who mothered the apostle Paul was married to the man who carried the cross.

Which is worth holding onto, because Simon did not volunteer for any of this. He was seized. Whatever he had planned for that morning was ruined by a soldier's hand on his shoulder, and he walked up the hill under a piece of timber that was not his, for a condemned man he had never met, in front of a crowd, at the worst possible moment. It was, by any ordinary reckoning, a disaster of a day. It is also the only reason anybody has ever heard of him, and it appears to have put his sons in the church and his family in the Scriptures.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Mark adds that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Golgotha is Aramaic for skull, and Matthew translates it for readers who would not know. The name most likely came from the shape of the outcrop rather than from bones lying about — Jewish burial customs make the second unlikely. It was outside the wall and beside a road, because the entire point of crucifixion was that people should see it on their way past. The writer of Hebrews makes something of that location: he suffered outside the gate, where the bodies of the sin offerings were burned (Heb 13:11-12).

Then the drink. Wine mixed with gall — Mark says myrrh — was a rough narcotic, and Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it to men going to execution as an act of mercy, on the strength of the proverb about giving strong drink to one who is perishing (Prov 31:6). It was the one kindness available on that road, and Matthew does not say who offered it.

When he tasted it, he would not drink it. Both halves matter. He tasted it, so he knew what it was and what it would do — the refusal is informed. And he refused it, which is the more remarkable given that he had every reason to take it and no one would have thought less of him for it.

The reason is in the garden. Twice that night he had prayed about a cup, and twice he had said that if it could not pass, he would drink it. He was not going to numb the cup he had agreed to drink. And there is a further note, easy to miss: at the table a few hours earlier he had told them he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drank it new with them in his Father's kingdom (26:29). He keeps that too. The next wine offered him is declined.

So the whole of it was borne awake. Everything that follows — six hours on the wood, the mockery, the darkness, the cry — was undergone by a man in full possession of his senses, because he had turned down the only anaesthetic on offer. There is a kind of love that will not take the edge off the thing it has agreed to carry, and this is the only recorded instance of it in the history of the world.
verseByVerse.note: Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” The drink was probably a drugged wine to dull pain; Jesus refused it.

parallels.desc: they gave me poison for food

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crucified him. Matthew does not describe it. Neither does Mark, Luke, or John. Four writers who were there or knew those who were give the central event of human history a subordinate clause, because their first readers needed no explanation whatever — and a modern reader needs it badly, since almost nothing about the word survives in ordinary speech.

Crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels, and the worst class of criminals; Roman law exempted citizens from it. The condemned was stripped naked, part of the humiliation, and fastened to the wood — nailed through the wrists, since the hands alone will not carry a body's weight, with the arms extended and slightly raised, and a nail driven through the feet onto a small block.

The design was engineered for duration. Hanging from outstretched arms makes exhaling possible and inhaling nearly impossible; to take a breath the victim had to push upward against the nail through his feet, lift the body a few inches, fill the lungs, and sag back down. Every breath was bought at that price, and the cycle could go on for hours or days. Death came by asphyxiation, exhaustion, or blood loss. When the Romans wanted to end it quickly — as they would that evening, before the Sabbath (Jn 19:31-32) — they broke the legs, so that the man could no longer push up, and it was over in minutes.

And it was public by design: a naked body at eye level beside a road, for as long as it took. Cicero called it the most cruel and horrifying of punishments and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. That the apostles went out and preached a crucified Messiah was therefore not merely a theological difficulty but a social obscenity — which is exactly what Paul meant by calling it a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks (1 Cor 1:23). Nobody invents a founder who died this way.

Then, while that is happening above them, the detail sit down and gamble for his clothes. A crucified man's garments were the perquisite of the execution party, and they divide them and throw dice for the last piece. It is written a thousand years earlier, in the psalm he will quote from the cross in a few hours: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (Ps 22:18). Four soldiers playing a game to pass a slow afternoon are, without the faintest idea of it, performing a line of Scripture.

Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. It is the flattest sentence in the chapter and one of the most terrible. This was a shift. They had done it before and would do it again next week; there was nothing to do now but wait for the man to die, so they sat in the shade with the dice and their lunch. The most significant six hours in the history of the universe were, to the men closest to it, a slow day at work. Some of the greatest things God has ever done have looked, to everyone standing nearby, like nothing much happening.
verseByVerse.note: The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And over his head they put the charge against him, which read: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews." Then two robbers were crucified with him, one on the right and one on the left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The board over his head is the titulus, the standard Roman practice of publishing the charge above the condemned so that passers-by would know what this man had done and take the lesson. Every crucifixion had one. Barabbas would have had one.

And the charge against Jesus of Nazareth, posted by the government of the greatest empire on earth, was this: This is Jesus, the King of the Jews. Nothing about blasphemy, nothing about the temple, nothing about the Sabbath. The only crime the authorities could state in writing was that he was the King.

The chief priests saw the problem immediately and asked Pilate to change it to say he claimed to be — and Pilate, who had given way on everything that morning, chose this of all things to be immovable about: what I have written I have written (Jn 19:22). A weak man's one act of stubbornness in the whole affair, and it fixed the truth over the cross in three languages where nobody could take it down.

Then the two robbers, one on either side — the word is lestai, which is the term used of brigands and insurgents rather than petty thieves, and they may well have been associates of Barabbas, in which case the middle cross was built for him.

Isaiah had put it in the same passage as the stripes: he was numbered with the transgressors (Isa 53:12). Not near them. Numbered with them — counted in, listed on the same docket, given the central position that the crowd would read as the worst of the three. That is precisely what the whole day was for. He was not executed alongside sinners by accident of scheduling; he was placed among them because he had agreed to be counted as one of them, which is the only way any of them could be counted as righteous.

John adds that the notice was written in three languages — Aramaic for the people of the land, Latin for the government, Greek for everybody else in the empire (Jn 19:20). Whatever Pilate intended by that, the effect is worth naming. The first public proclamation in writing that Jesus of Nazareth is King went up in the three languages of the known world, at the expense of the Roman state, over the head of a dying man, composed by a governor who did not believe a word of it and posted by soldiers who could not read most of it. The church would spend the next three centuries saying the same sentence and being killed for it. Rome said it first, by accident, in triplicate.
verseByVerse.note: The charge was written on a board for all to read. The “robbers” may have been insurgents.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mockery comes in three waves and Matthew records them in order of respectability: first the passers-by, then the clergy, then the men dying beside him. It begins with ordinary people on their way somewhere else.

Wagging their heads is a quotation before it is a gesture: all who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Ps 22:7). This is the second line of that psalm to be enacted at the cross in this chapter, and nobody doing it has the faintest idea. The soldiers played out verse 18 with their dice; the crowd is now playing out verse 7 with their necks.

Their taunt reaches back to the false witnesses of the night before, who had garbled his saying about the temple (26:61). Note what has happened to it: a distorted quotation from a collapsed prosecution has become street property within twelve hours. A charge does not have to survive cross-examination to survive in the mouths of a crowd, and this one is being shouted at a dying man by people who could not have said where they heard it.

But the opening words are the ones to notice: if you are the Son of God. Matthew has printed that sentence once before, in the fourth chapter, in the wilderness, from the mouth of the devil — if you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread; if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down (4:3, 6). Same opening, same logic, same offer: use the power, prove the title, take the shortcut, come down.

So the last temptation is the first temptation, arriving three years later through human voices, and it is exactly as reasonable as it was the first time and exactly as deadly. What the tempter wanted in the desert and the crowd wants at Golgotha is a Son of God who will not suffer. And the answer given is the same answer, only now it is not spoken but endured: he stays. The proof of his Sonship, which the mockers demanded and would not have accepted, is the very thing they were watching. He was never more evidently the Son of God than in the hours he refused to act like it.

parallels.desc: “If you are the Son of God”

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests, with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. He is the King of Israel; let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second wave is the clergy — chief priests, scribes and elders, the whole leadership of the nation, standing at a public execution to jeer at a dying man. It is worth registering how far a religion has to have gone for that to seem appropriate on the morning of Passover, and worth remembering that these were the most scrupulous men in Jerusalem, who would not enter the governor's headquarters for fear of defilement (Jn 18:28) and had no scruple whatever about this.

And notice they no longer address him. The passers-by shouted you; the priests talk about him in the third person, to each other, over his head — which is its own kind of contempt. He has stopped being a person in the conversation.

Then the sentence: He saved others; he cannot save himself. It may be the most accidentally accurate thing ever said about Jesus Christ. Every word is true and the meaning they intend is the opposite of the meaning it carries.

He saved others — a concession, dropped in as sarcasm, and it is an admission from the hostile witnesses that the works were real. They never denied the miracles; even at Golgotha, with nothing left to lose, the case against him is not that he did nothing but that he cannot do it now. And he cannot save himself is true as well, though not for the reason they think. Not a failure of power — he had told Peter in the garden about twelve legions. A refusal, and a necessity built into the thing he came to do. A substitute who steps out from under the weight is not a substitute. He could have saved himself or he could have saved them; there was never a version of the afternoon in which he did both.

Their offer — let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him — is worth taking at face value for a moment, because it is the demand every generation makes. Give us a sign we cannot explain away and we will believe. They would not. In three days he did something considerably harder than climbing down from a cross, and the response of these same men was to pay the guards to say the body was stolen (28:12-13). The problem was never the quantity of evidence. It has never once been the quantity of evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" And the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests' last taunt is not merely similar to Psalm 22; it is Psalm 22, almost word for word: He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him (Ps 22:8). The theological leadership of Israel, standing at the foot of the cross and reaching for the cruellest thing they can think of to say, produce a verbatim line of Scripture written for this occasion a thousand years earlier.

They knew that psalm. They had chanted it. And they could not hear themselves saying it, which is the strangest fact in a strange morning: men who had given their lives to the study of the sacred text stood in front of its fulfilment quoting it at him as an insult. There is no sharper illustration anywhere of the difference between knowing the Bible and understanding it.

Their reasoning is straightforward and it is the argument of Job's friends, and of a great many people since: if God delighted in him, God would rescue him; God has not rescued him; therefore God does not delight in him. The logic is clean and the conclusion is false, and the reason it is false is the whole of the Christian gospel. At that moment the Father's delight in the Son was total, and the Son was exactly where the Father's delight had sent him. Abandonment to the enemy's hands is not evidence of the Father's displeasure. It was, here, the proof of the plan.

That is worth holding onto by anyone who has done the same arithmetic about his own life. If God loved me, this would not be happening; it is happening; therefore. The finest man who ever lived was the most loved man who ever lived, and he was hanging on a cross while the clergy explained to the crowd that his situation proved otherwise.

Then the last line, and it is the bottom of the descent: the robbers who were crucified with him also reviled him in the same way. Two men in identical agony, with minutes of life left and nothing whatever to gain, spent some of it mocking the man beside them. Matthew records the universal rejection — passers-by, priests, and the dying — because he wants the darkness total before anything else is said. Luke will tell us that before the afternoon was over one of those two turned his head and asked to be remembered, and was in paradise that day. But Matthew leaves it here. Every human voice at Golgotha is against him, and he is dying for the owners of every one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Luke records that one of the two later repented.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–66 — The Death, the Burial, and the Guard at the Tomb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darkness covers the land from noon until three. Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, is offered sour wine, shouts once more and yields up his spirit. The temple curtain tears from top to bottom, the earth shakes, tombs open, and the centurion who has watched it all confesses him Son of God. The women who had followed from Galilee look on; Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for the body and buries it in his own new tomb; two Marys sit opposite it. On the Sabbath the council persuades Pilate to seal the stone and post a guard.
verseByVerse.theology: The cry of dereliction is the theological centre of the atonement, and two things must be held together or one of them will be lost. He is quoting — the opening line of Psalm 22, which names the whole psalm, a psalm that describes pierced hands and feet and garments divided by lot, and which ends not in darkness but in vindication and a worldwide people and the words he has done it. And he is not merely reciting: the forsakenness is real, for he was made sin for us and became a curse for us. Not the tearing apart of the Trinity — the Father never stopped loving the Son — but the full judicial weight of standing in the place of the guilty. He lost the sight of his Father's face without ever losing his grip on his Father's character, and he still said my God.
verseByVerse.examples: The curtain is the pastoral centre of this section. It hung across the way into the Most Holy Place, and its entire function was distance: one man, once a year, with blood, and no one else ever. At three in the afternoon, with no hand near it, it tore from the top down. So the barrier was not removed by anyone becoming fit to pass it; it was removed by a death, from God's side, downward, before the reader did anything at all. Anyone who has been waiting until he is clean enough to pray has been waiting for something that was dealt with on a Friday afternoon. And note who fills the rest of the section: the women who stayed when every apostle had run, and a member of the condemning council who found his courage on the one evening when there was nothing left to gain by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?" that is, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Midday to mid-afternoon — three hours of darkness, as at the Egyptian plague (Exod. 10:22), signaling judgment and the withdrawal of the Creator's blessing from creation. Then the cry: Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic, shouted with a loud voice — not a whisper of despair but a full-voiced cry of anguished prayer to God. This is the cry of dereliction, the most theologically weighty sentence in the Gospels. The Son, bearing the sin of the world (2 Cor. 5:21), experiences the Godforsakenness that is the just consequence of sin. The Father has not ceased to love the Son, but the Son bearing sin experiences the full weight of divine judgment upon it. This moment is the price of our forgiveness: not our Godforsakenness, but his.

Two things more must be said about this cry, because it is the verse people ask about above all others in the chapter. The first is that Jesus is quoting, and quoting an opening line. There were no chapter and verse numbers in his world; a text was named by the words it began with, the way we say "our Father" and mean the whole prayer. To cry out the first line of Psalm 22 in the hearing of people who knew the Psalter by heart was to put the entire psalm on the table.

And look at what is in it. Bones out of joint, a tongue sticking to the jaws, hands and feet pierced, bystanders staring and gloating, garments divided and lots cast for the clothing — written a thousand years before anyone in Jerusalem had seen a Roman cross. Matthew has already quoted three pieces of it in this very chapter (vv. 35, 39, 43) without needing to tell you why. In his extremity the Son reaches for the one psalm in Scripture that describes, line by line, what is being done to him.

Then see how that psalm ends. Not in darkness. "He has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him" (Ps 22:24). "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD" (v. 27). And the very last words of it, of a work done for a people not yet born: he has done it (v. 31) — which is remarkably close to what John records him saying moments later, when it was over: it is finished.

But the second thing must be said too, or the first will be misused. Some have taken the whole-psalm point to mean that Jesus was not truly forsaken at all, only reciting a hopeful poem to steady himself. That will not stand. The darkness was real, the cry was a real cry, and the New Testament means what it says when it tells us he was made sin for us and became a curse for us (2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13). He bore the judicial abandonment that our sin deserved — not the tearing apart of the Trinity, for the Father never stopped loving the Son and the Son never stopped being God, but the full weight of what it is to stand in the place of the guilty and receive what they had earned. Both are true at once: he entered a real forsakenness, and he entered it holding the psalm that ends in vindication. He lost the sight of his Father's face without ever losing his grip on his Father's character.

Was the darkness an eclipse? It cannot have been: Passover fell at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible, and an eclipse lasts minutes, not three hours. It was a sign from God, the judgment Amos foretold: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9).

Which leaves one small word that has carried more comfort than most sermons. Twice in that sentence he says my. My God, my God. He does not say "God, why have you abandoned me" — he says my God, and he says it to the very One he cannot feel. If you have ever prayed in the dark and got nothing back, and wondered whether the silence proved your faith had failed — it does not. That prayer is not the sound of faith collapsing. It is the sound of faith with everything else stripped off it, still addressing God as its own. He prayed it first, in a worse darkness than yours, and he prayed it so that you would never have to pray it alone.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders, hearing it, said, "This man is calling Elijah." And one of them at once ran and took a sponge, filled it with sour wine, and put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man is calling Elijah. The mishearing is easy enough — Eli sounds like the beginning of Eliyahu — and it may have been genuine confusion among soldiers and bystanders with little Aramaic, or it may have been one more piece of mockery. Either way it shows what was in the popular mind: Elijah was expected to come before the day of the LORD (Mal 4:5), and popular piety had him arriving to rescue the righteous in extremity.

They are looking for the wrong rescuer, and Matthew has already told his readers so. Coming down that mountain a few chapters back, Jesus had said plainly that Elijah had come already and they had not recognised him, and the disciples understood that he spoke of John the Baptist (17:12-13). John had been dead for months, executed at a birthday party. The help these bystanders are waiting for came, preached, and was beheaded, and they had not noticed.

Then someone runs for a sponge. Sour wine — posca, cheap vinegar-wine cut with water — was the standard drink of the Roman army; there would have been a jar of it on site for the execution detail. A reed is long enough to reach a man on a cross, which tells you the height of the thing: not far above the ground, near enough for the mockery to be conversational.

And that too is written: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (Ps 69:21). It is the fourth line of a psalm enacted at Golgotha in this chapter without a single participant knowing it.

The gesture itself is genuinely ambiguous and the Gospels leave it so. It may be a rough kindness — a dying man says he is thirsty and a soldier does the one thing available. It may be a way of keeping him conscious for the entertainment of seeing whether Elijah turns up. Very possibly it was both, in the same man, in the same movement; people are like that. What is certain is that this is the last thing any human being does for Jesus Christ before he dies: someone holds up a sponge of army vinegar on a stick, and it is more than anyone else in the crowd thought of doing.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: But the others said, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save him. The sentence is worth reading slowly, because of the posture it describes. They are not hostile here, exactly. They are interested.

Somebody has stepped forward with a sponge and the rest tell him to stop, because they would rather find out how it ends. A man is dying in front of them and it has become absorbing — and the small mercy of a drink is set aside so as not to interfere with the experiment.

That is a colder thing than the jeering of the priests, and more recognisable. Contempt at least engages; this is spectatorship. They have got as close to the cross as it is possible to stand, they can see everything, they are giving it their full attention, and they are waiting to see whether anything interesting happens.

And it is possible to be in exactly that position for years. A person can attend, listen attentively, follow the argument, enjoy the music, find the whole thing genuinely fascinating, and be waiting the entire time to see whether something will happen that settles it — while the thing that settles it is going on in front of him and has been all along. Proximity is not faith. Interest is not faith. The men closest to the cross on the day it happened were watching to see whether God would do something, and God was doing it.

They were also, of course, wrong about the rescue. They were watching for someone to come and take him down, and what was actually being accomplished in those minutes was a rescue on a scale that would have emptied the vocabulary of everyone present. No one came to save him. That was the point. He was saving them.

And it is worth adding, before anyone settles too comfortably into judging these bystanders, that one man on that hill was in exactly their position at noon and in a completely different one by three o'clock. The centurion had the same view, the same job, and considerably more blood on his hands, and he had watched with professional detachment for six hours. Standing where the spectators stood is not a verdict on anybody. Some of the people watching that afternoon out of idle curiosity went home changed, and the difference was not in the quality of their attention. It was in what God did with what they were looking at.

parallels.desc: Elijah before the day of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details, and both are unusual enough that they are the reason a Roman centurion said what he said a few verses later.

First, the loud cry. Death by crucifixion is death by exhaustion and asphyxiation; a man in his last minutes cannot get enough breath to speak, let alone shout. Every word Jesus spoke from the cross had to be bought by pushing up on the nail through his feet to fill his lungs. Executioners were accustomed to the voice failing hours before the end. This one shouted with his last breath — John tells us what the shout was: it is finished, one word in Greek, tetelestai, the word written across a bill that has been paid in full.

Second, the verb Matthew chooses for the death itself. Not he died and not he expired but he yielded up his spirit — aphiemi, to let go, to release, to send away. It is an active verb with Jesus as its subject. Luke has him commit his spirit to the Father; John says he handed it over. All three reach for language of a deliberate act rather than a body giving out.

Which is precisely what he had said would happen, in advance and in public: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again (Jn 10:18). The Romans did not take his life. They provided the occasion; he chose the moment.

Hold that beside everything else in the chapter and it reorders the whole scene. He has been handed over, bound, condemned, flogged, mocked, stripped, nailed and jeered at, and at every point he has appeared to be the one thing happening to everybody else's decisions. And the last act of the day is his. The centurion, who had watched a great many men die and had never seen one do it like that, drew the only conclusion available to him.

Note the small word again. This is the second loud cry from the cross; the first was the words of Psalm 22 at the ninth hour, four verses back. So the three hours of darkness are bracketed by two shouts — one that names the forsakenness, and one that announces the work finished. Between them lies whatever happened in the dark that Scripture does not describe. He went into it crying out a question and came out of it declaring a completed thing, and the interval belongs to the Father and the Son alone.

parallels.desc: I lay it down of my own accord

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. The tombs also were opened. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Several signs testify to the significance of Jesus' death. The temple curtain — a massive hanging — torn from top to bottom (from God's side, not human hands) signals the abolition of the barrier between God and humanity (Heb. 10:19–20). Earthquake and split rocks are apocalyptic signs of divine presence (Ps. 68:8; Hab. 3:6). The opening of tombs and raising of saints is a proleptic sign of the general resurrection that Jesus' own resurrection will inaugurate. The physical creation responds to the death of its Creator with seismic testimony. The torn curtain is the theological headline of the crucifixion: access to God is open, permanently and to anyone, through Christ.

Stay a moment longer with that curtain, because it was put there to keep people like you out, and it is worth knowing what its tearing means for you personally. It hung across the door of the Most Holy Place, and behind it was the presence of God, and the whole point of it was distance: no one went in, ever, except one man, once a year, with blood, and not without trembling. It was the visible form of a message every worshipper understood without being told — not yet, not you, not here. And at three in the afternoon on a Friday, with no hand near it, it was ripped from the top to the bottom, as if torn by the hand that first hung it.

Who were the saints who were raised? Matthew says only that they were holy people who had died, that the tombs opened at Jesus’ death, and that they came out after his resurrection and appeared to many in Jerusalem (v. 53). Most likely they were real, bodily raisings, a sign that Christ’s death had broken the power of death. What became of them afterwards Scripture does not say.

So hear what that says to the reader who has been standing at a distance from God, sure that he is the one person too unclean, too late, too far gone to come near. The barrier was not removed by your improving until you were fit to pass it. It was removed by a death. The way in was opened from God's side, downward, before you did anything at all — which means the invitation to "with confidence draw near" (Heb 4:16) is not for the people who have made themselves presentable. It is for the ones who know they never could. If you have been waiting until you are clean enough to pray, the curtain tore to tell you the waiting is over. Come in. The room that was sealed your whole life is open, and the blood that opened it was not yours.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection they went into the holy city and appeared to many. When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were filled with awe and said, "Truly this was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The raised saints appear after his resurrection — Matthew is careful about the sequence — as the firstfruits of the harvest of the new creation, and their appearing to many in Jerusalem is bodily, public testimony that death has been beaten.

This little scene is one of the strangest and most-asked-about passages in the Gospel, and honesty requires facing the questions rather than hurrying past them. Most take it as Matthew reports it: a real, bodily raising, a handful of Old Testament believers brought back as a living sign. A few careful scholars have wondered whether Matthew intends vivid apocalyptic imagery rather than bare reportage — the language of Ezekiel's opened graves (Ezek 37:12-13) pressed into service to declare what the cross achieved. That suggestion has been controversial, and the plain reading remains the safest.

Why does no other Gospel mention it? Much in each Gospel is unique to it, and this sign fits Matthew's Jewish, fulfilment-shaped purpose exactly. And note the careful timing: the tombs split open at the moment Jesus dies, but the saints do not emerge until after his resurrection — for Christ must be the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20), the first through the grave and out the other side, and none may go before him.

What became of them we are simply not told — whether, like Lazarus, they laid their bodies down again, or were taken up in his train. Scripture draws the curtain and there is no need to pry behind it. The meaning is unmistakable even where the details are veiled: at the instant the Author of life dies, the graves of his people burst open, because his dying has already begun to kill death, and the resurrection of the last day has pushed its first green shoots up through the crust of the old world.

Then the centurion. He is the officer commanding the execution detail, a professional who has done this many times, and he has spent six hours a few feet from the cross. He has watched the man refuse the drugged wine, pray for the men driving the nails, speak to his mother, cry out a psalm, and die with a shout when dying men cannot speak. Then the ground moves.

Truly this was the Son of God. It is the confession Israel's leadership refused, spoken by a pagan soldier who had just supervised the killing — and in Matthew's narrative he is the first human being to say it about the crucified Christ. A Roman officer, not a theologian, standing where the priests had stood jeering hours before. That this confession comes from the least likely mouth on the hill is Matthew's signal about where this gospel is going: it will cross every boundary of religion, race and background, and the first man over the line was on the wrong side of it that morning.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records the raised saints. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him, among whom were Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James and Joseph and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the darkness and the earthquake, Matthew turns the camera and shows us who is still there. There were also many women there. It is the first mention of them in the Passion narrative and it comes after everything, which is itself the point — they had been there the whole time.

Set it against the record of the men. Judas sold him. Peter denied him with oaths. The other ten left him and fled (26:56). Of the twelve, none is at the cross in Matthew's account. And of the women, many are, and Matthew names three of them, and two of those three will still be sitting opposite the tomb at the end of the chapter.

He tells us what they had been doing: they had followed him from Galilee, ministering to him — diakoneo, the word for practical service, which Luke fills out by saying they supported the work out of their own means (Lk 8:3). So the itinerant ministry of Jesus of Nazareth was in part underwritten by a group of women, one of whom he had delivered from seven demons, and who are mentioned almost nowhere until the moment everyone else has gone.

Looking on from a distance. There is no criticism in the phrase; a Roman execution site was cordoned and they could get no closer, and John records that at some point some of them were near enough for Jesus to speak to his mother. Whatever the distance, they did not use it as an exit. They could not stop it, could not help, could not touch him, and had nothing whatever to offer but the fact that when he looked out from the cross there were faces there that loved him.

And that turns out to matter enormously for reasons none of them could have known. These women watch him die. They watch where he is buried. They come back on the third morning. They are the continuous chain of witnesses across all three events — which is why the resurrection cannot be waved away as a mistake about the address. In a culture where a woman's testimony carried little weight in court, God arranged for the central facts of the Christian faith to rest on the eyesight of people nobody would have chosen. Nobody inventing a religion does that. And nobody who stayed that afternoon knew she was doing anything except refusing to leave.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake.

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.quote: When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew introduces him with one adjective: a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph. Mark calls him a respected member of the council, Luke a good and righteous man, John a disciple in secret for fear of the Jews. Matthew alone says rich, and he says it and the reader who knows Isaiah 53 will recall what stands in verse 9: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death. He does not stop to point it out. He simply uses the word and lets the reader who knows the chapter find it.

And the first half of that sentence had come true a few hours earlier. His grave was made with the wicked — two brigands, one on either side, and a common pit at the end of the day for whatever the executioners did not bother to hand over. Crucified bodies were normally left on the wood or thrown into a shared trench; that was part of the punishment, and Roman governors granted the release of a body as a favour and not as a right.

So consider what Joseph does. He is a member of the very council that condemned Jesus before dawn. He has kept his discipleship hidden for what looks like a considerable time. And now, on the evening of the execution, with the body of a man convicted of claiming to be a king hanging in public and every one of the Twelve in hiding, he goes to the governor's residence and asks for it by name.

There is no version of that request that leaves him anonymous afterwards. He has to give his name to Pilate's staff, state his connection to the deceased, and then be seen taking the body down in front of the execution detail and whoever else was still on the hill. His seat on the Sanhedrin, his standing, and his safety all go in the same conversation. Whatever fear had kept him quiet for three years stopped working the moment there was nothing left to hope for.

Which is worth noticing about courage. It did not arrive when the miracles were happening and being associated with Jesus looked promising. It arrived on the one evening when the cause was visibly finished, the leader was dead, and there was no possible advantage in it. There are people who cannot be brave while there is still something to win, and become unanswerable the moment everything is lost.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council (Mark, Luke); John adds Nicodemus. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: with a rich man in his death
not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in these two verses is done at speed, because the Sabbath begins at sunset and the light is going. And everything in them is done with care, which is the striking combination.

A clean linen shroud — bought that evening, since no one had prepared for this. John adds that Nicodemus came with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, an extravagant quantity, the sort of provision made for a king's burial. Two members of the council, working against the clock, handling a body that had been flogged and crucified and was ritually defiling to touch on the eve of a feast.

His own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. A rock-cut tomb was the burial of a wealthy family, quarried at expense and intended to hold generations; and this one was new, never used. Joseph gave away his own grave. He had made arrangements for his death, as prosperous men do, and he spent them on somebody else at a few hours' notice.

Then the stone. These were large discs set in a channel cut across the entrance, weighing in the region of a ton or more, rolled downhill into place easily enough and requiring several men to shift back. Matthew says he rolled it to the entrance and went away, which is the last thing anyone does in this Gospel before the Sabbath falls.

And here is the quiet providence in it. Every single element of this hurried, improvised, grief-stricken burial turns out, three days later, to be evidence. A tomb cut from solid rock, with one entrance and no other way in. A new tomb, containing no other body that could be confused with his. A wealthy owner, publicly named, whose property could be found and checked by anybody in Jerusalem. Two named women sitting opposite, watching it happen, so that nobody could later claim they went to the wrong grave. And a stone too heavy for a few frightened disciples to move quietly in the dark. Joseph thought he was performing the last service anyone could do for a dead friend. He was, in fact, sealing the case for the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, in wealthier tombs sometimes a disc-shaped stone rolled in a groove.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence, and Matthew gives it a verse of its own. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.

Everyone else has gone. Joseph rolled the stone and went away; the soldiers went back to barracks; the priests went to keep the feast. Two women sit down on the ground facing a closed grave as the light fails on the worst day of their lives, and Matthew does not tell us how long they stayed.

There was nothing to do. That is what makes the verse worth its space. They could not anoint the body — the Sabbath was starting. They could not move the stone. They could not pray him back, because it had not entered anyone's head that he was coming back; whatever he had said three times about the third day had gone straight past all of them, and the men who remembered it best were the chief priests, who are about to post a guard because of it. These two women are not waiting for a resurrection. They are sitting with a grave because they cannot bring themselves to leave it.

Anyone who has sat in a hospital corridor after the machines were switched off, or stayed at a graveside after the others had drifted back to the cars, knows precisely what they were doing and why there is no explaining it to somebody who has not. It accomplishes nothing. It is not a strategy. It is what love does when there is nothing left that love can do, and it is the last thing to go.

God took note of it. Their sitting there is why they knew the address; their knowing the address is why they came back on the third morning; and their coming back is why the first human beings to hear that Jesus Christ had risen from the dead were two women who had stayed at a tomb on a Friday evening when there was no reason to stay and no hope of anything at all. Faithfulness in the hours when it achieves nothing is not wasted. It is very often the thing God builds the next miracle on.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, that is, after the day of Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate and said, "Sir, we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and Pharisees go to Pilate on the Sabbath. It is worth pausing on that. These are the men who would not enter the governor's headquarters the previous morning for fear of ceremonial defilement before the feast; they are now transacting business with a Gentile official on the holy day itself, because they cannot rest.

And read what they say: we remember how that impostor said, while he was still alive, after three days I will rise.
